questions.stem: The water absorption of a FIRST CLASS burnt clay brick, after 24 hours of immersion in cold water, should not exceed:
options: 20 per cent of its dry weight
15 per cent of its dry weight
25 per cent of its dry weight
10 per cent of its dry weight
questions.solution:
**20 per cent of its dry weight.**

**The absorption limits:**

| Brick | Water absorption limit (24 h cold immersion) |
|---|---|
| **FIRST class** | **20 per cent** ← |
| **Second class** | **22 per cent** |
| **Third class** | **25 per cent** ← option (c) |
| **Class-designated bricks of grade above 12.5 N/mm² (IS 1077)** | **15 per cent** ← option (b) |
| **Bricks up to and including grade 12.5** | **20 per cent** |

> **So every distractor is a real absorption limit belonging to a different class of brick**, and identifying the class is the whole question.

**Why water absorption is limited — the reasons, which are not obvious:**

| Consequence of high absorption | Note |
|---|---|
| **The brick is POROUS, hence weaker and less durable** | Absorption is a proxy for the degree of burning |
| **It draws WATER OUT OF THE MORTAR before the mortar can hydrate** | **The joint is starved of water and the bond is weak — which is why bricks are SOAKED before laying** ← |
| **EFFLORESCENCE — soluble salts are carried in and deposited on drying** | Disfigures the wall, and the crystallisation can spall the surface |
| **DAMPNESS penetrates the wall** | Both rising and rain penetration |
| **FROST damage where freezing occurs** | Absorbed water expands on freezing and spalls the face |
| **Loss of thermal insulation** | Wet masonry conducts heat far better than dry |

> **The SECOND row is the one with the most immediate practical consequence and explains a universal site practice:**

> **A dry, absorbent brick laid in fresh mortar sucks the mixing water out of the joint within minutes.**

> **The mortar is then left without enough water to hydrate its cement, so it never gains its designed strength — and the failure is invisible, since the joint looks perfectly normal.**

> **That is why bricks are SOAKED — traditionally for several hours, until air bubbles cease rising — before being laid.**

> **And it is why the soaking must be sufficient but not excessive: a brick dripping wet floats on the mortar bed, the joint bleeds, and the courses settle out of level.**

> **The right condition is SATURATED BUT SURFACE DRY, which is the same specification used for aggregate in concrete mix design, and for the same reason: the material should neither take water from the mix nor add water to it.**

**The tests on bricks, since absorption is one of a family:**

| Test | Requirement / method |
|---|---|
| **COMPRESSIVE STRENGTH** | **Class-designated: 3.5, 5, 7.5, 10, 12.5, 15, 17.5, 20 N/mm² and above. A first class brick is traditionally taken as 10.5 N/mm² (105 kg/cm²)** ← |
| **WATER ABSORPTION** | **24 h cold immersion; ≤ 20 % for first class** ← this question |
| **EFFLORESCENCE** | **Repeated immersion and drying; the deposit graded NIL, SLIGHT, MODERATE, HEAVY or SERIOUS. "Slight" is the limit for first class** |
| **DIMENSIONAL TOLERANCE** | Measured on a stack of 20 bricks, so individual variation averages out |
| **HARDNESS** | A fingernail should leave no impression |
| **SOUNDNESS** | **Two bricks struck together should give a clear METALLIC RING and not break** |
| **STRUCTURE** | A broken brick should show a compact, uniform texture with no voids or lumps |

> **The DIMENSIONAL test's method deserves a note because it is a neat piece of specification design: measuring TWENTY bricks stacked together, rather than one brick, and comparing the total against twenty times the nominal size.**

> **That averages out the variation of individual bricks, which is inevitable in a fired product, while still catching a systematic error in the mould size.**

> **It measures what actually matters — whether twenty courses will come to the expected height — rather than what is easy to measure.**

> **The standard modular brick is 190 × 90 × 90 mm, becoming 200 × 100 × 100 mm with a 10 mm mortar joint, so a stack of twenty is a round 2 metres in the length direction.** That is why the number is twenty.

**The EFFLORESCENCE test and what it detects:**

> **Soluble salts — chiefly sulphates of sodium, magnesium and calcium — present in the clay or picked up from the ground.**

> **Water dissolves them, carries them to the surface, and evaporates, leaving a white crystalline deposit.**

> **The disfigurement is the visible problem; the SPALLING is the serious one, because crystallisation within the pores generates pressure sufficient to break the brick's face away.**

> **And magnesium sulphate is the most damaging because it crystallises with a large volume increase.**

> **The practical remedies are all about keeping the salts dry: an effective DPC, adequate copings and cills, and mortar of the appropriate strength.** Once salts are present in a brick, they cannot be removed — they can only be prevented from moving.

**Why a FIRST CLASS brick matters where it does:**

| Use | Class required |
|---|---|
| **Exposed FACE work, arches, cills, copings** | **FIRST class** ← |
| **Load-bearing walls generally** | First class |
| **Internal or plastered work** | Second class acceptable |
| **Temporary work, filling, soling** | Third class or brick bats |

> **The reason exposed work demands first class is that the exposed face carries all three burdens at once: it takes the weather, it shows any disfigurement, and it is the surface through which any moisture must enter or leave.**

> **A second class brick behind plaster is protected on both counts, so its higher absorption and poorer finish are of no consequence.**

> **That is a sensible allocation of a scarce material and worth understanding as a principle: specify the quality where the exposure demands it, not uniformly.**

examTip.trick: **First class: 20 per cent maximum after 24 h cold immersion.** Second class 22 %, third class 25 %, and class-designated bricks above grade 12.5 are limited to 15 %.
examTip.trap: **Every distractor is a real limit for a DIFFERENT class** — 15 % for high-grade class-designated bricks, 25 % for third class. Identify the class first.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bricks are SOAKED because a dry brick sucks the mixing water out of the mortar joint**, starving the cement of hydration water — an invisible failure. The right condition is SATURATED BUT SURFACE DRY, exactly as for aggregate in a concrete mix.

questions.stem: The microstructural feature that gives TMT (thermo-mechanically treated) reinforcing bars their combination of high strength and good ductility is:
options: A higher carbon content distributed uniformly through the bar
A cold-worked surface carrying large residual tensile stresses
A completely uniform martensitic structure through the whole section
A hard tempered MARTENSITIC RIM surrounding a ductile FERRITE-PEARLITE CORE
questions.solution:
**A hard tempered MARTENSITIC RIM around a ductile FERRITE-PEARLITE CORE.**

**How the structure is produced — the process explains the product:**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1. The bar leaves the final rolling pass at about 1000 °C** | Fully austenitic |
| **2. QUENCHING — it passes through a water box for a few SECONDS** | **The SURFACE is cooled below the martensite start temperature and transforms to MARTENSITE; the CORE remains hot and austenitic** ← the key step |
| **3. SELF-TEMPERING — quenching stops while the core is still hot** | **Heat flows OUTWARD from the core and TEMPERS the martensitic rim, relieving its brittleness** ← the elegant part |
| **4. ATMOSPHERIC COOLING on the cooling bed** | The core transforms slowly to a fine FERRITE-PEARLITE structure — strong and ductile |

> **The result is a bar with a graded structure: hard tempered martensite at the surface, a transition zone, and fine-grained ferrite-pearlite at the centre.**

**Why that arrangement is exactly what a reinforcing bar needs:**

> **The two requirements of reinforcement are in conflict in a homogeneous material: STRENGTH and DUCTILITY normally trade against one another.**

> **The TMT bar resolves the conflict by putting each property where it is needed:**

| Property | Where it comes from | Why it is needed there |
|---|---|---|
| **STRENGTH** | **The hard martensitic RIM** | **In bending and tension the OUTER fibres carry the highest stress** ← |
| **DUCTILITY** | **The soft ferrite-pearlite CORE** | **Allows the bar to be bent, and to yield with large elongation before fracture** |
| **Weldability** | **The LOW CARBON content — strength comes from heat treatment, not carbon** | Welding a high-carbon bar risks brittle heat-affected zones |
| **Corrosion resistance** | **A dense, uniform surface with NO residual stress** | Better than a cold-worked bar |
| **Fire (elevated temperature) performance** | Better than cold-worked bars, which lose strength as the cold work anneals out | |

> **So the graded structure is not a curiosity of the process — it is the reason the bar performs as it does, and the process was designed to achieve it.**

**The comparison with the bars TMT displaced:**

| | **MILD STEEL (Fe 250)** | **CTD / TOR (cold twisted deformed)** | **TMT (Fe 500, Fe 500D, Fe 550)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **How strength is obtained** | **Composition alone** | **COLD WORKING — twisting and stretching** | **HEAT TREATMENT (quench + self-temper)** ← |
| **Carbon content** | Low | **Higher** | **LOW** |
| **Residual stresses** | None | **HIGH — locked in by the cold twisting** | **Low** |
| **Ductility (elongation)** | **Excellent (23 %+)** | **Poorer (14.5 %)** | **Good (14.5-18 %)** |
| **Weldability** | Excellent | **Poor — needs care** | **GOOD** |
| **Corrosion resistance** | Good | **POOR — the twisted surface and residual stress accelerate it** ← | **Good** |
| **Bendability on site** | Excellent | Poorer; can crack | Good |
| **Behaviour in fire** | Retains strength | **Loses strength as the cold work anneals** | Better |
| **Sharp yield point** | **YES — a definite plateau** | **NO** | **NO** |

> **The CORROSION row explains why CTD bars have been almost entirely displaced, and it is worth stating the mechanism:**

> **Cold twisting leaves the bar's surface with high residual TENSILE stress and a distorted grain structure.**

> **Both accelerate corrosion — tensile stress promotes stress-corrosion cracking, and the disturbed surface offers more sites for attack.**

> **In the humid, chloride-bearing conditions of much of South Asia, that difference in durability matters more than any small difference in strength.**

> **So TMT bars represent a genuine improvement rather than a marketing distinction, and the reason is metallurgical.**

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **(a) Higher carbon throughout** | **The OPPOSITE. TMT bars are LOW-carbon — the strength comes from the heat treatment, and the low carbon is what makes them WELDABLE** ← |
| **(b) Cold-worked surface with residual stresses** | **That describes a CTD/TOR bar, and the residual stresses are a DEFECT** |
| **(c) Uniform martensite throughout** | **Would give a very strong and BRITTLE bar — unusable as reinforcement, which must be bent and must yield ductilely** |

> **Option (c) deserves the note because it is the plausible over-reach: if hard martensite is good at the surface, why not everywhere?**

> **Because untempered martensite is brittle, and a fully martensitic bar would fracture rather than yield.**

> **Reinforcement must be DUCTILE, since the entire limit-state design philosophy depends on the steel yielding before the concrete crushes — that is what makes the failure gradual and gives warning.**

> **A brittle reinforcing bar would defeat under-reinforced design entirely.**

**The grades and the D designation, since it matters for seismic work:**

| Grade | Yield strength | Minimum elongation | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Fe 415** | **415 N/mm²** | **14.5 %** | Being superseded |
| **Fe 500** | **500 N/mm²** | **12 %** | **The general standard** |
| **Fe 500D** | **500 N/mm²** | **16 %** | **D for DUCTILE — higher elongation, tighter limits on carbon, sulphur and phosphorus** ← |
| **Fe 550, Fe 600** | Higher | Lower | Special applications |

> **The D GRADES exist for SEISMIC design and IS 13920 requires them, for a direct reason:**

> **A structure surviving an earthquake does so by forming plastic hinges that absorb energy through large inelastic rotations.**

> **Those rotations demand large steel STRAINS — far beyond yield — so the reinforcement must be able to elongate substantially without fracturing.**

> **A bar meeting only the 12 per cent minimum may fracture at the strain a plastic hinge demands, and a fractured bar ends the hinge's capacity abruptly.**

> **So specifying Fe 500D rather than Fe 500 in a seismic zone is not a refinement but a requirement**, and it is the same principle as the R factor obliging ductile detailing: the design credits ductility, so the materials must actually possess it.

examTip.trick: **A hard tempered MARTENSITIC RIM (strength, where bending stress is highest) around a ductile FERRITE-PEARLITE CORE (ductility, for bending and yielding).**
examTip.trap: **Option (a) inverts it — TMT bars are LOW-carbon**, which is exactly what makes them weldable; strength comes from heat treatment. And (b) describes a CTD bar, whose residual stresses are a defect.
examTip.mnemonic: **Self-tempering is the elegant step**: quenching stops while the core is still hot, and that heat flows outward to temper the brittle rim. And use **Fe 500D** in seismic work — plastic hinges demand strains a 12 %-elongation bar may not survive.

questions.stem: The maximum permissible AGGREGATE CRUSHING VALUE for aggregate used in concrete for WEARING SURFACES is:
questions.solution:
**30 per cent.**

**The permissible crushing values:**

| Use | Maximum aggregate crushing value |
|---|---|
| **Concrete for WEARING SURFACES — runways, roads, pavements, floors** | **30 per cent** ← |
| **Concrete OTHER than wearing surfaces** | **45 per cent** ← option (a) |

> **So option (a) 45 per cent is the limit for ordinary structural concrete**, offered as though it applied to a wearing surface — a correct number in the wrong role.

> **The pattern is the same one that appears throughout aggregate specification: the STRICTER limit applies to the surface that traffic actually rubs.**

**The test itself:**

| Element | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Sample** | **Aggregate passing 12.5 mm and retained on 10 mm, in a standard cylinder** |
| **Load** | **400 kN (40 tonnes), applied GRADUALLY over 10 MINUTES** ← |
| **Measured** | **The percentage of material passing a 2.36 mm sieve after crushing** |
| **Formula** | **Crushing value = (weight passing 2.36 mm / total weight) × 100** |

> **The GRADUAL loading over ten minutes is the defining feature and is what distinguishes this test from the IMPACT test, which applies a sudden blow.**

> **So the crushing value measures resistance to a slowly applied COMPRESSIVE load — that is, STRENGTH — while the impact value measures resistance to a SUDDEN shock, that is, TOUGHNESS.**

> **The two are genuinely different properties: a strong but brittle aggregate can have a good crushing value and a poor impact value.**

**Why option (c) 10 per cent is a well-made distractor:**

> **It refers to the TEN PERCENT FINES VALUE, which is a different test with a different output.**

| | **Aggregate CRUSHING value** | **TEN PERCENT FINES value** |
|---|---|---|
| **What is fixed** | **The LOAD (400 kN)** | **The RESULT (10 per cent fines)** |
| **What is measured** | **The percentage of fines produced** | **The LOAD required to produce 10 per cent fines** ← |
| **Units of the answer** | **Per cent** | **kN** |
| **Suits** | **Strong aggregate** | **WEAK aggregate** |
| **A high value means** | **WEAK aggregate (more fines)** | **STRONG aggregate (more load needed)** |

> **The two tests are inverses of each other, and the last row is the trap worth noting: the two indices run in OPPOSITE directions.**

> **A high crushing value is BAD; a high ten-percent-fines value is GOOD.**

> **And the reason both exist is a real limitation of the crushing test: for a WEAK aggregate, the standard 400 kN load crushes so much of the sample that the result exceeds about 30 per cent, and beyond that the test becomes insensitive and unreliable.**

> **So IS 2386 directs that where the crushing value exceeds 30 per cent, the TEN PERCENT FINES test should be used instead** — which is a good example of a specification acknowledging the limits of its own test rather than pretending it applies everywhere.

**The four mechanical aggregate tests, and which property each measures:**

| Test | Property | Limit for a wearing surface |
|---|---|---|
| **CRUSHING value** | **STRENGTH — resistance to gradual compression** | **30 %** ← |
| **IMPACT value** | **TOUGHNESS — resistance to sudden shock** | **30 %** |
| **ABRASION value (Los Angeles)** | **HARDNESS — resistance to wear** | **30 %** |
| **SOUNDNESS (sulphate test)** | **DURABILITY — resistance to weathering** | 12-18 % loss |

> **The convenient coincidence that all three of the first limits are 30 per cent for wearing surfaces is worth knowing, and so is the fact that the corresponding limits for NON-wearing concrete differ: 45 per cent for crushing and impact.**

> **The relation between the impact and crushing values is roughly one-to-one for most aggregates, which is why the IMPACT test is often used as a quicker substitute: it needs no compression testing machine, only a standard hammer, and can be done in the field.**

> **That is a real practical advantage on a remote site, and it is the reason the impact test survives alongside the more fundamental crushing test.**

**Why aggregate strength matters less than one might expect — an honest qualification:**

> **In ordinary concrete, the aggregate is NOT the weakest link. The cement paste and the paste-aggregate INTERFACE are.**

> **So a stronger aggregate does not give proportionally stronger concrete, and beyond a point it gives none: a normal-strength concrete's strength is governed by its water-cement ratio, not by its stone.**

> **Aggregate strength becomes governing in two situations:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **HIGH-STRENGTH concrete (above about M60)** | **The paste is now stronger than the stone, so the AGGREGATE becomes the weakest link and its strength governs** ← |
| **WEARING SURFACES** | **The aggregate is exposed directly to traffic; the paste is worn away and the stone takes the load** |

> **That is why the crushing value limit is stricter for wearing surfaces specifically, and why high-strength concrete mix design begins with a search for strong aggregate.**

> **For ordinary M20 or M25 structural concrete, an aggregate at 40 per cent crushing value is entirely satisfactory** — which is what the 45 per cent limit reflects, and why the specification distinguishes the two cases rather than imposing one strict limit everywhere.

examTip.trick: **30 per cent for WEARING surfaces, 45 per cent for other concrete.** Option (a) is the non-wearing limit — a correct number in the wrong role.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) 10 % refers to the TEN PERCENT FINES test, whose answer is a LOAD in kN, not a percentage** — and the two indices run in OPPOSITE directions: a high crushing value is bad, a high ten-percent-fines value is good.
examTip.mnemonic: **Gradual load = CRUSHING (strength); sudden blow = IMPACT (toughness); tumbling with steel spheres = ABRASION (hardness).** And aggregate strength governs only for wearing surfaces and for concrete above about M60 — below that, the PASTE is the weak link.

questions.stem: In the fineness test on ordinary Portland cement by dry sieving, the residue left on the 90 micron IS sieve should not exceed:
questions.solution:
**10 per cent by weight.**

**The two methods of measuring fineness:**

| Method | What it gives | OPC requirement |
|---|---|---|
| **DRY SIEVING on a 90 micron sieve** | **The percentage RETAINED — a crude but quick index** | **Not more than 10 per cent** ← |
| **BLAINE AIR PERMEABILITY** | **The SPECIFIC SURFACE in m²/kg — a much better measure** | **Not less than 225 m²/kg** |

> **Both are specified, and the second is the more meaningful: sieving on a 90 micron sieve tells you only how much cement is COARSER than 90 microns, and says nothing about the distribution of the 90 per cent that passes.**

> **Since a typical cement's mean particle size is around 15 microns, almost all of it passes the sieve, and the test is measuring only the tail of the distribution.**

> **The BLAINE test measures the total surface area of all the particles, which is what actually determines the rate of hydration** — so it is the test that reflects the property of interest.

> **That distinction is worth understanding: the sieve test is a QUICK CONTROL check, and the Blaine test is the measurement.**

**Why FINENESS matters — the effects, and both directions:**

| Effect of GREATER fineness | Note |
|---|---|
| **FASTER hydration and EARLIER strength gain** | **More surface area is exposed to water, so the reaction proceeds faster** ← |
| **Greater HEAT of hydration, released sooner** | The other side of the same coin |
| **Better workability and cohesion; less bleeding** | The fine particles hold water |
| **Improved strength at all ages, up to a point** | |
| **GREATER SHRINKAGE** | More paste surface, more drying shrinkage |
| **More prone to AIR-SET and deterioration in storage** | **A fine cement absorbs atmospheric moisture faster** ← |
| **Higher grinding cost** | Grinding is the most energy-intensive step in cement manufacture |
| **Greater water demand for the same consistency** | Which partly offsets the strength gain |

> **The trade-off is genuine and it is why a MINIMUM fineness is specified but not a maximum: finer is better for strength and worse for shrinkage, storage life and cost.**

> **The specified minimum of 225 m²/kg ensures adequate reactivity; producers commonly grind to 300-350 m²/kg for 43 and 53 grade cements, and rapid-hardening cement is finer still.**

> **The AIR-SET point in the sixth row has a direct practical consequence worth stating: cement deteriorates in storage, and a fine cement deteriorates faster.**

| Storage period | Approximate strength loss |
|---|---|
| **3 months** | **20 per cent** |
| **6 months** | **30 per cent** |
| **12 months** | **40 per cent** |
| **24 months** | **50 per cent** |

> **So cement more than about three months old should be retested before use, and cement stored through a monsoon in a damp godown may be substantially weaker than its grade suggests.**

> **The practical field test is simple and worth knowing: thrust a hand into a bag of cement, and it should feel COOL (not warm, which indicates hydration has begun) and should not contain LUMPS that resist finger pressure.**

> **Lumps that crush easily are harmless; lumps that do not are hydrated cement and are lost.**

**Why the SEVEN-DAY strength is not the whole story — the connection to fineness:**

> **Fineness accelerates the reaction without changing the total amount of cement available to react.**

> **So a finer cement reaches a given strength SOONER, and its ULTIMATE strength is not proportionally greater.**

> **That is why a rapid-hardening cement's 3-day strength approximates an OPC's 7-day strength, while their 28-day strengths are much closer together.**

> **And it explains a practical consequence for construction: rapid-hardening cement buys FORMWORK CYCLE TIME, not final strength — which is exactly what a repetitive construction programme values, and why it is worth its premium there and nowhere else.**

**The other cement tests and their requirements, for completeness:**

| Test | Requirement (OPC 43 grade) |
|---|---|
| **FINENESS — sieve** | **≤ 10 % residue on 90 micron** ← |
| **Fineness — Blaine** | **≥ 225 m²/kg** |
| **SETTING TIME — initial** | **≥ 30 minutes** |
| **Setting time — final** | **≤ 600 minutes (10 hours)** |
| **SOUNDNESS — Le Chatelier expansion** | **≤ 10 mm** |
| **Soundness — autoclave** | **≤ 0.8 per cent** |
| **COMPRESSIVE STRENGTH — 3 days** | **≥ 23 N/mm²** |
| **Compressive strength — 7 days** | **≥ 33 N/mm²** |
| **Compressive strength — 28 days** | **≥ 43 N/mm²** |

> **The TWO soundness tests exist because they detect DIFFERENT causes of unsoundness:**

> **LE CHATELIER detects expansion due to FREE LIME (uncombined CaO), which slakes slowly and expands.**

> **The AUTOCLAVE test detects expansion due to FREE MAGNESIA (MgO), which hydrates much more slowly still and is only revealed by the accelerated high-pressure steam conditions.**

> **So a cement can pass Le Chatelier and fail the autoclave test, and both are required.**

> **All forms of unsoundness share the same signature and the same danger: DELAYED EXPANSION in concrete that has already hardened**, which appears months or years after the concrete was accepted, and which no amount of later inspection can prevent.

examTip.trick: **Residue on the 90 micron sieve: not more than 10 per cent.** The better measure is the BLAINE specific surface, minimum 225 m²/kg.
examTip.trap: **The sieve test measures only the tail of the distribution** — a typical cement's mean particle is about 15 microns, so nearly all of it passes. It is a quick control check; Blaine is the measurement.
examTip.mnemonic: **Finer cement = faster strength AND more heat, more shrinkage, shorter storage life.** Hence a minimum is specified and no maximum. And cement loses roughly 20 % in 3 months, 30 % in 6 — retest anything older, and check that a bag feels COOL with no hard lumps.

questions.stem: The type of shallow foundation consisting of a single continuous slab covering the entire plan area of the structure, adopted where the soil is weak and the loads are heavy, is:
questions.solution:
**A RAFT (mat) foundation.**

**Why a raft is used — the two distinct reasons:**

> **FIRST — TO REDUCE THE BEARING PRESSURE.**

> **Spreading the whole building's load over its entire footprint gives the largest possible bearing area, and hence the lowest possible pressure on the soil.**

> **If the total load is 20,000 kN and the building covers 500 m², the raft applies 40 kN/m² — where isolated footings covering only 15 per cent of the area would apply nearly 270 kN/m².**

> **On a soil that cannot carry 270 kN/m² but can carry 40, the raft is what makes the building possible.**

> **SECOND — TO CONTROL DIFFERENTIAL SETTLEMENT, which is often the more important reason.**

> **A raft is a single stiff structural element, so it settles more or less as a unit.**

> **Isolated footings on variable soil settle independently by different amounts, and DIFFERENTIAL settlement is what damages a building.**

> **So a raft converts a differential settlement problem into a total settlement problem — and total settlement, provided it is uniform, does remarkably little harm.**

> **A building that settles 75 mm uniformly is undamaged (services and drains must accommodate it); one that settles 25 mm at one column and 5 mm at the next is cracked.**

> **That trade is the essence of raft design and worth understanding as the primary justification rather than a secondary benefit.**

**When a raft becomes the natural choice:**

| Condition | Note |
|---|---|
| **The soil is WEAK and the loads heavy** | ← the stem's case |
| **The soil is ERRATIC — pockets of soft material** | **The raft bridges over them** |
| **Isolated footings would cover more than about HALF the plan area** | **At that point a raft is cheaper and simpler than many footings with formwork between them** ← a useful rule of thumb |
| **A BASEMENT is required** | The raft doubles as the basement floor and the water barrier |
| **UPLIFT or BUOYANCY must be resisted** | The raft's weight and area resist flotation |
| **Structures sensitive to differential settlement** | Silos, chimneys, machinery foundations |
| **Where soil may be lost by scour or subsidence** | Mining areas |

> **The rule of thumb in the third row is genuinely useful in practice: once the footings' total area approaches half the building's footprint, the excavation, formwork and reinforcement of separate footings costs more than a single continuous slab.**

**Why each distractor is a different thing — and each solves a different problem:**

| Foundation | When it is used |
|---|---|
| **ISOLATED (pad) footing** | **One column on its own footing — the default where the soil is adequate** |
| **COMBINED footing** | **TWO OR MORE columns on ONE footing — used when columns are so close that their separate footings would overlap, or when one is near a boundary** ← |
| **STRAP (cantilever) footing** | **Two separate footings joined by a stiff BEAM (the strap), which transfers moment between them — used when a column is at a property line and its footing cannot be centred beneath it** ← |
| **RAFT** | The whole area ✓ |

> **The STRAP footing deserves explanation because its purpose is subtle and it is the cleverest of the group:**

> **A column on a property boundary cannot have a footing centred under it — the footing would trespass.**

> **An eccentric footing beneath it would be loaded off-centre, producing a non-uniform bearing pressure and a tendency to rotate.**

> **The STRAP BEAM connects that footing rigidly to the next column's footing, and the interior footing provides the counterbalancing reaction that resists the rotation.**

> **So the two footings act as a couple, and the eccentric one is held level by its neighbour.**

> **It is a genuinely elegant solution to a boundary constraint, and it uses no more material than the two footings would have needed anyway.**

> **A COMBINED footing solves the same boundary problem differently — by making one footing serve both columns, shaped (often trapezoidal) so that its centroid coincides with the resultant of the two column loads.**

> **Which of the two to use is largely a question of the distance between the columns: close together, a combined footing; far apart, a strap.**

**The types of raft, since "raft" covers several forms:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **FLAT plate raft** | **A uniform-thickness slab — simplest; suits light, closely spaced columns** |
| **Flat plate thickened under columns** | Local thickening where punching shear governs |
| **Beam and slab raft** | **Beams in both directions with the slab between — stiffer for the same concrete** ← |
| **Cellular (box) raft** | **Two slabs with cross walls between — extremely stiff; used for very heavy or settlement-sensitive structures** |
| **Piled raft** | **A raft supported partly on soil and partly on piles — the piles reduce and even out the settlement** |

> **The PILED RAFT deserves a note because it is the modern approach for tall buildings and is conceptually interesting: rather than treating piles as the sole support (and the raft as merely a cap), the design deliberately shares the load between the two.**

> **The soil beneath the raft carries a substantial share, and the piles are placed where they most reduce differential settlement — typically concentrated toward the centre, where a raft on soil would settle most.**

> **So the piles are used as SETTLEMENT REDUCERS rather than as load carriers, and far fewer are needed than a piles-only design would require.**

> **That is a considerable saving, and it depends on analysing the raft, the piles and the soil as one interacting system rather than as separate elements** — which is why it became practical only with numerical analysis.

**The FLOATING FOUNDATION concept, since it is the limiting case of the raft idea:**

> **If a raft is built in an excavation, the soil REMOVED had weight, and that weight was previously carried by the ground beneath.**

> **If the weight of the building EQUALS the weight of the soil excavated, the net increase in stress on the soil is ZERO — and in principle the building causes NO settlement at all.**

> **That is a FLOATING or COMPENSATED foundation, and it is used for heavy buildings on very soft soils.**

> **The arithmetic is straightforward: soil at 18 kN/m³ excavated to 5 m depth relieves 90 kN/m², which is a substantial building's worth of load.**

> **The practical difficulty is the construction: a deep excavation in soft ground requires support, dewatering, and control of heave — and the structure must resist BUOYANCY when the groundwater returns, since a hollow box below the water table wants to float.**

> **So the concept is sound and the execution is demanding**, which is why compensated foundations are found under heavy buildings in cities built on soft ground — Mexico City being the classic example.

examTip.trick: **A RAFT is one continuous slab over the whole plan area** — used where the soil is weak, the loads heavy, or the ground erratic.
examTip.trap: **A STRAP footing joins two footings by a stiff BEAM so a boundary column's eccentric footing is held level by its neighbour; a COMBINED footing makes ONE footing serve two columns.** Both solve the boundary problem, differently.
examTip.mnemonic: **A raft's main benefit is converting DIFFERENTIAL settlement into TOTAL settlement** — and uniform total settlement does little harm while differential settlement cracks buildings. Rule of thumb: once footings would cover half the footprint, a raft is cheaper.

questions.stem: The temporary support consisting of INCLINED members bearing against a wall and against the ground, provided to prevent a wall that is out of plumb or bulging from collapsing, is called:
questions.solution:
**A RAKING SHORE.**

**The three kinds of shoring, and what each supports:**

| Shore | Arrangement | Supports against |
|---|---|---|
| **RAKING shore** | **INCLINED members from the ground to the wall, with a wall plate, needles and a sole plate** | **LATERAL movement of a wall — bulging, leaning, out of plumb** ← |
| **FLYING (horizontal) shore** | **HORIZONTAL members spanning BETWEEN TWO PARALLEL WALLS, with no ground support** | **Lateral movement, where the ground between cannot be occupied** |
| **DEAD (vertical) shore** | **VERTICAL props with needles through the wall, carrying the load above** | **VERTICAL load — used when the wall BELOW is to be removed or rebuilt** ← |

> **The distinction is between what is being resisted: RAKING and FLYING shores resist LATERAL movement; a DEAD shore carries VERTICAL load.**

> **And between raking and flying: a RAKING shore needs GROUND to bear on; a FLYING shore needs an OPPOSITE WALL.**

**Why a FLYING shore is used at all, given that a raking shore is simpler:**

> **A raking shore occupies the ground in front of the wall — which blocks a street, a footpath, an access or a working area.**

> **A FLYING shore spans between two parallel walls (typically the flank walls of adjoining buildings after an intermediate building has been demolished) and leaves the ground entirely CLEAR.**

> **That is its whole advantage, and it is a considerable one in a town: a street can remain open beneath a flying shore.**

> **Its limitation is that it requires two walls at roughly the same level and a span it can economically cover — usually under about 9 metres.**

**The parts of a RAKING SHORE, since the components are examined:**

| Part | Function |
|---|---|
| **RAKERS (the inclined members)** | **Carry the thrust; usually 45° to 75° to the horizontal** ← |
| **WALL PLATE** | **A vertical timber against the wall face, distributing the rakers' thrust over the wall** |
| **NEEDLES** | **Short members passing THROUGH the wall plate INTO the wall, so the shore engages the wall rather than merely pressing on its plaster** ← the critical detail |
| **CLEATS** | Fixed above the needles to prevent them slipping |
| **SOLE PLATE** | **A timber bedded in the ground, INCLINED so that the rakers bear square on it** |
| **Hoop iron / bolts** | Bind the rakers to the wall plate |
| **Bracing** | Ties the rakers together |

> **The NEEDLES are the detail that makes the difference between a working shore and a decorative one, and it is worth understanding why:**

> **A raker simply pressing against a wall's surface can only push. It cannot prevent the wall moving outward at any point except where it bears, and it relies on friction and on the plaster.**

> **A NEEDLE let into the wall engages the MASONRY itself, so the shore acts on the wall's structure and the thrust is delivered into the courses rather than onto the render.**

> **And the needles are placed to coincide with FLOOR LEVELS wherever possible, because a wall is stiffest and best able to receive a concentrated thrust where a floor ties into it.**

> **Pushing against the middle of an unrestrained storey height can bulge the wall further** — so a shore incorrectly positioned can cause the damage it was installed to prevent.

> **The RAKER ANGLE matters for the same reason: the flatter the raker, the greater the horizontal component of its thrust but the more ground it occupies; the steeper it is, the less useful it is at resisting lateral movement.**

> **The usual compromise is 45° to 75°, with the topmost raker steepest.**

> **And the SOLE PLATE must be inclined so that the raker bears PERPENDICULAR to it — otherwise the thrust has a component along the plate and the shore tends to slide.**

**Why UNDERPINNING — option (c) — is a different operation entirely:**

> **UNDERPINNING is not a temporary support at all. It is the PERMANENT strengthening or deepening of an existing FOUNDATION.**

| Reason for underpinning | Note |
|---|---|
| **The existing foundation has settled or is inadequate** | Remedial |
| **A deeper basement is to be built alongside** | **The neighbour's foundation must be taken below the new excavation** ← |
| **The load on the structure is to be increased** | Additional storeys |
| **The soil beneath has deteriorated** | Washout, subsidence |

> **The methods include the traditional PIT method (excavating short lengths in a planned sequence and building up beneath), needle beams and piers, PILE underpinning (mini-piles either side with needle beams), and JET GROUTING or grout injection to strengthen the soil in place.**

> **The PIT method's essential rule is worth knowing because it is what makes the operation safe: the work proceeds in SHORT ALTERNATE LENGTHS — typically 1.2 to 1.5 m — never in a continuous run.**

> **The unexcavated lengths between them support the wall while each section is underpinned, so the wall is never unsupported over a distance it cannot span.**

> **Excavating a continuous trench beneath a wall removes its support entirely and the wall fails — which is exactly what the alternate-bay sequence prevents.**

> **That sequencing rule appears throughout temporary works: excavate, remove or replace in bays, never continuously.** It is the same principle as staged loading of an embankment and as opening only part of a formwork at a time.

**The general purpose of shoring, and its relation to the other temporary works:**

| Operation | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **SHORING** | **Support an existing STRUCTURE — a wall or building** ← |
| **STRUTTING / TIMBERING** | **Support the SIDES OF AN EXCAVATION** |
| **SCAFFOLDING** | **Provide a WORKING PLATFORM — not a structural support at all** |
| **CENTERING** | Temporary support for an arch or dome while it is built |
| **FORMWORK / SHUTTERING** | Mould and support fresh concrete until it can carry itself |

> **The SCAFFOLDING distinction is worth being firm about, because the terms are loosely used on site: a scaffold carries WORKERS AND MATERIALS, and a shore carries the BUILDING.**

> **Using a scaffold to support a structure, or a shore as a working platform, is a category error with real consequences — the loads, the factors of safety and the failure modes are entirely different.**

examTip.trick: **RAKING shore: inclined, ground to wall, resists LATERAL movement. FLYING shore: horizontal between two walls, leaves the ground clear. DEAD shore: vertical, carries VERTICAL load while the wall below is rebuilt.**
examTip.trap: **Option (c) UNDERPINNING is not temporary support at all** — it is the permanent deepening or strengthening of an existing foundation, done in SHORT ALTERNATE bays of 1.2-1.5 m so the wall is never unsupported.
examTip.mnemonic: **The NEEDLES are what make a raking shore work** — they engage the MASONRY rather than pressing on the plaster, and they are placed at FLOOR levels where the wall can receive the thrust. A shore pushing mid-storey can bulge the wall it was meant to save.

questions.stem: The centroid of a semicircular AREA of radius 60 mm lies, measured from its diameter, at a distance of:
questions.solution:
**25.46 mm.**

**The standard result:**

> **For a semicircular AREA, the centroid lies at  ȳ = 4r / (3π)  from the diameter.**

> **= 4 × 60 / (3 × 3.1416) = 240 / 9.4248 = 25.46 mm** ✓

> **As a fraction of the radius: 4/(3π) = 0.4244 r** — so the centroid sits at about 42 per cent of the radius, a little BELOW the mid-radius.

**Why it is below the mid-radius — the physical reason:**

> **A semicircle is WIDE near its diameter and NARROW near its crown.**

> **So more of its area lies close to the diameter than far from it, and the centroid is pulled toward the diameter.**

> **A rectangle of the same height would have its centroid at 0.5r; the semicircle's is at 0.424r.**

> **That sanity check is worth making — the answer must be LESS than r/2 = 30 mm** — which immediately eliminates option (a) 30.00 mm and option (d) 38.20 mm.

**Every distractor is a real centroid of a related figure — which is the design of the question:**

| Option | Figure it belongs to | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| **30.00 mm** | **A RECTANGLE or a semi-elliptical guess** | **r/2** |
| **25.46 mm** | **SEMICIRCULAR AREA (lamina)** ✓ | **4r/3π = 0.4244 r** |
| **22.50 mm** | **SOLID HEMISPHERE** | **3r/8 = 0.375 r** ← |
| **38.20 mm** | **SEMICIRCULAR ARC (a wire, not an area)** | **2r/π = 0.6366 r** ← |

> **The distinction between the AREA and the ARC in the last row is the one most often confused and is worth fixing firmly:**

> **A semicircular AREA (a flat plate) has its centroid at 4r/3π = 0.424 r.**

> **A semicircular ARC (a bent wire, with no area) has its centroid at 2r/π = 0.637 r — much further out.**

> **The reason is that an ARC has all its material at the FULL radius, so nothing is pulled inward, while an AREA has material at every radius from zero outward.**

> **So the arc's centroid is well outside the area's, and the two formulae look similar enough to be swapped by accident.**

**The standard centroids worth having automatically:**

| Figure | Centroid |
|---|---|
| **Triangle** | **h/3 from the base** |
| **Semicircular AREA** | **4r/3π = 0.424 r from the diameter** ← |
| **Quarter circle** | **4r/3π from BOTH straight edges** |
| **Semicircular ARC** | **2r/π = 0.637 r** |
| **Quarter circular arc** | **2r/π from both edges** |
| **Circular SECTOR, half-angle α** | **(2r sin α)/(3α), α in radians** |
| **Solid HEMISPHERE** | **3r/8 = 0.375 r** |
| **Solid CONE or pyramid** | **h/4 from the base** |
| **Parabolic spandrel (area under y = kx²)** | 3h/10 from the base |
| **Semi-parabolic area (under a parabola)** | 3h/5 from the base |

> **Note the pleasing consistency: the SECTOR formula reduces to the others.**

> **For a semicircle α = π/2: (2r sin 90°)/(3 × π/2) = 2r/(3π/2) = 4r/3π** ✓

> **So the sector result is the general one and the semicircle and quarter circle are special cases — which means only one formula need be remembered if the reduction is understood.**

**Where semicircular centroids are actually needed:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Composite section properties** | **A section made of rectangles and semicircles — a slotted plate, a rounded flange, a keyhole section** ← |
| **Semicircular arches and their thrust lines** | |
| **Circular water tanks and their wall pressures** | |
| **Half-round channels and culverts** | Hydraulic radius and section properties |
| **Locating the neutral axis of a composite beam** | |

> **The COMPOSITE SECTION method is where this result gets used, and the procedure is worth setting out because it is the common thread of the whole subchapter:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Divide the section into simple figures whose areas and centroids are known** |
| **2** | **Choose a convenient REFERENCE AXIS — usually an edge or a line of symmetry** |
| **3** | **Compute ȳ = Σ(A_i ȳ_i)/ΣA_i** |
| **4** | **For a HOLE or a removed part, take its area as NEGATIVE** ← |
| **5** | **Then find I about the centroid using the PARALLEL AXIS theorem: I = Σ(I_Gi + A_i d_i²)** |

> **Step 4 is the technique that makes awkward shapes easy: a plate with a semicircular notch is treated as the full rectangle MINUS a semicircle, and the semicircle's area and first moment enter the sums with a negative sign.**

> **That converts a shape with no standard formula into two shapes that both have one, and it is far less error-prone than integrating.**

> **And step 5's parallel axis theorem is essential and easily under-applied: the term A d² is often much LARGER than I_G itself for a part far from the centroid, so omitting it is not a small error.**

> **For a semicircle of radius 60 mm at 100 mm from the reference axis: A = 5655 mm², A d² = 5655 × 10,000 = 56.5 × 10⁶ mm⁴, against I_G of only about 1.76 × 10⁶ mm⁴** — the transfer term is thirty times the part's own second moment.

> **Which is the general lesson: for a composite section, the material's POSITION usually matters far more than its own shape.**

examTip.trick: **Semicircular AREA: ȳ = 4r/3π = 0.424 r = 25.46 mm.** Sanity check: it must be LESS than r/2 = 30 mm, because a semicircle is wide near its diameter.
examTip.trap: **Every distractor is a real centroid of a related figure**: r/2 for a rectangle, 3r/8 for a solid HEMISPHERE, and 2r/π = 0.637 r for a semicircular ARC — the confusion most often made, since an arc has all its material at full radius.
examTip.mnemonic: **The SECTOR formula (2r sinα)/(3α) reduces to all of them** — at α = π/2 it gives 4r/3π. And in composite sections, treat a hole as NEGATIVE area, and never omit the A d² transfer term: it is often thirty times the part's own I_G.

questions.stem: A rectangular section is 100 mm wide and 200 mm deep. Its moment of inertia about an axis coinciding with its BASE (the 100 mm edge) is:
questions.solution:
**266.7 × 10⁶ mm⁴.**

**By the PARALLEL AXIS theorem:**

> **I_base = I_G + A d²**

| Term | Computation | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **I_G = bd³/12** | **100 × 200³/12 = 100 × 8 × 10⁶/12** | **66.67 × 10⁶ mm⁴** ← option (b) |
| **A** | **100 × 200** | **20,000 mm²** |
| **d** | **200/2 = 100 mm** | |
| **A d²** | **20,000 × 100²** | **200 × 10⁶ mm⁴** |
| **I_base** | **66.67 + 200** | **266.7 × 10⁶ mm⁴** ✓ |

**And the direct formula confirms it:**

> **I_base = b d³ / 3 = 100 × 8 × 10⁶/3 = 266.7 × 10⁶ mm⁴** ✓

> **So the two routes agree, and it is worth noticing the relation between the coefficients: bd³/3 is exactly FOUR TIMES bd³/12.**

**Why the base value is four times the centroidal one — a result worth understanding:**

> **I_base / I_G = (bd³/3)/(bd³/12) = 4**

> **So moving the axis from the centroid to the base MULTIPLIES the second moment by FOUR.**

> **The reason is that the transfer term A d² = 200 × 10⁶ is THREE TIMES the section's own I_G of 66.67 × 10⁶.**

> **And that is the general lesson of the parallel axis theorem: for an axis outside the section, the TRANSFER TERM usually dominates.**

> **The material's DISTANCE from the axis matters more than its own distribution about its own centroid.**

> **Which is exactly why an I-section works, why a hollow shaft works and why a hollow column works — three problems, one principle: get the material far from the axis.**

**The distractors, each identifiable:**

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| **266.7 × 10⁶** | ✓ **bd³/3, about the base** |
| **66.7 × 10⁶** | **bd³/12 — about the CENTROIDAL axis; the transfer term omitted** ← the intended trap |
| **133.3 × 10⁶** | **db³/3 = 200 × 10⁶/3... or twice I_G — an intermediate slip** |
| **333.3 × 10⁶** | **bd³/3 with d and b interchanged in part, or 100 × 200³/2.4** |

> **Option (b) is the error the question is built to catch: computing I_G and forgetting that the axis specified is NOT the centroidal one.**

> **Reading which AXIS is asked for is the whole task, and the option set makes both available.**

**The parallel axis theorem, stated properly and with its one condition:**

> **I_AB = I_G + A d²**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **The two axes must be PARALLEL** | Hence the name |
| **One of them MUST pass through the CENTROID** | **This is the condition most often violated** ← |
| **d is the perpendicular distance between them** | |
| **The transfer term is always POSITIVE** | **So I is MINIMUM about the centroidal axis** |

> **The second condition is the trap in more advanced problems: the theorem CANNOT be used to transfer directly between two NON-centroidal parallel axes.**

> **To go from axis 1 to axis 2, both offset from the centroid, one must transfer BACK to the centroid first and then out again:**

> **I₂ = I₁ − A d₁² + A d₂²**

> **Applying I₂ = I₁ + A d² with d the distance between the two non-centroidal axes gives a wrong answer, and it is a genuinely common mistake.**

> **The fourth row states a useful consequence: since A d² is always positive, the second moment of area is MINIMUM about an axis through the centroid.**

> **That is why the centroidal axis is the NEUTRAL AXIS in pure bending — the section resists bending least efficiently about it, which is to say the stresses are distributed most evenly, which is the condition of pure bending.**

**The companion PERPENDICULAR AXIS theorem, since the two are used together:**

> **I_z = I_x + I_y**, where z is perpendicular to the plane of the area and x, y lie in it, all three meeting at a point.

> **I_z is the POLAR moment of inertia, J.**

> **For a circle: I_x = I_y = πd⁴/64, so J = πd⁴/32** ✓ — which is where the familiar factor of two between I and J comes from.

> **For this rectangle about its centroid: I_x = bd³/12 = 66.67 × 10⁶ and I_y = db³/12 = 200 × 100³/12 = 16.67 × 10⁶.**

> **So J = 66.67 + 16.67 = 83.3 × 10⁶ mm⁴.**

> **Note that the perpendicular axis theorem applies only to PLANE areas (laminae), and it requires all three axes to be CONCURRENT** — two conditions worth stating, since the theorem is otherwise applied loosely.

**The standard second moments, for reference:**

| Section | About the centroidal axis | About the base or edge |
|---|---|---|
| **Rectangle b × d** | **bd³/12** | **bd³/3** ← |
| **Triangle, base b, height h** | **bh³/36** | **bh³/12 (about the base)** |
| **Circle, diameter d** | **πd⁴/64** | **5πd⁴/64 (about a tangent)** |
| **Semicircle, radius r** | **0.1098 r⁴** | **πr⁴/8 (about the diameter)** |
| **Hollow rectangle** | (BD³ − bd³)/12 | — |
| **Hollow circle** | **π(D⁴ − d⁴)/64** | — |

> **The TRIANGLE row shows the same four-fold pattern in a different guise: bh³/12 about the base against bh³/36 about the centroid is a ratio of THREE, not four — because the triangle's centroid is at h/3 rather than h/2.**

> **Check: I_base = bh³/36 + (bh/2)(h/3)² = bh³/36 + bh³/18 = bh³/36 + 2bh³/36 = 3bh³/36 = bh³/12** ✓

> **So the ratio depends on where the centroid sits, and it is 4 for a rectangle and 3 for a triangle** — which is a good reason to derive rather than to memorise these relations.

examTip.trap: **Option (b) 66.7 × 10⁶ is bd³/12 — the CENTROIDAL value, transfer term omitted.** Reading which AXIS is asked for is the whole task.
examTip.mnemonic: **The parallel axis theorem needs ONE axis through the CENTROID** — to go between two offset axes, transfer back to the centroid first: I₂ = I₁ − Ad₁² + Ad₂². And the transfer term usually DOMINATES (here 3× the section's own I_G), which is why I-sections and hollow shafts work.

questions.stem: The method of reducing levels in a levelling survey that provides an arithmetical CHECK on ALL the staff readings, including the intermediate sights, is:
questions.solution:
**The RISE AND FALL method.**

**The two methods of reduction compared:**

| | **HEIGHT OF INSTRUMENT (collimation)** | **RISE AND FALL** |
|---|---|---|
| **How it works** | **Compute the height of the line of collimation, then RL = HI − staff reading** | **Compare each reading with the PREVIOUS one to find a RISE or a FALL, then apply it** |
| **Arithmetical check** | **ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL** | **ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL** ← |
| **Are INTERMEDIATE sights checked?** | **NO** ← | **YES — every reading enters a rise or a fall** |
| **Speed** | **FASTER — fewer computations** | Slower |
| **Suits** | **Many intermediate sights: longitudinal sections, contouring, cross-sections** | **Few intermediate sights: precise levelling, fly levelling, benchmark transfer** ← |
| **Error detection** | Detects errors in backsights and foresights only | **Detects an error in ANY reading** |

> **The THREE-part check of the rise and fall method is its defining advantage:**

> **ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = (last RL − first RL)**

> **All three quantities must agree. The collimation method has only the first and third, so an intermediate sight can be misrecorded or mis-reduced and the check will still balance.**

**Why that difference exists — the mechanism:**

> **In the COLLIMATION method, an intermediate reading is used ONCE: subtracted from the height of instrument to give its RL. It enters no sum that is checked.**

> **So if it is written down wrongly, its RL is wrong, and nothing in the arithmetic reveals it.**

> **In the RISE AND FALL method, each reading is compared with BOTH its neighbours — it forms the second term of one comparison and the first term of the next.**

> **So every reading appears TWICE in the rise and fall columns, and an error in it produces an inconsistency that the check catches.**

> **That is the whole reason for the method's existence, and it is why precise levelling uses it despite being slower.**

**The choice in practice — a genuine trade:**

> **The methods are not ranked; they suit different work.**

| Survey | Method |
|---|---|
| **Longitudinal section of a road, with a reading every 20 m** | **COLLIMATION — dozens of intermediate sights, and speed matters more than checking each** ← |
| **Contouring a site by grid levelling** | Collimation |
| **Transferring a benchmark over several kilometres** | **RISE AND FALL — few readings, each critical** |
| **Precise levelling for a dam, a long tunnel, or settlement monitoring** | Rise and fall |
| **Fly levelling to establish a temporary benchmark** | Rise and fall |

> **The reasoning is proportionality: where there are two hundred intermediate readings whose individual accuracy matters little, checking each is not worth the effort — and a gross error in a section level shows up as an obvious kink in the plotted profile anyway.**

> **Where there are six readings and the final RL will govern a structure's setting-out, every one must be verified arithmetically.**

> **So the plotted PROFILE is itself a check in the first case, and the arithmetic must be the check in the second.** That is a sensible allocation of effort.

**Why option (a) is the near miss:**

> **The collimation method is a perfectly valid and more commonly used method of reduction — it simply lacks the check on intermediate sights.**

> **So the question is not asking which method is better but which provides the fuller CHECK, and the answer is unambiguous.**

**Why options (b) and (d) are different operations altogether:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **(b) TACHEOMETRY** | **A method of measuring DISTANCES and ELEVATIONS by stadia hairs or by tangential readings, without chaining — a survey METHOD, not a reduction method** ← |
| **(d) RECIPROCAL levelling** | **A FIELD PROCEDURE for levelling across a river or valley where the instrument cannot be placed midway: observations are taken from both banks and the mean taken** |

> **RECIPROCAL LEVELLING deserves the note because it addresses a genuine problem and does so elegantly:**

> **Where an obstacle prevents balanced sights, curvature, refraction and collimation errors no longer cancel.**

> **Taking observations from BOTH banks and averaging the two apparent differences of level cancels all three, because each error affects the two sets equally and in opposite senses.**

> **So it is a field remedy for a specific geometric obstruction, not a way of reducing a level book.**

**The levelling terms, since the reduction depends on using them correctly:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **BACKSIGHT (BS)** | **The FIRST reading after setting up the instrument, taken on a point of KNOWN RL** |
| **FORESIGHT (FS)** | **The LAST reading before moving the instrument, taken on a point whose RL is required and which becomes the next backsight** ← |
| **INTERMEDIATE SIGHT (IS)** | **Any reading between the backsight and the foresight from the same set-up** |
| **CHANGE POINT (turning point)** | **The point on which both an FS and the following BS are taken** |
| **HEIGHT OF INSTRUMENT (HI)** | RL of the point + backsight reading |
| **REDUCED LEVEL (RL)** | The elevation of a point above the datum |
| **BENCH MARK (BM)** | A point of known RL — GTS, permanent, arbitrary or temporary |

> **The FORESIGHT definition contains the point that matters for the arithmetic: a foresight is not merely "the last reading" but the reading on the CHANGE POINT, which carries the level forward to the next instrument position.**

> **So the number of foresights equals the number of instrument set-ups, and ΣBS and ΣFS each have exactly that many terms.**

> **A level book with unequal numbers of backsights and foresights has an error of recording — which is itself a check worth applying before any arithmetic.**

> **And the CHANGE POINT is the one place where the staff must NOT be moved between the foresight and the following backsight**, because the whole chain of levels depends on both readings being taken on the identical point. Moving the staff there breaks the survey silently, and no arithmetical check will reveal it.

examTip.trick: **RISE AND FALL gives a THREE-part check: ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL.** The collimation method has only the first and third, so intermediate sights are unchecked.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is not wrong as a method** — it is faster and more commonly used. The question asks which CHECKS all readings, and only rise-and-fall does, because each reading appears TWICE in the rise/fall columns.
examTip.mnemonic: **Collimation for many intermediate sights (sections, contouring) — the plotted profile is its own check. Rise and fall for few, critical readings (benchmark transfer, precise levelling).** And never move the staff at a CHANGE POINT: no arithmetic will catch it.

questions.stem: For a PRELIMINARY or approximate estimate of a building at the early planning stage, the method most commonly used is:
questions.solution:
**The PLINTH AREA method.**

**How it works:**

> **Estimated cost = PLINTH AREA × plinth area RATE**

> **The plinth area is the built-up area measured at floor level, taken over the EXTERNAL dimensions of the building including the walls.**

> **The rate is derived from the actual cost of recently completed buildings of similar type, specification and locality, divided by their plinth area.**

> **For a 200 m² building at a rate of Rs 25,000 per m²: estimated cost = Rs 50,00,000.**

**Why it is the method of choice for a preliminary estimate:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Requires only the AREA — no drawings beyond a sketch plan** | **Usable before the design exists** ← the decisive advantage |
| **Very fast — a single multiplication** | |
| **Rates are readily available from completed work** | Public works departments publish them |
| **Accurate enough for a decision to proceed** | ±10 to 15 per cent for a familiar building type |
| **Easily understood by a client** | A cost per square metre is intuitive |

> **The FIRST row is why the method exists: at the stage when a client asks "roughly what will this cost?", there are no drawings to measure.**

> **A detailed estimate cannot be prepared without a design, and the design cannot be commissioned without a budget — so a method that needs only an area breaks the circularity.**

**What the plinth area rate must be matched on — where the method goes wrong:**

| Factor | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **TYPE of building** | **A hospital, a warehouse and a house differ by a factor of three or more per m²** ← |
| **SPECIFICATION and finishes** | Marble against cement flooring changes the rate substantially |
| **NUMBER OF STOREYS** | **A multi-storey building has a lower rate per m² (the roof and foundation are shared) up to a point, then higher (lifts, services, structure)** |
| **LOCALITY** | Transport, labour rates and material availability |
| **DATE — with an index adjustment for inflation** | **A rate from three years ago must be escalated** |
| **Height of storey** | A taller storey costs more per m² of floor |
| **Services included or excluded** | Electrical, sanitary, lifts, HVAC |

> **The method's accuracy depends ENTIRELY on the comparability of the rate, and that is its real limitation:**

> **The arithmetic cannot be wrong; the RATE can be, and there is nothing in the calculation to reveal it.**

> **So a plinth area estimate is only as good as the judgement in selecting the rate — which means it should be prepared by someone with knowledge of local completed costs, and it should always state WHICH buildings the rate derives from.**

> **An estimate quoting a rate without its basis is not verifiable and should not be relied upon**, which is worth insisting on professionally.

**The other approximate methods, and when each is preferred:**

| Method | Basis | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **PLINTH AREA** | **Cost per m² of plinth area** | **Buildings generally** ← |
| **CUBICAL CONTENT (cubic rate)** | **Cost per m³ of volume (plinth area × height from floor to roof)** | **Buildings with unusual storey heights — a hall, an auditorium, a factory** ← |
| **UNIT BASE (unit rate)** | **Cost per FUNCTIONAL UNIT** | **Schools (per pupil), hospitals (per bed), cinemas (per seat), water tanks (per litre), roads (per km)** |
| **Approximate quantity** | Cost per metre run of wall, including everything in it | Slightly more detailed; walls dominate the cost |
| **Bay method** | Cost of one repeating bay × number of bays | Factory sheds, warehouses |
| **Service unit method** | Cost per service unit — per kW, per MLD | Plant and infrastructure |

> **The CUBICAL CONTENT method's advantage over plinth area is worth understanding, because it addresses a real defect:**

> **Plinth area takes no account of HEIGHT. A single-storey building with a 3 m ceiling and an auditorium with a 9 m ceiling have the same plinth area and utterly different costs.**

> **Cubical content includes the height, so it discriminates correctly between them.**

> **Which is why the cubic method is preferred for halls, factories, godowns and any building whose height departs from the ordinary.**

> **And the UNIT BASE method is the most useful of all at the very earliest stage, before even a plan area is known:**

> **A client who says "we need a 50-bed hospital" has given enough for a unit-base estimate, and nothing at all for a plinth area estimate** — since the plinth area itself has yet to be determined.

> **So the three methods form a sequence of increasing information: unit base needs only the FUNCTION, plinth area needs the AREA, cubical content needs the area and the HEIGHT.**

> **Choosing the right one is a matter of what is actually known at the time.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| **(a) DETAILED quantity method** | **The FULL, ITEM-BY-ITEM estimate: every item measured from drawings, multiplied by its rate from a rate analysis. The most accurate and the one used for TENDERING — and it needs complete drawings** ← |
| **(b) CENTRE LINE method** | **Not an estimating METHOD at all — it is a technique for computing the LENGTHS of walls WITHIN a detailed estimate** |
| **(c) UNIT BASE method** | **A real approximate method, but suited to functional units (per bed, per pupil), not the general building case** |

> **Option (b) is the instructive error: the centre line method and the long wall-short wall method are two ways of computing wall lengths inside a detailed estimate.**

> **They are at a completely different level of the hierarchy from the plinth area method — one is a technique within a detailed estimate, the other is an alternative to preparing a detailed estimate at all.**

**The types of estimate, since "preliminary" is one of several:**

| Estimate | Purpose | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| **PRELIMINARY (approximate, abstract)** | **Administrative approval; deciding whether to proceed** | **±10-15 %** ← |
| **PLINTH AREA estimate** | The usual form of the above | |
| **DETAILED estimate** | **Technical sanction, tendering, agreement** | **±5 %** |
| **REVISED estimate** | **When the detailed estimate is exceeded by more than a stated percentage (commonly 5 %)** |
| **SUPPLEMENTARY estimate** | **For ADDITIONAL work not in the original scope** ← |
| **ANNUAL REPAIR / maintenance estimate** | Recurring upkeep |
| **Complete estimate** | All ancillary costs — land, fees, contingency, supervision |

> **The distinction between a REVISED and a SUPPLEMENTARY estimate is worth being firm about, since it is administratively consequential:**

> **A REVISED estimate covers the SAME work at a higher cost — an overrun.**

> **A SUPPLEMENTARY estimate covers ADDITIONAL work — a change of scope.**

> **They require different justifications and different approvals, and describing a scope change as an overrun (or the reverse) misrepresents what happened.**

> **That is a matter of professional honesty in reporting as much as of procedure: an overrun reflects on the original estimate, and a scope change reflects on the original brief.**

examTip.trick: **PLINTH AREA method: cost = plinth area × a rate derived from comparable completed buildings.** It needs only an AREA, so it works before a design exists.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) the CENTRE LINE method is not an estimating method** — it is a technique for computing wall LENGTHS inside a DETAILED estimate, a different level of the hierarchy entirely.
examTip.mnemonic: **Three approximate methods in order of information needed: UNIT BASE (function only — per bed, per pupil), PLINTH AREA (area), CUBICAL CONTENT (area and HEIGHT).** Use the cubic method for halls and factories, where plinth area ignores the height.

questions.stem: A saturated soil sample has a water content of 40 % and a specific gravity of solids of 2.70. Its void ratio is:
questions.solution:
**1.08.**

**The fundamental relation:**

> **e S = w G**

> **This single equation connects the four basic index quantities and is the most useful identity in soil mechanics.**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **e** | **Void ratio** | to find |
| **S** | **Degree of saturation** | **1.0 (saturated)** |
| **w** | **Water content** | **0.40** |
| **G** | **Specific gravity of solids** | **2.70** |

**The computation:**

> **e × 1.0 = 0.40 × 2.70**

> **e = 1.08** ✓

**Why the relation holds — the derivation in two lines:**

> **Take the volume of solids as unity, so the volume of voids is e.**

> **Mass of solids = G ρ_w × 1. Mass of water = w × G ρ_w.**

> **Volume of water = w G ρ_w / ρ_w = w G.**

> **Degree of saturation S = volume of water / volume of voids = wG / e.**

> **Hence e S = w G** ✓

> **Deriving it from the phase diagram once means it never needs to be memorised, and every index problem yields to the same picture: SET THE VOLUME OF SOLIDS TO ONE and write everything in terms of e, w, G and S.**

**Why the answer exceeds 1, which surprises people:**

> **A void ratio of 1.08 means the VOIDS OCCUPY MORE VOLUME THAN THE SOLIDS.**

> **That is entirely normal for a soft clay, and void ratios of 2 or 3 occur in very soft marine and organic clays.**

> **The reason is that clay particles are PLATY and build open, flocculated structures held together by electrochemical forces at the particle contacts** — a card-house arrangement with a great deal of empty space.

> **A sand, whose grains are bulky and pack like ball bearings, cannot do this: its void ratio is confined to roughly 0.4 to 1.0 by geometry alone.**

| Soil | Typical void ratio |
|---|---|
| **Dense sand** | **0.4-0.5** |
| **Loose sand** | **0.7-0.9** |
| **Stiff clay** | **0.5-0.8** |
| **Soft clay** | **1.0-2.0** ← this sample |
| **Organic clay, peat** | **2-15** |

> **So a void ratio of 1.08 with 40 per cent water content describes a soft clay — a compressible material whose settlement, not its bearing capacity, will usually govern a design on it.**

**The related quantities, since one question can ask for any of them:**

> **POROSITY:  n = e/(1+e) = 1.08/2.08 = 0.519 = 51.9 %**

> **SATURATED unit weight:  γ_sat = (G + e)/(1 + e) × γ_w = (2.70 + 1.08)/2.08 × 9.81 = 17.83 kN/m³**

> **DRY unit weight:  γ_d = G/(1+e) × γ_w = 2.70/2.08 × 9.81 = 12.73 kN/m³**

> **SUBMERGED unit weight:  γ' = γ_sat − γ_w = 17.83 − 9.81 = 8.02 kN/m³**

> **Check:  γ_sat = γ_d (1 + w) = 12.73 × 1.40 = 17.82 kN/m³** ✓ — the two routes agree, which confirms the void ratio.

> **That last check is worth making a habit of: γ = γ_d(1+w) holds for ANY soil at ANY saturation**, so it verifies a set of computed values in one multiplication.

**Why e is used rather than porosity n, since both describe the same thing:**

> **The VOID RATIO takes the volume of SOLIDS as its reference, and the volume of solids DOES NOT CHANGE when a soil compresses.**

> **POROSITY takes the TOTAL volume as its reference, and the total volume changes continuously as the soil compresses.**

> **So a change in void ratio is directly proportional to a change in volume, while a change in porosity is not.**

> **That is why the whole theory of consolidation is written in terms of e — the e-log σ' curve, the compression index C_c = Δe/Δ(log σ'), the settlement formula Δe/(1+e₀) × H.**

> **Choosing an unchanging reference is what makes the algebra tractable**, and it is the same reasoning that makes engineers work in strain rather than in length.

examTip.trick: **e S = w G.** With S = 1, e = 0.40 × 2.70 = **1.08.** One relation covers the whole family of index problems.
examTip.trap: **A void ratio above 1 is normal, not an error** — it means the voids exceed the solids, which soft clays do routinely because platy particles build open flocculated structures. Sand is confined to about 0.4-1.0 by packing geometry.
examTip.mnemonic: **Derive it from the phase diagram: set the volume of SOLIDS to one.** And check any set of computed unit weights with γ = γ_d(1+w), which holds for any soil at any saturation.

questions.stem: A soil has a liquid limit of 55 %, a plastic limit of 25 % and a natural water content of 34 %. Its liquidity index is:
questions.solution:
**0.30.**

**The liquidity index:**

> **I_L = (w − w_P) / I_P**, where **I_P = w_L − w_P** is the plasticity index.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Liquid limit w_L** | **55 %** |
| **Plastic limit w_P** | **25 %** |
| **PLASTICITY INDEX I_P = 55 − 25** | **30 %** |
| **Natural water content w** | **34 %** |

**The computation:**

> **I_L = (34 − 25) / 30 = 9 / 30 = 0.30** ✓

**What the answer MEANS — the point of the index:**

> **The liquidity index locates the soil's NATURAL water content on the scale between its plastic limit (0) and its liquid limit (1).**

| I_L | Consistency | State |
|---|---|---|
| **> 1** | **Water content ABOVE the liquid limit** | **A LIQUID — it will flow; very sensitive** |
| **0.75-1.0** | Very soft | — |
| **0.5-0.75** | Soft | — |
| **0.25-0.5** | **Medium stiff** | ← I_L = 0.30 |
| **0-0.25** | Stiff | — |
| **< 0** | **Water content BELOW the plastic limit** | **Semi-solid to solid; desiccated** |

> **So I_L = 0.30 describes a soil in the lower part of its plastic range — a MEDIUM STIFF clay, workable and stable but by no means strong.**

> **The index is more informative than the water content alone, and that is precisely why it exists: 34 per cent water is very wet for a sand and very dry for a peat.**

> **What matters is the water content RELATIVE TO THE SOIL'S OWN LIMITS**, and the liquidity index supplies exactly that comparison.

**The CONSISTENCY INDEX, its complement:**

> **I_C = (w_L − w) / I_P = (55 − 34)/30 = 21/30 = 0.70**

> **And note:  I_L + I_C = 1 always** — 0.30 + 0.70 = 1.00 ✓

> **The two indices measure the same thing from opposite ends: the liquidity index counts UP from the plastic limit, the consistency index counts DOWN from the liquid limit.**

> **So a HIGH consistency index means a STIFF soil, and a high liquidity index means a soft one** — and their sum is the check on both.

**Why option (d) 1.36 is the designed distractor:**

> **1.36 = 34/25 — the water content divided by the plastic limit, which is not any defined index.**

> **And option (b) 0.45 = (55 − 34)/(55 − 25 + something), or a mis-set subtraction.**

> **Option (a) 0.55 is simply the liquid limit as a decimal, offered to catch a candidate who reads the wrong line of the stem.**

> **The defence is to compute the PLASTICITY INDEX first as a separate step — 30 per cent — and only then form the ratio.** Writing it down as its own line makes the subsequent division hard to get wrong.

**The full set of Atterberg-derived indices, since papers ask for any of them:**

| Index | Formula | Tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **PLASTICITY index I_P** | **w_L − w_P** | **The WIDTH of the plastic range — how much water the soil can absorb while staying plastic** |
| **LIQUIDITY index I_L** | **(w − w_P)/I_P** | **Where the natural water content sits in that range** ← |
| **CONSISTENCY index I_C** | **(w_L − w)/I_P** | The same, counted from the other end |
| **FLOW index I_F** | The slope of the w vs log N line in the Casagrande test | Rate of loss of strength with water |
| **TOUGHNESS index I_T** | **I_P / I_F** | Shear strength at the plastic limit |
| **SHRINKAGE index I_S** | **w_P − w_S** | Range over which the soil is semi-solid |
| **ACTIVITY A** | **I_P / (% finer than 2 μm)** | **The MINERALOGY — how active the clay fraction is** |

> **ACTIVITY is the one worth understanding beyond its formula, because it identifies the clay mineral:**

| Activity | Classification | Mineral |
|---|---|---|
| **< 0.75** | **Inactive** | **KAOLINITE — stable, low swell** |
| **0.75-1.25** | Normal | **ILLITE** |
| **> 1.25** | **Active** | **MONTMORILLONITE — the swelling clay** ← |

> **A high activity is a warning: montmorillonitic clay swells on wetting and shrinks on drying, and it will lift a lightly loaded floor slab or crack a boundary wall through seasonal moisture change alone.**

> **That is the practical value of the index tests. They are cheap, quick and performed on a REMOULDED sample — so they say nothing about the soil's in-situ structure or strength — but they identify what the soil IS, and hence what it will do.**

> **A plasticity index of 30 with a liquid limit of 55 plots above the A-line on the plasticity chart, classifying this soil as CH — an inorganic clay of HIGH plasticity** — which is consistent with a material to be treated with respect on any project involving foundations, fill or pavement subgrade.

examTip.trick: **Compute I_P first as its own line: 55 − 25 = 30.** Then I_L = (34 − 25)/30 = **0.30.**
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 0.55 is just the liquid limit as a decimal**, and (d) 1.36 = 34/25, which is no defined index. Writing I_P down separately makes the division hard to misform.
examTip.mnemonic: **I_L + I_C = 1 always** — 0.30 + 0.70 ✓ — so each checks the other. And ACTIVITY (I_P ÷ % clay) identifies the mineral: below 0.75 kaolinite, above 1.25 MONTMORILLONITE, the swelling clay that cracks walls through seasonal moisture change.

questions.stem: At a depth of 6 m in a saturated sand deposit of saturated unit weight 19 kN/m³, the water table stands at the ground surface. Taking γ_w = 9.81 kN/m³, the effective vertical stress at that depth is:
questions.solution:
**55.1 kPa.**

**Step 1 — the TOTAL vertical stress:**

> **σ_v = γ_sat × z = 19 × 6 = 114 kPa**

**Step 2 — the PORE WATER pressure:**

> **The water table is AT THE SURFACE, so the water is 6 m deep at this point:**

> **u = γ_w × z = 9.81 × 6 = 58.86 kPa**

**Step 3 — TERZAGHI'S effective stress principle:**

> **σ' = σ − u**

> **σ' = 114 − 58.86 = 55.14 kPa ≈ 55.1 kPa** ✓

**The shorter route, which is worth using:**

> **σ' = γ' × z**, where **γ' = γ_sat − γ_w** is the SUBMERGED (buoyant) unit weight.

> **γ' = 19 − 9.81 = 9.19 kN/m³**

> **σ' = 9.19 × 6 = 55.14 kPa** ✓

> **Same answer in one step instead of three, and it is the form to use whenever the water table is at or above the surface.**

> **Note that option (d) 9.2 kPa is the submerged UNIT WEIGHT itself, offered as a stress** — a distractor aimed at a candidate who computes γ' and forgets to multiply by the depth.

> **And options (a) 114 and (c) 58.9 are the TOTAL stress and the PORE PRESSURE respectively — the two intermediate quantities, each offered as the answer.**

> **So all three distractors are steps along the correct path, which means the calculation must be carried to its end rather than stopped when a familiar-looking number appears.**

**Why EFFECTIVE stress is the quantity that matters — Terzaghi's principle:**

> **The single most important idea in soil mechanics is that the mechanical behaviour of a soil is governed by the EFFECTIVE stress, not the total stress.**

> **Strength:  τ = c' + σ' tan φ'**

> **Compressibility: the e-log σ' curve, in terms of effective stress**

> **The reason is physical: TOTAL stress is carried partly by the soil SKELETON and partly by the WATER in the pores.**

> **Water has no shear strength and cannot hold the grains together. Only the part of the stress transmitted GRAIN TO GRAIN — the effective stress — presses the particles into contact and generates friction.**

> **So a soil's strength depends on σ' alone, and any change in pore pressure changes the strength even when the total stress has not moved at all.**

**The consequences of that, which are the whole of practical soil mechanics:**

| Situation | What happens |
|---|---|
| **The water table RISES** | **u increases, σ' FALLS, strength FALLS** — many slope failures occur after prolonged rain for exactly this reason ← |
| **A rapid drawdown behind an earth dam** | **The total stress falls but the pore pressure lags, so σ' falls sharply — a classic slope stability case** |
| **Loading a clay quickly** | **The load is carried initially by the WATER (Δu = Δσ), so σ' does not change and there is no immediate strength gain** |
| **Consolidation over time** | **Water drains, u dissipates, σ' rises, and the clay gains strength and settles** |
| **QUICKSAND / boiling at an excavation base** | **Upward seepage reduces σ' to ZERO — the soil has NO strength at all** |
| **Pumping groundwater from beneath a city** | **u falls, σ' RISES, and the ground SETTLES — regional subsidence** |
