> **The head loss per unit length is 10.19/500 = 0.0204 m per metre, that is a hydraulic gradient of about 1 in 49.**

> **That is STEEP for a water main: a 2 m/s velocity in a 200 mm pipe is on the high side, and the loss reflects it.**

| Typical design velocity | Application |
|---|---|
| **0.6-1.0 m/s** | **Gravity mains where head is precious** |
| **1.0-1.5 m/s** | **Normal distribution mains** |
| **1.5-2.5 m/s** | **Pumping mains, where pumping cost is traded against pipe cost** ← |
| **Above 3 m/s** | **Avoided — noise, erosion and severe head loss** |

> **The economics behind that table are worth stating: a LARGER pipe costs more to lay but has a lower head loss, so it costs less to pump through for the whole of its life.**

> **The ECONOMIC DIAMETER is the one minimising the sum of the capital cost and the capitalised pumping cost, and it typically lands in the 1 to 2 m/s range** — which is why the design velocities above are what they are, rather than being arbitrary conventions.

**The V² dependence, which is the most consequential feature:**

> **Head loss goes as the SQUARE of the velocity, hence as the square of the discharge.**

| Change | Effect on h_f |
|---|---|
| **DOUBLE the flow** | **× 4** |
| **HALVE the diameter (at the same flow)** | **The velocity quadruples AND D halves: × 4² × 2 = × 32** ← |
| **Double the length** | **× 2** |

> **The second row is the striking one and it is worth deriving, because it explains why pipe sizing is so sensitive.**

> **At constant discharge, V ∝ 1/D², so V² ∝ 1/D⁴, and with the 1/D already in the formula:**

> **h_f ∝ 1/D⁵ at constant discharge**

> **A FIFTH POWER. Increasing a pipe's diameter by just 15 per cent halves its head loss.**

> **That extreme sensitivity is why the choice of pipe diameter dominates the hydraulic design of any pipeline, and why an apparently small increase in size can transform a scheme's pumping cost.**

**How f itself is obtained, since the stem simply gives it:**

| Flow regime | Friction factor |
|---|---|
| **LAMINAR (Re < 2000)** | **f = 64/Re — exact, independent of roughness** |
| **Turbulent, smooth pipe** | **Blasius: f = 0.316/Re^{0.25} for Re up to 10⁵** |
| **Turbulent, transitional** | **COLEBROOK-WHITE — implicit, solved iteratively or read from the MOODY diagram** ← |
| **Fully rough turbulent** | **f depends on RELATIVE ROUGHNESS ε/D ALONE, not on Re** |

> **The last row is the important qualitative result: in FULLY ROUGH turbulent flow the friction factor stops depending on the Reynolds number altogether.**

> **On the Moody diagram those are the horizontal lines to the right, and their existence is why an old, rough pipe's friction factor can be quoted as a single number without reference to the flow rate.**

> **It also means that in that regime h_f is exactly proportional to V², which is the assumption the empirical formulae (Hazen-Williams, Manning) build in** — and it is why those formulae work well for water mains and poorly for laminar or transitional flow.

**And the MINOR losses, which this calculation omits:**

> **h_minor = K V²/2g**, summed over the fittings.

| Fitting | K (approximate) |
|---|---|
| **Sudden enlargement to a large tank (exit)** | **1.0** |
| **Sharp-edged entry** | **0.5** |
| **90° elbow** | **0.9** |
| **Gate valve, fully open** | **0.2** |
| **Globe valve, fully open** | **10** |
| **Bend, long radius** | 0.2-0.4 |

> **For this pipe V²/2g = 0.204 m, so each unit of K costs about 0.2 m — small against the 10.2 m of friction loss over 500 m.**

> **Which is the general rule: in a LONG pipeline the friction loss dominates and minor losses may be neglected; in a SHORT one with many fittings the reverse is true.**

> **The usual criterion is L/D: above about 1000, minor losses are negligible. Here L/D = 2500, so ignoring them is entirely justified** — but a 5 m length of the same pipe with three bends and a valve would be governed almost entirely by them.

examTip.trap: **Two conventions differ by a factor of 4** — the DARCY factor (f ≈ 0.02, no extra 4) and the FANNING factor (f' ≈ 0.005, needs 4f'). The numerical value of f tells you which is intended.
examTip.mnemonic: **At constant discharge h_f ∝ 1/D⁵** — a fifth power, so a 15 % larger pipe halves the loss. That sensitivity is why diameter dominates pipeline design. And minor losses are negligible when L/D exceeds about 1000 (here 2500).

questions.stem: Three pipes are connected in PARALLEL between two junctions. Which quantity is the SAME in all three pipes?
questions.solution:
**The HEAD LOSS.**

**The two connection arrangements, and what each shares:**

| Arrangement | SAME in every pipe | ADDS across the pipes |
|---|---|---|
| **SERIES** | **DISCHARGE Q** | **HEAD LOSS: h_f = h₁ + h₂ + h₃** |
| **PARALLEL** | **HEAD LOSS h_f** ← | **DISCHARGE: Q = Q₁ + Q₂ + Q₃** |

> **The two cases are exact duals of one another, and knowing one gives the other by exchange.**

**Why the head loss must be equal in parallel pipes:**

> **All three pipes START at the same junction and END at the same junction.**

> **The head at the upstream junction is a single value; the head at the downstream junction is a single value.**

> **So the DIFFERENCE between them — the head loss — is the same number for every path connecting them.**

> **It cannot be otherwise: if two pipes joining the same two points had different head losses, the head at one junction would have two different values simultaneously, which is impossible.**

> **That is the whole argument, and it is worth phrasing exactly that way because it makes the result inevitable rather than something to be recalled.**

> **It is precisely the same reasoning as Kirchhoff's voltage law in an electrical circuit: the potential difference between two nodes is unique, whatever path is taken between them.**

**Why the DISCHARGE is not equal — and how it divides:**

> **Each pipe carries the flow that ITS OWN resistance permits under the common head loss.**

> **From Darcy-Weisbach, with h_f fixed:**

> **h_f = f L V²/(2gD) = f L Q²/(2gD × A²)**

> **Solving for Q:  Q ∝ √(D⁵/(f L))**

> **So a pipe that is SHORTER, WIDER or SMOOTHER carries MORE of the flow.**

> **And the D^{5/2} dependence is very strong: a pipe of twice the diameter, same length and roughness, carries 2^{2.5} = 5.66 times the flow.**

> **Which means that in a parallel arrangement the LARGEST pipe carries the overwhelming majority of the discharge, and a small pipe added in parallel with a large one contributes very little.**

> **That is a genuinely useful practical conclusion: reinforcing a main by laying a small parallel pipe is nearly futile, while replacing it with one slightly larger is highly effective.**

**Why the other options fail:**

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **(a) Discharge** | **This is the SERIES answer. In parallel the discharges ADD** |
| **(b) Velocity** | **Depends on the diameter and the resistance; no reason for it to be equal** |
| **(c) Diameter** | **Nothing requires parallel pipes to be the same size — indeed they usually are not** |

> **Option (a) is the deliberate trap because it is the correct answer to the SERIES case, and the two arrangements are constantly confused.**

> **The memory device that fixes it: in SERIES the water has NO CHOICE but to pass through every pipe, so the flow is common. In PARALLEL the water has a choice, so it distributes — but every route spans the same pressure drop.**

**The EQUIVALENT PIPE, since that is what these rules are for:**

> **A network can be reduced to a single pipe of equivalent resistance:**

| Arrangement | Equivalent |
|---|---|
| **SERIES** | **L_e/D_e⁵ = L₁/D₁⁵ + L₂/D₂⁵ + L₃/D₃⁵** (equal f) |
| **PARALLEL** | **√(D_e⁵/L_e) = √(D₁⁵/L₁) + √(D₂⁵/L₂) + √(D₃⁵/L₃)** |

> **The D⁵ terms are the direct consequence of h_f ∝ Q²L/D⁵, and both formulae are simply that relation rearranged for the appropriate common quantity.**

> **Note how they mirror the electrical analogy: series resistances ADD, and parallel CONDUCTANCES add.** Here L/D⁵ plays the part of resistance and √(D⁵/L) the part of conductance.

**Why parallel pipes are laid in practice:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **To INCREASE the capacity of an existing main** | **Laying a second pipe alongside rather than replacing the first** ← |
| **REDUNDANCY — one pipe can be taken out for repair** | **Often the decisive reason for a critical main** |
| **To stage the capital expenditure** | Build the second pipe when demand grows |
| **Where a single pipe of the required size is unavailable or unhandleable** | Practical limits on manufacture and transport |

> **The REDUNDANCY argument frequently outweighs the hydraulic one: a city's trunk main that cannot be isolated for repair is a single point of failure, and two pipes each of 70 per cent capacity may be preferable to one of 100 per cent.**

> **That is a design judgement about reliability rather than about hydraulics, and it is the kind of consideration that distinguishes engineering from calculation.**

**A worked illustration of the flow division, to make the D^{5/2} rule concrete:**

> **Three pipes between the same junctions, all 500 m long with f = 0.02, of diameters 300, 200 and 150 mm.**

| Pipe | D (m) | D^{2.5} | Share of the total flow |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **0.30** | **0.0493** | **57 %** |
| **2** | **0.20** | **0.0179** | **21 %** |
| **3** | **0.15** | **0.00872** | **10 %** |
| — | — | Σ = 0.0759 | — |

> **Recomputing the percentages against the sum: 65 %, 24 %, 11 %.**

> **So the 300 mm pipe carries nearly two thirds of the flow and the 150 mm pipe barely a tenth**, though it is half the larger pipe's diameter.

> **That distribution is the practical face of the fifth-power law, and it is why hydraulic capacity is bought with diameter and almost nothing else.**

examTip.trick: **PARALLEL: head loss common, discharges ADD. SERIES: discharge common, head losses ADD.** The two are exact duals.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) discharge is the SERIES answer**, and the two arrangements are constantly swapped. Fix it by reasoning: parallel pipes join the same two junctions, so the head DIFFERENCE between them is one unique number — Kirchhoff's voltage law.
examTip.mnemonic: **In parallel, Q ∝ D^{2.5}**, so a 300 mm pipe carries about six times a 150 mm one. Reinforcing a main with a small parallel pipe is nearly futile; capacity is bought with diameter and almost nothing else.

questions.stem: For a rectangular channel carrying a discharge of 12 m³/s per metre width, the critical depth is:
questions.solution:
**2.45 m.**

**The critical depth for a rectangular channel:**

> **y_c = (q²/g)^{1/3}**

> **where q is the discharge PER UNIT WIDTH.**

**The computation:**

> **q = 12 m³/s per metre**

> **y_c = (12²/9.81)^{1/3} = (144/9.81)^{1/3} = (14.68)^{1/3}**

> **The cube root of 14.68: since 2.4³ = 13.82 and 2.5³ = 15.63, the answer lies between.**

> **2.45³ = 14.71 — close enough.**

> **y_c = 2.45 m** ✓

> **Extracting a cube root without a calculator is done exactly that way: bracket it between two obvious cubes and interpolate.**

**Where the formula comes from — the condition Fr = 1:**

> **Critical flow is defined by Fr = 1, that is V = √(g y) for a rectangular channel (where the hydraulic depth equals the flow depth).**

> **With V = q/y:**

> **q/y = √(g y)**

> **q = y √(g y) = √(g y³)**

> **q² = g y³**

> **y_c = (q²/g)^{1/3}** ✓

> **So the formula is nothing more than the Froude number set to one, and it can be rebuilt in three lines if forgotten.**

**The properties of critical depth, which is why it matters:**

| Property | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Fr = 1** | **The defining condition** |
| **SPECIFIC ENERGY is MINIMUM** for the given discharge | **E_min = 1.5 y_c** ← |
| **DISCHARGE is MAXIMUM** for the given specific energy | The dual statement |
| **Velocity head = HALF the depth** | **V_c²/2g = y_c/2** |
| **The flow is a CONTROL** | Depth and discharge are uniquely related there |

> **The relation E_min = 1.5 y_c is worth having, and it follows immediately:**

> **E = y + V²/2g, and at critical V²/2g = y/2, so E_c = y_c + y_c/2 = 1.5 y_c**

> **Here E_min = 1.5 × 2.45 = 3.68 m** — the least specific energy with which 12 m³/s per metre can possibly be passed.

> **That is a hard physical limit: no channel, however designed, can carry 12 m³/s/m with less than 3.68 m of specific energy.** Attempting it forces the flow to back up until it has that energy.

**The specific energy curve and the ALTERNATE DEPTHS:**

> **For a given discharge, plotting E against y gives a curve with a MINIMUM at the critical depth and two branches:**

| Branch | Depth | Regime |
|---|---|---|
| **Upper branch** | **y > y_c** | **SUBCRITICAL — deep and slow** |
| **Lower branch** | **y < y_c** | **SUPERCRITICAL — shallow and fast** |

> **So for any specific energy above the minimum there are TWO possible depths carrying the same discharge — the ALTERNATE DEPTHS.**

> **For instance at E = 5 m, this discharge could flow at about 4.55 m deep and slow, or about 1.35 m deep and fast.**

> **Which of the two actually occurs is settled not by energy but by the CONTROLS at the ends of the reach**, and that is one of the genuinely subtle points in open channel hydraulics.

> **A HYDRAULIC JUMP is the transition from the lower branch to the upper — from supercritical to subcritical — and it is accompanied by an ENERGY LOSS, which is why it appears as a jump rather than a smooth passage back along the curve.**

> **Note the asymmetry: a flow can pass smoothly from subcritical to supercritical (accelerating over a weir or a steepening slope), but the reverse transition is always abrupt and dissipative.**

**Why the distractors are placed where they are:**

| Option | Origin |
|---|---|
| **(a) 1.83 m** | Roughly (q²/g)^{1/3} with q mis-set, or 2/3 of the critical depth |
| **(b) 2.45 m** | ✓ |
| **(c) 3.06 m** | **Close to E_min/1.2, or 1.25 y_c — a plausible-looking value** |
| **(d) 1.22 m** | **Exactly HALF the answer — from taking a square root instead of a cube root somewhere** |

> **A magnitude check settles it quickly: 12 m³/s per metre is a substantial flow, and at the critical depth the velocity is V_c = q/y_c = 12/2.45 = 4.9 m/s — which is √(9.81 × 2.45) = 4.9 m/s ✓.**

> **That internal check — that V_c must equal √(g y_c) — verifies the answer completely and costs one square root.** It is the best available guard against a cube-root slip.

**Why critical depth is engineered deliberately:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **FLOW MEASUREMENT** | **Force the flow to critical and one depth measurement gives the discharge — the principle of the VENTURI FLUME, the broad-crested weir and the standing-wave flume** ← |
| **Control section for profile computation** | Profiles are computed away from it in both directions |
| **ENERGY DISSIPATION** | A hydraulic jump downstream of a spillway destroys energy |
| **Free overfall** | Critical depth occurs a short distance upstream of the brink |
| **Channel transitions** | Choking is checked against the critical condition |

> **The MEASUREMENT application is the most valuable, because it turns a difficult problem into an easy one.**

> **Measuring a discharge normally requires knowing the velocity distribution — a laborious business with a current meter.**

> **But at a critical section the depth and the discharge are uniquely related, so a single staff gauge reading gives the flow.**

> **That is why irrigation systems are full of deliberately constructed critical-flow structures: they are self-measuring, they need no moving parts, and a reading can be taken by anyone.**

> **And the FREE OVERFALL result is worth knowing as a field observation: at the brink of a drop, the depth is about 0.7 y_c, and critical depth occurs roughly 3 to 4 y_c upstream of it.** So a channel ending in a fall carries its own measuring section, if one knows where to look.

examTip.trap: **Check it with V_c = √(g y_c):** here q/y_c = 12/2.45 = 4.9 and √(9.81 × 2.45) = 4.9 ✓. That costs one square root and catches any cube-root slip — option (d) is exactly half the answer.
examTip.mnemonic: **At critical flow, velocity head = HALF the depth, so E_min = 1.5 y_c = 3.68 m** — a hard limit on the energy needed to pass this discharge. And a critical section is SELF-MEASURING, which is why irrigation systems are full of them.

questions.stem: A 6-hour unit hydrograph has a peak discharge of 90 m³/s. For a storm of 6 hours producing 4 cm of effective rainfall, the peak of the resulting flood hydrograph, with a base flow of 15 m³/s, is:
questions.solution:
**375 m³/s.**

**Step 1 — what a UNIT hydrograph is.**

> **A UNIT HYDROGRAPH is the direct runoff hydrograph resulting from ONE UNIT (in SI, 1 cm) of EFFECTIVE RAINFALL falling uniformly over the catchment in the specified duration.**

> **Every part of that definition carries weight:**

| Element | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **ONE UNIT** | **1 cm of effective rainfall — the ordinates scale linearly with depth** |
| **EFFECTIVE rainfall** | **Rainfall MINUS losses; the part that becomes DIRECT RUNOFF** ← |
| **DIRECT runoff only** | **BASE FLOW is EXCLUDED from a unit hydrograph and must be added back separately** ← |
| **The specified DURATION** | **A 6-hour UH applies to 6-hour storms; a different duration needs the S-curve or the UH method to convert** |
| **Uniformly over the catchment** | The rainfall distribution is assumed even |

**Step 2 — scale the peak by the rainfall depth.**

> **The unit hydrograph's defining property is LINEARITY: 4 cm of effective rainfall in the same duration produces ordinates FOUR TIMES as large.**

> **Direct runoff peak = 4 × 90 = 360 m³/s**

**Step 3 — add the base flow.**

> **Total peak discharge = 360 + 15 = 375 m³/s** ✓

**Why each distractor is placed where it is:**

| Option | Origin |
|---|---|
| **(a) 90 m³/s** | **The unit hydrograph peak UNSCALED** — the answer for 1 cm of rainfall with no base flow |
| **(b) 345 m³/s** | **The base flow SUBTRACTED instead of added** |
| **(c) 375 m³/s** | ✓ |
| **(d) 360 m³/s** | **The DIRECT RUNOFF peak with the base flow OMITTED — the commonest error** ← |

> **Option (d) is the trap that matters, because a unit hydrograph deals ONLY in direct runoff.**

> **The base flow is never part of a unit hydrograph and must always be added back separately — which is not pedantry but the definition of the tool.**

> **The question asks for the peak of the FLOOD hydrograph, meaning the total discharge in the river, so the base flow belongs in the answer.**

**The two assumptions that make the method work — and their limits:**

| Assumption | Statement | Where it fails |
|---|---|---|
| **LINEARITY (proportionality)** | **Ordinates scale directly with the rainfall depth** | **Very large storms: the catchment's response is not truly linear, and extreme events give proportionally larger peaks** |
| **SUPERPOSITION** | **Hydrographs from successive rainfall blocks ADD, offset in time** | Where the catchment condition changes during the storm |
| **TIME INVARIANCE** | **The same rainfall always gives the same hydrograph** | **Seasonal changes in vegetation, land use change, urbanisation** ← |

> **The TIME INVARIANCE assumption is the one most often violated in practice and the most consequential: a unit hydrograph derived from records of the 1980s may not describe a catchment that has since been urbanised.**

> **Urbanisation makes a catchment's response FASTER and SHARPER — a higher peak arriving sooner — because paved surfaces and drains replace infiltration and overland flow.**

> **So a flood design based on an old unit hydrograph for a developing catchment will UNDERESTIMATE the peak, and the error is on the unsafe side.**

> **Which is a real limitation to state rather than a caveat to note in passing: hydrological models describe the catchment they were calibrated on.**

**SUPERPOSITION worked out, since it is the method's real power:**

> **If the storm had been 4 cm in the first 6 hours followed by 2 cm in the next 6, the flood hydrograph would be built by adding:**

> **4 × (the UH ordinates), plus 2 × (the UH ordinates shifted 6 hours later), plus the base flow.**

> **The peak of the sum is NOT simply 6 × 90, because the two component peaks occur at different times and do not coincide.**

> **Computing it requires the full ordinate table, and that is the ordinary work of flood estimation** — the single-block case in this question is the simplest instance of it.

**How a unit hydrograph is DERIVED, since it must come from somewhere:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Select an ISOLATED storm of roughly the required duration with a good rainfall and streamflow record** |
| **2** | **SEPARATE the base flow from the observed hydrograph (straight line, or the master depletion curve)** |
| **3** | **Compute the volume of direct runoff and divide by the catchment area to get the EFFECTIVE RAINFALL depth in cm** |
| **4** | **DIVIDE every direct runoff ordinate by that depth** — giving the ordinates for 1 cm |
| **5** | **Average several such unit hydrographs from different storms, matching the PEAKS and the TIME TO PEAK rather than averaging ordinates blindly** |

> **Step 5 contains a real subtlety: a straight arithmetic average of several unit hydrographs, each with its peak at a slightly different time, produces a flattened curve with too low a peak.**

> **The correct practice is to average the peak magnitudes and the times to peak separately, then sketch a curve through those averaged characteristics with the correct unit volume beneath it.**

> **That is a good example of a case where the obvious statistical operation gives the wrong engineering answer.**

**The SYNTHETIC unit hydrograph, for catchments with no records:**

> **Where no gauged data exist — which is the usual situation in Nepal — a SYNTHETIC unit hydrograph is derived from the catchment's physical characteristics:**

| Method | Based on |
|---|---|
| **SNYDER's** | **Basin length, length to the centroid, and regional coefficients C_t and C_p** |
| **SCS DIMENSIONLESS UH** | **A standard curve shape scaled by the time of concentration** |
| **Clark's / Nash's instantaneous UH** | Routing through a linear reservoir |
| **CWC regional formulae (India, and used in Nepal)** | Regionally calibrated relations |

> **The essential caution with all of them is that the regional coefficients were calibrated on catchments elsewhere, and transferring them to a Himalayan catchment of very different steepness and geology is an extrapolation.**

> **So a synthetic unit hydrograph is a defensible estimate in the absence of data and not a substitute for measurement** — which is the argument for the gauging that Nepal's ungauged basins conspicuously lack.

examTip.trick: **Scale the UH peak by the effective rainfall, then ADD the base flow: 4 × 90 = 360, plus 15 = 375 m³/s.**
examTip.trap: **Option (d) 360 omits the base flow** — the commonest error. A unit hydrograph contains DIRECT RUNOFF ONLY, by definition, so base flow is always a separate addition.
examTip.mnemonic: **A UH is 1 cm of EFFECTIVE rainfall in a STATED duration, direct runoff only.** Its three assumptions are linearity, superposition and TIME INVARIANCE — and the last fails on an urbanising catchment, where an old UH underestimates the peak.

questions.stem: A simply supported beam of span 8 m carries a uniformly distributed load of 12 kN/m over its whole span. The maximum bending moment is:
questions.solution:
**96 kNm.**

**The standard result:**

> **M_max = w L² / 8**

> **= 12 × 8² / 8 = 12 × 64 / 8 = 96 kNm** ✓

> **The maximum occurs at MIDSPAN, where the shear force is zero.**

**Why the maximum bending moment occurs where the shear is zero:**

> **The two are related by  dM/dx = V.**

> **A maximum of M therefore requires dM/dx = 0, that is V = 0.**

> **For this beam the shear varies linearly from +48 kN at the left support to −48 kN at the right, crossing zero at midspan** — which is where the bending moment peaks.

> **That relation is the most useful single fact in beam analysis: FIND WHERE THE SHEAR CROSSES ZERO AND THE MOMENT IS MAXIMUM THERE.**

> **It removes the need to differentiate anything, and it works for any loading, including unsymmetrical cases where midspan is NOT the critical point.**

**The complete set of relations, since they come as a family:**

> **dV/dx = −w   and   dM/dx = V**

| Loading | Shear force diagram | Bending moment diagram |
|---|---|---|
| **No load** | **CONSTANT** | **LINEAR** |
| **Point load** | **A STEP** | **A KINK (change of slope)** |
| **UNIFORM load (UDL)** | **LINEAR** | **PARABOLIC** ← this beam |
| **Linearly varying load** | **PARABOLIC** | **CUBIC** |
| **A couple applied** | No change | **A STEP in the moment** |

> **The rule: each integration raises the order by one, so the moment diagram is always one degree "smoother" than the shear diagram, which is one degree smoother than the load.**

> **Sketching the diagrams by that rule alone, without computing anything, is a reliable check on any calculated result** — a UDL that produces a triangular moment diagram means a mistake has been made somewhere.

**Why the distractors are where they are:**

| Option | Origin |
|---|---|
| **(a) 48 kNm** | **The maximum SHEAR FORCE (wL/2 = 48 kN), offered as a moment** |
| **(b) 96 kNm** | ✓ |
| **(c) 192 kNm** | **wL²/4 — the formula for a CENTRAL POINT LOAD applied to a UDL** |
| **(d) 24 kNm** | wL²/32, or a mis-set denominator |

> **Option (c) is the serious trap, because wL/4 and wL²/8 are the two most-used results and are easily interchanged:**

| Loading on a simply supported span | M_max |
|---|---|
| **Central POINT load W** | **W L / 4** |
| **UNIFORM load w per metre** | **w L² / 8** ← |

> **The way to keep them apart is DIMENSIONAL: a point load W is a force, so WL/4 has the dimensions of a moment directly. A UDL w is a force per length, so it needs L² to become a moment.**

> **Checking the dimensions takes a second and cannot be misremembered, whereas the denominators 4 and 8 can be.**

**The useful comparison — a UDL against an equal total load applied centrally:**

> **The total load on this beam is 12 × 8 = 96 kN.**

> **If that same 96 kN were applied as a single central point load, the moment would be:**

> **M = WL/4 = 96 × 8/4 = 192 kNm**

> **So the SAME total load concentrated at midspan produces TWICE the bending moment of the distributed case.**

> **That factor of two is worth carrying, because it makes the physical point: a load spread along a beam is far gentler than the same load concentrated.**

> **And it explains why a beam that carries its design distributed load comfortably may be overstressed by a heavy point load of the same magnitude — a plant item, a stack of material, or a wheel.**

> **Which is a genuine site hazard: temporary storage of materials at midspan of a slab designed for a uniform load is a common cause of cracking.**

**The full picture for this beam, for design:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Reaction at each support** | **wL/2 = 48 kN** |
| **Maximum shear (at the supports)** | **48 kN** |
| **Maximum bending moment (at midspan)** | **96 kNm** ← |
| **Maximum deflection (at midspan)** | **5wL⁴/(384 EI)** |
| **Point of maximum moment** | **Midspan, where V = 0** |
| **Points of contraflexure** | **None — the moment is positive throughout** |

> **The absence of contraflexure points is worth noting: a SIMPLY SUPPORTED beam under downward load has SAGGING moment everywhere, so the tension is in the BOTTOM fibre along the whole span and the main reinforcement stays at the bottom.**

> **A CONTINUOUS beam is quite different — it hogs over the supports, so tension moves to the TOP there, and the reinforcement must follow.** Locating the contraflexure points is what determines where the top steel can be curtailed, which is why they matter in detailing.

examTip.trick: **M_max = wL²/8 = 12 × 64/8 = 96 kNm**, at midspan where the shear crosses zero.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) 192 kNm applies the CENTRAL POINT LOAD formula WL/4 to a UDL.** Keep them apart DIMENSIONALLY: W is a force so WL/4 is already a moment; w is force per length so it needs L².
examTip.mnemonic: **Find where the shear crosses ZERO and the moment peaks there** — dM/dx = V, so no differentiation is needed, and it works for unsymmetrical loading too. And the same total load applied centrally would double the moment to 192 kNm.

questions.stem: A cantilever 4 m long carries a uniformly distributed load of 10 kN/m over its entire length. The bending moment at the fixed end is:
questions.solution:
**80 kNm.**

**The standard result:**

> **M_fixed = w L² / 2**

> **= 10 × 4² / 2 = 10 × 16 / 2 = 80 kNm** ✓

**The derivation, which takes one line and makes the formula unnecessary:**

> **Total load = w L = 10 × 4 = 40 kN**

> **Its resultant acts at the CENTROID of the load, that is at L/2 = 2 m from the fixed end.**

> **Moment at the fixed end = 40 × 2 = 80 kNm** ✓

> **That route — TOTAL LOAD TIMES THE DISTANCE TO ITS CENTROID — works for any load distribution on a cantilever and is worth using in preference to remembering formulae.**

> **For a triangular load with its maximum at the free end, for instance, the resultant is wL/2 acting at 2L/3 from the fixed end, giving M = wL²/3 — obtained by the same reasoning without a new formula.**

**Why the cantilever coefficient is 1/2 and the simply supported one 1/8:**

| Beam | Loading | M_max | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Simply supported** | **UDL w** | **wL²/8** | **1** |
| **Propped cantilever** | **UDL w** | **wL²/8 at the fixed end** | **1** |
| **Fixed both ends** | **UDL w** | **wL²/12 at the supports** | **0.67** |
| **CANTILEVER** | **UDL w** | **wL²/2** | **4** ← |

> **A cantilever of the same span and load carries FOUR TIMES the moment of a simply supported beam.**

> **The physical reason: a simply supported beam is held up at BOTH ends, so each end carries half the load over half the span. A cantilever is held at ONE end only, which must resist the whole load acting at its full lever arm.**

> **That factor of four is why cantilevers are so much heavier than simply supported spans, and why a cantilevered balcony or canopy of even modest projection needs a substantial root section.**

> **Option (a) 20 kNm is wL²/8 — the simply supported value applied to a cantilever — and it is the designed trap, understating the moment by a factor of four.**

> **Option (d) 160 kNm is wL² without the ½; option (b) 40 kNm is the total load, offered as a moment.**

**The critical detail about a cantilever — the SIGN of the moment:**

> **A cantilever HOGS: the moment is NEGATIVE, and the TENSION is in the TOP fibre.**

> **So the main reinforcement in a reinforced concrete cantilever goes at the TOP, and it must be ANCHORED PROPERLY INTO THE SUPPORTING MEMBER.**

> **That anchorage is the single most important detail in a cantilever, and its failure is the commonest cause of cantilever collapse.**

| Detailing requirement | Why |
|---|---|
| **Main steel at the TOP** | **Tension is in the top fibre** ← |
| **Full anchorage into the support beyond the point of contraflexure** | **A bar that stops at the face of the support has nothing to develop its force against** |
| **The bar must be held DOWN during concreting** | **Top steel that is trodden down becomes bottom steel, and the cantilever has no tension reinforcement at all** ← |
| **Deflection checked carefully** | The span/depth ratio for a cantilever is only 7, against 20 for simply supported |

> **The third row is not a theoretical concern. Cantilever slabs have collapsed because the top reinforcement was displaced downward by site traffic before the concrete was placed, and there is no redundancy in a cantilever to save it.**

> **A simply supported beam whose steel is mislocated is weakened; a cantilever whose top steel has been pushed down has no strength at all at the section that matters.**

**Why a cantilever has no redundancy — and what that means:**

> **A cantilever is a DETERMINATE structure with a single load path.**

> **There is no alternative route for the load to reach the support, so the failure of any one element at the root is the failure of the whole.**

> **A continuous beam, by contrast, can redistribute: if one section yields, the moment sheds to the adjacent spans and the structure often survives.**

> **That difference is why cantilevers are treated with extra caution in codes and in practice** — a larger factor of safety in effect, achieved through detailing rules rather than through the load factors.

**The deflection, since it usually governs a cantilever:**

> **δ_free end = w L⁴ / (8 E I)**

> **Compare the simply supported case: δ = 5wL⁴/(384 EI) = wL⁴/(76.8 EI).**

> **So a cantilever deflects 76.8/8 = 9.6 times as much as a simply supported beam of the same span, load and section.**

> **Nearly TEN TIMES the deflection, and four times the moment.**

> **Which is why IS 456's basic span-to-depth ratio for deflection control is 7 for a cantilever against 20 for a simply supported beam and 26 for a continuous one.**

> **A cantilever must be roughly three times as deep as a simply supported beam of the same span to be equally stiff**, and that requirement — not the bending stress — is usually what fixes its size.

examTip.trick: **Total load × distance to its centroid: 40 kN × 2 m = 80 kNm.** That route works for any load distribution and beats remembering wL²/2.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 20 kNm is the simply supported value wL²/8** — understating a cantilever by a factor of FOUR. A cantilever is held at one end only, so it resists the whole load at its full lever arm.
examTip.mnemonic: **A cantilever HOGS: tension in the TOP fibre, so main steel at the TOP and fully anchored into the support.** Top steel trodden down during concreting leaves a cantilever with no tension reinforcement at all — and no redundancy to save it.

questions.stem: A steel bar of 25 mm diameter and 2 m length carries an axial tensile load of 60 kN. Taking E = 200 GPa, its elongation is:
questions.solution:
**1.22 mm.**

**The relation:**

> **δ = P L / (A E)**

**Step 1 — the area:**

> **A = πd²/4 = π × 25²/4 = π × 625/4 = 490.9 mm²**

**Step 2 — the elongation:**

> **δ = (60,000 × 2000) / (490.9 × 200,000)**

> **= 1.2 × 10⁸ / 9.818 × 10⁷**

> **= 1.222 mm ≈ 1.22 mm** ✓

**The unit discipline that makes this reliable:**

> **Work entirely in N and mm, and the answer comes out in mm with no conversion:**

| Quantity | In N-mm units |
|---|---|
| **P = 60 kN** | **60,000 N** |
| **L = 2 m** | **2000 mm** |
| **A** | **490.9 mm²** |
| **E = 200 GPa** | **200,000 N/mm² (= 200,000 MPa)** |

> **The single most useful conversion in structural work: 1 GPa = 1000 N/mm², so steel's E = 200 GPa = 2 × 10⁵ N/mm².**

> **Sticking to N and mm throughout avoids every unit error in this class of problem**, because stress comes out in N/mm² (= MPa) and length in mm automatically.

**Why the distractors are placed as they are:**

| Option | Origin |
|---|---|
| **(a) 1.22 mm** | ✓ |
| **(b) 0.61 mm** | **Exactly half — from using L = 1 m, or halving the area error** |
| **(c) 2.44 mm** | **Exactly double — from L = 4 m or a factor-of-two slip in the area** |
| **(d) 0.31 mm** | **A quarter of the answer — from using the diameter squared without the π/4, or d = 50 mm** |

> **All three are factor-of-two errors, which is characteristic: the arithmetic is straightforward, and the errors available are all in the area or the length.**

> **The check: compute the STRESS first, as its own step.**

> **σ = P/A = 60,000/490.9 = 122.2 N/mm²**

> **Then δ = σL/E = 122.2 × 2000/200,000 = 1.222 mm** ✓

> **Splitting the calculation that way has a further benefit: the intermediate stress of 122 MPa can be judged for reasonableness.**

**Judging the result — is this bar working sensibly?**

| Check | Value | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| **Stress** | **122 MPa** | **Comfortable — Fe 415 steel yields at 415 MPa, so the utilisation is about 30 %** |
| **Strain** | **δ/L = 1.222/2000 = 6.11 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.061 %** | **Well within the elastic range** |
| **Yield strain of Fe 415** | **0.87 × 415/200,000 = 0.0018 = 0.18 %** | **The bar is at about a third of its yield strain** |

> **So the bar is elastic and lightly stressed, and Hooke's law applies — which is the assumption δ = PL/AE requires.**

> **That check matters because the formula is valid ONLY below the proportional limit.** Beyond yield, the extension is no longer proportional to the load and the calculation would be meaningless.

**The AXIAL STIFFNESS, which is the useful way to see the result:**

> **k = AE/L = 490.9 × 200,000/2000 = 49,090 N/mm ≈ 49 kN/mm**

> **So this bar extends about 1 mm for every 49 kN applied, and δ = P/k = 60/49 = 1.22 mm** ✓

> **Expressing a member as a SPRING of stiffness AE/L is the step that makes the whole of structural analysis systematic — it is the basis of the stiffness method and of every matrix analysis program.**

> **Note what the stiffness depends on: DIRECTLY on the area and the modulus, INVERSELY on the length.**

> **A longer member is more flexible; a thicker or stiffer one is stiffer.** Both are intuitive, and having them in one expression means the behaviour of a bar can be predicted without calculation.

**The related quantities, since a question can ask for any of them:**

| Quantity | Expression | Value here |
|---|---|---|
| **Stress** | **P/A** | **122.2 MPa** |
| **Strain** | **σ/E = δ/L** | **6.11 × 10⁻⁴** |
| **Elongation** | **PL/AE** | **1.222 mm** ← |
| **LATERAL strain** | **−μ × axial strain** | **−0.3 × 6.11×10⁻⁴ = −1.83 × 10⁻⁴** |
| **Change in DIAMETER** | **lateral strain × d** | **−1.83×10⁻⁴ × 25 = −0.0046 mm (a contraction)** |
| **STRAIN ENERGY stored** | **½ P δ = P²L/(2AE)** | **½ × 60,000 × 1.222 = 36.7 N·m = 36.7 J** |

> **The DIAMETER CHANGE is worth computing once: the bar gets 1.22 mm longer and 0.0046 mm thinner.**

> **The lateral contraction is tiny in absolute terms but it is real, and in a constrained situation it matters — a bolt tightened in a hole, a bar cast into concrete, or a member prevented from contracting laterally develops stresses from exactly this effect.**

> **And the STRAIN ENERGY of 36.7 J is the quantity that energy methods (Castigliano's theorems, virtual work) are built on** — the same deflection can be obtained by differentiating that energy with respect to the load, which is often the easier route in a complex structure.

examTip.trap: **All three distractors are factor-of-two or -four errors in the area or the length.** Split the calculation: σ = P/A = 122 MPa first, then δ = σL/E — which also lets the stress be judged for reasonableness.
examTip.mnemonic: **Treat the bar as a SPRING of stiffness AE/L = 49 kN/mm**, so δ = P/k. That view is the basis of the whole stiffness method. And δ = PL/AE holds ONLY below the proportional limit — check the strain is elastic.

questions.stem: For a material with a modulus of elasticity of 200 GPa and a modulus of rigidity of 80 GPa, Poisson's ratio is:
questions.solution:
**0.25.**

**The elastic constants relation:**

> **E = 2 G (1 + μ)**

> **200 = 2 × 80 × (1 + μ)**

> **200 = 160 (1 + μ)**

> **1 + μ = 1.25**

> **μ = 0.25** ✓

**The three relations among the four elastic constants:**

| Relation | Links |
|---|---|
| **E = 2 G (1 + μ)** | **E, G, μ** ← used here |
| **E = 3 K (1 − 2μ)** | **E, K (bulk modulus), μ** |
| **E = 9 K G / (3K + G)** | **E, K, G** |

> **An ISOTROPIC material has only TWO independent elastic constants, so any two of E, G, K and μ determine the other two.**

> **That is a genuinely important fact: it means a full elastic characterisation requires only two tests, and it is why a tension test (giving E and μ) is sufficient for most purposes.**

**The bulk modulus of this material, since the second relation gives it:**

> **K = E / [3(1 − 2μ)] = 200 / [3(1 − 0.5)] = 200/1.5 = 133.3 GPa**

> **Check with the third relation:  E = 9KG/(3K+G) = 9 × 133.3 × 80/(400 + 80) = 96,000/480 = 200 GPa** ✓

> **The three relations are consistent, which confirms the value of μ.** Cross-checking through a second relation is the reliable way to verify an elastic constant.

**Why μ = 0.25 is the value to expect for steel — and why 0.3 is also quoted:**

| Material | Poisson's ratio |
|---|---|
| **Cork** | **≈ 0 — it barely bulges when compressed** |
| **Concrete** | **0.10-0.20** |
| **CAST IRON** | **0.21-0.26** |
| **STEEL** | **0.27-0.30 (commonly taken as 0.3)** |
| **Aluminium** | **0.33** |
| **Copper, brass** | **0.34-0.35** |
| **RUBBER** | **≈ 0.4999 — very nearly incompressible** |
| **Clay (undrained)** | **0.5 — no volume change** |

> **The value 0.25 emerging here is what the given data require, and it is close to the cast iron range.**

> **Note that E = 200 GPa with G = 80 GPa gives μ = 0.25 exactly, whereas real steel with μ = 0.3 would have G = E/[2(1.3)] = 77 GPa.**

> **So the numbers in the stem are the tidy examination version of steel's properties, and recognising that is useful: G ≈ 0.4E is the practical relation for steel, since 1/[2(1+0.3)] = 0.385.**

**Why μ CANNOT exceed 0.5 — the physical limit:**

> **From  K = E/[3(1 − 2μ)]:**

> **As μ → 0.5, the denominator → 0 and K → INFINITY.**

> **An infinite bulk modulus means the material cannot change volume at all — it is INCOMPRESSIBLE.**

> **And for μ > 0.5, K would be NEGATIVE, meaning the material would EXPAND under hydrostatic compression — a physical impossibility for a stable material.**

> **So 0.5 is a hard upper bound, and option (a) 0.50 represents the limiting incompressible case rather than a real elastic solid.**

> **The lower bound for a stable isotropic material is −1, from the same kind of argument on G** — and materials with negative Poisson's ratio (auxetic materials, certain foams and lattices) do exist and get thicker when stretched, which is counter-intuitive but real.

**What Poisson's ratio physically IS:**

> **μ = − (lateral strain) / (axial strain)**

> **Stretch a bar and it gets THINNER; the ratio of the thinning to the stretching is μ.**

> **The minus sign in the definition makes μ positive for ordinary materials, since the two strains have opposite signs.**

> **For a bar under axial tension the volumetric strain is:**

> **ΔV/V = ε (1 − 2μ)**

> **With μ = 0.25, ΔV/V = 0.5 ε — so the bar's volume INCREASES by half the axial strain.**

> **At μ = 0.5 the volumetric strain would be zero: the bar would get exactly as much thinner as it got longer, conserving volume.**

> **Which is why undrained saturated clay is assigned μ = 0.5 — it cannot change volume without water leaving it, so within the undrained period it behaves as an incompressible elastic solid.**

> **That is a case where an idealised limiting value is the physically correct choice rather than an approximation**, and it is the basis of the elastic settlement formulae for immediate settlement on clay.

**Where μ matters in practice:**

| Application | Role of μ |
|---|---|
| **Lateral earth pressure AT REST** | **K₀ = μ/(1−μ) for an elastic soil** ← |
| **Immediate settlement of a footing on clay** | **The elastic formula contains (1 − μ²)** |
| **Stress distribution beneath a footing (Boussinesq)** | **Independent of μ for vertical stress — a convenient result** |
| **Thick cylinders and pressure vessels** | Hoop and radial strains are coupled through μ |
| **Plane stress against plane strain** | The distinction is expressed through μ |
| **Confined concrete** | Lateral expansion is what the confinement resists |

> **The CONFINED CONCRETE case deserves a note because it is the mechanism behind spiral reinforcement in columns.**

> **Concrete under axial compression tries to expand laterally by μ times the axial strain.**

> **A close spiral or closely spaced ties RESIST that expansion, putting the concrete into triaxial compression — in which state it is markedly stronger and much more ductile.**

> **So Poisson's ratio is the reason spiral reinforcement works at all**, and it is why a spirally reinforced column is credited with higher strength in the codes than a tied one.

examTip.trap: **Option (a) 0.50 is the physical UPPER LIMIT, not an answer** — at μ = 0.5 the bulk modulus becomes infinite and the material incompressible. Above it, K would be negative, which no stable material permits.
examTip.mnemonic: **An isotropic material has only TWO independent elastic constants**, so verify through a second relation: K = E/[3(1−2μ)] = 133.3 GPa, and 9KG/(3K+G) returns 200 GPa ✓. For steel in practice, G ≈ 0.4E.

questions.stem: The effective length of a column of actual length L with BOTH ENDS FIXED is:
questions.solution:
**0.5 L.**

**The four standard end conditions:**

| End condition | Effective length L_e | Euler load relative to hinged-hinged |
|---|---|---|
| **BOTH ENDS HINGED (pinned)** | **L** | **1 (the reference case)** |
| **BOTH ENDS FIXED** | **0.5 L** | **4** ← |
| **One end FIXED, one HINGED** | **0.707 L** | **2** |
| **One end FIXED, one FREE (a flagpole)** | **2 L** | **0.25** |

> **Note that all four values appear as options, so the end condition in the stem must be read carefully.**

**What EFFECTIVE LENGTH means — the idea that makes the table intelligible:**

> **The EFFECTIVE LENGTH is the length of an equivalent PIN-ENDED column that would buckle at the same load.**

> **Geometrically, it is the distance between successive POINTS OF ZERO MOMENT (points of inflection) in the buckled shape.**

> **For a column FIXED AT BOTH ENDS, the buckled shape has inflection points at the QUARTER POINTS, so the length between them is L/2** ✓

> **For a FIXED-FREE column, the buckled shape is half of a pin-ended column of length 2L — hence L_e = 2L.**

> **Sketching the buckled shape and looking for the inflection points recovers every value in the table without memorising it**, which is why the geometric definition is worth holding rather than the numbers.

**Why the Euler load scales as 1/L_e²:**

> **P_cr = π² E I / L_e²**

> **So fixing both ends of a column HALVES its effective length and hence QUADRUPLES its buckling load.**

> **And releasing one end entirely (fixed-free) DOUBLES the effective length and cuts the capacity to a QUARTER.**

> **The full range across the four cases is therefore 16 TO 1 — from fixed-fixed to fixed-free.**

> **That is an enormous range for a change that costs nothing but connection detailing, and it is why end restraint is one of the most economical things a designer can improve in a compression member.**

**The practical caution, which the code embodies:**

> **The theoretical values assume PERFECT restraint, and real connections are never perfect.**

> **A "fixed" end in a real frame provides partial restraint that depends on the stiffness of the members framing into it.**

> **IS 800 therefore gives more conservative values for design:**

| Condition | Theoretical L_e | IS 800 recommended L_e |
|---|---|---|
| **Both ends fixed (effectively held in position and restrained in direction)** | **0.5 L** | **0.65 L** ← |
| **Both ends held in position, one restrained in direction** | 0.707 L | **0.80 L** |
| **Both ends held in position, neither restrained** | **L** | **1.0 L** |
| **One end fixed, other free** | 2 L | **2.0 L** |

> **Note that the code's value of 0.65 L is deliberately larger than the theoretical 0.5 L, because no practical connection achieves full fixity.**

> **Claiming the theoretical value in a design would overstate the capacity, and the difference is not small: (0.65/0.5)² = 1.69, so the theoretical value would overstate the buckling load by nearly 70 per cent.**

> **That gap between theory and code is worth understanding rather than resenting: the theory tells you the mechanism, and the code tells you what to rely on.**

**The SLENDERNESS RATIO, which is what the effective length feeds into:**

> **λ = L_e / r**, where r = √(I/A) is the radius of gyration.

| Slenderness | Behaviour | Governing failure |
|---|---|---|
| **λ < 30-40** | **SHORT column** | **CRUSHING — the material's strength governs** |
| **λ = 40-120** | **INTERMEDIATE** | **A combination; the Rankine or Perry-Robertson formulae apply** |
| **λ > 120** | **LONG, SLENDER column** | **ELASTIC BUCKLING — Euler's formula applies** ← |

> **The critical insight about Euler's formula is that it contains E AND I BUT NOT THE YIELD STRENGTH.**

> **So a slender column's buckling load does NOT depend on the strength of its steel at all.**

> **Using high-strength steel for a slender column is therefore WASTED MONEY — it buckles at the same load as mild steel of the same section.**

> **That is a genuinely valuable conclusion: to strengthen a slender column, change its GEOMETRY (a larger or better-shaped section, or a shorter effective length by adding a brace), not its material.**

> **And adding an intermediate brace is the most effective intervention available: bracing a pin-ended column at midheight halves its effective length and quadruples its capacity, for the cost of one member.**

**Why the radius of gyration governs the SECTION SHAPE chosen:**

> **r = √(I/A), so for a given AREA of material, a section with a larger I has a larger r and a lower slenderness.**

> **Which means material placed FAR FROM THE CENTROID is what resists buckling.**

| Section | Efficiency in compression |
|---|---|
| **Hollow circular tube** | **The best — material uniformly far from the centroid, equal r about every axis** ← |
| **Hollow square (box)** | Very good |
| **Built-up section with plates spread apart** | Good, and adjustable |
| **I-section** | **Good about the major axis, POOR about the minor — buckling occurs about the WEAK axis** |
| **Solid circular or square** | **Poor — most material near the centroid** |

> **The I-section point is critical in practice: a column buckles about its WEAKEST axis, so the minimum radius of gyration governs, and an I-section used as a column is far less efficient than as a beam.**

> **That is why steel columns are so often hollow sections or built-up boxes rather than the I-sections used for beams** — and why an I-section column needs bracing about its minor axis if it is to be used at all.

examTip.trick: **Both ends fixed: L_e = 0.5 L.** The four values — L, 0.5L, 0.707L, 2L — all appear as options, so read the end condition carefully.
examTip.trap: **Sketch the buckled shape and find the INFLECTION POINTS** — the effective length is the distance between them. For fixed-fixed they are at the quarter points, giving L/2. That recovers every value without memorising.
examTip.mnemonic: **P_cr ∝ 1/L_e², so the four cases span 16 to 1.** Euler's formula contains E and I but NOT the yield strength — so high-strength steel is wasted on a slender column. Change the GEOMETRY or add a BRACE instead.

questions.stem: A rectangular section is 200 mm wide and 300 mm deep. Its section modulus about the horizontal centroidal axis is:
questions.solution:
**3.0 × 10⁶ mm³.**

**The section modulus:**

> **Z = I / y_max = (bd³/12) / (d/2) = b d² / 6**

**The computation:**

> **Z = 200 × 300² / 6 = 200 × 90,000 / 6 = 18,000,000/6 = 3.0 × 10⁶ mm³** ✓

> **The intermediate values are worth writing down: I = bd³/12 = 200 × 2.7×10⁷/12 = 4.5 × 10⁸ mm⁴, and y_max = 150 mm, so Z = 4.5×10⁸/150 = 3.0 × 10⁶ mm³** ✓

**What the section modulus is FOR:**

> **The flexure formula:  σ = M y / I**

> **The maximum stress occurs at the extreme fibre, y = y_max, so:**

> **σ_max = M / Z**

> **So Z is the single geometric property that converts a bending moment directly into the maximum stress — which is why it exists as a named quantity rather than being computed from I each time.**

> **And rearranged, it is the design equation: Z_required = M / σ_allowable.**

> **A designer with a moment and a permissible stress computes a required Z and picks a section from the tables** — which is exactly how steel beam sections are selected in practice.

**Why the depth matters so much more than the width:**

> **Z = bd²/6, so Z is proportional to b to the FIRST power and to d to the SECOND.**

| Change | Effect on Z |
|---|---|
| **DOUBLE the width** | **× 2** |
| **DOUBLE the depth** | **× 4** ← |

> **And for the moment of inertia the disparity is greater still: I = bd³/12, so doubling the depth multiplies I by EIGHT.**

> **Consider this section turned on its side — 300 mm wide and 200 mm deep:**

> **Z = 300 × 200²/6 = 300 × 40,000/6 = 2.0 × 10⁶ mm³**

> **That is option (b), and it is only TWO THIRDS of the correct value.**

> **So the SAME piece of timber or steel is 50 per cent stronger in bending when used with its long dimension VERTICAL.**

> **Which is why joists are laid on edge and never flat, and it is the most immediately practical consequence of the whole topic.**

> **Option (b) is therefore a well-made distractor: it is the section modulus about the OTHER axis, and a candidate who confuses b with d gets it.**

> **The defence is to identify which dimension is the DEPTH — the one in the plane of bending, measured parallel to the load — and square that one.**

**The other distractors:**

| Option | Origin |
|---|---|
| **(a) 1.0 × 10⁶** | **bd²/18, or a mis-set denominator** |
| **(b) 2.0 × 10⁶** | **The section modulus about the WEAK axis (b and d interchanged)** ← |
| **(c) 3.0 × 10⁶** | ✓ |
| **(d) 9.0 × 10⁶** | **bd²/2 — using y_max = d/6, or omitting the 3 in the denominator** |

**The standard section properties, since they are constantly needed:**

| Section | I about the centroidal axis | Z | y_max |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RECTANGLE b × d** | **b d³/12** | **b d²/6** | **d/2** |
| **Rectangle about its BASE** | **b d³/3** | — | — |
| **CIRCLE, diameter d** | **π d⁴/64** | **π d³/32** | **d/2** |
| **TRIANGLE, base b, height h** | **b h³/36** | — | **2h/3 from apex** |
| **Hollow circle, D and d** | **π(D⁴ − d⁴)/64** | **π(D⁴−d⁴)/(32D)** | **D/2** |

> **The distinction between bd³/12 (centroidal) and bd³/3 (about the base) is one of the commonest confusions**, and the parallel axis theorem connects them:

> **I_base = I_G + A h² = bd³/12 + bd × (d/2)² = bd³/12 + bd³/4 = bd³/3** ✓

> **Which is a factor of FOUR difference, so choosing the wrong one is a serious error.** The rule: unless the axis is stated otherwise, section properties are about the CENTROIDAL axis.

**Why an I-SECTION beats a rectangle — the point the section modulus makes:**

> **The bending stress varies LINEARLY from zero at the neutral axis to a maximum at the extreme fibre.**

> **So material near the neutral axis is doing almost nothing, while material at the extreme fibres carries the stress.**

> **An I-SECTION removes material from where it is idle (the middle) and concentrates it where it works (the flanges).**

> **The result is a far higher Z for the same weight of material** — which is the entire reason the I-section exists.

| Section, same area 60,000 mm² | Approximate Z |
|---|---|
| **Rectangle 200 × 300** | **3.0 × 10⁶ mm³** ← |
| **An I-section of the same area and 300 mm depth** | **Roughly 5-6 × 10⁶ mm³** |

> **Nearly double the strength for the same weight, from geometry alone.**

> **The web remains necessary, of course — it carries the SHEAR and holds the flanges apart — but it can be thin, and the material saved goes into the flanges.**

> **That trade is the origin of every rolled steel section in the tables, and it is worth being able to explain rather than merely to use.**

examTip.trick: **Z = bd²/6 = 200 × 90,000/6 = 3.0 × 10⁶ mm³.** The DEPTH is the dimension in the plane of bending, and it is the one that gets squared.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) 2.0 × 10⁶ is the section modulus about the OTHER axis** — b and d interchanged. The same member is 50 % stronger with its long dimension vertical, which is why joists are laid on edge.
examTip.mnemonic: **Z ∝ b but ∝ d²; I ∝ d³.** And unless stated otherwise, section properties are about the CENTROIDAL axis — bd³/12, not the bd³/3 about the base, a factor of four apart.

questions.stem: A plane truss has 11 members, 7 joints and 3 reaction components. Its degree of static indeterminacy is:
questions.solution:
**Zero — the truss is statically DETERMINATE.**

**The criterion for a plane truss:**

> **D_s = (m + r) − 2j**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **m** | **Number of MEMBERS** | **11** |
| **r** | **Number of REACTION components** | **3** |
| **j** | **Number of JOINTS** | **7** |

**The computation:**

> **D_s = (11 + 3) − 2 × 7 = 14 − 14 = 0** ✓

> **So the truss is JUST DETERMINATE — solvable by statics alone, with no redundant members.**

**Where the criterion comes from — the counting argument:**

> **UNKNOWNS: one axial force in each member (m), plus each reaction component (r), giving m + r unknowns.**

> **EQUATIONS: at each joint, the forces are concurrent, so only TWO equations of equilibrium apply — ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0. With j joints, that is 2j equations.**

> **Comparing them:**

| Result | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **m + r = 2j** | **DETERMINATE — as many equations as unknowns** ← |
| **m + r > 2j** | **INDETERMINATE by the excess; extra members or reactions are REDUNDANT** |
| **m + r < 2j** | **A MECHANISM (unstable) — not enough members to hold the shape** |

> **Note the crucial detail: only TWO equations per joint, not three.**

> **The moment equation ΣM = 0 is automatically satisfied at a truss joint because all the member forces pass THROUGH the joint and so have no moment about it.**

> **Using 3j instead of 2j is the commonest error in this calculation, and it makes every truss look like a mechanism.**

**The internal and external split, which the single number conceals:**

> **D_s = D_se + D_si**

| Component | Formula | Here |
|---|---|---|
| **EXTERNAL indeterminacy D_se** | **r − 3** (for a plane structure) | **3 − 3 = 0** |
| **INTERNAL indeterminacy D_si** | **m − (2j − 3)** | **11 − (14 − 3) = 11 − 11 = 0** |
| **TOTAL** | **Their sum** | **0** ✓ |

> **So this truss is determinate both externally and internally — the reactions can be found from the three overall equilibrium equations, and the member forces then follow joint by joint.**

> **Splitting the calculation this way is worth doing, because the two kinds of indeterminacy are dealt with quite differently:**

> **EXTERNAL indeterminacy means too many SUPPORTS — a truss on three rollers plus a pin, say — and it is resolved by considering support settlement or by choosing a redundant reaction.**

> **INTERNAL indeterminacy means too many MEMBERS — extra diagonals in a panel — and it is resolved by considering the compatibility of member deformations.**

> **A structure can be internally indeterminate and externally determinate, or the reverse, and knowing which tells you what kind of analysis is needed.**

**The PERFECT TRUSS relation, which is the same statement:**

> **For a plane truss on three reaction components, determinacy requires:**

> **m = 2j − 3**

> **Here: 2 × 7 − 3 = 11 = m** ✓

> **The −3 accounts for the three overall equilibrium equations that fix the truss's position in the plane rather than its member forces.**

> **And the relation has a neat physical reading: the simplest stable plane truss is a TRIANGLE (m = 3, j = 3, and 2×3 − 3 = 3 ✓), and every additional joint requires exactly TWO more members to fix its position.**

> **So a perfect truss can be built up from a triangle by adding joints two members at a time — which is the SIMPLE TRUSS construction, and it guarantees determinacy by the way it is assembled.**

**A caution the criterion does not cover — and it matters:**

> **SATISFYING THE COUNT DOES NOT GUARANTEE STABILITY.**

> **A truss can have m + r = 2j exactly and still be unstable, if the members are arranged badly.**

| Instance of the trap | Problem |
|---|---|
| **A panel with NO diagonal, while another panel has TWO** | **The count balances, but the undiagonalled panel is a mechanism that will rack** ← |
| **Three reactions all PARALLEL** | Cannot resist a force perpendicular to them |
| **Three reaction lines CONCURRENT at a point** | Cannot resist a moment about that point |
| **A joint where all members are COLLINEAR** | The joint can move perpendicular to them |

> **The first row is the classic case: move a diagonal from one panel to another and the arithmetic is unchanged while the truss becomes useless.**

> **So the count is a NECESSARY but not a SUFFICIENT condition, and the arrangement must also be inspected.**

> **That is an important general lesson about structural criteria: a formula tells you about the bookkeeping, and only a look at the structure tells you whether it works.**

**The space truss version, for completeness:**

> **For a SPACE truss:  D_s = (m + r) − 3j**, since each joint has THREE equations of concurrent-force equilibrium.

> **And the perfect space truss relation is m = 3j − 6**, the −6 being the six equations of overall equilibrium in three dimensions.

> **The simplest stable space truss is a TETRAHEDRON (m = 6, j = 4, and 3×4 − 6 = 6 ✓), and each additional joint needs THREE members** — the exact three-dimensional analogue of the triangle rule.

examTip.trick: **D_s = (m + r) − 2j = (11 + 3) − 14 = 0 — determinate.** Only TWO equations per joint, because all member forces pass through it and ΣM = 0 is automatic.
examTip.trap: **Using 3j instead of 2j makes every truss look like a mechanism** — the commonest error here. And check the split: D_se = r − 3 = 0, D_si = m − (2j − 3) = 0, which tells you what kind of analysis is needed.
examTip.mnemonic: **The count is NECESSARY but not SUFFICIENT.** Move a diagonal from one panel to another and the arithmetic is unchanged while the truss becomes a mechanism. Always look at the arrangement as well as the numbers.

questions.stem: A three-hinged parabolic arch of span 20 m and central rise 5 m carries a uniformly distributed load of 20 kN/m over its whole span. The horizontal thrust at each support is:
questions.solution:
**200 kN.**

**The standard result:**

> **H = w L² / (8 h)**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **w** | **UDL intensity** | **20 kN/m** |
| **L** | **Span** | **20 m** |
| **h** | **Central RISE** | **5 m** |

**The computation:**

> **H = 20 × 20² / (8 × 5) = 20 × 400/40 = 8000/40 = 200 kN** ✓

**The derivation, which takes three lines and explains the formula:**

> **By symmetry, each support carries a vertical reaction V = wL/2 = 20 × 20/2 = 200 kN.**

> **Take moments about the CROWN HINGE for the left half of the arch. A hinge transmits no moment, which is the extra equation that makes a three-hinged arch determinate.**

> **Forces on the left half, taken about the crown:**

| Force | Lever arm about the crown | Moment |
|---|---|---|
| **V = 200 kN at the left support** | **L/2 = 10 m** | **200 × 10 = 2000 kNm** |
| **H at the left support** | **h = 5 m** | **H × 5** |
| **The half of the UDL, 20 × 10 = 200 kN** | **Its centroid at L/4 = 5 m** | **200 × 5 = 1000 kNm** |

> **ΣM_crown = 0:  200 × 10 − H × 5 − 200 × 5 = 0**

> **2000 − 5H − 1000 = 0**

> **H = 1000/5 = 200 kN** ✓

> **Being able to derive it means the formula need not be trusted blindly — and the same method handles any loading, including unsymmetrical cases where no formula exists.**

**The key result about a parabolic arch under a UDL — worth knowing beyond the arithmetic:**

> **For a THREE-HINGED PARABOLIC arch carrying a UDL over its FULL span, the bending moment is ZERO EVERYWHERE.**

> **The arch carries the load in PURE COMPRESSION along its axis.**

> **The reason is that the parabola is exactly the FUNICULAR SHAPE for a uniform load — the shape a flexible cable would take under that load, inverted.**

> **A cable can carry only tension; inverted, the same shape carries only compression.**

> **So the parabolic arch under a UDL is the ideal case: no bending, no shear across the section, only axial thrust.**

> **That is why masonry arches, which cannot resist tension or bending, work at all — provided the load is close to what the shape was designed for.**

**And the corollary, which is the practical caution:**

> **If the load is NOT the one the shape suits, bending moments appear.**

| Loading on a parabolic arch | Result |
|---|---|
| **UDL over the FULL span** | **ZERO bending moment — pure axial thrust** ← |
| **UDL over HALF the span** | **Significant bending moment; the maximum occurs at about the quarter points** |
| **A single POINT load** | Substantial bending |
| **A UDL on a CIRCULAR arch** | Bending occurs — a circle is not the funicular shape for a UDL |

> **So the HALF-SPAN loading case is usually the governing design condition for an arch**, not the full load — which is counter-intuitive and is exactly the sort of thing that catches an unwary designer.

> **In a masonry arch bridge, an unsymmetrical live load (a vehicle on one half) is therefore more onerous than the same load spread over the whole span.**

> **Which is why the funicular ideal is a starting point rather than a design: a real arch must have enough section to carry the bending its non-ideal loadings produce.**

**The H ∝ 1/h relation, which governs the design choice:**

> **The thrust is INVERSELY proportional to the rise.**

| Rise h | H | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **10 m (rise/span = 1/2)** | **100 kN** | **A tall arch — low thrust** |
| **5 m (1/4)** | **200 kN** | ← this arch |
| **2.5 m (1/8)** | **400 kN** | **A flat arch — high thrust** |
| **1 m (1/20)** | **1000 kN** | Very flat — enormous thrust |

> **So a FLAT arch produces a very LARGE horizontal thrust, and a TALL one a small thrust.**

> **That is the central trade in arch design: a flat arch is elegant, uses less material in the rib and gives more headroom beneath, but it pushes the abutments apart very hard.**

> **And the abutments — or the ties, or the rock they bear on — must take that thrust. An arch on weak foundations is a poor idea, and a flat arch on weak foundations is a disaster.**

> **Note that options (b) 100 and (c) 400 are the answers for rises of 10 m and 2.5 m — so the option set punishes a misread rise.**

**Why an arch is used at all, since a beam would be simpler:**

> **A simply supported beam of the same span and load would carry M_max = wL²/8 = 20 × 400/8 = 1000 kNm.**

> **The parabolic three-hinged arch carries the same load with ZERO bending moment — at the price of a 200 kN horizontal thrust at each support.**

> **So the arch has TRADED BENDING FOR THRUST.**

> **That is a very favourable trade whenever the ground can supply the horizontal reaction, because a member in pure compression can be far lighter than one in bending — and materials like masonry and concrete are strong in compression and weak in tension.**

> **It is why arches and vaults were the only way to span significant distances before structural steel, and why the arch remains the natural form for a long-span bridge in a rock gorge** — a situation, incidentally, that Nepal supplies in abundance.

**The three-hinged against two-hinged and fixed arches:**

| Arch | Reactions | D_s | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| **THREE-HINGED** | 4 | **0 — DETERMINATE** | **Unaffected by settlement, temperature or shrinkage** ← |
| **TWO-HINGED** | 4 | **1** | Common in steel; needs the strain energy method |
| **FIXED** | 6 | **3** | Stiffest; most sensitive to settlement and temperature |

> **The three-hinged arch's insensitivity to support movement and temperature is its great practical advantage, and it follows directly from being determinate: a determinate structure develops NO stresses from imposed deformations.**

> **A fixed arch on ground that settles differentially, or in a climate of large temperature range, develops substantial secondary stresses that must be designed for.**

> **So the choice among the three is a judgement about the FOUNDATIONS and the ENVIRONMENT as much as about the loads** — which is a good illustration of why structural form is chosen before it is calculated.

examTip.trick: **H = wL²/(8h) = 20 × 400/40 = 200 kN.** Or derive it: take moments about the crown HINGE for one half — the hinge transmits no moment, which is what makes the arch determinate.
examTip.trap: **Options (b) 100 and (c) 400 are the answers for rises of 10 m and 2.5 m** — H is INVERSELY proportional to the rise, so a misread rise is a large error. A flat arch pushes its abutments apart very hard.
examTip.mnemonic: **A parabolic arch under a FULL-span UDL has ZERO bending moment** — the parabola is the funicular shape, so the load is carried in pure compression. But HALF-span loading produces real bending, and it usually governs the design.

questions.stem: The central deflection of a simply supported beam of span L carrying a central point load W is:
questions.solution:
**W L³ / (48 E I).**

**The standard deflection formulae, which must be kept distinct:**

| Beam and loading | Maximum deflection | Location |
|---|---|---|
| **Simply supported, CENTRAL POINT load W** | **W L³ / (48 E I)** ← | Midspan |
| **Simply supported, UDL w** | **5 w L⁴ / (384 E I)** | Midspan |
| **CANTILEVER, point load W at the free end** | **W L³ / (3 E I)** | Free end |
| **Cantilever, UDL w** | **w L⁴ / (8 E I)** | Free end |
| **Both ends FIXED, central point load W** | **W L³ / (192 E I)** | Midspan |
| **Both ends fixed, UDL w** | **w L⁴ / (384 E I)** | Midspan |
| **Propped cantilever, UDL w** | **w L⁴ / (185 E I)** | Near 0.4L from the prop |

> **Every one of the distractors in this question is a genuine formula from that table applied to the wrong case, which is what makes the option set well formed:**

> **Option (a) WL³/3EI is the CANTILEVER with an end point load.**

> **Option (c) 5wL⁴/384EI is the simply supported beam with a UDL.**

> **Option (d) WL³/192EI is the FIXED-ENDED beam with a central point load.**

**How to tell them apart WITHOUT memorising — two reliable checks:**

> **FIRST — the POWER OF L tells you the load type.**

| Load | Power of L | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **A POINT load W (a force)** | **L³** | **W already has force units, so L³ is needed to balance EI** |
| **A UDL w (force per length)** | **L⁴** | **w carries a 1/length, so an extra L is needed** |

> **That is a DIMENSIONAL argument, and it is decisive: a formula with a point load and L⁴, or a UDL and L³, is simply wrong.**

> **It eliminates option (c) immediately, since the stem gives a point load W.**

> **SECOND — the DENOMINATOR tells you the restraint, and the bigger it is, the stiffer the beam.**

| Denominator (point load) | Beam | Relative deflection |
|---|---|---|
| **3** | **CANTILEVER — the most flexible** | **64 × the fixed case** |
| **48** | **Simply supported** | **4 × the fixed case** |
| **192** | **FIXED both ends — the stiffest** | **1** |

> **The ordering follows physical sense: more restraint means less deflection, so a larger denominator.**

> **And the ratios are worth noting: a cantilever deflects 16 TIMES as much as a simply supported beam of the same span and load, and 64 times as much as a fixed-ended one.**

> **So between the two checks — the power of L and the size of the denominator — the correct formula can be identified without recall.**

**Where the 48 comes from, for those who want it:**

> **By double integration, or by the moment-area method, the midspan deflection of a simply supported beam under a central point load is:**

> **δ = (1/EI) × [area of the M/EI diagram] × [distance to its centroid]**

> **The bending moment diagram is a triangle with peak WL/4 at midspan.**

> **Taking the left half: area = ½ × (L/2) × (WL/4) = WL²/16, with its centroid at (2/3)(L/2) = L/3 from the support.**

> **Deflection at midspan = (WL²/16)(L/3)/EI = WL³/(48 EI)** ✓

> **The moment-area method is worth knowing precisely because it turns a differential equation into the geometry of a diagram**, and for a case like this it is quicker than integration.

**Why deflection matters as much as strength — and often more:**

> **A beam has to satisfy TWO independent requirements, and either may govern:**

| Limit state | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **STRENGTH (limit state of collapse)** | **The section must resist the moment and shear** |
| **SERVICEABILITY (deflection)** | **The deflection must be within a limit the building can tolerate** ← |

> **IS 456's deflection limits:**

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| **Total deflection, including creep and shrinkage** | **span/250** |
| **Deflection after partitions and finishes are erected** | **span/350 or 20 mm, whichever is LESS** |

> **The second limit is the one that catches designers, and the reason is worth understanding.**

> **A beam may deflect a good deal while the structure is being built, and that deflection does no harm — the finishes have not been applied yet.**

> **But deflection occurring AFTERWARD cracks the plaster, jams the doors and breaks the glazing.**

> **And much of a concrete beam's deflection occurs LATE, through CREEP, which continues for years.**

> **So the governing check is on the long-term deflection increment, not the immediate one** — which is why IS 456 requires creep and shrinkage to be included and why the span/depth ratio rules exist as a simple way of satisfying it.

**The span/depth check, since it is how deflection is usually controlled in practice:**

| Beam | Basic span/effective depth ratio |
|---|---|
| **CANTILEVER** | **7** |
| **Simply supported** | **20** |
| **Continuous** | **26** |

> **Satisfying that ratio, with the code's modification factors for tension steel, compression steel and flanged sections, is deemed to satisfy the deflection requirement without a calculation.**

> **And the ordering — 7, 20, 26 — is the same physical ordering as the deflection formulae: the more restraint, the stiffer, the slenderer the beam may be.**

> **So the two topics are the same idea expressed twice, once as a formula for analysis and once as a ratio for design.**

examTip.trick: **Simply supported, central point load: δ = WL³/(48EI).** Every distractor is a real formula for a different case — cantilever (3), UDL (5wL⁴/384), fixed ends (192).
examTip.trap: **Check the POWER OF L: a point load gives L³, a UDL gives L⁴** — a dimensional argument that eliminates option (c) at once. Then the DENOMINATOR ranks the restraint: 3 cantilever, 48 simply supported, 192 fixed.
examTip.mnemonic: **A cantilever deflects 16× a simply supported beam and 64× a fixed-ended one**, same span and load. And deflection often governs, not strength — especially the increment AFTER finishes are erected (span/350 or 20 mm), because concrete creep continues for years.

questions.stem: A propped cantilever of span 8 m carries a uniformly distributed load of 16 kN/m over its whole length. The reaction at the simply supported (propped) end is:
questions.solution:
**48 kN.**

**The standard result:**

> **R_prop = 3 w L / 8**

> **= 3 × 16 × 8 / 8 = 48 kN** ✓

**The complete set of results for this classic case:**

| Quantity | Expression | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Total load** | **w L** | **128 kN** |
| **Reaction at the PROP** | **3wL/8** | **48 kN** ← |
| **Reaction at the FIXED end** | **5wL/8** | **80 kN** |
| **Fixing MOMENT at the built-in end** | **wL²/8** | **128 kNm** |
| **Maximum POSITIVE (sagging) moment** | **9wL²/128, at 3L/8 from the prop** | **72 kNm at 3 m** |
| **Point of CONTRAFLEXURE** | **at L/4 from the fixed end** | **2 m from the fixed end** |
| **Maximum deflection** | **wL⁴/(185 EI), near 0.42L from the prop** | — |

> **The two reactions sum to 128 kN ✓ — which is the check to make first, since 3/8 + 5/8 = 1.**

> **Note that option (a) 64 kN is HALF the total load — the answer if the beam were simply supported at both ends — and option (d) 96 kN has no clean derivation but sits close to the fixed-end reaction.**

> **Option (b) 32 kN is wL/4.**

**Why the propped end carries LESS than half — the physical reading:**

> **A simply supported beam would put 64 kN on each support.**

> **The propped cantilever's FIXED end is STIFFER than a simple support: it resists rotation as well as translation.**

> **A stiffer support attracts more load.**

> **So the fixed end takes 80 kN (five eighths) and the prop only 48 kN (three eighths).**

> **The general principle behind that — LOAD FLOWS TO STIFFNESS — is the single most useful idea in indeterminate structural analysis, and it is worth stating explicitly:**

> **In an indeterminate structure, the distribution of forces depends on the RELATIVE STIFFNESSES of the members and supports, not on their strengths.**

> **Which has a consequence that surprises people: making one part of a structure stiffer attracts MORE load to it, not less.**

> **A designer who stiffens a member hoping to relieve it achieves the opposite.**

**How the result is obtained — the compatibility method, in three steps:**

> **The propped cantilever has 4 unknown reaction components (3 at the fixed end, 1 at the prop) and 3 equations of equilibrium, so D_s = 1: ONE redundant.**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **REMOVE the redundant — take away the prop, leaving a plain cantilever** |
| **2** | **Compute the deflection at the prop position under the load: δ₁ = wL⁴/(8EI) downward** |
| **3** | **Compute the deflection there due to a unit upward force: δ₂ = L³/(3EI) per unit force** |
| **4** | **Apply COMPATIBILITY — the real deflection at the prop is ZERO: R × L³/(3EI) = wL⁴/(8EI)** |
| **5** | **Solve:  R = 3wL/8** ✓ |

> **That is the whole method of consistent deformation, and this is its cleanest example.**

> **The essential idea: an indeterminate structure needs an extra condition beyond equilibrium, and the extra condition is always a statement about DEFORMATION — here, that the prop does not move.**

> **Equilibrium alone cannot distinguish between the possible distributions; compatibility selects the right one.**

**Why the propped cantilever is the useful case to know:**

> **It is the SIMPLEST indeterminate beam, so it appears constantly — and it also describes several real situations:**

| Real situation | Why it is a propped cantilever |
|---|---|
| **An END SPAN of a continuous beam** | **Fixed (by continuity) at the interior support, simply supported at the wall** ← |
| **A cantilever retaining wall stem with a base slab and a prop** | — |
| **A sheet pile wall with a single anchor** | Fixed in the soil below, propped by the anchor |
| **A beam built into a wall at one end and resting on a column at the other** | Directly |
| **A slab spanning between a fixed and a free edge** | The one-way equivalent |

> **The END SPAN case is the most frequent, and it explains why the propped cantilever's coefficients appear in the moment coefficient tables for continuous beams.**

**Comparing the three UDL cases, since the comparison is instructive:**

| Beam | Max moment | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Simply supported** | **wL²/8 = 128 kNm** | **Midspan (sagging)** |
| **PROPPED CANTILEVER** | **wL²/8 = 128 kNm** | **At the FIXED END (hogging)** ← |
| **Fixed both ends** | **wL²/12 = 85 kNm** | At the supports (hogging) |

> **The striking result is that the propped cantilever has the SAME maximum moment as the simply supported beam — wL²/8 — but at the FIXED END and HOGGING rather than at midspan and sagging.**

> **So propping does not reduce the peak moment at all; it MOVES it and changes its sign.**

> **What propping DOES improve substantially is the DEFLECTION: wL⁴/185EI against 5wL⁴/384EI = wL⁴/76.8EI — a reduction of about 60 per cent.**

> **And FIXING BOTH ENDS is what reduces the moment, to wL²/12.**
