> **In a looped system, water circulates past every point on its way to somewhere else, so the residual is maintained without deliberate flushing.**

> **That is the strongest argument for looping and it is a WATER QUALITY argument rather than a hydraulic one, which is often overlooked.**

**Why the reliability is poor — the single point of failure:**

> **If a main bursts, or must be shut for a repair or a new connection, EVERY consumer downstream of the break loses supply.**

> **There is no alternative route, because there is only one route.**

> **In a looped system the same break is isolated between two valves, and water reaches the affected area the other way round the loop — with reduced pressure, but supplied.**

> **So the choice between layouts is a choice about what happens on a bad day, and the dead end system's economy is bought entirely at the expense of that day.**

**Why the dead end system is nevertheless used:**

> **It is the CHEAPEST layout by a considerable margin: less pipe, fewer valves, and simple hydraulic design.**

> **And its hydraulic calculation is TRIVIAL — the discharge in each pipe is simply the sum of the demands beyond it, determined by inspection with no iteration at all.**

> **A looped network, by contrast, is INDETERMINATE: the flow divides between the routes according to their relative resistances, and the analysis requires iteration.**

| Layout | Analysis |
|---|---|
| **DEAD END** | **Determinate — flows found by inspection** ← |
| **LOOPED (grid iron, ring)** | **INDETERMINATE — requires HARDY CROSS or a matrix method** |

> **So the dead end system suits a small town, a growing settlement where the eventual layout is unknown, or a hill village along a road** — and Nepal's hill topography frequently makes it the only practicable arrangement, since settlements are strung along ridges and valleys rather than laid out on a grid.

> **The honest conclusion: the dead end system is the right answer where the town's shape or budget forbids looping, and the operational cost is the flushing programme it requires.**

**HARDY CROSS analysis, since looped networks need it:**

> **The method balances the flows in each loop iteratively:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **ASSUME a flow distribution satisfying continuity at every junction** |
| **2** | **Compute the head loss round each loop; for a balanced network the algebraic sum must be ZERO** |
| **3** | **Compute the correction  ΔQ = −Σh_f / (n Σ(h_f/Q))**, with n = 2 for Darcy-Weisbach, 1.85 for Hazen-Williams |
| **4** | **APPLY the correction to every pipe in the loop and repeat until the sums are acceptably small** |

> **The two conditions the method enforces are exactly the two conservation laws:**

> **CONTINUITY at each junction — inflow equals outflow. (Kirchhoff's current law.)**

> **ZERO HEAD LOSS round each closed loop — the head at a point is unique. (Kirchhoff's voltage law.)**

> **Note that step 1 requires continuity to be satisfied from the start and step 3 preserves it, since the same correction is applied to every pipe in the loop.**

> **So the iteration is entirely about satisfying the SECOND condition, and that is what makes the method converge reliably.**

> **In practice the analysis is done by software (EPANET being the standard free tool), but the Hardy Cross procedure remains worth understanding because it makes clear WHAT the software is solving** — and because a hand check of one loop is the best way to detect a badly built model.

examTip.trick: **The DEAD END system is the only one of the four with a SINGLE path to each consumer** — which produces both defects at once: stagnation at every branch end and total loss of supply downstream of any break.
examTip.trap: **The strongest argument for looping is WATER QUALITY, not hydraulics:** in a dead end the chlorine residual decays away exactly at the furthest points, and the remedy is a permanent flushing programme.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dead end networks are DETERMINATE — flows found by inspection; looped networks are INDETERMINATE and need HARDY CROSS.** That method enforces continuity at junctions and zero head loss round each loop — Kirchhoff's two laws applied to water.

questions.stem: The balancing storage of a service reservoir is usually taken as approximately what fraction of the maximum daily demand?
questions.solution:
**About ONE THIRD of the maximum daily demand.**

**The three components of a service reservoir's capacity:**

| Component | Purpose | Typical provision |
|---|---|---|
| **BALANCING (equalising) storage** | **Absorb the difference between the steady inflow and the varying hourly demand** | **About one third of the maximum daily demand** ← |
| **BREAKDOWN storage** | **Maintain supply while a pump, main or plant unit is out of service** | **1.5 to 2 hours of maximum daily demand, or up to 25 % of it** |
| **FIRE storage** | **Reserve for fire fighting** | **From the fire demand formula, commonly 1 to 4 hours of fire flow** |

> **The three are added, and the total commonly comes to something between one third and one half of the maximum daily demand.**

> **The BALANCING component alone is the one asked for here, and one third is the usual figure — though it should be determined from a MASS CURVE analysis for any particular town rather than assumed.**

**How the balancing storage is actually determined — the mass curve:**

> **The correct method is graphical or tabular, and the principle is simple:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Plot the CUMULATIVE DEMAND against time over 24 hours, from the town's hourly demand pattern** |
| **2** | **Plot the CUMULATIVE SUPPLY as a straight line (steady pumping) over the pumping hours** |
| **3** | **Measure the MAXIMUM VERTICAL ORDINATE between the two curves on each side** |
| **4** | **The required storage is the SUM of the maximum surplus and the maximum deficit** ← |

> **Step 4 is the one that is easy to get wrong: the storage must accommodate BOTH the largest accumulated excess of supply over demand AND the largest accumulated deficit.**

> **Taking only the deficit would leave nowhere to put the night-time surplus; taking only the surplus would run the tank dry in the morning peak.**

> **So the two are added, and the result is the balancing storage.**

> **For a typical urban demand pattern with 24-hour pumping the answer comes out at roughly one third of the daily demand — which is where the rule of thumb originates.**

**Why the PUMPING HOURS change the answer so much:**

| Pumping regime | Balancing storage required |
|---|---|
| **24-hour steady pumping** | **About 25-35 % of the daily demand** ← |
| **Pumping for 16 hours** | **Around 40-45 %** |
| **Pumping for 8 hours only (off-peak electricity)** | **Can exceed 60-70 %** |

> **The relation is intuitive: the SHORTER the pumping period, the MORE storage is needed, because the tank must hold enough to cover the hours when nothing is being pumped in.**

> **And that produces a real economic trade-off worth stating:**

> **PUMPING ONLY AT NIGHT uses cheap off-peak electricity and permits smaller pumps to run at full load, but it requires a much larger and more expensive reservoir.**

> **CONTINUOUS PUMPING needs the least storage but the largest total pump capacity and pays peak electricity rates.**

> **The optimum depends on the local tariff structure and on the cost of storage, and it is a genuine design decision rather than a matter of convention.**

**Why a service reservoir is provided at all — the four functions:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **EQUALISE supply and demand** | **The primary function — lets the plant run steadily while consumption varies** ← |
| **Provide RESERVE against breakdown** | Supply continues while a repair is made |
| **Maintain PRESSURE in the distribution system** | **An elevated reservoir sets the hydraulic grade line** |
| **Reduce the size of the treatment plant, pumps and rising main** | **Sized for 1.8 × average rather than 2.7 ×** |

> **The PRESSURE function is the one that determines the reservoir's LEVEL rather than its volume, and it is subject to its own criteria:**

| Requirement | Value |
|---|---|
| **Minimum residual pressure at the consumer's ferrule** | **7 m of water for single-storey, 12 m for two-storey, 17 m for three-storey** |
| **Maximum pressure in the mains** | **Around 70 m — above that, leakage and fitting failures multiply** |

> **The maximum limit is as important as the minimum and is more often neglected: leakage from a given hole increases with the square root of the pressure, and the number of pipe and fitting failures rises steeply with it.**

> **So excessive pressure in the lower parts of a hilly distribution zone is a direct cause of water loss — and PRESSURE-REDUCING VALVES or ZONING by contour are the remedy.**

> **In a hill town such as those throughout Nepal, that zoning is not optional: a single reservoir serving a 100 m fall in ground level would give either no pressure at the top or 100 m of pressure at the bottom.**

**The reservoir's other design features, briefly:**

| Feature | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Two or more COMPARTMENTS** | **So one can be cleaned or repaired while the other remains in service** ← |
| **Inlet and outlet at OPPOSITE ends** | **To promote circulation and avoid short-circuiting and dead zones** |
| **Floor sloped to a sump with a washout** | For cleaning |
| **Ventilation, screened against insects and birds** | Air movement without contamination |
| **Overflow and scour arrangements** | Safety against overfilling |
| **Access covers, locked** | Security against contamination |

> **The two-compartment requirement is the one most often economised away and most regretted: a single-compartment reservoir cannot be cleaned without shutting off the town, so in practice it never gets cleaned.**

> **And the INLET AND OUTLET AT OPPOSITE ENDS detail is the same water-quality principle as looping the network: water must be made to move through the whole volume, or part of it stagnates and the chlorine residual is lost there.**

examTip.trick: **Balancing storage ≈ ONE THIRD of the maximum daily demand**, with breakdown storage (1.5-2 hours) and fire storage added on top.
examTip.trap: **The mass curve requires the maximum SURPLUS and the maximum DEFICIT to be ADDED** — taking only one leaves nowhere to put the night surplus, or runs the tank dry in the morning peak.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shorter pumping hours need MORE storage** — 8-hour off-peak pumping can need 60-70 % of the daily demand against 30 % for continuous. That is the real trade: cheap electricity against an expensive tank.

questions.stem: In a conventional surface water treatment plant, the unit process that immediately FOLLOWS filtration is:
questions.solution:
**DISINFECTION.**

**The conventional treatment train, in order:**

| Order | Unit process | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **SCREENING** | **Remove floating debris, leaves and large solids** |
| **2** | **AERATION (where needed)** | **Remove taste, odour, CO₂; oxidise iron and manganese** |
| **3** | **PLAIN SEDIMENTATION (grit removal)** | **Settle the coarse, readily settleable silt** |
| **4** | **COAGULATION** | **Add alum or another coagulant; destabilise the colloidal particles** |
| **5** | **FLOCCULATION** | **Gentle stirring to grow the destabilised particles into settleable FLOC** |
| **6** | **SEDIMENTATION (clarification)** | **Settle out the floc — removes most of the turbidity** |
| **7** | **FILTRATION** | **Remove the residual floc and fine particles — the final polishing** |
| **8** | **DISINFECTION** | **Kill the remaining pathogens and leave a protective residual** ← |
| **9** | **(Optional) fluoridation, pH correction, softening** | As required |

> **So disinfection is the LAST step, and there are two independent reasons for it.**

**Why disinfection must come LAST — the two reasons:**

> **FIRST — TURBIDITY SHIELDS PATHOGENS.**

> **Particles protect bacteria and viruses from chlorine and from UV light. Disinfecting turbid water is unreliable, however much chlorine is added.**

> **So the water must be clarified and filtered FIRST, so that the disinfectant can actually reach the organisms.**

> **SECOND — THE RESIDUAL MUST SURVIVE INTO THE DISTRIBUTION SYSTEM.**

> **Chlorine is added not only to kill what is in the water at the plant but to leave a RESIDUAL of 0.1 to 0.2 mg/L that continues to protect the water all the way to the consumer's tap.**

> **Any subsequent treatment process would consume that residual: a filter would strip it, and the whole protective purpose would be defeated.**

> **So disinfection is placed last because it is the only process whose product must reach the consumer unaltered.**

> **Options (a), (b) and (d) all name processes that come BEFORE filtration, which is what makes them wrong** — and their ordering among themselves is the other half of this topic.

**COAGULATION and FLOCCULATION — the pair most often confused:**

| | **COAGULATION** | **FLOCCULATION** |
|---|---|---|
| **What happens** | **The colloidal particles' surface CHARGE is neutralised, destabilising them** | **The destabilised particles COLLIDE and grow into large floc** |
| **Mechanism** | **CHEMICAL — a coagulant is added** | **PHYSICAL — gentle mixing brings particles together** |
| **Mixing** | **RAPID, violent, brief (30-60 seconds)** | **SLOW, gentle, prolonged (20-40 minutes)** |
| **Why that mixing** | **To disperse the coagulant through the whole volume before it is consumed locally** | **Fast mixing would TEAR the fragile floc apart** ← |

> **The mixing intensities are OPPOSITE, and that is the practical heart of the distinction.**

> **The velocity gradient G is the design parameter: around 300-1000 s⁻¹ for rapid mixing, and only 10-75 s⁻¹ for flocculation.**

> **A flocculator run too fast produces small, weak floc that will not settle; run too slow, the particles never meet.**

> **So flocculation is a genuinely delicate process and the commonest cause of poor clarifier performance is a flocculator that is mixing too vigorously.**

**Why colloids need coagulation at all — the physical reason:**

> **Colloidal clay particles carry a NEGATIVE surface charge, so they REPEL one another and never collide.**

> **And they are so small (0.001 to 1 μm) that Brownian motion keeps them suspended indefinitely — their settling velocity under gravity is negligible.**

> **Plain sedimentation would take weeks to remove them.**

> **ALUM (aluminium sulphate) supplies trivalent Al³⁺ ions, which compress the repulsive double layer around each particle and let them approach; the hydrolysed aluminium hydroxide also forms a sticky floc that ENMESHES particles as it settles.**

> **So coagulation converts an unsettleable colloid into a settleable floc, and the two subsequent processes — flocculation and sedimentation — grow it and remove it.**

> **The alum reaction also produces acid, which consumes ALKALINITY and lowers the pH:**

> **Al₂(SO₄)₃·18H₂O + 3Ca(HCO₃)₂ → 2Al(OH)₃ + 3CaSO₄ + 6CO₂ + 18H₂O**

> **Which is why a water of low natural alkalinity needs LIME or SODA ASH added with the alum, and why the optimum pH for alum coagulation (about 6.5 to 8.5, with the best floc around 7) must be maintained.**

> **A JAR TEST — coagulating several samples at different doses and pH values and comparing the settled turbidity — is how the dose is determined, and it must be repeated as the raw water changes.**

**FILTRATION — what it actually does:**

| Removal mechanism | Note |
|---|---|
| **STRAINING** | The obvious one, and the least important for fine particles |
| **SEDIMENTATION within the pores** | Particles settle onto the grain surfaces |
| **ADSORPTION and adhesion to the grains** | **The principal mechanism for particles far smaller than the pores** ← |
| **Biological action (in slow sand filters)** | **The SCHMUTZDECKE — a biological mat that removes organisms actively** |

> **The point worth understanding is that a rapid sand filter with 0.5 mm sand has pores far larger than the particles it removes, so it does NOT work by straining.**

> **It works by particles adhering to the grain surfaces as the water threads past them — which is why a filter's performance depends on the coagulation upstream: uncoagulated particles do not adhere and pass straight through.**

> **So filtration cannot be considered independently of coagulation, and a plant with a poorly dosed coagulant produces poor filtered water however good the filters are.**

| | **SLOW sand filter** | **RAPID sand filter** |
|---|---|---|
| **Rate** | **100-200 L/m²/h** | **4000-5000 L/m²/h** — some 30 times faster |
| **Pre-treatment** | **None needed** | **Coagulation and sedimentation essential** |
| **Cleaning** | **Scrape the top 20-25 mm by hand, every 1-3 months** | **BACKWASH, every 24-48 hours** |
| **Bacterial removal** | **98-99 % — excellent, biological** | **80-90 % — relies on subsequent disinfection** |
| **Land required** | **LARGE** | Small |
| **Suits** | **Small towns, low turbidity, low skill availability** ← | **Cities, variable raw water** |

> **The slow sand filter deserves respect rather than dismissal: it needs no chemicals, no power, no skilled operator and no backwash system, and it removes bacteria better than a rapid filter does.**

> **For a Nepali hill town with a reasonably clear spring source and no reliable electricity, it is frequently the correct choice** — and its limitation is land and its intolerance of high turbidity, not its performance.

examTip.trick: **Screening → aeration → plain sedimentation → coagulation → flocculation → sedimentation → FILTRATION → DISINFECTION.** All three distractors come before filtration.
examTip.trap: **Disinfection is last for TWO reasons: turbidity shields pathogens from chlorine, and the RESIDUAL must survive into the mains.** Any later process would strip the residual and defeat its purpose.
examTip.mnemonic: **Coagulation is CHEMICAL with RAPID mixing (G ≈ 300-1000 s⁻¹); flocculation is PHYSICAL with GENTLE mixing (G ≈ 10-75 s⁻¹)** — opposite intensities, because fast mixing tears the fragile floc apart. That is the commonest cause of poor clarifier performance.

questions.stem: The minimum free residual chlorine that should be maintained at the consumer's tap is about:
questions.solution:
**About 0.2 mg/L.**

**The residual chlorine requirements:**

| Location and condition | Free residual chlorine |
|---|---|
| **At the CONSUMER'S TAP, normal conditions** | **0.2 mg/L** ← |
| **At the far end of the distribution system, minimum** | **0.1 mg/L** |
| **After 30 minutes' contact at the plant** | **0.5 mg/L** |
| **During an EPIDEMIC or after a contamination event** | **1.0 mg/L or more** |
| **Taste threshold for most consumers** | **Around 0.3-0.5 mg/L, and lower for some** |

> **So 0.2 mg/L at the tap is the working target, and the constraint at the upper end is TASTE, not toxicity.**

> **Option (c) 0.1 mg/L is the absolute minimum at the extremity of the network, so it is a real value from the same range — which makes it the designed distractor.**

**Why a RESIDUAL is maintained at all — the crucial concept:**

> **Chlorine is added for TWO distinct purposes, and the second is the one this question is about:**

| Purpose | Where it acts |
|---|---|
| **PRIMARY DISINFECTION** | **At the plant — kill the pathogens present in the filtered water** |
| **A PROTECTIVE RESIDUAL** | **Throughout the distribution system — guard against contamination entering downstream of the plant** ← |

> **The second purpose is what distinguishes chlorine from most alternatives and is the main reason it remains dominant worldwide.**

> **A distribution system is not sterile and not sealed: mains leak, pressures fluctuate, repairs are made, cross-connections occur, and every one of those events can admit contamination.**

> **A residual disinfectant in the water provides a continuing barrier against exactly those events, and it also serves as an INDICATOR: a sudden loss of residual is evidence that something has entered the main.**

> **So the residual is both a protection and a monitoring tool, and losing it is a loss of both.**

**The FREE and COMBINED distinction — which the word "free" in the stem signals:**

> **Chlorine added to water forms HYPOCHLOROUS ACID:**

> **Cl₂ + H₂O → HOCl + HCl**

> **HOCl ⇌ H⁺ + OCl⁻**

| Form | Name | Disinfecting power |
|---|---|---|
| **HOCl (hypochlorous acid)** | **FREE available chlorine** | **The most powerful form — about 80 times stronger than OCl⁻** ← |
| **OCl⁻ (hypochlorite ion)** | Free available chlorine | **Much weaker** |
| **Chloramines (NH₂Cl etc.)** | **COMBINED available chlorine** | **Weak — about 1/25 of HOCl — but PERSISTENT** |

> **The balance between HOCl and OCl⁻ depends on pH, and this is the single most important operational fact about chlorination:**

| pH | Proportion as HOCl |
|---|---|
| **6.0** | **97 %** |
| **7.0** | **75 %** |
| **7.5** | **50 %** |
| **8.0** | **25 %** |
| **9.0** | **3 %** |

> **So chlorination is FAR MORE EFFECTIVE AT LOW pH.**

> **A water at pH 8.5 needs several times the contact time or dose of the same water at pH 7 for the same kill, because most of the chlorine is present as the weak hypochlorite ion.**

> **That is why pH control is part of disinfection practice and not merely a separate quality parameter, and why adding lime for corrosion control can inadvertently impair disinfection if it is done before rather than after chlorination.**

**CHLORAMINES and the BREAKPOINT curve, since "free" residual implies going past it:**

> **If AMMONIA is present in the water, chlorine reacts with it in preference to acting as a free residual:**

| Stage of the breakpoint curve | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1. Initial dose** | **Chlorine is consumed by reducing agents (Fe²⁺, Mn²⁺, H₂S, organics) — NO residual appears** |
| **2. Rising limb** | **Chloramines form; the COMBINED residual rises with dose** |
| **3. Falling limb** | **Further chlorine DESTROYS the chloramines — the residual FALLS as more is added** ← the counter-intuitive part |
| **4. The BREAKPOINT** | **The minimum — all ammonia has been oxidised** |
| **5. Beyond the breakpoint** | **FREE available chlorine appears and rises linearly with dose** |

> **The falling limb is the feature that surprises: adding MORE chlorine REDUCES the measured residual, over a range of doses.**

> **An operator who responds to a low residual by increasing the dose slightly may make it lower still, which is a real and documented operational trap.**

> **The remedy is to dose PAST the breakpoint decisively — SUPER-CHLORINATION — so that a free residual is established.**

> **Which is what "free residual chlorine" in a specification means: the plant must be dosing beyond the breakpoint.**

**The other chlorination practices, since the terminology recurs:**

| Practice | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **PLAIN chlorination** | **Chlorine as the ONLY treatment — for a clear, protected source** |
| **PRE-chlorination** | **Before the other treatment units — controls algae and helps coagulation** |
| **POST-chlorination** | **After filtration — the normal practice** ← |
| **DOUBLE chlorination** | Both pre and post |
| **SUPER-chlorination** | **A large dose to get past the breakpoint or to deal with heavy contamination** |
| **DE-chlorination** | **Removing the excess afterward (SO₂, sodium thiosulphate, activated carbon) where the taste would be objectionable** |
| **BREAK-POINT chlorination** | Dosing exactly past the breakpoint |

> **The disinfection efficacy is governed by the CT VALUE — the product of concentration and contact time — so a lower dose with longer contact can achieve the same kill as a higher dose briefly.**

> **That is why a contact tank or a length of main between the dosing point and the first consumer is part of the design, and why a plant that doses at the outlet of the clear water tank achieves far better disinfection than one dosing into the rising main.**

**And the honest limitation of chlorine, which must be stated:**

| Organism | Susceptibility to chlorine |
|---|---|
| **Bacteria (E. coli, Vibrio cholerae, Salmonella)** | **Very susceptible — readily killed** |
| **Viruses** | **Susceptible, needing a higher CT** |
| **GIARDIA cysts** | **RESISTANT — needs a high CT** |
| **CRYPTOSPORIDIUM oocysts** | **ESSENTIALLY IMMUNE to practical chlorine doses** ← |

> **CRYPTOSPORIDIUM is the reason filtration cannot be replaced by chlorination: no achievable chlorine dose reliably inactivates its oocysts, and the only effective barriers are FILTRATION, UV or ozone.**

> **The 1993 Milwaukee outbreak — over 400,000 people affected from a properly chlorinated supply — established the point conclusively.**

> **So the treatment train's multiple barriers are not redundancy but necessity: each barrier catches something the others miss, and chlorination alone is a barrier with a known and serious gap.**

examTip.trick: **0.2 mg/L free residual at the consumer's tap; 0.1 mg/L minimum at the far end; 0.5 mg/L after 30 minutes at the plant; 1.0 mg/L or more during an epidemic.**
examTip.trap: **Option (c) 0.1 is the minimum at the network extremity** — a real figure from the same range. And the upper constraint is TASTE (0.3-0.5 mg/L), not toxicity.
examTip.mnemonic: **Chlorination is far more effective at LOW pH: 75 % as powerful HOCl at pH 7 but only 25 % at pH 8.** And on the breakpoint curve's FALLING limb, adding more chlorine LOWERS the residual — dose decisively past the breakpoint. CRYPTOSPORIDIUM is immune to chlorine entirely.

questions.stem: The minimum self-cleansing velocity that should be developed in a sanitary sewer is about:
questions.solution:
**About 0.6 m/s.**

**The velocity limits for a sewer:**

| Limit | Value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **MINIMUM (self-cleansing) velocity** | **0.6 m/s at the design flow; 0.8 m/s preferred** | **Below this, SOLIDS SETTLE and the sewer silts up** ← |
| **MAXIMUM (non-scouring) velocity** | **3.0 m/s** | **Above this, the sewer's INVERT is ERODED by grit** |

> **So the design must keep the velocity between about 0.6 and 3.0 m/s — a band, not a single target.**

> **Option (d) 3.0 m/s is the MAXIMUM limit from the same pair, and option (b) 0.3 m/s is roughly the minimum for a storm drain carrying no organic solids.**

**Why a MINIMUM velocity is needed — and it is the defining constraint of sewer design:**

> **Sewage carries SUSPENDED SOLIDS, including grit, faecal matter and organic debris.**

> **If the velocity falls below the settling velocity of those solids, they DEPOSIT on the invert.**

> **The consequences compound:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The cross-section is reduced** | Capacity falls, so the velocity falls further — a vicious circle |
| **Deposited organic matter DECOMPOSES ANAEROBICALLY** | **Producing HYDROGEN SULPHIDE — see below** ← |
| **Blockages develop** | Eventually a surcharge and an overflow |
| **Manual cleaning becomes necessary** | **Dangerous, unpleasant work in a confined space** |

> **The point about the vicious circle is important: siltation is SELF-AGGRAVATING, so a sewer that begins to silt continues to.**

> **Which is why the self-cleansing velocity must be achieved at the MINIMUM expected flow, not the design maximum.**

**The HYDROGEN SULPHIDE problem, which is the most serious consequence:**

> **Anaerobic decomposition of the deposited organic matter and of the sewage itself produces H₂S gas.**

| Effect of H₂S | Note |
|---|---|
| **CROWN CORROSION of concrete sewers** | **H₂S rises to the sewer's crown, is oxidised by Thiobacillus bacteria to SULPHURIC ACID, which dissolves the concrete from the inside** ← |
| **Lethal toxicity** | **H₂S kills at a few hundred ppm, and it PARALYSES THE SENSE OF SMELL at low concentration — so a worker stops smelling it just as it becomes dangerous** |
| **Explosive with air** | A further hazard in confined spaces |
| **Odour nuisance** | The complaint that reveals the problem |

> **CROWN CORROSION is the classic mode of failure of concrete sewers, and its mechanism is worth knowing precisely because it is counter-intuitive: the sewer is destroyed at its TOP, where no sewage flows, rather than at its invert.**

> **The gas rises, condenses on the damp crown, and the bacteria living in that condensate manufacture sulphuric acid in situ.**

> **The remedies are to maintain self-cleansing velocities, to ventilate the sewer so the gas is carried away, and in aggressive situations to line the crown or use a resistant material such as vitrified clay, HDPE or a PVC-lined pipe.**

> **And the WORKER SAFETY point deserves emphasis: the loss of the sense of smell at moderate H₂S concentration means the natural warning disappears exactly when it is needed, which is why entry into a sewer or manhole requires gas testing and forced ventilation rather than a sniff at the opening.**

**Why a MAXIMUM velocity is also needed:**

> **Sewage carries GRIT — sand, silt and small stones washed in from roads and from infiltration.**

> **At high velocity that grit ABRADES the invert of the pipe, wearing it away over years and eventually exposing reinforcement or breaching the pipe.**

> **The 3.0 m/s limit protects the pipe, and where the topography forces steeper gradients the remedy is a DROP MANHOLE — dissipating the fall in a controlled structure rather than accelerating the flow along the pipe.**

> **In Nepal's hill towns that constraint is constant: natural gradients far exceed what a sewer can use, so sewer design there is largely a matter of arranging drops.**

**How self-cleansing velocity is achieved at LOW flow — the design difficulty:**

> **A sewer must carry the peak flow at the end of its design period AND be self-cleansing at the minimum flow at the beginning of it.**

> **Those two requirements pull in opposite directions: a pipe large enough for the future peak runs almost empty now, at a low depth and hence a low velocity.**

> **The devices used to resolve it:**

| Device | How it works |
|---|---|
| **Design the gradient for self-cleansing at MINIMUM flow** | **The governing criterion, not the peak** ← |
| **A CIRCULAR section running part full** | **Fortunately, velocity at half depth EQUALS velocity at full depth — see the note below** |
| **EGG-SHAPED (ovoid) section** | **Narrow at the invert, so a small flow is DEEPER and faster** |
| **A CUNETTE — a small channel formed in the invert** | Concentrates the dry-weather flow |
| **FLUSHING tanks or automatic siphons at the head of the system** | Periodic scouring |
| **Separate small-diameter sewers for the early phase** | Staged construction |

> **The EGG-SHAPED sewer is the classical answer and a genuinely elegant one: by narrowing the section at the bottom, a small flow occupies a greater depth and so achieves a higher velocity than it would in a circular pipe of the same capacity.**

> **It is now rarely built, because circular pipes are mass-produced and cheap while ovoid sections must be formed in situ or specially cast** — an instance of manufacturing economics defeating hydraulic elegance.

**The hydraulic property that makes circular sewers workable — worth knowing:**

> **For a circular pipe running PART FULL:**

| Depth of flow | Velocity relative to full-flow | Discharge relative to full-flow |
|---|---|---|
| **0.5 d (half depth)** | **1.00 — EQUAL to full-flow velocity** ← |
| **0.8 d** | **1.14 — the MAXIMUM velocity** |
| **0.938 d** | **1.07 — the MAXIMUM DISCHARGE** |
| **1.0 d (full)** | **1.00** |
| **0.3 d** | **0.78** |

> **Two remarkable results sit in that table.**

> **FIRST — a sewer flowing HALF FULL has exactly the SAME velocity as one flowing full**, because the hydraulic radius happens to be identical at those two depths.

> **SECOND — the maximum DISCHARGE occurs at about 94 per cent of the depth, NOT when the pipe is full.**

> **The second is because as the pipe fills the last few per cent, the wetted perimeter grows faster than the area, so the hydraulic radius and hence the velocity fall.**

> **A consequence worth stating: a sewer designed to run just short of full carries MORE than one designed to run exactly full** — which is why sewers are conventionally designed to flow at about 0.8 of the depth at peak flow, leaving air space above for ventilation as well.

examTip.trick: **Sewer velocity band: MINIMUM 0.6 m/s (self-cleansing), MAXIMUM 3.0 m/s (non-scouring).** Option (d) is the other end of the same pair.
examTip.trap: **Self-cleansing must be achieved at the MINIMUM flow, not the design peak** — a pipe sized for the future peak runs nearly empty now. Siltation is self-aggravating, so a sewer that starts to silt continues to.
examTip.mnemonic: **Deposits decompose anaerobically to H₂S, which rises and is oxidised at the CROWN to sulphuric acid** — concrete sewers fail at the top, not the invert. And H₂S paralyses the sense of smell just as it becomes lethal, which is why manhole entry needs gas testing, not a sniff.

questions.stem: A circular sewer flowing at HALF its depth has a velocity that is:
questions.solution:
**EQUAL to the full-flow velocity.**

**Why — the hydraulic radius is identical at the two depths:**

> **The velocity by Manning's equation depends on the HYDRAULIC RADIUS: V = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2}.**

> **For a circular pipe of diameter d:**

| Condition | Area A | Wetted perimeter P | R = A/P |
|---|---|---|---|
| **FULL** | **πd²/4** | **πd** | **d/4** |
| **HALF full** | **πd²/8** | **πd/2** | **d/4** ← |

> **Both the area and the wetted perimeter are exactly HALVED, so their ratio is UNCHANGED.**

> **With the same R, the same n and the same slope S, the velocity must be the same** ✓

> **That is a clean and complete proof, and it takes two lines — which is why it is worth deriving rather than remembering.**

**But the DISCHARGE is halved, and the distinction matters:**

> **Q = A V, and the area is halved while the velocity is unchanged.**

> **So a sewer at half depth carries HALF the discharge at the SAME velocity.**

> **That combination is what makes circular sewers practicable: a sewer running at half its design flow is still self-cleansing.**

> **Which resolves much of the design difficulty described above — a pipe sized generously for a future peak still scours itself at half that flow.**

**The full part-full relationships, which this question is one entry of:**

| Depth ratio d/D | Velocity ratio V/V_full | Discharge ratio Q/Q_full |
|---|---|---|
| **0.2** | **0.62** | **0.09** |
| **0.3** | **0.78** | **0.20** |
| **0.5** | **1.00** ← | **0.50** |
| **0.6** | **1.07** | **0.67** |
| **0.8** | **1.14 — the MAXIMUM velocity** | **0.98** |
| **0.938** | **1.07** | **1.08 — the MAXIMUM DISCHARGE** ← |
| **1.0 (full)** | **1.00** | **1.00** |

> **Two results in that table are genuinely surprising and both are worth understanding.**

> **FIRST — the MAXIMUM VELOCITY occurs at about 0.8 of the depth, not when the pipe is full.**

> **SECOND — the MAXIMUM DISCHARGE occurs at about 0.94 of the depth, and it EXCEEDS the full-flow discharge by about 8 per cent.**

**Why the maxima are not at full depth — the explanation:**

> **As a circular pipe fills beyond about 80 per cent, the WETTED PERIMETER grows faster than the AREA.**

> **Picture the last quarter of the pipe filling: the water surface is narrow (the pipe is curving inward at the top), so little area is added — but a great deal of pipe wall is being wetted.**

> **So the hydraulic radius R = A/P starts to FALL, and with it the velocity.**

> **The discharge Q = AV is a product of a rising A and a falling V, and it peaks just before the pipe is full.**

> **That is a purely geometric result about circles, and it has a practical consequence: A SEWER DESIGNED TO RUN JUST SHORT OF FULL CARRIES MORE THAN ONE DESIGNED TO RUN EXACTLY FULL.**

**Why sewers are designed to run at about 0.8 depth at the peak flow:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Maximum VELOCITY occurs there** | **Best self-cleansing at the design condition** ← |
| **Discharge is 98 % of full-bore** | **Almost no capacity is given up** |
| **AIR SPACE is left above the flow** | **VENTILATION — essential for carrying away H₂S and sewer gas** ← |
| **A margin against surcharge** | Peak flows exceed estimates |
| **Room for the flow to accelerate without pressurising** | A pressurised sewer leaks outward at every joint |

> **The VENTILATION reason is the decisive one and is often the least discussed.**

> **A sewer running full has no air space, so sewer gas cannot move along it, and H₂S accumulates against the crown where it does its damage.**

> **A sewer running at 0.8 depth has a continuous air passage from manhole to manhole, and the air movement induced by the flowing sewage carries the gas away to the ventilating columns.**

> **So the 20 per cent of unused cross-section is not spare capacity being wasted — it is a functional part of the design**, and filling it would create the corrosion and safety problems described above.

**Note also the STORM SEWER contrast, since the design philosophy differs:**

| | **SANITARY sewer** | **STORM sewer** |
|---|---|---|
| **Design flow** | **Peak dry-weather flow plus infiltration** | **The design storm's peak runoff** |
| **Design depth at peak** | **About 0.8 D — air space retained** | **May be designed to run FULL, or even surcharged briefly** |
| **Self-cleansing velocity** | **0.6-0.8 m/s — organic solids** | **0.3-0.5 m/s adequate — grit only, no organics** |
| **Gas problem** | **H₂S — serious** | **Negligible** |
| **Flow variation** | Continuous, moderate variation | **Zero for most of the year, then very large** |

> **The last row is the fundamental difference: a storm sewer is DRY most of the time and carries an enormous flow occasionally, while a sanitary sewer carries a modest flow continuously.**

> **Which is why the two are separated in modern practice (the SEPARATE system) rather than combined: a combined sewer must be sized for the storm flow, and it then carries the small sanitary flow at a velocity far too low to be self-cleansing.**

> **Worse, a combined sewer OVERFLOWS during a storm, discharging diluted but untreated sewage to the receiving water — the combined sewer overflow problem that older cities spend heavily to remedy.**

> **So the separate system's advantage is not merely hydraulic: it keeps the sewage in the sewer during exactly the conditions when a combined system would spill it.**

examTip.trick: **At half depth both the AREA and the WETTED PERIMETER halve, so R = A/P is unchanged — hence the same velocity.** The DISCHARGE, though, is halved.
examTip.trap: **Maximum velocity is at 0.8 D and maximum DISCHARGE at 0.94 D, exceeding full-bore by 8 %** — because beyond 80 % the wetted perimeter grows faster than the area, so R and V fall.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sewers are designed at 0.8 D because the AIR SPACE is functional, not spare capacity** — it ventilates the H₂S that would otherwise corrode the crown. A sewer running full has nowhere for the gas to go.

questions.stem: The BOD removal efficiency of a well-designed PRIMARY sedimentation tank in a sewage treatment plant is about:
questions.solution:
**About 30 per cent (typically 30 to 35 per cent).**

**The removal efficiencies through a conventional treatment plant:**

| Unit | BOD removal | Suspended solids removal |
|---|---|---|
| **Screens and grit chamber** | **Negligible (0-5 %)** | **5-10 %** |
| **PRIMARY sedimentation** | **30-35 %** ← | **50-70 %** |
| **Secondary treatment — ACTIVATED SLUDGE** | **85-95 % (of the settled sewage)** | **85-95 %** |
| **Secondary treatment — TRICKLING FILTER** | **80-90 %** | **80-90 %** |
| **OVERALL, primary plus secondary** | **85-95 %** | **85-95 %** |
| **Tertiary treatment** | **Up to 99 % overall** | — |

> **Note the important asymmetry in the primary tank's performance: it removes 50 to 70 per cent of the SUSPENDED SOLIDS but only 30 to 35 per cent of the BOD.**

> **Option (d) 60 % is the SUSPENDED SOLIDS figure, offered for BOD — which is what makes it the designed distractor.**

**Why primary sedimentation removes so much more SS than BOD — the reason is the substance of the question:**

> **A settling tank removes what SETTLES.**

> **BOD in sewage is present in three forms:**

| Form of BOD | Removed by plain sedimentation? |
|---|---|
| **SETTLEABLE organic solids** | **YES — this is the 30 % that comes out** ← |
| **COLLOIDAL organic matter** | **NO — too small to settle in the available time** |
| **DISSOLVED organic matter** | **NO — cannot be settled at all, by any tank** |

> **Roughly a third of sewage BOD is in settleable form, and that is precisely what a primary tank achieves.**

> **The remaining two thirds — colloidal and dissolved — requires BIOLOGICAL treatment, because the only practical way to remove dissolved organic matter is to let microorganisms EAT it and then settle the microorganisms.**

> **That is the entire logic of secondary treatment, and it explains why a sewage works cannot consist of settling tanks alone however large they are made.**

> **A settling tank of infinite size would still leave the dissolved BOD untouched.**

**What BOD actually measures, since the number is central:**

> **BIOCHEMICAL OXYGEN DEMAND is the mass of oxygen consumed by microorganisms in oxidising the organic matter in a sample, under standard conditions:**

| Standard condition | Value |
|---|---|
| **Incubation period** | **5 DAYS** |
| **Temperature** | **20 °C** |
| **Result reported as** | **BOD₅ at 20 °C, in mg/L** |

> **The 5-day, 20 °C convention is arbitrary but universal, and it matters because BOD is a RATE-dependent measurement: the 5-day figure is about 68 per cent of the ultimate BOD.**

> **Typical values:**

| Water | BOD₅ (mg/L) |
|---|---|
| **Raw domestic sewage** | **200-400** |
| **After primary sedimentation** | **130-270** |
| **After secondary treatment** | **20-30** |
| **Discharge standard, typical** | **30 mg/L or less** |
| **Clean river water** | **Below 2** |

> **So a plant taking 300 mg/L sewage down to 30 mg/L is achieving 90 per cent removal — which is the conventional performance target and matches the table above.**

**Why BOD is used at all, given its awkwardness — and the alternatives:**

| Test | Measures | Time | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BOD₅** | **BIODEGRADABLE organic matter** | **5 DAYS** | **The regulatory standard, but far too slow for process control** ← |
| **COD (chemical oxygen demand)** | **TOTAL oxidisable matter, biodegradable or not** | **2-3 HOURS** | **Always HIGHER than BOD; the ratio BOD/COD indicates biodegradability** |
| **TOC (total organic carbon)** | Organic carbon | **Minutes** | Instrumental, needs correlation |

> **The BOD/COD RATIO is the genuinely useful derived quantity:**

| BOD₅/COD | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| **Above 0.5** | **Readily biodegradable — biological treatment will work well** |
| **0.3-0.5** | Biodegradable with acclimatised organisms |
| **Below 0.3** | **POORLY biodegradable — biological treatment alone will not suffice; suspect industrial or toxic content** ← |

> **Domestic sewage typically has BOD/COD around 0.5 to 0.6.**

> **A ratio well below 0.3 in what is supposed to be domestic sewage is evidence of an industrial discharge into the sewer, and it is a warning that the biological plant may be inhibited or killed.**

> **So the ratio functions as a diagnostic, and it is why both tests are run rather than the faster one alone.**

**The primary tank's design parameters, since the efficiency depends on them:**

| Parameter | Typical value |
|---|---|
| **DETENTION time** | **2 to 2.5 hours** |
| **SURFACE OVERFLOW RATE** | **30-45 m³/m²/day** ← the governing parameter |
| **Weir loading rate** | **125-500 m³/m/day** |
| **Depth** | **2.5-3.5 m** |
| **Sludge production** | **About 0.7-0.9 % of the sewage volume** |

> **The SURFACE OVERFLOW RATE is the parameter that actually governs removal, and understanding why is worth the effort:**

> **A particle is removed if it can settle from the water surface to the floor during the time the water takes to pass through the tank.**

> **That condition works out as: settling velocity ≥ (flow rate ÷ surface area) — which is exactly the surface overflow rate.**

> **So removal depends on the tank's PLAN AREA and NOT on its DEPTH.**

> **A remarkable and useful result: making a settling tank DEEPER does not improve its removal efficiency at all; making it WIDER does.**

> **Depth is provided for sludge storage, for hydraulic stability and to avoid scour of the settled sludge — not for settling performance.**

> **Which is the theoretical basis of the HIGH-RATE or TUBE SETTLER: inserting inclined plates or tubes multiplies the effective settling area within the same tank volume, and so multiplies the capacity.** A retrofit of tube settlers can double an existing clarifier's throughput without enlarging it at all.

examTip.trick: **Primary sedimentation removes 30-35 % of BOD but 50-70 % of SUSPENDED SOLIDS.** Option (d) 60 % is the solids figure offered for BOD.
examTip.trap: **Only about a third of sewage BOD is SETTLEABLE** — the rest is colloidal and dissolved, and no settling tank of any size can remove dissolved organic matter. That is why biological secondary treatment is unavoidable.
examTip.mnemonic: **Removal depends on the tank's PLAN AREA, not its DEPTH** — the surface overflow rate is the governing parameter. Which is why TUBE SETTLERS work: more settling area in the same volume can double a clarifier's capacity.

questions.stem: Under Nepal's Environment Protection Act and Rules, the environmental study that requires a PUBLIC HEARING in the affected area is:
questions.solution:
**The ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT ASSESSMENT (EIA).**

**The tiers of environmental study under Nepal's regime:**

| Study | Applies to | Public hearing | Approving authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BRIEF ENVIRONMENTAL STUDY (BES)** | **The smallest projects with minor impacts** | **NOT required** | **The concerned body / local level** |
| **INITIAL ENVIRONMENTAL EXAMINATION (IEE)** | **Projects of moderate scale and impact** | **NOT required** | **The concerned MINISTRY** |
| **ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT ASSESSMENT (EIA)** | **Large projects with significant impacts** | **REQUIRED** ← | **Ministry of Forests and Environment** |

> **The graduated structure is the point: the depth of study, the level of approval and the extent of public involvement all increase with the scale of the likely impact.**

> **That is a proportionate regulatory design — a small project is not put through the same process as a large one — and it is common to environmental regimes worldwide.**

**Why the PUBLIC HEARING is attached to the EIA specifically:**

> **An EIA applies to projects whose impacts are SIGNIFICANT and which typically involve LAND ACQUISITION, DISPLACEMENT, or effects on the livelihoods and environment of a local population.**

> **Those affected have a legitimate interest in being heard, and they frequently possess information the proponent does not: local hydrology, seasonal use of resources, cultural and religious sites, existing grievances.**

> **So the public hearing serves two purposes at once:**

| Purpose | Note |
|---|---|
| **PROCEDURAL — a right to be heard about a decision affecting one's own place** | **A matter of legitimacy** |
| **SUBSTANTIVE — the study is improved by local knowledge** | **Local people know things a visiting consultant cannot** ← |

> **The second purpose is the one engineers most often underrate and most often regret.**

> **A hydropower EIA that has not asked local people where the river floods, which spring the village drinks from, or which grove is a shrine will produce a document that is technically competent and practically wrong.**

> **And a project that proceeds on such a document meets opposition later, at far greater cost than the hearing would have taken.**

**The EIA process in sequence, since the hearing is one step of several:**

| Step | Content |
|---|---|
| **1. SCREENING** | **Decide which tier of study applies — BES, IEE or EIA** |
| **2. SCOPING** | **Determine WHICH impacts will be studied and in what depth; a scoping document is prepared** |
| **3. TERMS OF REFERENCE** | **Approved by the ministry; defines the study's content** |
| **4. Baseline data collection** | **Physical, biological, socio-economic and cultural environment as it stands** |
| **5. Impact PREDICTION and evaluation** | Magnitude, extent, duration, significance |
| **6. MITIGATION measures** | **Avoid, minimise, mitigate, compensate — in that order of preference** ← |
| **7. ALTERNATIVES analysis** | **Including the NO-PROJECT alternative** |
| **8. PUBLIC HEARING in the affected area** | **A notice at the site and in a national daily; the hearing recorded** |
| **9. Environmental MANAGEMENT PLAN and monitoring plan** | How the mitigation will actually be delivered |
| **10. Report submission, review and approval** | By the Ministry of Forests and Environment |
| **11. MONITORING and AUDITING during and after implementation** | **Compliance, impact and environmental audit** |

> **Note that SCREENING is step 1 and is a decision, not a study — which is why option (b) is wrong: screening determines which study is needed and involves no hearing.**

**The MITIGATION HIERARCHY in step 6, which is the professional core of the exercise:**

| Preference | Measure |
|---|---|
| **1. AVOID** | **Change the design or location so the impact does not occur at all** ← always the best |
| **2. MINIMISE** | Reduce the magnitude, extent or duration |
| **3. MITIGATE / rectify** | Repair or restore after the impact |
| **4. COMPENSATE** | **Offset the residual impact — replacement planting, resettlement, payment** — the last resort |

> **The hierarchy is not a menu but an ORDER, and the reason is worth stating: an avoided impact is certain, whereas a compensated one depends on the compensation actually being delivered and actually working.**

> **Compensatory afforestation that is planted and not maintained, or a resettlement site without water, compensates nothing.**

> **So a design change that avoids an impact is worth more than a large compensation budget — which is an argument for doing the environmental assessment EARLY, while the design can still be changed.**

> **An EIA conducted after the design is frozen can only document impacts and propose compensation; one conducted during design can prevent them.** That is the single most useful thing to understand about the process.

**The MONITORING and AUDITING stage, which is where the process most often fails:**

| Stage | What it checks |
|---|---|
| **COMPLIANCE monitoring** | **Are the committed mitigation measures actually being implemented?** |
| **IMPACT monitoring** | **Are the predicted impacts occurring, and at the predicted magnitude?** |
| **ENVIRONMENTAL AUDIT** | **Conducted 2 years after operation begins, by the Ministry — an independent check** ← |

> **The honest observation about environmental assessment in practice is that the report is usually produced conscientiously and the MONITORING is frequently neglected.**

> **A mitigation measure promised in an approved EIA and never implemented is worse than one never promised, because it secured the approval on a false basis.**

> **The two-year environmental audit exists precisely to close that gap, and its value depends entirely on whether it is carried out.**

**Why this matters for a civil engineer rather than only for an environmental specialist:**

> **The mitigation measures in an EIA are largely ENGINEERING measures, and they must be designed and built by engineers:**

| Impact | Engineering mitigation |
|---|---|
| **Reduced flow downstream of a diversion** | **An ENVIRONMENTAL FLOW release — in Nepal, at least 10 % of the minimum monthly average flow** ← |
| **Fish migration blocked** | **A fish ladder or bypass channel** |
| **Sediment released during construction** | Silt traps, staged excavation, timing outside the monsoon |
| **Spoil disposal** | Designed and stabilised disposal areas, not tipping over the hillside |
| **Slope instability from road cutting** | Bioengineering, retaining structures, drainage |
| **Dust and noise** | Water spraying, working hours, barriers |

> **The ENVIRONMENTAL FLOW requirement — a minimum of 10 per cent of the minimum monthly average flow to be released downstream of any diversion in Nepal — is the one that most directly affects hydropower design.**

> **It is water that cannot be used for generation, and so it appears in the energy calculation as a permanent deduction from the smallest flows** — precisely the dry-season flows that matter most.

> **Which is why it is a real design constraint rather than a formality, and why it must be included from the feasibility stage rather than discovered at approval.**

examTip.trick: **Only the EIA requires a PUBLIC HEARING.** BES and IEE do not, and SCREENING is a decision about which study applies, not a study at all.
examTip.trap: **The tiers rise together — depth of study, level of approval and public involvement.** BES goes to the concerned body, IEE to the ministry, EIA to the Ministry of Forests and Environment.
examTip.mnemonic: **The mitigation hierarchy is an ORDER, not a menu: AVOID, minimise, mitigate, COMPENSATE last** — because an avoided impact is certain while compensation depends on delivery. Which is why an EIA done DURING design prevents impacts, and one done after can only document them.

questions.stem: A field is delivered 60 hectare-cm of water, of which 48 hectare-cm is stored in the root zone. The water application efficiency is:
questions.solution:
**80 per cent.**

**The definition:**

> **Water application efficiency  η_a = (water stored in the ROOT ZONE / water DELIVERED to the field) × 100**

> **= 48/60 × 100 = 80 %** ✓

**The family of irrigation efficiencies, which must be kept distinct:**

| Efficiency | Definition | Where the loss occurs |
|---|---|---|
| **CONVEYANCE efficiency η_c** | **Water delivered to the field / water diverted at the head** | **SEEPAGE and evaporation from canals and watercourses** |
| **APPLICATION efficiency η_a** | **Water stored in the root zone / water delivered to the field** ← | **Deep percolation below the root zone, and surface runoff off the field** |
| **STORAGE efficiency η_s** | **Water stored in the root zone / water NEEDED in the root zone** | Under-irrigation |
| **DISTRIBUTION (uniformity) efficiency η_d** | **How EVENLY the water is spread over the field** | Uneven application |
| **USE efficiency / consumptive use efficiency** | Water consumed by the crop / water depleted from the root zone | Weeds, evaporation from the soil surface |
| **OVERALL (project) efficiency** | **η_c × η_a** | **Everything** |

> **Note that the numerator and denominator move down the chain: each efficiency takes the previous one's output as its input.**

> **So the OVERALL efficiency is the PRODUCT, and that is where the sobering arithmetic lies:**

> **With a conveyance efficiency of 70 per cent (a fair unlined system) and this application efficiency of 80 per cent:**

> **Overall = 0.70 × 0.80 = 0.56, that is 56 per cent.**

> **Nearly half the water diverted from the river never reaches a crop root — and a poorly maintained system does considerably worse, with overall efficiencies of 30 to 40 per cent widely reported.**

**Why STORAGE and APPLICATION efficiency are different — and can move in opposite directions:**

> **This is the conceptual point of the topic and it is genuinely useful.**

> **APPLICATION efficiency asks: of the water I put on the field, how much stayed where the roots are?**

> **STORAGE efficiency asks: of the water the crop needed, how much did I actually supply?**

> **Consider two contrasting irrigations of a field needing 60 ha-cm:**

| Case | Delivered | Stored in root zone | η_a | η_s |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **UNDER-irrigation** | **40** | **40** | **100 %** | **67 %** |
| **OVER-irrigation** | **100** | **60** | **60 %** | **100 %** |

> **The under-irrigated field has PERFECT application efficiency and poor storage efficiency — nothing was wasted, but the crop was starved.**

> **The over-irrigated field has perfect storage efficiency and poor application efficiency — the crop got what it needed, and 40 ha-cm was wasted to deep percolation.**

> **So a HIGH application efficiency is not automatically good: it can be a symptom of under-irrigation.**

> **Both must be looked at together, which is why the set of efficiencies exists rather than a single number.**

**Where the application losses go, and why deep percolation is doubly harmful:**

| Loss | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **DEEP PERCOLATION below the root zone** | **Wasted water AND it raises the WATER TABLE, causing waterlogging and salinity** ← |
| **SURFACE RUNOFF off the field** | Wasted water, plus soil erosion and nutrient loss |
| **Evaporation during application** | Small for surface methods; significant for sprinklers in hot dry wind |

> **The DEEP PERCOLATION entry is the one worth dwelling on: over-irrigation does not merely waste water, it actively DAMAGES the land.**

> **The percolating water raises the water table toward the root zone, and once capillary rise reaches it, salts are delivered to the surface and concentrated there by evaporation.**

> **So an irrigator applying too much water is simultaneously wasting a scarce resource and salinising the field.**

> **That is the mechanism by which irrigation has destroyed agricultural land throughout history, and it is why over-irrigation is a more serious fault than under-irrigation even though it looks like generosity.**

**The application efficiencies achievable by different methods:**

| Method | Application efficiency |
|---|---|
| **Wild flooding** | **30-50 %** |
| **Border strip** | **60-75 %** |
| **Check basin** | **60-80 %** |
| **FURROW** | **60-80 %** ← the common field method |
| **SPRINKLER** | **70-85 %** |
| **DRIP (trickle)** | **85-95 %** ← the highest |

> **DRIP irrigation achieves its efficiency by delivering water directly to the root zone of each plant, so there is almost nothing to percolate or run off, and very little soil surface is wetted for evaporation.**

> **Its further advantage is that FERTILISER can be delivered with the water (fertigation), applied precisely where the roots are.**

> **Its disadvantages are honest ones: high capital cost, a requirement for CLEAN water (emitters clog readily, so filtration is essential), vulnerability to rodent and mechanical damage, and a need for a pressurised supply.**

> **So drip suits high-value crops — vegetables, orchards, cash crops — and is rarely economic for cereals at prevailing water prices.**

> **Which is the honest conclusion: the technically best method is not always the appropriate one, and the choice depends on the value of the crop and the cost of water rather than on efficiency alone.**

**And the reason efficiency matters more than it used to:**

> **In most irrigated regions the easily developed water resources are already committed.**

> **New supply must come from expensive storage, from deep groundwater, or from another basin — or from EFFICIENCY.**

> **Raising a system's overall efficiency from 40 to 55 per cent releases as much water as a substantial new reservoir, without inundating anything or displacing anyone.**

> **That is why canal lining, watercourse improvement, on-farm water management and volumetric charging attract the attention they do: they are the cheapest remaining source of irrigation water in most of South Asia.**

examTip.trick: **Application efficiency = water stored in the ROOT ZONE ÷ water DELIVERED to the field = 48/60 = 80 %.**
examTip.trap: **A HIGH application efficiency can be a symptom of UNDER-irrigation** — an under-watered field wastes nothing and starves the crop. Application and STORAGE efficiency must be read together, which is why both exist.
examTip.mnemonic: **Overall efficiency is the PRODUCT: 0.70 conveyance × 0.80 application = 56 %.** And deep percolation is doubly harmful — wasted water that also raises the water table and salinises the land, which is why over-irrigation is worse than under-irrigation.

questions.stem: A canal system has a culturable command area of 5000 hectares, of which 2000 hectares is irrigated in the rabi season. The intensity of irrigation for rabi is:
questions.solution:
**40 per cent.**

**The definition:**

> **Intensity of irrigation = (area irrigated in the season / CULTURABLE COMMAND AREA) × 100**

> **= 2000/5000 × 100 = 40 %** ✓

**The area definitions, which are the substance of this topic:**

| Area | Definition |
|---|---|
| **GROSS COMMAND AREA (GCA)** | **The TOTAL area that can be commanded — everything within the canal's boundary, INCLUDING villages, roads, ponds, forests and barren land** |
| **CULTURABLE COMMAND AREA (CCA)** | **The part of the GCA that is CULTIVABLE — land that can grow a crop** ← the denominator here |
| **Culturable cultivated area** | The part of the CCA actually under cultivation |
| **Culturable uncultivated area** | Cultivable but left fallow |
| **Unculturable area** | **GCA − CCA: the villages, roads, water bodies and waste** |

> **The intensity of irrigation is always taken on the CCA, never the GCA — because irrigating a village or a road is meaningless.**

> **Using the GCA would be the error, and it would understate the intensity.**

**Why intensities are computed per SEASON and then added:**

> **Nepal and northern India have two principal crop seasons and one minor one:**

| Season | Months | Typical crops |
|---|---|---|
| **KHARIF (monsoon)** | **June to October** | **RICE, maize, millet, sugarcane** |
| **RABI (winter)** | **October to March** | **WHEAT, barley, gram, mustard, potato** |
| **Zaid / hot weather** | **March to June** | Vegetables, fodder, some maize |

> **Since the seasons do not overlap, the SAME LAND can be irrigated twice or three times in a year.**

> **So the intensities ADD, and the annual intensity can exceed 100 per cent:**

| Case | Kharif | Rabi | Annual intensity |
|---|---|---|---|
| **This system, if kharif intensity were 60 %** | **60 %** | **40 %** | **100 %** |
| **A well-supplied system** | **80 %** | **70 %** | **150 %** |
| **An intensively cropped system with a zaid crop** | 90 % | 80 % | **170-200 %** |

> **An annual intensity above 100 per cent is therefore not an error — it means the land is being cropped more than once a year, which is precisely what irrigation is for.**

> **That is worth being clear about, because a figure above 100 per cent looks like a mistake until the reason is understood.**

**Why the intensity is a DESIGN parameter, not merely a statistic:**

> **The canal's capacity depends on the intensity of irrigation, because the intensity determines how much of the command area must be watered at once.**

> **The design chain runs:**

| Step | Quantity |
|---|---|
| **1** | **CCA × intensity of irrigation = area to be irrigated in the season** |
| **2** | **Area ÷ DUTY = discharge required at the head** ← |
| **3** | **Add conveyance losses working upstream from the field to the head** |
| **4** | **The result is the canal's design discharge — its FULL SUPPLY DISCHARGE** |

> **For this system in rabi, with a wheat duty of say 1800 ha/cumec at the field:**

> **Discharge at the field = 2000/1800 = 1.11 cumec**

> **With a conveyance efficiency of 70 per cent, the head discharge = 1.11/0.70 = 1.59 cumec.**

> **So the intensity of irrigation is what converts an area into a canal size — and choosing it is one of the fundamental decisions in project planning.**

**And the reason the intensity is set BELOW 100 per cent deliberately:**

> **A designer could size the canal to irrigate the whole CCA in each season, giving intensities of 100 per cent throughout.**

> **It is almost never done, and the reasons are worth understanding:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **The WATER is not available** | **The river's dry-season flow limits what can be supplied** ← usually the binding constraint |
| **A larger canal costs more** | Capital cost rises with capacity |
| **Not all farmers will irrigate** | Some grow rainfed crops, some leave land fallow |
| **Spreading water THINLY over a large area may serve more people** | **A policy choice: equity against intensity** ← |
| **Crop rotation requires fallow land** | Agronomic necessity |

> **The fourth row is the interesting one, and it is a genuine question of policy rather than of engineering.**

> **A fixed quantity of water can be used to irrigate a SMALL area WELL — high intensity, high yields, few beneficiaries — or a LARGE area LIGHTLY, giving each farmer a protective irrigation that saves the crop from failure without maximising its yield.**

> **The second approach is called PROTECTIVE irrigation and the first PRODUCTIVE irrigation, and the choice between them has been argued over for a century.**

| | **PROTECTIVE irrigation** | **PRODUCTIVE irrigation** |
|---|---|---|
| **Water spread** | **Thinly, over a large area** | **Generously, over a small area** |
| **Intensity** | **LOW (30-40 %)** ← as here | **HIGH (70-100 %)** |
| **Purpose** | **Prevent crop FAILURE and famine over a wide area** | **MAXIMISE yield and production** |
| **Beneficiaries** | Many, each lightly served | Fewer, each well served |
| **Historical context** | **Famine protection in colonial India** | Post-Green-Revolution production goals |

> **A rabi intensity of 40 per cent, as in this question, is characteristic of a PROTECTIVE system** — and recognising that tells you something about the project's purpose from a single number.

> **The honest observation is that neither approach is simply correct: protective irrigation serves more households and produces less food per unit of water, and which matters more is a question about objectives rather than about hydraulics.**

examTip.trick: **Intensity = area irrigated in the season ÷ CCA = 2000/5000 = 40 %.** Always on the CULTURABLE command area, never the gross.
examTip.trap: **Seasonal intensities ADD, so the ANNUAL intensity can exceed 100 %** — which is not an error but the point of irrigation: the same land cropped twice or three times a year.
examTip.mnemonic: **The intensity converts an AREA into a CANAL SIZE: CCA × intensity ÷ duty, plus conveyance losses.** And a low intensity like 40 % characterises PROTECTIVE irrigation — water spread thinly to prevent crop failure over a wide area, rather than to maximise yield on a small one.

questions.stem: Using Lacey's regime theory, the wetted perimeter of a channel carrying a discharge of 16 m³/s is:
questions.solution:
**19.0 m.**

**Lacey's regime perimeter equation:**

> **P = 4.75 √Q**

> **= 4.75 × √16 = 4.75 × 4 = 19.0 m** ✓

> **The numbers are chosen so that √16 = 4 exactly, which is what makes this a one-step calculation.**

**Lacey's three regime equations, which together fix the channel completely:**

| Equation | Gives |
|---|---|
| **P = 4.75 √Q** | **The WETTED PERIMETER** ← |
| **A = 2.28 Q^{5/6} / f^{1/3}**  (or  R = 0.47(Q/f)^{1/3}) | **The AREA and hence the hydraulic radius** |
| **S = f^{5/3} / (3340 Q^{1/6})** | **The BED SLOPE** |

> **THREE equations, and three unknowns to find — so the design is DETERMINATE and a unique channel section results.**

> **That completeness is Lacey's decisive advantage over Kennedy, whose single equation left the B/y ratio to be assumed by the designer.**

**Working this channel out completely, to show the method:**

> **Take a silt factor f = 1.0 (Kennedy's standard fine sandy silt).**

| Quantity | Computation | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Wetted perimeter** | **4.75 × 4** | **19.0 m** |
| **Hydraulic radius** | **R = 0.47 (16/1)^{1/3} = 0.47 × 2.52** | **1.184 m** |
| **Area** | **A = P R = 19.0 × 1.184** | **22.5 m²** |
| **Mean velocity** | **V = Q/A = 16/22.5** | **0.711 m/s** |
| **Bed slope** | **S = 1^{5/3}/(3340 × 16^{1/6}) = 1/(3340 × 1.587)** | **1 in 5300** |

> **A velocity of 0.71 m/s and a slope of 1 in 5300 are entirely typical of a distributary canal in alluvium — which confirms that the numbers are being used correctly.**

> **Note the check available: A = P × R holds by definition, so the three quantities must be mutually consistent.**

**Why the perimeter goes as √Q — the dimensional reasoning:**

> **For geometrically similar channels, area scales with the square of a length, so a length scales with √A.**

> **And Lacey's other relations make A roughly proportional to Q^{5/6}, so a length scales roughly as Q^{5/12} — close to the √Q = Q^{1/2} of the perimeter equation.**

> **So the √Q form is what dimensional similarity would suggest, and Lacey's coefficient 4.75 was fitted to observations on canals in regime.**

> **Note the consequence: a channel carrying FOUR times the discharge has only TWICE the perimeter.**

> **Large channels are therefore proportionally more efficient — more area per unit of wetted perimeter — which is the same economy of scale that makes a large pipe more efficient than a small one.**

**The SILT FACTOR f, since two of the three equations need it:**

> **f = 1.76 √m_r**, where m_r is the mean particle size in millimetres.

| Material | m_r (mm) | Silt factor f |
|---|---|---|
| **Very fine silt** | **0.05** | **0.4** |
| **Fine silt** | **0.08** | **0.5** |
| **Medium silt** | **0.16** | **0.7** |
| **Standard silt** | **0.32** | **1.0** ← |
| **Medium sand** | **0.50** | **1.25** |
| **Coarse sand** | **0.72** | **1.5** |
| **Fine gravel** | **2.0** | **2.5** |

> **Note what f does and does NOT affect:**

| Quantity | Depends on f? |
|---|---|
| **PERIMETER P = 4.75√Q** | **NO — independent of the silt** ← |
| **Hydraulic radius R = 0.47(Q/f)^{1/3}** | **YES — coarser silt gives a SHALLOWER channel** |
| **Slope S = f^{5/3}/(3340 Q^{1/6})** | **YES, strongly — the 5/3 power** |

> **That the PERIMETER is independent of the silt is a striking feature of Lacey's theory: a channel carrying a given discharge has the same width regardless of what it is cut in, and only its depth and slope change.**

> **And the slope's f^{5/3} dependence is very strong: coarse sand (f = 1.5) requires a slope 1.5^{5/3} = 1.97 times steeper than standard silt — nearly double.**

> **Which makes physical sense: coarser material needs more energy to keep it moving, and a steeper slope supplies it.**

**Lacey against Kennedy, stated compactly since this is the perennial comparison:**

| | **KENNEDY (1895)** | **LACEY (1930)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Silt parameter** | **CVR, m** | **SILT FACTOR, f** |
| **Number of equations** | **ONE** | **THREE** |
| **Determinate?** | **NO — B/y assumed** | **YES** ← |
| **Slope** | **From Kutter/Manning separately** | **Given by the theory** |
| **Length scale for silt suspension** | **DEPTH — eddies from the bed only** | **HYDRAULIC RADIUS — the whole perimeter** |
| **Regime states distinguished?** | **No** | **YES — initial and final regime** |
| **Section shape** | Trapezoidal, assumed | **SEMI-ELLIPTICAL** |

> **Lacey's INITIAL and FINAL REGIME distinction is worth a note, since it is his most practically useful refinement.**

> **A newly excavated canal has an ARTIFICIAL slope and a bed not yet in equilibrium with its sediment load. Over years of operation it adjusts — scouring here, silting there — until it reaches its FINAL regime.**

> **Designing for the final regime means the canal will not change shape after commissioning, which is what a designer wants.**

> **A canal designed for the initial condition will silt or scour its way to the regime section anyway, damaging its offtakes and structures in the process** — which is why the distinction matters and is not merely a theoretical nicety.

**And the honest limitation of both theories:**

> **They apply only to a channel in ALLUVIUM, carrying a SMALL sediment load, running with a STEADY discharge, and free to adjust its own section.**

> **A LINED channel meets none of those conditions and needs none of these theories: it is designed by Manning's equation for the required discharge, with velocity limits set by the lining material rather than by the silt.**

> **So the regime theories, for all their historical importance, apply to a diminishing share of new construction** — and knowing when they do not apply is as useful as being able to use them.

examTip.trap: **The PERIMETER is independent of the silt factor** — only the hydraulic radius and the slope depend on f. So a channel of given discharge has the same width whatever it is cut in.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lacey gives THREE equations (P, R, S), so the design is DETERMINATE** — which is exactly what Kennedy's single equation could not do. And the slope's f^{5/3} dependence is strong: coarse sand needs nearly double the slope of standard silt.

questions.stem: In canal design, the depth of cutting at which the quantity of excavation exactly equals the quantity required for the banks is called the:
questions.solution:
**The BALANCING DEPTH.**

**What it is:**

> **A canal is generally constructed partly in CUTTING and partly in FILLING — excavated below the natural ground and banked above it.**

> **The excavated material is used to build the banks.**

> **The BALANCING DEPTH is the depth of cutting at which the volume EXCAVATED exactly equals the volume NEEDED for the banks.**

> **At that depth there is no surplus spoil to dispose of and no borrow material to import.**

**Why it matters — the economics:**

| If the cutting is | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **SHALLOWER than the balancing depth** | **Not enough material for the banks — BORROW pits are needed, with the cost of excavating, hauling and compacting imported fill** |
| **DEEPER than the balancing depth** | **SURPLUS spoil — which must be hauled away and disposed of, occupying land and costing money** |
| **EQUAL to the balancing depth** | **NEITHER — the cheapest condition** ← |

> **So the balancing depth is an ECONOMIC optimum in earthwork, and it is why canal alignments are chosen to keep the cutting close to it wherever the topography allows.**

> **The saving is not trivial: hauling surplus spoil or importing borrow can be a substantial fraction of a canal's construction cost, and it involves land acquisition for the spoil or the borrow area on top of the earthmoving itself.**

**How it is calculated:**

> **Equate the two areas in cross-section:**

> **Area of CUTTING = Area of the two BANKS (plus an allowance for bulking and shrinkage, and for the banks' own compaction)**

> **For a trapezoidal canal of bed width B, side slope 1:z, and depth of cutting d:**

> **Area of cutting = (B + z d) d**

> **That is set equal to the required cross-sectional area of the banks — which depends on the bank top width, the freeboard, the service road and the bank side slopes — and the resulting quadratic in d is solved.**

> **In practice a BULKING or SHRINKAGE allowance is applied: excavated soil placed and compacted in a bank occupies a different volume from its in-situ state, typically requiring 10 to 25 per cent more excavation than the bank's finished volume.**

> **So the true balancing depth is somewhat GREATER than a naive equal-area calculation gives, and neglecting the allowance leaves a project short of fill.**

**Why the other options are wrong — each is a real and different quantity:**

| Option | What it really is |
|---|---|
| **(a) CRITICAL depth** | **The depth at which the Froude number is 1 and the specific energy is minimum — an OPEN CHANNEL HYDRAULICS quantity** |
| **(b) NORMAL depth** | **The depth of UNIFORM flow, at which the bed slope exactly balances the friction — from Manning's equation** |
| **(c) BALANCING depth** | ✓ **An EARTHWORK quantity** |
| **(d) REGIME depth** | **The depth given by Lacey's regime equations for a channel in equilibrium with its sediment** |

> **The instructive feature of that table is that three of the four are HYDRAULIC quantities and the answer is an EARTHWORK one.**

> **So the question is testing whether the candidate reads the stem — "the quantity of excavation equals the quantity required for the banks" is unmistakably about earth, not water.**

> **The word "depth" in a canal context invites a hydraulic answer, and the option set exploits that expectation.**

**The related canal cross-section terminology, since it is asked as a family:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **FREEBOARD** | **The height of the bank above the full supply level — 0.3 m for small canals up to 0.75-0.9 m for large ones** |
| **BERM** | **A horizontal shelf left between the cutting slope and the bank, at ground level** ← see below |
| **DOWEL (dowla)** | A small embankment on the bank top, along the service road, to prevent vehicles running into the canal |
| **SPOIL BANK** | Surplus excavated material stacked alongside where the cutting exceeds the balancing depth |
| **BORROW PIT** | Excavation outside the canal to obtain fill where the cutting is short of the balancing depth |
| **SERVICE ROAD / INSPECTION path** | On the bank top, for maintenance access |
| **Counter berm / catch water drain** | Intercepts hillside runoff before it reaches the canal |

> **The BERM deserves explanation because its purposes are several and not obvious:**

| Purpose of a berm | Note |
|---|---|
| **Provides a margin against the bank sliding into the canal** | **The principal structural purpose** ← |
| **Gives the cutting slope room to weather and slough without reaching the bank** | — |
| **Increases the seepage path from the canal to the outside** | Reduces seepage and improves stability |
| **Provides a working space for maintenance** | — |
| **Reduces the water velocity near the bank at high stage** | Protects the toe |

> **Berms WIDEN with age: as the cutting slope weathers back, the berm naturally extends, and a well-designed canal allows for it rather than fighting it.**

> **That is a good example of designing with a slow natural process rather than against it** — the berm is left generous initially, and the canal reaches a stable geometry without intervention.

**The CANAL ALIGNMENT choices, since the balancing depth depends on them:**

| Alignment | Description | Cross-drainage works needed |
|---|---|---|
| **RIDGE (watershed) canal** | **Follows the ridge line between two drainages** | **NONE or very few — every drain runs away from it** ← |
| **CONTOUR canal** | **Follows a contour along a hillside** | **MANY — it crosses every drain on the slope** |
| **SIDE SLOPE canal** | **Runs down a side slope, parallel to the drainage** | **Few** |

> **The RIDGE alignment is the ideal and the reason is exactly the cross-drainage question raised earlier: a canal on a watershed has no drainage crossing it, so no aqueducts, siphons or super passages are required at all.**

> **It also commands land on BOTH sides, doubling the area served per kilometre of canal.**

> **A CONTOUR canal, by contrast, commands land on one side only and must cross every stream on the hillside — which is why hill irrigation is so much more expensive per hectare than plains irrigation, and why Nepal's hill schemes are dominated by the cost of their crossings.**

examTip.trick: **BALANCING DEPTH — the depth of cutting at which the excavation exactly supplies the banks**, so there is neither surplus spoil to haul away nor borrow to import.
