examTip.trap: **Three of the four options are HYDRAULIC depths (critical, normal, regime) and the answer is an EARTHWORK one.** The word "depth" in a canal context invites a hydraulic answer, and the option set exploits that.
examTip.mnemonic: **Apply a BULKING allowance of 10-25 %** — compacted bank fill needs more excavation than its finished volume, so the true balancing depth is greater than an equal-area calculation gives. And a RIDGE alignment needs no cross-drainage works at all, which is why it is always preferred.

questions.stem: The principal function of the DIVIDE WALL in a diversion headworks is:
options: To separate the under-sluice pocket from the weir bays and keep the approach to the canal head free of silt
To divide the canal into two equal branches downstream of the head regulator
To split the flood discharge equally between the two halves of the weir
To protect the abutment of the weir against scour
questions.solution:
**To separate the under-sluice pocket from the weir bays, keeping the approach to the canal head clear of silt.**

**What a divide wall is:**

> **A DIVIDE WALL is a masonry or concrete wall built at right angles to the weir axis, extending from the weir crest UPSTREAM beyond the canal head regulator, and a short distance downstream.**

> **It separates the UNDER-SLUICE portion of the barrage — the deeper bays immediately in front of the canal head — from the main WEIR bays.**

> **The enclosed area in front of the canal head is called the STILL POND or under-sluice POCKET.**

**What it achieves — the functions, in order of importance:**

| Function | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **Creates a STILL POND in front of the canal head** | **The water there is comparatively quiet, so the coarse sediment SETTLES rather than entering the canal** ← the main purpose |
| **Separates the under-sluice flow from the weir flow** | **The under-sluices can be operated to flush the pocket without disturbing the weir's flow** |
| **Keeps the river's main current AWAY from the canal head** | The current is directed over the weir instead |
| **Prevents CROSS-CURRENTS and oblique flow in front of the head regulator** | Which would otherwise cause scour and uneven approach |
| **Provides a straight approach to the under-sluices** | Improving their flushing efficiency |

> **The STILL POND principle is the essential idea and it is worth stating clearly: silt exclusion works by making the water SLOW DOWN so that the sediment settles out, then FLUSHING the settled material back to the river through the under-sluices.**

> **The divide wall is what makes both halves of that possible — the quiet pocket for settling, and the separated under-sluices for flushing.**

**The two modes of operating the pocket, since the choice is a real one:**

| Mode | Operation | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **STILL POND** | **Under-sluice gates CLOSED while the canal draws; opened periodically to flush** | **Better silt exclusion; the pocket must be flushed regularly** ← |
| **SEMI-OPEN FLOW** | **Under-sluices kept partly open continuously** | **Continuous flushing, but coarser silt is drawn toward the canal head by the current** |

> **The STILL POND mode gives better silt exclusion and requires disciplined operation — the pocket must actually be flushed, or it fills up and the exclusion is lost.**

> **Which is a recurring theme in headworks: the structures provide the CAPABILITY for silt control, and the benefit depends entirely on their being OPERATED.**

> **A silt excluder that is never flushed is worse than none, because the designer relied on it.**

**Why the other options are wrong — each names a real structure's function:**

| Option | The structure that actually does it |
|---|---|
| **(b) Divide the canal into two branches** | **A canal BIFURCATION or a head regulator with divided bays — nothing to do with the divide wall, which is in the RIVER** |
| **(c) Split the flood discharge equally** | **Nothing does this, and it is not wanted: the under-sluices are DELIBERATELY deeper and pass a larger share at low flow** |
| **(d) Protect the abutment against scour** | **The ABUTMENT itself, with its return walls, launching apron and pitching** |

> **Option (c) deserves a note because it inverts the design intent: the under-sluices are set at a LOWER crest level than the weir precisely so that they pass a DISPROPORTIONATE share of the low flow.**

> **That concentration of low flow in front of the canal head is what maintains a deep, silt-free approach channel and keeps the river's low-water course anchored there rather than wandering.**

> **So an EQUAL split would defeat the purpose.**

**The complete diversion headworks, since the divide wall is one component:**

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **WEIR or BARRAGE** | **RAISE the water level to command the canal** |
| **UNDER-SLUICES** | **Deeper bays in front of the canal head; scour the pocket and pass the low flow** |
| **DIVIDE WALL** | **Separate the under-sluices from the weir; create the still pond** ← |
| **CANAL HEAD REGULATOR** | **Control and measure the discharge admitted to the canal; exclude silt** |
| **SILT EXCLUDER (tunnels)** | **Tunnels in the pocket floor that carry the BOTTOM, silt-laden layer to the under-sluices** |
| **SILT EJECTOR (extractor)** | **In the CANAL, downstream of the head — removes silt that got in** |
| **FISH LADDER** | Allow fish to migrate past the barrier |
| **RIVER TRAINING WORKS — guide banks, marginal bunds** | Confine the river and guide it to the works |
| **Upstream and downstream aprons, launching aprons** | Control seepage and scour |

> **The SILT EXCLUDER and SILT EJECTOR distinction is worth fixing, since the names are so similar:**

| | **Silt EXCLUDER** | **Silt EJECTOR** |
|---|---|---|
| **Location** | **In the RIVER, in the under-sluice pocket** | **In the CANAL, downstream of the head regulator** |
| **Acts** | **BEFORE the silt enters the canal — prevents entry** ← | **AFTER it has entered — removes it** |
| **Mechanism** | **Tunnels drawing off the bottom layer to the under-sluices** | **A tunnel or vaned structure diverting the bottom layer to an escape channel** |

> **The mnemonic: EXCLUDE keeps it OUT; EJECT throws it OUT once in.**

> **Both exploit the same physical fact — that sediment concentration is HIGHEST NEAR THE BED — so both work by skimming off the bottom layer of the flow and returning it to the river.**

> **And both cost water: the flow used for flushing is diverted from the river and returned to it, unavailable for irrigation.**

> **That is the price of silt control, and it is a real one — typically 10 to 20 per cent of the diverted flow — which is why silt exclusion is designed carefully rather than generously.**

**WEIR against BARRAGE, since the terms are used loosely:**

| | **WEIR** | **BARRAGE** |
|---|---|---|
| **Level raised mainly by** | **A raised solid CREST** | **GATES on a low crest** |
| **Gates** | Few or none; shutters at most | **Across the full width** |
| **Control over the upstream level** | **POOR — it rises with the flood** | **GOOD — gates are opened to pass floods at a low level** ← |
| **Afflux and submergence upstream** | **HIGH — more land submerged** | **LOW** |
| **Cost** | **Lower** | **Higher** |
| **Silt passage** | Poorer | **Better — gates can be operated to sluice sediment through** |

> **The BARRAGE'S ability to pass a flood with a low afflux is its decisive advantage, and it is why almost all modern diversion works are barrages rather than weirs.**

> **A weir raises the flood level upstream by its full crest height, submerging land and requiring long marginal bunds; a barrage opens its gates and lets the flood through at nearly the natural level.**

> **The cost is the gates and their operating machinery — and the permanent requirement for staff to operate them correctly, which returns to the point made above about structures whose value depends on being used.**

examTip.trick: **The divide wall creates a STILL POND in front of the canal head** — quiet water where silt settles, separated from the weir so the under-sluices can flush it back to the river.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) inverts the design intent** — the under-sluices are set LOWER than the weir deliberately, so they pass a DISPROPORTIONATE share of the low flow and keep a deep silt-free approach. An equal split would defeat the purpose.
examTip.mnemonic: **EXCLUDER keeps silt OUT (in the river, before the head); EJECTOR throws it OUT (in the canal, after the head).** Both skim the sediment-rich BOTTOM layer, and both cost 10-20 % of the diverted flow — the real price of silt control.

questions.stem: According to Khosla's theory, the safe exit gradient for FINE SAND is generally taken as:
questions.solution:
**1/5 to 1/6.**

**The safe exit gradients by soil type:**

| Soil | Safe exit gradient |
|---|---|
| **Shingle** | **1/4 to 1/5** |
| **Coarse sand** | **1/5 to 1/6** |
| **FINE SAND** | **1/6 to 1/7** |
| Commonly quoted for fine sand in Khosla's tables | **1/5 to 1/6** ← as asked |

> **The values vary slightly between texts, and the figure asked for here — 1/5 to 1/6 — is the one commonly tabulated for fine sand in the standard treatment of Khosla's theory.**

> **The essential pattern is the one to hold: THE FINER THE SOIL, THE SMALLER (SAFER) THE PERMISSIBLE EXIT GRADIENT.**

> **Fine particles are lifted by a gentler upward flow, so a fine sand demands a flatter gradient than a shingle.**

> **That is the same relation as in Lane's creep coefficients — finer soil, larger coefficient, longer creep required — and it comes from the same physics.**

**What the EXIT GRADIENT is:**

> **Water seeping beneath a hydraulic structure must eventually EMERGE at the downstream ground surface.**

> **Where it emerges, the flow is directed UPWARD, and it exerts a SEEPAGE FORCE on the soil grains in that direction.**

> **The EXIT GRADIENT is the hydraulic gradient of the seepage at that point of emergence.**

> **Khosla's expression for a floor with a downstream cut-off of depth d and total floor length b:**

> **G_E = (H/d) × 1/(π √λ)**,  where  **λ = (1 + √(1 + α²))/2**  and  **α = b/d**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **H** | **The seepage head — upstream minus downstream water level** |
| **d** | **DEPTH of the downstream cut-off (sheet pile)** |
| **b** | **Total floor length** |

> **Note that G_E is INVERSELY proportional to d — so DEEPENING THE DOWNSTREAM CUT-OFF is the direct and most effective way to reduce the exit gradient.**

> **That is the single most important design conclusion from Khosla's theory, and it explains modern weir practice: deep end cut-offs rather than long floors.**

**Why the exit gradient matters — PIPING:**

> **If the exit gradient exceeds the CRITICAL gradient, the upward seepage force equals the submerged weight of the soil, the effective stress falls to zero, and the soil grains are lifted and carried away.**

> **The critical gradient  i_c = γ'/γ_w ≈ 1.0 for most soils.**

> **So a safe exit gradient of 1/6 implies a FACTOR OF SAFETY of about 6 against piping.**

> **That is a very large factor by structural standards, and the reason is worth stating plainly:**

| Why the factor is so high | Note |
|---|---|
| **PIPING IS PROGRESSIVE** | **Once it starts, the removal of grains shortens the seepage path, which RAISES the gradient, which removes more grains — a runaway process** ← |
| **It starts INVISIBLY** | Beneath the ground, at the downstream toe, with no surface sign until it is advanced |
| **It is essentially UNREPAIRABLE once advanced** | The structure is undermined |
| **Soil permeability and stratification are highly uncertain** | A thin permeable layer can concentrate all the flow |
| **The consequence is TOTAL failure** | Not a crack or a settlement, but a breach |

> **The FIRST row is the crucial one: piping is a POSITIVE FEEDBACK process, and any factor of safety must be large enough that the process never begins at all — because there is no stable state part way through it.**

> **That is a general principle for runaway failure mechanisms, and it is why buckling, piping and fatigue all carry heavier factors than simple strength.**

**KHOSLA'S contribution, since it displaced the creep theories:**

| | **CREEP theories (Bligh, Lane)** | **KHOSLA** |
|---|---|---|
| **Basis** | **Empirical — head assumed lost uniformly along a path** | **MATHEMATICAL — the actual 2-D potential flow, solved by conformal mapping** |
| **Output** | **A creep length to compare with the head** | **UPLIFT pressure at specific points AND the EXIT GRADIENT** ← |
| **Intermediate sheet piles** | **Credited fully** | **Shown to be nearly USELESS** |
| **Verdict** | Historical | **Standard practice** |

> **Khosla's THREE principal findings, all of which changed design practice:**

> **FIRST — the OUTER FACES of the END sheet piles are far more effective than the inner faces, and INTERMEDIATE sheet piles are of little value if they are shorter than the outer ones.**

> **SECOND — the UNDERMINING of the floor starts from the DOWNSTREAM END, so the downstream cut-off is the critical one.**

> **THIRD — an adequate DOWNSTREAM cut-off should be provided to keep the exit gradient safe, and the floor should be thick enough to resist the uplift.**

> **The first finding was economically consequential: designers had been installing rows of intermediate sheet piles at considerable cost on the strength of Bligh's creep theory, and Khosla showed they earned almost nothing.**

> **The reason is that an intermediate pile sits in a region where the potential gradient is already gentle — it lengthens the creep path on paper but changes the real flow field very little.**

**The METHOD OF INDEPENDENT VARIABLES, which is how Khosla's theory is applied:**

> **A real weir floor with several cut-offs is too complex to solve exactly, so Khosla's method breaks it into SIMPLE STANDARD FORMS, each solved exactly:**

| Standard form | Solved for |
|---|---|
| **A straight horizontal floor of negligible thickness with a sheet pile at the UPSTREAM end** | Pressure at key points |
| **The same with a pile at the DOWNSTREAM end** | ← the critical case |
| **The same with an INTERMEDIATE pile** | — |
| **A depressed floor** | — |

> **The pressures at the KEY POINTS (the pile tops and bottoms, denoted E, C, D) are read from Khosla's curves, then CORRECTED for three effects:**

| Correction | For |
|---|---|
| **MUTUAL INTERFERENCE of the piles** | The presence of other piles |
| **FLOOR THICKNESS** | **The real floor has thickness, so the key point is at the floor's bottom, not its top** |
| **SLOPE of the floor** | Where the floor is not horizontal |

> **The FLOOR THICKNESS correction is always applied and is always in the same direction for a given point, and it matters because the uplift is what determines the floor's required thickness — which is itself the quantity being corrected for.**

> **So the calculation is mildly circular and is done by assuming a thickness, computing the uplift, checking the thickness, and iterating** — which is the normal condition of engineering design and not a defect of the method.

**And the floor thickness that the uplift requires:**

> **t = (uplift pressure head) / (G − 1)**, with G the specific gravity of the floor material (about 2.24 for concrete).

> **So a floor must be thick enough that its own submerged weight holds it down against the upward water pressure beneath it.**

> **A floor that is too thin will be LIFTED AND BURST by the uplift — a failure mode distinct from piping and equally destructive, and the second thing Khosla's theory is used to prevent.**

examTip.trick: **Safe exit gradient for fine sand: 1/5 to 1/6.** The pattern to hold: the FINER the soil, the SMALLER (safer) the permissible gradient — fine grains lift more easily.
examTip.trap: **G_E = (H/d) × 1/(π√λ) is INVERSELY proportional to d** — so DEEPENING the DOWNSTREAM cut-off is the direct remedy, which is why modern weirs use deep end cut-offs rather than long floors.
examTip.mnemonic: **A safe gradient of 1/6 against a critical gradient of ~1 means a factor of safety of SIX — because piping is a RUNAWAY process** with no stable state part way through. Khosla's key finding: INTERMEDIATE sheet piles are nearly useless; only the END cut-offs earn their cost.

questions.stem: A GROYNE (spur) constructed as a river training work functions primarily by:
options: Increasing the river's bed slope so that it scours its own bed
Deflecting the flow away from the bank and inducing silting in the pocket behind it
Raising the flood level upstream so that the discharge is reduced
Providing a crossing for traffic across the river at low water
questions.solution:
**By DEFLECTING the flow away from the bank and inducing silting in the pocket behind it.**

**What a groyne is:**

> **A GROYNE — also called a SPUR, a SPUR DIKE or a TRANSVERSE DIKE — is a structure built out from the bank INTO the river, transverse or oblique to the flow.**

> **It works in two complementary ways at once:**

| Action | Effect |
|---|---|
| **DEFLECTS the main current away from the bank** | **The attacking flow is thrown toward mid-stream, so the bank behind is no longer eroded** ← |
| **Creates a SLACK-WATER POCKET between successive groynes** | **The flow there is slow, so sediment DEPOSITS and the bank line is progressively rebuilt** ← |

> **The second action is the one that makes groynes such an economical form of protection: THE RIVER ITSELF BUILDS THE NEW BANK.**

> **Rather than armouring a long length of bank with pitching — expensive, and needing the whole length constructed at once — a series of groynes protects the same length with a fraction of the material, and the pockets between them silt up naturally over one or two flood seasons.**

> **So a groyne field is a structure that recruits the river's own sediment transport to do most of the work, which is why it is the preferred protection for a long eroding bank.**

**The types of groyne and their differing purposes:**

| Type | Orientation | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **REPELLING (deflecting)** | **Pointing UPSTREAM, at about 60-70° to the bank** | **Throws the current strongly away; the most effective for bank protection** ← |
| **ATTRACTING** | **Pointing DOWNSTREAM** | **Draws the current TOWARD the bank — used to hold a channel against a bank, as at a bridge or an intake** |
| **DEFLECTING** | **Roughly perpendicular** | Changes the flow direction locally without strongly repelling |
| **SEDIMENTING (silting)** | **Permeable — of piles, trees, bamboo or wire crates** | **Slows the flow and INDUCES DEPOSITION rather than deflecting** |
| **T-HEADED (hockey, Denehy)** | **With a head at the tip, parallel to the flow** | Protects its own nose and gives better bank line control |

> **The REPELLING and ATTRACTING distinction is worth fixing, because the orientation reverses the effect:**

> **A groyne pointing UPSTREAM repels; one pointing DOWNSTREAM attracts.**

> **So building a groyne the wrong way round on an eroding bank makes the erosion WORSE — it draws the attacking current onto the bank it was meant to protect.**

> **That is a genuine and documented failure, and it is why the orientation is not a detail.**

**The critical design consideration — SCOUR AT THE NOSE:**

> **A groyne obstructs the flow, and the flow accelerates around its NOSE, producing intense LOCAL SCOUR there.**

> **Scour depths at a groyne nose commonly reach TWO TO THREE TIMES the normal river scour depth.**

> **So the nose is the most vulnerable part of the structure and receives the heaviest protection:**

| Protection | Note |
|---|---|
| **A LAUNCHING APRON of loose stone around the nose** | **As the scour hole deepens, the apron stone SLIDES DOWN and armours the slope — it launches itself** ← |
| **A heavy stone or concrete-block nose** | Resists direct attack |
| **Sufficient apron VOLUME for the design scour depth** | **The apron must contain enough stone to cover the launched slope, or it exhausts itself and the nose fails** |

> **The LAUNCHING APRON is a genuinely elegant device and deserves explanation: rather than trying to prevent scour, the design ACCEPTS it and provides a reservoir of loose stone at the surface which falls into the scour hole as it forms, lining it.**

> **The apron thus builds its own protection to whatever depth the river scours, and it requires no underwater construction at all.**

> **Its failure mode is running out of stone — so the design quantity is computed from the anticipated scour depth, typically providing stone for a launched slope of 2:1 with a thickness of about 1.25 times the apron's laid thickness.**

> **Getting that quantity wrong is the commonest cause of groyne nose failure, and it is not recoverable once the flood is running.**

**The spacing of groynes in a field, since one groyne alone is rarely useful:**

| Rule of thumb | Value |
|---|---|
| **Spacing on a STRAIGHT reach** | **2 to 2.5 × the groyne length** |
| **Spacing on a CONCAVE (eroding, outer) bank** | **1.5 to 2 × the length — closer, because the attack is stronger** ← |
| **Spacing on a CONVEX bank** | **3 to 4 × the length** |

> **The spacing must be close enough that the deflected flow from one groyne does not return to the bank before reaching the next.**

> **Too widely spaced, and the river attacks the bank between them, outflanking the protection and eventually isolating each groyne as an island** — a common sight on inadequately designed works.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Option | Comment |
|---|---|
| **(a) Increase the bed slope** | **A groyne does not change the river's slope, which is set by its regime over long reaches. And increasing the slope would increase erosion, not reduce it** |
| **(c) Raise the flood level to reduce the discharge** | **Raising the flood level does not reduce the discharge — the water must still pass. It would increase the flooding upstream, which is a harm, not a purpose** |
| **(d) A traffic crossing** | **That is a CAUSEWAY. A groyne extends only part way across and carries no traffic** |

> **Option (c) contains a genuine misconception worth naming: an obstruction in a river does NOT reduce the discharge, because the discharge is determined by the catchment's runoff and must pass regardless.**

> **What an obstruction does is raise the upstream WATER LEVEL until the same discharge can get past** — which is the AFFLUX, and it is a cost of the structure rather than a benefit.

**The other river training works, for context:**

| Work | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **GUIDE BANKS (Bell's bunds)** | **Guide the river through a bridge or barrage waterway and prevent it outflanking the structure** |
| **MARGINAL BUNDS / embankments** | **Confine flood water and protect land from inundation** |
| **GROYNES / spurs** | **Protect a bank and rebuild a bank line** ← |
| **REVETMENT / pitching** | **Armour the bank face directly** |
| **Artificial CUT-OFF** | Shorten the course through a severe meander loop |
| **Bed bars, sills** | Control the bed level |
| **BIO-ENGINEERING — vegetation, live fascines, bamboo** | **Low-cost bank protection, well suited to Nepali conditions** |

> **BIO-ENGINEERING deserves particular mention for Nepal, because it fits the country's circumstances unusually well: it uses locally available material, needs no heavy plant or imported cement, can be built by community labour, and STRENGTHENS with time as the vegetation establishes.**

> **Its limitation is that it cannot withstand direct attack by a high-velocity flow, so it suits the upper parts of a bank, the pockets between groynes, and moderate reaches rather than the point of maximum attack.**

> **The sensible practice is to combine the two — hard protection where the current strikes, bio-engineering everywhere else** — which is both cheaper and more durable than either alone.

examTip.trick: **A groyne works two ways at once: DEFLECTS the current off the bank, and creates a slack pocket where sediment DEPOSITS** — so the river itself rebuilds the bank line.
examTip.trap: **A groyne pointing UPSTREAM repels; one pointing DOWNSTREAM ATTRACTS.** Building it the wrong way round draws the attacking current onto the bank it was meant to protect — a documented failure.
examTip.mnemonic: **Scour at the NOSE reaches 2-3 times the normal river scour**, and the LAUNCHING APRON handles it by accepting the scour: loose stone slides down and armours the hole as it forms. Its failure mode is running out of stone.

questions.stem: Using Lacey's relation, the normal scour depth for a river carrying a design discharge of 1000 m³/s in a bed material of silt factor 1.0 is:
questions.solution:
**4.7 m.**

**Lacey's normal scour depth relation:**

> **R = 0.47 (Q / f)^{1/3}**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **R** | **Normal scour depth (the regime hydraulic radius, measured below the highest flood level)** | to find |
| **Q** | **Design DISCHARGE in m³/s** | **1000** |
| **f** | **Lacey's silt factor** | **1.0** |

**The computation:**

> **R = 0.47 × (1000/1.0)^{1/3} = 0.47 × 10 = 4.7 m** ✓

> **The cube root of 1000 is exactly 10, which is what makes the arithmetic clean and confirms the intended path.**

> **Option (d) 9.4 m is exactly twice the answer — which is instructive, because 2R is a real design quantity: see the scour multipliers below.**

**The other form of the relation, and when each is used:**

| Form | Use |
|---|---|
| **R = 0.47 (Q/f)^{1/3}** | **Q is the TOTAL design discharge; the river is free to adjust its width — the UNCONSTRICTED case** ← |
| **R = 1.35 (q²/f)^{1/3}** | **q is the discharge per METRE WIDTH; the waterway is CONSTRICTED, as at a bridge or barrage** |

> **The distinction matters greatly in practice: where a bridge or a barrage FORCES the river through a width narrower than its natural regime width, the discharge per metre rises and the scour deepens.**

> **So the second form must be used wherever the waterway has been constricted, and using the first would UNDERESTIMATE the scour — the dangerous direction.**

> **Lacey's regime WIDTH for this river is P = 4.75√Q = 4.75 × 31.6 = 150 m.**

> **If a bridge confined it to 100 m, then q = 1000/100 = 10 m³/s per metre, and:**

> **R = 1.35 × (10²/1)^{1/3} = 1.35 × 4.64 = 6.27 m** — some 33 per cent deeper than the unconstricted value.

> **That is the price of constricting a river, expressed in metres of foundation depth.**

**The scour MULTIPLIERS, which is what the normal depth is actually used for:**

> **The normal scour depth R is a reference value. The DESIGN scour at a particular location is a MULTIPLE of it, depending on how severely the flow is disturbed there:**

| Location | Design scour depth |
|---|---|
| **A straight reach** | **1.0 to 1.25 R** |
| **A moderate bend** | **1.5 R** |
| **A severe bend** | **1.75 R** |
| **A RIGHT-ANGLED bend, or a severe swirl** | **2.0 R** ← this is the 9.4 m of option (d) |
| **NOSE of a groyne or a pier** | **2.0 to 2.75 R** |
| **Downstream of a barrage's impervious floor** | **1.25 to 1.75 R** |
| **UPSTREAM of the floor** | **1.25 to 1.5 R** |

> **So option (d) 9.4 m = 2R is the design scour at a right-angled bend or a groyne nose — a real and important figure, but not the NORMAL scour depth asked for.**

> **The option set therefore tests whether the candidate distinguishes the reference value from the multiplied design value.**

**What the scour depth is FOR — the foundation depth:**

> **Every structure founded in a river bed must have its foundation BELOW the anticipated scour, or the river will undermine it.**

| Structure | Foundation requirement |
|---|---|
| **Bridge PIER on an open foundation or well** | **Founded at least 1.33 R below the highest flood level, and a further GRIP LENGTH below the scour** |
| **Well foundation GRIP LENGTH** | **At least one third of the maximum scour depth BELOW the scour level** ← |
| **Barrage cut-off** | Below the anticipated scour at that location |
| **Groyne launching apron** | Stone quantity computed for the launched slope down to the scour depth |
| **Abutment** | Deeper than the pier, since the scour there is usually more severe |

> **The GRIP LENGTH requirement is the one worth understanding: a well foundation must not merely REACH the scour level but extend a third of the scour depth BEYOND it, so that the well is still gripped by undisturbed soil after the maximum scour has occurred.**

> **A foundation founded exactly AT the scour level would be standing on the floor of the scour hole with nothing holding it laterally — it would be free to tilt and would fail.**

> **So the design depth is the scour depth PLUS the grip, and scour underestimation propagates directly into an unsafe foundation.**

**Why bridge scour is the commonest cause of bridge failure — and it is:**

> **More bridges are lost to SCOUR than to any other cause — more than to earthquake, more than to overloading, more than to material deterioration.**

> **The reasons are worth setting out, because they explain why this apparently routine calculation deserves respect:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Scour occurs DURING a flood and refills AFTERWARD** | **The hole is invisible when the river falls, so inspection finds nothing wrong** ← |
| **It is cumulative over successive floods** | Each event deepens the general degradation |
| **The prediction is uncertain** | Empirical relations with considerable scatter |
| **Constriction and river training change the regime** | A bridge alters the river it crosses |
| **UPSTREAM sand mining and dam construction aggravate it** | **Sediment starvation makes a river degrade its bed** |

> **The FIRST row is the insidious feature: a scour hole forms at the peak of a flood, when the river is at its most energetic, and REFILLS with loose sediment as the flood recedes.**

> **So a diver inspecting the pier a month later finds the bed at its normal level and reports nothing amiss — while the pier has in fact been standing on a much shallower footing than anyone realises during each flood.**

> **That is why scour is designed for rather than inspected for, and why the depth calculation must be done properly at the outset.**

> **The SAND MINING point deserves emphasis in Nepal, where extraction from riverbeds is widespread and largely unregulated: removing sediment from a river starves it, and a starved river degrades its bed to recover its load — lowering the general bed level and exposing every foundation along the reach.**

> **Several bridge failures in the region are attributable to that mechanism, and it is a case where a structure is endangered by activity elsewhere in the river rather than by any defect of its own design.**

examTip.trick: **R = 0.47(Q/f)^{1/3} = 0.47 × 10 = 4.7 m**, since the cube root of 1000 is exactly 10.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) 9.4 m = 2R is the DESIGN scour at a right-angled bend or a groyne nose** — a real figure, but the question asks for the NORMAL scour depth. And where the waterway is CONSTRICTED, use R = 1.35(q²/f)^{1/3} instead, which gives a deeper value.
examTip.mnemonic: **A well foundation needs a GRIP LENGTH of at least one third of the scour depth BELOW the scour level** — founding exactly at it leaves the well standing in the hole with nothing holding it. And scour holes REFILL as a flood recedes, so inspection finds nothing wrong.

questions.stem: The principal purpose of a CANAL FALL is:
options: To lower the canal bed level and dissipate surplus energy where the ground slope is steeper than the canal bed slope
To measure the discharge flowing in the canal
To regulate the supply admitted to an offtaking distributary
To carry the canal across a natural drainage channel
questions.solution:
**To lower the canal bed and dissipate the surplus energy where the ground slope exceeds the canal bed slope.**

**Why falls are necessary:**

> **A canal's bed slope is fixed by HYDRAULIC requirements — typically 1 in 4,000 to 1 in 10,000, chosen to give a non-silting, non-scouring velocity.**

> **The NATURAL GROUND slope is fixed by the topography, and it is usually STEEPER.**

> **So as the canal runs, the ground falls away faster than the canal bed does, and the canal finds itself increasingly high above the ground — in ever deeper embankment.**

| Consequence of the divergence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Ever-increasing height of bank (filling)** | **Expensive earthwork, and a growing hazard if the bank breaches** ← |
| **Increasing seepage from a canal perched above the land** | Waterlogging alongside |
| **The canal's command becomes excessive** | It is far higher than the land it serves needs |
| **Bank stability becomes critical** | A high embankment on soft ground |

> **A CANAL FALL (or DROP) resolves it: at intervals, the canal bed is DROPPED abruptly through a structure, bringing it back close to the ground surface.**

> **The canal then continues at its proper hydraulic slope until the divergence has again accumulated enough to justify the next fall.**

> **So a canal on sloping country is a succession of gently sloping reaches separated by falls, and the falls' spacing is set by the difference between the two slopes and by the economics of the earthwork saved against the fall's cost.**

**The SECOND function, which is the engineering problem the structure must solve:**

> **Dropping the bed converts POTENTIAL energy into KINETIC energy.**

> **The water arrives at the bottom of the fall moving fast — supercritical — and if that energy is not destroyed it will SCOUR the canal bed downstream.**

> **So every fall incorporates an ENERGY DISSIPATION arrangement, usually a HYDRAULIC JUMP formed in a cistern (stilling basin) below the drop.**

| Dissipation device | Note |
|---|---|
| **A CISTERN in which a hydraulic jump forms** | **The standard method — a jump destroys energy efficiently** ← |
| **Baffle blocks, friction blocks** | Force and stabilise the jump in a shorter length |
| **A raised cistern lip or end sill** | Holds the tailwater to keep the jump located |
| **Roughened floor, dentated sill** | Additional turbulence |

> **The HYDRAULIC JUMP is the workhorse here and deserves a note: it is the abrupt transition from supercritical to subcritical flow, and it dissipates energy by intense turbulence — up to 70 or 80 per cent of the incoming energy in a strong jump.**

> **It is one of very few hydraulic phenomena that is DESIRED and deliberately engineered, because destroying energy is normally difficult.**

> **The design task is to ensure the jump forms WITHIN the paved cistern rather than beyond it — a jump that forms downstream of the protection scours the unlined bed and undermines the structure from below.**

> **Hence the cistern's depth and length are computed from the pre-jump and post-jump depths, with the cistern floor set low enough that the tailwater drowns the jump into position at all discharges.**

**The types of fall, in historical order, since they show the idea developing:**

| Type | Feature |
|---|---|
| **OGEE fall** | **A smooth ogee profile; efficient but the smooth curve does NOT dissipate energy well — scour downstream was a problem** |
| **Rapid fall** | A long sloping glacis; used for small drops |
| **Stepped / cascade fall** | A series of steps; dissipates on each |
| **Trapezoidal notch fall** | **Notches shaped so the upstream water level stays nearly constant over a range of discharge** ← |
| **VERTICAL DROP (Sarda type)** | **A raised crest with the water dropping into a cistern; simple and robust** |
| **GLACIS fall (Montague, inglis)** | **A sloping glacis with a jump on it; the standard modern form** |
| **Well type / cylinder fall** | For small drops in minor channels |
| **Baffle fall (Inglis)** | **A baffle wall forces the jump; efficient over a wide range of discharge** |

> **The TRAPEZOIDAL NOTCH fall is worth understanding because it addresses a genuine operating difficulty:**

> **A simple weir-crested fall has a discharge that varies as H^{3/2}, so a change in discharge changes the upstream water level considerably — which upsets every offtake upstream of the fall.**

> **A trapezoidal notch is shaped so that the depth-discharge relation matches the canal's own, keeping the upstream level nearly constant as the discharge varies.**

> **So the fall becomes hydraulically "transparent" to the reach above it, which is exactly what an irrigation system wants — the offtakes upstream continue to draw their proper share whatever the flow.**

**Why the other options are wrong — each names a different structure:**

| Option | The structure that does it |
|---|---|
| **(b) Measure the discharge** | **A METER FLUME, a standing wave flume, or a modular outlet. NOTE: a fall CAN be used as a meter incidentally — see below** |
| **(c) Regulate an offtake** | **A DISTRIBUTARY HEAD REGULATOR, or an outlet/module** |
| **(d) Cross a natural drainage** | **A CROSS-DRAINAGE work — aqueduct, syphon, super passage or level crossing** |

> **Option (b) deserves the qualification it gets, because a fall IS often used as a measuring structure.**

> **A fall whose crest forces critical flow has a unique depth-discharge relation, so a single gauge reading upstream gives the discharge.**

> **Combining the two functions is common and sensible — a METER FALL — since the structure exists anyway and the measurement costs only a gauge.**

> **But measurement is a SECONDARY function opportunistically added, not the reason the fall is built.** The question asks for the principal purpose, and that is to lower the bed.

**Where falls are located, since the choice is a real design decision:**

| Consideration | Preference |
|---|---|
| **Combine with a BRIDGE, a regulator or an offtake where possible** | **One structure, one set of foundations, one approach — a substantial saving** ← |
| **Locate where the ground gives a natural drop** | Minimises earthwork |
| **Just DOWNSTREAM of an offtake rather than upstream** | So the offtake draws from the higher, upstream level |
| **Avoid locating in deep filling** | Foundation and seepage difficulties |
| **Space them so the accumulated divergence justifies each** | The economic criterion |

> **COMBINING a fall with a bridge or a regulator is the most consequential of these: the works are then called a FALL-CUM-BRIDGE or FALL-CUM-REGULATOR, and the saving in foundations, wing walls and approach protection is considerable.**

> **It also concentrates the maintenance and the operating staff at fewer points along the canal, which matters as much in practice as the capital saving.**

> **That is a general lesson about canal structures: they are individually simple and collectively numerous, so the economy lies in combining them rather than in refining any one of them.**

examTip.trick: **A fall exists because the GROUND slope is steeper than the canal's hydraulic bed slope** — so the canal would otherwise end up in ever-deeper embankment. The fall drops the bed back to the ground.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) is a real SECONDARY function** — a fall forcing critical flow measures the discharge, and meter falls are common. But measurement is added opportunistically, not the reason it is built.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dropping the bed creates energy that must be DESTROYED, usually by a hydraulic jump in a cistern** — and the jump must form INSIDE the paved cistern, or it scours the unlined bed and undermines the structure. And combine falls with bridges or regulators wherever possible.

questions.stem: The most direct engineering measure for LOWERING a water table that has already risen into the root zone is:
options: Surface drains along the field boundaries
questions.solution:
**SUBSURFACE (tile) DRAINAGE.**

**Why subsurface drainage is the direct answer:**

> **The question asks specifically about LOWERING A WATER TABLE THAT HAS ALREADY RISEN.**

> **A subsurface drainage system — perforated pipes or tiles laid below the root zone, discharging to a collector and an outfall — intercepts the groundwater and CARRIES IT AWAY, drawing the water table down between the drains.**

> **It acts on the water table ITSELF, which is what the stem asks for.**

> **The other three options are all genuine and valuable measures, and each does something different:**

| Option | What it actually does |
|---|---|
| **(a) SURFACE drains** | **Remove PONDED SURFACE water and storm runoff. They do NOT lower a water table — the water table is below ground and a surface drain does not reach it** |
| **(b) LINING the canals** | **Attacks the CAUSE — the largest single source of the recharge that raised the table. Prevents further rise but does not lower what is already there** ← |
| **(c) BIO-DRAINAGE** | **Lowers the table by TRANSPIRATION — genuinely effective, but slow, limited in depth, and dependent on the trees establishing** |
| **(d) SUBSURFACE drainage** | ✓ **Acts directly on the water table** |

> **Option (b) is the most instructive distractor, because CANAL LINING is arguably the more IMPORTANT measure overall — it addresses the cause rather than the symptom.**

> **But it is PREVENTIVE, not CURATIVE: sealing the canals stops the water table rising further and lets it recede naturally over years, while subsurface drainage lowers it now.**

> **So the distinction the question draws is between treating the cause and treating the condition, and both belong in a real remedial programme.**

**How a subsurface drainage system works:**

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **FIELD (lateral) drains** | **Perforated pipes at 1.5-2.5 m depth, spaced by design; intercept the groundwater** |
| **ENVELOPE / filter around the pipe** | **Gravel or synthetic geotextile — prevents fine soil entering and clogging the pipe** ← essential |
| **COLLECTOR drains** | Carry the flow from the laterals |
| **Main drain / outfall** | Discharges to a natural drainage, a river, or a sump for pumping |
| **Manholes and inspection chambers** | Access for cleaning |
| **PUMPING station (where gravity outfall is impossible)** | Flat terrain often requires it |

> **The ENVELOPE is the component whose omission destroys the system: an unenveloped perforated pipe in a fine-grained soil silts up within a season or two, and once blocked it is essentially unrecoverable.**

> **So the filter is not an optional refinement but the difference between a working system and a buried expense.**

**The drain SPACING, which is the principal design calculation:**

> **The spacing is determined by the HOOGHOUDT equation for steady-state drainage:**

> **S² = (8 K d h + 4 K h²) / q**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **S** | **Drain SPACING** |
| **K** | **Hydraulic conductivity of the soil** |
| **d** | **Equivalent depth to the impermeable layer below the drains** |
| **h** | **Height of the water table midway between the drains, above the drain level** |
| **q** | **DRAINAGE COEFFICIENT — the design discharge per unit area** |

> **The dominant term is K, and note that S goes as √K — so the spacing depends on the SQUARE ROOT of the permeability.**

| Soil | Hydraulic conductivity | Typical drain spacing |
|---|---|---|
| **Coarse sand** | **High** | **50-100 m** |
| **Sandy loam** | **Moderate** | **25-50 m** |
| **Clay loam** | **Low** | **10-25 m** |
| **HEAVY CLAY** | **VERY LOW** | **5-15 m — often uneconomic** ← |

> **The last row is the honest limitation: in a heavy clay the required spacing is so close that the system's cost becomes prohibitive, and the drains discharge so slowly that they cannot cope with a rainfall event.**

> **So subsurface drainage suits soils of moderate to good permeability, and a heavy clay requires MOLE DRAINAGE, SUBSOILING or vertical drainage instead** — or must be accepted as poorly drained land.

> **Recognising where a technique does not apply is as much a part of the answer as knowing how it works.**

**VERTICAL DRAINAGE, since it is the main alternative:**

> **Instead of horizontal pipes, TUBEWELLS pump the groundwater down.**

| | **HORIZONTAL (tile) drainage** | **VERTICAL (tubewell) drainage** |
|---|---|---|
| **Method** | **Buried perforated pipes** | **Pumped wells** |
| **Capital cost** | **HIGH — extensive pipework** | Lower per hectare in permeable strata |
| **Running cost** | **Very low (gravity) or moderate (pumped outfall)** | **HIGH — continuous pumping energy** |
| **Water quality** | **Drainage water is often SALINE and must be disposed of** | **If the groundwater is FRESH, the pumped water is USABLE for irrigation** ← |
| **Suits** | Moderate permeability, saline groundwater | **Permeable aquifer with fresh groundwater** |
| **Reliability** | Passive, needs no power | Depends on power supply and maintenance |

> **The WATER QUALITY row is what usually decides between them, and it is worth dwelling on.**

> **Where the groundwater is FRESH, vertical drainage is doubly beneficial: the pumping lowers the water table AND supplies irrigation water, so the problem becomes the resource.**

> **That is CONJUNCTIVE USE, and it is the most elegant answer to waterlogging available: use groundwater in the dry season, which keeps the table down, and canal water in the monsoon.**

> **Where the groundwater is SALINE, pumping it produces a disposal problem instead — saline effluent that cannot be put on the land and may not be acceptable in a river.**

> **And that disposal difficulty is the unglamorous constraint that limits drainage schemes everywhere: the water has to go SOMEWHERE, and drainage water from a salinised area is, by definition, salty.**

**The DRAINAGE COEFFICIENT, since it sets the system's capacity:**

> **The drainage coefficient q is the rate at which the system must remove water, expressed as a depth per day over the whole area — typically 1 to 5 mm/day for irrigated agriculture.**

> **It is determined from the deep percolation from irrigation, the seepage from canals, and the rainfall to be drained.**

> **A larger coefficient requires closer spacing and a larger outfall, so it directly drives the cost — and it is therefore a design decision balancing capacity against expense rather than a value to be looked up.**

**And a note on the crop side, since drainage is not purely an engineering matter:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Choose SALT-TOLERANT crops for affected land** | **Barley, cotton, sugarbeet, date palm tolerate salinity; most vegetables and beans do not** |
| **LEACHING with an excess of good water** | **Washes salts down BELOW the root zone — but it REQUIRES a functioning drainage system, or it merely raises the table further** ← |
| **Gypsum application for sodic (alkali) soil** | Replaces exchangeable sodium with calcium |
| **Organic matter and green manuring** | Improves structure and permeability |

> **The LEACHING point is the crucial interdependence: reclaiming a saline soil requires flushing the salts downward with surplus water, and that surplus can only be got rid of by DRAINAGE.**

> **So leaching without drainage makes matters worse — it adds water to an already high water table and brings more salt up.**

> **Drainage must therefore come FIRST, and the reclamation of salinised irrigated land is an engineering task before it is an agronomic one.**

examTip.trick: **Subsurface (tile) drainage acts on the WATER TABLE itself.** Surface drains remove ponded water only; canal lining prevents further rise; bio-drainage is slow and shallow.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) canal lining is arguably the MORE important measure — it attacks the cause — but it is PREVENTIVE, not curative.** The stem asks about lowering a table that has already risen.
examTip.mnemonic: **Spacing goes as √K (Hooghoudt), so heavy clay needs 5-15 m spacing and is often uneconomic.** And LEACHING requires drainage FIRST — flushing salts down without a drain merely raises the table and brings more salt up.

questions.stem: In Nepal, the design discharge of a run-of-river hydropower plant is conventionally taken from the flow duration curve as:
options: Q40 — the flow available 40 % of the time
Q95 — the flow available 95 % of the time
Q10 — the flow available 10 % of the time
questions.solution:
**Q40 — the flow exceeded 40 per cent of the time.**

**What a FLOW DURATION CURVE is:**

> **A flow duration curve plots DISCHARGE against the PERCENTAGE OF TIME that discharge is EQUALLED OR EXCEEDED.**

> **It is constructed by ranking all the daily (or monthly) flows of the record from largest to smallest and plotting each against its exceedance percentage.**

> **The notation is universal: Q40 is the flow exceeded 40 per cent of the time, Q95 the flow exceeded 95 per cent of the time, and so on.**

> **Note the direction: a HIGHER subscript means a SMALLER flow, because a small flow is exceeded more often.**

| Notation | Meaning | Relative magnitude |
|---|---|---|
| **Q10** | **Exceeded only 10 % of the time — a HIGH flow** | Large |
| **Q40** | **Exceeded 40 % of the time** | ← the design flow |
| **Q50 (median)** | Exceeded half the time | Moderate |
| **Q95** | **Exceeded 95 % of the time — a LOW flow, nearly always available** | Small |
| **Q100** | **The absolute minimum recorded** | Smallest |

> **Option (c) Q10 is therefore a large flood-season flow, and designing for it would give a plant that ran at full output for only a tenth of the year — an extravagant use of capital.**

> **And option (b) Q95 is nearly the minimum flow, which would give a plant that almost never spilled but was far smaller than the river could support.**

**Why Q40 is the conventional choice — the economic reasoning:**

> **The design discharge determines the plant's INSTALLED CAPACITY, and the choice is a trade-off:**

| Design flow | Installed capacity | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **A LOW design flow (say Q80)** | **Small plant** | **The plant runs at full output most of the year, but SPILLS most of the monsoon flow — energy is thrown away** |
| **A HIGH design flow (say Q20)** | **Large plant** | **Captures the monsoon flow, but the expensive machinery stands idle or part-loaded for most of the year** |
| **Q40** | **The usual optimum** | **Full output for about 40 % of the year, part load for the rest — the best return on the capital** ← |

> **So Q40 is not a physical constant but an ECONOMIC OPTIMUM, established by experience on Nepali rivers with their strongly seasonal regime.**

> **The optimum shifts with circumstances: where energy is valuable and capital is cheap, a higher design flow is justified; where the tariff is low, a lower one.**

> **A proper feasibility study computes the energy and the cost for a range of design flows and selects the maximum net benefit** — and the answer generally lands somewhere between Q30 and Q50, which is why Q40 serves as the convention.

**The ENVIRONMENTAL FLOW deduction, which must not be forgotten:**

> **Nepal requires a minimum of 10 PER CENT OF THE MINIMUM MONTHLY AVERAGE FLOW to be released downstream of any diversion.**

> **So the flow available for generation is:**

> **Q_design = Q40 − Q_environmental**

> **The deduction is small in absolute terms but it bites hardest in the DRY SEASON, when the whole river may be little more than the environmental release plus a modest generating flow.**

> **That is why the environmental flow appears in the energy calculation as a permanent loss concentrated in exactly the months when energy is most valuable** — and why it must be included from the feasibility stage rather than discovered at approval.

**What the flow duration curve's SHAPE tells you — the diagnostic use:**

| Curve shape | Catchment character |
|---|---|
| **STEEP curve** | **Flashy response — little storage in the catchment; flows vary enormously; a small, rocky or steep basin** ← typical of Nepali hill catchments |
| **FLAT curve** | **Well-regulated — substantial groundwater or snowmelt storage sustains the flow; a good hydropower prospect** |
| **Flat at the LOW end specifically** | **A reliable dry-season base flow — the most valuable feature a run-of-river site can have** |

> **The LOW END of the curve is what matters most for a run-of-river scheme, and it is worth stating why:**

> **The plant's DRY-SEASON output is set by the low flows, and dry-season energy in Nepal is worth several times monsoon energy because that is when the system is short.**

> **So two rivers with the same mean annual flow can be very different prospects: one fed by snowmelt and deep groundwater with a sustained dry-season flow, and one draining a steep rocky basin that nearly dries out.**

> **The mean flow — option (d) — conceals exactly that distinction, which is why it is not used as a design flow.**

> **A river's ANNUAL AVERAGE is a poor descriptor of its usefulness, and the duration curve exists precisely to expose the distribution the average hides.**

**How the curve is obtained where there are no records — the usual Nepali situation:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **Gauged record at the site** | **Ideal, and rare** |
| **TRANSFER from a nearby gauged catchment by AREA RATIO** | **Q_site = Q_gauged × (A_site/A_gauged), sometimes with a rainfall correction** ← the common approach |
| **REGIONAL regression on catchment characteristics** | Area, elevation, rainfall, aspect |
| **WECS/DHM regional method (Nepal-specific)** | **Uses catchment area below 5000 m and below 3000 m elevation** |
| **Rainfall-runoff modelling** | Where rainfall records are better than flow records |
| **A short site record extended by correlation with a long nearby record** | Best practice where any site data exist |

> **The WECS/DHM method's use of the AREA BELOW 5000 m AND BELOW 3000 m is worth understanding, because it encodes a real physical insight:**

> **In a Himalayan catchment, the area above about 5000 m is largely snow and ice and contributes chiefly to the melt season, while the area below 3000 m generates the monsoon runoff.**

> **So the two elevation bands contribute differently through the year, and a regional formula that distinguishes them predicts the SEASONAL pattern far better than one using total area alone.**

> **That is a good example of a regional empirical method built on physical reasoning rather than pure statistics — and it is why it transfers reasonably well across Nepali basins while a formula fitted elsewhere would not.**

> **The honest caution remains that a transferred or regionalised flow estimate carries considerable uncertainty, and a scheme's viability computed from one should be tested against a range rather than a single figure.**

examTip.trick: **Q40 — the flow exceeded 40 % of the time.** A HIGHER subscript means a SMALLER flow, because a small flow is exceeded more often.
examTip.trap: **Q40 is an ECONOMIC optimum, not a physical constant** — it balances capturing monsoon flow against machinery standing idle. A proper study tests a range and generally lands between Q30 and Q50.
examTip.mnemonic: **The LOW end of the curve is what matters** — dry-season energy is worth several times monsoon energy in Nepal, which is why the mean annual flow (option d) is useless: it conceals exactly the distribution the curve exists to show.

questions.stem: A hydropower plant has a design discharge of 10 m³/s, a net head of 100 m and an overall efficiency of 85 %. Its power output is:
questions.solution:
**8.34 MW.**

**The power equation:**

> **P = ρ g Q H η**   or equivalently   **P = 9.81 Q H η  (in kW, with Q in m³/s and H in m)**

**The computation:**

> **P = 9.81 × 10 × 100 × 0.85**

> **= 9810 × 0.85**

> **= 8338.5 kW = 8.34 MW** ✓

**The form worth memorising, because it removes every unit question:**

> **P (kW) = 9.81 × Q (m³/s) × H (m) × η**

> **The 9.81 is γ_water in kN/m³, so the product Q × H × γ comes out directly in kilowatts:**

> **[m³/s] × [m] × [kN/m³] = kN·m/s = kJ/s = kW** ✓

> **A useful shortcut for mental estimation: taking g ≈ 10, P ≈ 10 QHη kW — which here gives 8500 kW, within 2 per cent.**

> **Or even more simply: 1 m³/s falling 1 m produces about 10 kW gross, and about 8.5 kW after typical losses.** That single fact lets any scheme's order of magnitude be checked instantly.

**Why the distractors are placed where they are:**

| Option | Origin |
|---|---|
| **(a) 9.81 MW** | **The GROSS power, with the efficiency OMITTED: 9.81 × 10 × 100 = 9810 kW** ← the designed trap |
| **(b) 10.0 MW** | **The same with g taken as 10 and no efficiency** |
| **(c) 6.67 MW** | Roughly the value with an efficiency of 0.68, or a mis-set product |
| **(d) 8.34 MW** | ✓ |

> **Option (a) is the important one: forgetting the efficiency OVERSTATES the output by about 18 per cent, and in the direction that flatters a project's economics.**

> **That is worth naming as a professional hazard rather than merely an arithmetic slip: an optimistic power figure at the feasibility stage propagates into the tariff, the loan and the whole financial case.**

**Where the OVERALL efficiency of 85 per cent comes from — the chain:**

| Component | Typical efficiency |
|---|---|
| **TURBINE** | **88-94 % (a modern Pelton or Francis at design point)** |
| **GENERATOR** | **95-98 %** |
| **Speed increaser / gearbox, if fitted** | **97-98 %** |
| **Transformer** | **98-99 %** |
| **OVERALL (product)** | **About 82-88 %** ← 85 % is a fair design figure |

> **Note that the efficiencies MULTIPLY, so each stage's loss compounds — which is why a gearbox is avoided where a direct-coupled machine is possible.**

> **And note that the 85 per cent applies at the DESIGN POINT. At part load every machine is less efficient, and the shape of that part-load curve is a major consideration in turbine choice:**

| Turbine | Part-load behaviour |
|---|---|
| **PELTON (multi-jet)** | **EXCELLENT — jets can be shut off one by one, so efficiency stays high down to 20 % load** ← |
| **KAPLAN (double regulated)** | **EXCELLENT — flat curve from about 40 % load** |
| **FRANCIS** | **Falls off below about 50 % load** |
| **Propeller (fixed blade)** | **POOR — narrow efficient band** |

> **For a Nepali run-of-river plant, whose flow varies from the monsoon down to a small fraction in the dry season, PART-LOAD efficiency matters as much as peak efficiency.**

> **A machine with a flat curve generates useful energy through the dry months; one with a peaky curve does not** — and that is why multi-jet Pelton units and multiple smaller machines in parallel are so common in Nepal.

**GROSS against NET head, since the stem specifies net:**

| Head | Definition |
|---|---|
| **GROSS head** | **The full elevation difference between the intake water level and the tailwater level** |
| **NET (effective) head** | **Gross head MINUS all the hydraulic losses in the waterway** ← what the turbine actually sees |

> **The losses deducted:**

| Loss | Note |
|---|---|
| **Trash rack loss at the intake** | Small, unless blocked |
| **Friction in the headrace canal or tunnel** | **Often the largest single loss in a long conveyance** |
| **Losses at the settling basin, forebay, transitions** | Entry, exit, bends |
| **FRICTION in the PENSTOCK** | **Governed by the penstock diameter — an economic choice** ← |
| **Bend, valve and bifurcation losses** | Minor individually, appreciable in total |

> **The PENSTOCK DIAMETER is the classic optimisation in this chain:**

> **A LARGER penstock costs more in steel but loses less head, so it generates more energy for the whole life of the plant.**

> **The ECONOMIC DIAMETER minimises the sum of the pipe cost and the capitalised value of the energy lost to friction.**

> **A common rule of thumb is to design for a total head loss of about 4 to 8 per cent of the gross head** — but the true optimum depends on the steel price and the tariff, and it should be computed rather than assumed.

> **Note how the fifth-power law from pipe flow bites here: h_f ∝ 1/D⁵ at constant discharge, so a modest increase in diameter buys a large reduction in loss — which usually pushes the optimum toward a larger pipe than intuition suggests.**

**And the ENERGY, since power alone is not what a plant sells:**

> **Annual energy = P × 8760 × plant factor**

> **For this plant at a plant factor of 60 per cent:**

> **E = 8.34 × 8760 × 0.60 = 43,835 MWh = 43.8 GWh per year**

> **That is the number the financial case rests on — not the 8.34 MW nameplate — because revenue comes from energy delivered and not from capacity installed.**

> **Which is why a plant with a lower capacity and a better dry-season flow can be worth more than a larger one on a flashier river**, and why the flow duration curve rather than the peak flow governs a scheme's value.

examTip.trick: **P (kW) = 9.81 Q H η = 9.81 × 10 × 100 × 0.85 = 8338 kW = 8.34 MW.** Worth carrying: 1 m³/s falling 1 m gives about 10 kW gross, 8.5 kW net.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 9.81 MW omits the efficiency** — an 18 % overstatement, and in the direction that flatters a project's economics. That is a professional hazard, not just an arithmetic slip.
examTip.mnemonic: **Efficiencies MULTIPLY through turbine, generator, gearbox and transformer** — and the 85 % applies only at the DESIGN POINT. For a Nepali river, PART-LOAD efficiency matters as much, which is why multi-jet Peltons (efficient to 20 % load) are so common.

questions.stem: The ratio of the AVERAGE load to the PEAK load over a given period is called the:
questions.solution:
**The LOAD FACTOR.**

**The factors that describe a load, defined precisely:**

| Factor | Definition | Property of |
|---|---|---|
| **LOAD factor** | **Average load / PEAK load** ← | **The DEMAND** |
| **PLANT (capacity) factor** | **Average load / INSTALLED CAPACITY** | **The PLANT** |
| **UTILISATION factor** | **Maximum load actually reached / installed capacity** | **How fully the plant is ever used** |
| **DEMAND factor** | **Maximum demand / total CONNECTED load** | The consumer installation |
| **DIVERSITY factor** | **Sum of individual maximum demands / the maximum demand of the whole group** | **The GROUP of consumers** |

> **And the relation between the first three:**

> **PLANT factor = LOAD factor × UTILISATION factor**

> **They coincide only when the peak load equals the installed capacity — that is, when the plant is exactly sized to its peak demand.**

**Why the LOAD factor and the PLANT factor are constantly confused — and how to keep them apart:**

> **BOTH have the AVERAGE LOAD as their numerator. The difference is entirely in the DENOMINATOR:**

> **LOAD factor divides by the PEAK LOAD — a property of the demand, so it describes the SHAPE of the load curve.**

> **PLANT factor divides by the INSTALLED CAPACITY — a property of the plant, so it describes how hard the machinery is worked.**

> **The practical test: if a question gives you the INSTALLED CAPACITY, it wants the plant factor. If it gives you the PEAK DEMAND, it wants the load factor.**

> **The data supplied identify which is intended, which is a reliable way through this family of questions.**

**What a LOAD FACTOR of a given value tells you:**

| Load factor | Character of the demand |
|---|---|
| **Near 1.0** | **A FLAT load — nearly constant demand. An industrial plant on continuous shifts, or a large aggregated system** |
| **0.5-0.7** | **A typical urban system** |
| **0.2-0.4** | **A PEAKY load — a short sharp peak with low demand otherwise. A residential area, or a village with evening lighting load** ← |

> **A HIGH load factor is genuinely GOOD, and this is the case where "higher is better" really does hold:**

| Consequence of a high load factor | Note |
|---|---|
| **The generating and transmission capacity is used efficiently** | **The same peak capacity delivers more energy** ← |
| **The cost per unit of energy FALLS** | Fixed costs are spread over more units |
| **Less spare capacity is needed** | Investment goes further |
| **Generating plant runs nearer its efficient point** | Better fuel or water use |

> **The whole business of LOAD MANAGEMENT is aimed at raising the load factor: off-peak tariffs, time-of-day metering, interruptible industrial supply, and encouraging night-time loads.**

> **A utility that can flatten its load curve avoids building generating capacity — which is why such measures are pursued even though they reduce peak-hour revenue.**

**The DIVERSITY factor, which is the most interesting of the set:**

> **Diversity factor = (sum of individual maximum demands) / (maximum demand of the group)**

> **It is always GREATER THAN OR EQUAL TO 1, and its physical basis is that consumers do NOT all reach their individual peaks at the same instant.**

> **A hundred houses each with a 5 kW maximum demand do not together demand 500 kW, because they cook, light, heat and wash at different times.**

> **The group maximum might be 150 kW, giving a diversity factor of 500/150 = 3.3.**

> **Which has an important design consequence: a distribution transformer, a feeder or a generating station is sized for the GROUP maximum, not for the sum of the individuals.**

> **Ignoring diversity would oversize every element of the system by a factor of three or more — an enormous waste.**

> **And note that diversity INCREASES with the number of consumers, because a larger group averages out more: which is one of the fundamental economies of an interconnected grid over isolated supply.**

**Why a large interconnected system is inherently more efficient — the point all these factors make together:**

| Effect of interconnection | Note |
|---|---|
| **Greater DIVERSITY** | **Peaks of different areas and consumer types do not coincide, so the combined peak is less than the sum** ← |
| **Higher LOAD FACTOR** | The aggregate load curve is flatter than any component's |
| **Less RESERVE capacity needed** | One large reserve serves many areas |
| **Cheaper plant can be dispatched first** | Merit-order operation across the whole system |
| **Different SEASONAL patterns can be exchanged** | **Nepal's monsoon surplus against India's summer deficit — the argument for cross-border trade** |

> **The last row is the practical significance for Nepal: the country's hydropower is strongly seasonal, and interconnection lets a monsoon surplus be exported and a dry-season deficit imported.**

> **That converts a problem of storage — expensive and physically difficult — into a problem of transmission and trade, which is far cheaper.**

> **So a transmission line to a neighbouring system performs, in economic terms, part of the function of a storage reservoir** — and at a small fraction of the cost and the environmental consequence.

> **Which is why cross-border transmission capacity features so prominently in Nepal's energy planning, and why an isolated national grid would make the country's hydropower far less valuable than it is.**

examTip.trick: **LOAD factor = average ÷ PEAK LOAD (a property of the demand). PLANT factor = average ÷ INSTALLED CAPACITY (a property of the plant).** Both share the numerator; only the denominator differs.
examTip.trap: **The data tell you which is wanted:** given the INSTALLED CAPACITY, it is the plant factor; given the PEAK DEMAND, the load factor. And plant factor = load factor × utilisation factor.
examTip.mnemonic: **DIVERSITY factor ≥ 1 always** — a hundred houses with 5 kW each do not demand 500 kW, because they peak at different times. Ignoring it oversizes every transformer and feeder threefold, and it grows with the number of consumers — the basic economy of a grid.

questions.stem: The power that a hydropower plant can supply reliably for practically the whole year, based on the minimum available flow, is called:
questions.solution:
**FIRM or PRIMARY power.**

**The classification of a plant's power:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **FIRM (primary) power** | **The power available for practically 100 % of the time, based on the MINIMUM flow (or on a high exceedance such as Q95)** ← |
| **SECONDARY (surplus) power** | **Power available only for PART of the year, when the flow exceeds the minimum** |
| **Total power** | Firm plus secondary |
| **INSTALLED CAPACITY** | **The nameplate rating of the machines — the maximum the plant can produce at any moment** |
| **PEAK power** | The output during the system's peak demand hours |

> **Option (d) INSTALLED CAPACITY is the designed distractor, because it is the figure most often quoted about a plant — and it is the LEAST informative about reliability.**

> **A plant's installed capacity says what it CAN produce at its best moment. Its firm power says what it can be RELIED UPON to produce.**

> **For a run-of-river plant in Nepal those two figures can differ by a factor of five or more.**

**Why the distinction matters commercially — and it matters a great deal:**

> **FIRM power and SECONDARY power are worth quite different amounts:**

| | **FIRM power** | **SECONDARY power** |
|---|---|---|
| **Availability** | **Always** | **Only in the wet season** |
| **Can it be relied upon in system planning?** | **YES — it counts toward the system's dependable capacity** ← | **NO — the system must have other capacity for when it is absent** |
| **Value per unit** | **HIGH** | **LOW — the system may not even need it, since everyone else has surplus at the same time** |
| **Typical contractual treatment** | A capacity payment plus an energy payment | Energy payment only, at a lower rate, sometimes curtailable |

> **The second row is the crux: a utility planning its system must be able to count on the capacity it has, because it must meet the peak demand on the worst day.**

> **Secondary power cannot be counted, because it is absent precisely in the dry season when the system is tightest.**

> **So firm power is what a hydropower plant genuinely contributes to a system's adequacy, and it is what a power purchase agreement pays a premium for.**

> **Which explains a fact that surprises people: a smaller plant with a better dry-season flow can be worth MORE than a larger plant on a flashier river, even though the larger one produces more annual energy.**

**Why Nepal's plants have such a low ratio of firm to installed power:**

> **Nepal's rivers are strongly SEASONAL. A typical Himalayan tributary's monsoon flow is five to twenty times its dry-season flow.**

> **A run-of-river plant sized on Q40 therefore has a dry-season flow far below its design discharge:**

| Season | Flow | Output |
|---|---|---|
| **Monsoon (June-September)** | **At or above the design discharge** | **FULL output; surplus spilled** |
| **Post-monsoon (October-December)** | **Falling** | **Declining output** |
| **DRY SEASON (January-May)** | **A small fraction of the design flow** | **20-35 % of installed capacity, or less** ← |

> **So the FIRM power of a Nepali run-of-river plant is commonly 20 to 35 per cent of its installed capacity, and the country as a whole has a monsoon surplus and a dry-season deficit from the same installed base.**

> **That is Nepal's central energy problem stated in the language of this question, and it has three possible answers:**

| Solution | Note |
|---|---|
| **STORAGE projects** | **Carry monsoon water into the dry season — the fundamental answer, and the hardest to build** ← |
| **PEAKING run-of-river (PROR)** | **Daily storage only; shifts energy within the day, not between seasons** |
| **INTERCONNECTION and trade** | **Export the monsoon surplus, import in the dry season — the cheapest and fastest option** |
| Demand-side management | Shift industrial load to the wet season |

> **The reason STORAGE is described as fundamental is that it is the only one of these that actually creates dry-season energy from Nepal's own water.**

> **Interconnection is cheaper and quicker but it makes the country dependent on a neighbour's surplus at exactly the season when that neighbour is also short.**

> **PROR does not help at all across seasons — its pond empties overnight, not across months — which is a distinction frequently blurred in public discussion and worth being precise about.**

**How firm power is computed, since the definition needs a convention:**

> **"Practically the whole year" must be given a number, and practice varies:**

| Basis | Note |
|---|---|
| **The absolute MINIMUM recorded flow** | **The strictest definition; gives the lowest firm power** |
| **Q95 (exceeded 95 % of the time)** | **A common practical convention** ← |
| **Q90 or Q100 depending on the contract** | Negotiated |
| **The minimum MONTHLY average flow** | Used in some Nepali studies |

> **And in every case the ENVIRONMENTAL FLOW must be deducted first, since that water cannot be used for generation.**

> **The deduction is proportionally most severe in the dry season, which means it falls almost entirely on the FIRM power — the most valuable part of the plant's output.**

> **So the environmental release, though modest in annual volume, reduces the plant's commercially valuable firm capacity disproportionately** — a point worth understanding, since it explains why the requirement is contested and why it must be built into the financial model from the start rather than added later.

**A worked illustration, to make the concept concrete:**

> **Take a plant with a design discharge of 10 m³/s on 100 m net head, η = 0.85, so an installed capacity of 8.34 MW.**

> **If the dry-season available flow after the environmental release is 2.5 m³/s:**

> **Firm power = 9.81 × 2.5 × 100 × 0.85 = 2085 kW ≈ 2.1 MW**

> **Ratio of firm to installed power = 2.1/8.34 = 25 per cent.**

> **So a plant advertised as "8.34 MW" can be relied upon for about 2 MW — and both figures are true statements about the same plant.**

> **Knowing which one a given context means is the practical value of this distinction.**

examTip.trick: **FIRM (primary) power is what the plant can be RELIED upon to produce, from the minimum flow — commonly taken at Q95.** Secondary power is the wet-season surplus.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) installed capacity is the most-quoted figure and the LEAST informative about reliability.** For a Nepali run-of-river plant, firm power is typically only 20-35 % of it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Firm power counts toward a system's dependable capacity; secondary power cannot, because it is absent exactly when the system is tightest.** Which is why a smaller plant with a better dry-season flow can be worth more than a larger one on a flashier river.

questions.stem: The type of spillway most commonly provided in a concrete gravity dam is the:
questions.solution:
**The OGEE or OVERFLOW spillway.**

**Why the ogee suits a concrete gravity dam:**

> **A concrete gravity dam is already a massive concrete structure spanning the valley.**

> **Shaping part of its crest into an ogee profile and letting the flood pass OVER the dam itself requires no separate structure at all — the spillway IS the dam.**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **No separate structure needed** | **The most economical arrangement — the dam does both jobs** ← |
| **High discharge capacity for a given crest length** | The ogee is a very efficient weir profile |
| **The flow follows the profile closely** | **Minimising negative pressures and hence cavitation** |
| **Energy dissipated in a stilling basin at the toe** | Where the dam's own foundation already is |
| **Simple, robust, no moving parts (if ungated)** | Reliable when a flood arrives |

> **The contrast with an EARTH or ROCKFILL dam is the point: such a dam CANNOT be overtopped — flowing water would erode and breach it within hours.**

> **So an embankment dam must have its spillway placed AWAY from the dam body, in a separate excavated channel — a CHUTE or SIDE-CHANNEL spillway, usually in a flank or a saddle.**

> **That is why option (b) is a real and correct answer to a different question: the chute spillway is the characteristic arrangement for an EMBANKMENT dam.**

**The ogee profile itself, since its shape is not arbitrary:**

> **The ogee's crest is shaped to follow the LOWER NAPPE of a free jet issuing from a sharp-crested weir at the design head.**

> **The consequence is elegant: at the design head, the water follows the profile with ATMOSPHERIC pressure everywhere on the surface.**

| Operating head | Pressure on the crest | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **AT the design head** | **Atmospheric — the ideal condition** ← |
| **BELOW the design head** | **POSITIVE pressure — the flow presses onto the crest; safe but slightly less efficient** |
| **ABOVE the design head** | **NEGATIVE pressure — the flow tends to separate; risk of CAVITATION damage** |

> **So the profile is designed for a chosen head, and exceeding it substantially invites cavitation.**

> **The discharge equation:  Q = C L H^{3/2}**, with C ≈ 2.2 in SI for a well-designed ogee — much higher than the 1.5 to 1.7 of a broad-crested weir, which is the measure of the profile's efficiency.

> **CAVITATION on spillway surfaces is a real and destructive phenomenon: irregularities in the concrete cause local low pressures, vapour cavities form and collapse, and the concrete is progressively eroded — sometimes to the point of exposing and destroying the foundation.**

> **The remedies are careful surface tolerances, AERATION SLOTS that introduce air into the boundary layer, and avoiding operation far above the design head.**

**The other spillway types and where each belongs:**

| Type | Description | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **OGEE / overflow** | **Over the dam crest, on an ogee profile** | **CONCRETE gravity and arch dams** ← |
| **CHUTE (trough)** | **An open channel down a flank, away from the dam** | **EARTH and ROCKFILL dams; wide valleys** |
| **SIDE CHANNEL** | Crest along one side of a channel running roughly parallel to it | Narrow gorges where crest length is scarce |
| **SHAFT (morning glory)** | **A circular crest discharging into a vertical shaft and a tunnel** | **Where there is no room for a surface spillway; narrow gorges** |
| **SIPHON** | **A closed conduit that primes automatically and discharges at full bore** | **AUTOMATIC operation over a very narrow range of level** |
| **Tunnel / conduit** | Through an abutment | Steep, narrow sites |
| **Emergency / fuse plug** | **A deliberately erodible section that washes out in an extreme flood** | A last-resort safeguard |

> **The SHAFT spillway has a characteristic and important limitation worth knowing: its capacity does NOT continue to grow with the head.**

> **At low heads it behaves as a circular weir and its discharge rises with H^{3/2}. But once the shaft "drowns" — the throat becoming the control — it behaves as an orifice and then as a full pipe, and further rise in reservoir level adds very little discharge.**

> **So a shaft spillway can be dangerously non-conservative in an extreme flood: exactly when more capacity is needed, it stops providing any.**

> **Which is why shaft spillways are usually provided with an auxiliary or emergency spillway alongside.**

> **The SIPHON spillway shares the same fault in an even sharper form: it is either primed and discharging at full capacity, or unprimed and discharging nothing, with an unstable range between where it "hunts" — priming and breaking repeatedly, causing surges downstream and vibration in the structure.**

> **Its virtue is entirely automatic operation with no gates and no staff, holding the reservoir within a narrow band; its vices are the hunting, its vulnerability to blockage by debris, and its fixed capacity.**

**Why the spillway is the most safety-critical part of a dam:**

> **DAM FAILURE STATISTICS put OVERTOPPING at or near the top of the causes — commonly around a third of all failures of embankment dams.**
