> **The chain is short and unforgiving: a flood larger than the spillway can pass raises the reservoir above the dam crest, water flows over an embankment not designed for it, erosion begins, and a breach follows within hours.**

| Contributing failure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Spillway capacity underestimated** | **The design flood was too small — an estimation problem** |
| **Spillway BLOCKED by debris or a landslide** | **Trees, ice and slope failures have all done it** ← |
| **Gates failed to open** | Power failure, mechanical failure, no operator present |
| **Approach channel silted or obstructed** | Capacity lost gradually and invisibly |

> **The BLOCKAGE case deserves emphasis in the Himalayan context: a landslide into the reservoir or across the spillway approach is entirely plausible in Nepal, and it can remove the spillway's capacity at exactly the moment — a heavy monsoon — when it is needed.**

> **Which is the argument for an UNGATED spillway wherever the hydrology permits, and for an emergency or fuse-plug spillway as a second line of defence.**

> **An ungated ogee has no machinery to fail, no power supply to lose and no operator to be absent — and in a country where a flood may arrive at night in a monsoon with the access road washed out, that reliability is worth more than the storage a gated crest would add.**

examTip.trick: **A concrete dam can be overtopped safely, so the OGEE spillway is formed in the dam crest itself** — no separate structure. An EMBANKMENT dam cannot be overtopped, so it needs a CHUTE spillway away from the dam body.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) chute is the correct answer for an EARTH or ROCKFILL dam** — the distinction is whether the dam can take water over it.
examTip.mnemonic: **The ogee follows the lower nappe of a free jet, so at the DESIGN head the pressure is atmospheric** — above it, negative pressure risks CAVITATION. And SHAFT and SIPHON spillways stop gaining capacity once drowned or primed, so they need an emergency spillway alongside.

questions.stem: The highest level to which water is normally stored in a reservoir during operation, and to which the top of the live storage corresponds, is the:
questions.solution:
**The FULL RESERVOIR LEVEL (FRL).**

**The reservoir levels, from the bottom up:**

| Level | Definition |
|---|---|
| **River bed level** | The natural bed at the dam |
| **MINIMUM DRAWDOWN LEVEL (MDDL)** | **The lowest level to which the reservoir may be drawn in operation — the top of the DEAD storage and the bottom of the LIVE storage** |
| **FULL RESERVOIR LEVEL (FRL)** | **The HIGHEST level to which the reservoir is normally filled — the top of the LIVE storage** ← |
| **MAXIMUM WATER LEVEL (MWL) / highest flood level** | **The level reached TEMPORARILY while the design flood is being passed — the top of the SURCHARGE storage** |
| **TOP OF DAM** | MWL plus freeboard for waves and settlement |

> **And the storage zones they bound:**

| Storage | Between |
|---|---|
| **DEAD storage** | **Bed level and MDDL — reserved for sediment; cannot be drawn** |
| **LIVE (useful) storage** | **MDDL and FRL — the working volume** ← |
| **SURCHARGE storage** | **FRL and MWL — TEMPORARY, during a flood only** |

> **Option (b) MAXIMUM WATER LEVEL is the designed distractor, and it is a real and important level — but it is reached only TRANSIENTLY while a flood passes, and the water above FRL cannot be retained because the spillway will discharge it.**

> **That is the precise distinction: FRL is the highest level the reservoir is PERMITTED TO HOLD; MWL is the highest level it will momentarily REACH.**

**Why FRL and the spillway crest are related but not the same:**

> **Option (c) CREST LEVEL invites the assumption that the spillway crest is at FRL, and for an UNGATED spillway that is essentially true.**

| Spillway | Relation of crest to FRL |
|---|---|
| **UNGATED (free overflow)** | **The crest IS at FRL — water above the crest simply flows away** |
| **GATED** | **The crest is BELOW FRL, and FRL is at the top of the closed gates** ← |

> **The gated arrangement is what makes gates worth their cost: storage is gained in the depth between the spillway crest and the gate top, and that depth can be very valuable.**

> **A 5 m gate on a spillway 200 m wide over a reservoir of 50 km² area stores 250 million cubic metres in that band alone.**

> **The price is the machinery, the operating staff and the risk that the gates fail to open when a flood arrives — which returns to the reliability argument for ungated spillways.**

**Why the FRL is such a consequential decision in a project:**

> **The FRL determines almost everything about a storage project:**

| Determined by FRL | Note |
|---|---|
| **The LIVE STORAGE, and hence the firm power and the irrigable area** | **The project's whole benefit** ← |
| **The AREA SUBMERGED** | **Land, forest, villages, roads, cultural sites** |
| **The number of people DISPLACED** | **Usually the binding political constraint** ← |
| **The dam height, and hence its cost** | Cost rises faster than height |
| **The head available for generation** | — |

> **The submergence and displacement consequences are what make the FRL decision political as much as technical, and it is worth being clear about the trade:**

> **RAISING the FRL by a few metres can add disproportionate storage, because a reservoir is widest at the top — the area-capacity curve is steepest there.**

> **But the same few metres may submerge a village, a road or a stretch of valley floor that is the best agricultural land in the area — because valley floors are where people live and farm.**

> **So the marginal storage gained at the top of a reservoir is cheap in dam terms and expensive in human terms**, and the FRL is set where those two curves cross rather than where the engineering optimum alone would place it.

> **That is a genuinely difficult judgement and it is not an engineering calculation, though engineering must supply the numbers on which it is made.**

**The AREA-CAPACITY curves, which are the tool for all of this:**

> **Two curves are prepared from the topographic survey:**

| Curve | Plots |
|---|---|
| **ELEVATION-AREA** | **Water surface area against elevation** |
| **ELEVATION-CAPACITY** | **Cumulative volume against elevation — the integral of the first** |

> **From them the storage between any two levels is read directly, and they are the basis of every reservoir computation: flood routing, yield analysis, sedimentation studies, and the FRL decision itself.**

> **They must be REVISED periodically over a reservoir's life, because sedimentation changes them: the dead storage fills and the curves shift upward.**

> **A reservoir operated for decades on its original curves is being managed on data that no longer describe it** — and repeat bathymetric surveys are the only way to know how much storage actually remains.

> **In a Himalayan reservoir with its very high sediment yield, that re-survey is not a formality: the loss of capacity can be several per cent per decade.**

**FLOOD ROUTING through the reservoir, since it is what fixes MWL:**

> **The MWL is not chosen but COMPUTED, by routing the design flood through the reservoir and its spillway:**

| Input | Note |
|---|---|
| **The design flood HYDROGRAPH** | Inflow against time |
| **The reservoir's ELEVATION-CAPACITY curve** | How much the reservoir absorbs per metre of rise |
| **The spillway's DISCHARGE-ELEVATION relation** | How much the spillway passes per metre of head |
| **The starting reservoir level (usually FRL)** | The conservative assumption |

> **The routing solves the continuity equation step by step — inflow minus outflow equals the rate of change of storage — and yields the peak reservoir level and the peak outflow.**

> **The essential result of any routing is ATTENUATION: the peak OUTFLOW is always LESS than the peak INFLOW, because the reservoir stores part of the flood volume while the peak passes.**

> **That attenuation is a genuine flood-control benefit of a storage reservoir, and it accrues even to a project built for power or irrigation.**

> **And it explains why a reservoir kept deliberately BELOW FRL during the flood season provides much greater flood protection — the empty space absorbs more of the peak.**

> **Which is a real operating conflict: flood control wants the reservoir low before a flood, and power and irrigation want it full.** Resolving that conflict is what a reservoir operating rule curve exists to do.

examTip.trick: **FRL is the highest level the reservoir is PERMITTED to HOLD; MWL is the highest level it momentarily REACHES while passing the design flood.** Live storage lies between MDDL and FRL.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) crest level equals FRL only for an UNGATED spillway.** With gates, the crest is BELOW FRL and the gained storage between crest and gate top is what makes gates worth their cost.
examTip.mnemonic: **A reservoir is widest at the top, so raising FRL a few metres adds disproportionate storage — and submerges the valley floor where people live and farm.** That is why the FRL decision is political as well as technical.

questions.stem: The settling basin of a high-head Pelton turbine plant is normally designed to remove suspended particles larger than about:
questions.solution:
**About 0.2 mm.**

**The design particle sizes by turbine type:**

| Turbine and head | Particle size to be removed |
|---|---|
| **PELTON, high head (above ~200 m)** | **0.15-0.2 mm** ← |
| **Francis, medium head** | **0.2-0.3 mm** |
| **Kaplan, low head** | **0.3-0.5 mm** |

> **The pattern: THE HIGHER THE HEAD, THE FINER THE PARTICLE THAT MUST BE REMOVED.**

**Why higher head demands finer removal — the reason is the substance of the question:**

> **Erosion damage to a turbine depends on the IMPACT VELOCITY of the particles, and that velocity is set by the head:**

> **v = √(2gH)**

| Head | Jet velocity | Relative erosive power |
|---|---|---|
| **20 m (Kaplan)** | **19.8 m/s** | **1** |
| **100 m (Francis)** | **44.3 m/s** | — |
| **400 m (Pelton)** | **88.6 m/s** | — |

> **And erosion rate varies roughly as the CUBE of the impact velocity — some references use exponents from 2.5 to 3.5.**

> **Taking the cube: (88.6/19.8)³ = 4.47³ = 89.**

> **So the same sediment is roughly NINETY TIMES more erosive at 400 m head than at 20 m.**

> **That single number explains the whole design practice: a high-head plant cannot tolerate what a low-head plant shrugs off, so its settling basin must catch much finer material.**

> **Options (c) 1.0 mm and (d) 5.0 mm are far too coarse — they are the sizes handled by a GRAVEL TRAP, not a settling basin.**

> **And option (a) 0.05 mm is finer than a settling basin can economically achieve: a basin to settle 0.05 mm particles would need to be enormous, since settling velocity falls as the SQUARE of the particle diameter.**

**Why 0.05 mm is impractical — the settling arithmetic:**

> **By Stokes' law for fine particles, the settling velocity goes as d²:**

| Particle diameter | Settling velocity (approximate) |
|---|---|
| **1.0 mm (coarse sand)** | **~100 mm/s** |
| **0.2 mm (fine sand)** | **~20 mm/s** ← |
| **0.05 mm (coarse silt)** | **~2 mm/s** |
| **0.01 mm (silt)** | **~0.08 mm/s** |

> **The basin's required LENGTH is proportional to the settling time, hence inversely proportional to the settling velocity:**

> **L = (Q/B) × (d/w)** roughly, where w is the settling velocity — so removing 0.05 mm rather than 0.2 mm needs a basin about TEN TIMES longer.

> **A basin 40 m long becomes 400 m long, which is not buildable on a Himalayan hillside at any reasonable cost.**

> **So 0.2 mm represents a practical compromise: fine enough to protect the machine substantially, coarse enough to be achieved in a basin of buildable size.**

> **The residual finer material passes through and DOES erode the turbine — slowly — and that residual erosion is accepted and dealt with by periodic runner repair rather than prevented.**

> **That is an honest statement of the position: sediment erosion in Himalayan hydropower is MANAGED, not eliminated.**

**The sediment handling sequence in a run-of-river scheme:**

| Structure | Removes | Location |
|---|---|---|
| **TRENCH WEIR / intake with a rack** | **BOULDERS and cobbles — they pass over the rack** | At the river |
| **GRAVEL TRAP** | **GRAVEL and coarse sand, 2 mm and above** | Immediately after the intake |
| **SETTLING (desilting) BASIN** | **SAND, down to about 0.2 mm** ← | Before the headrace or forebay |
| **FOREBAY** | **A final settling opportunity, plus a stilling area** | At the penstock head |
| **Trash rack at the penstock** | Floating debris and leaves | At the forebay |

> **The sequence is graded — each structure removes what the previous one let through and what the next cannot handle — which is the same principle as a water treatment train.**

> **Omitting the GRAVEL TRAP is a false economy that recurs: gravel entering the settling basin deposits at its head, occupies the volume intended for sand, and must be dug out by hand.**

**How a settling basin works and its key design parameters:**

| Parameter | Typical value or requirement |
|---|---|
| **Flow-through velocity** | **0.2-0.4 m/s — slow enough for particles to settle, fast enough to avoid deposition of what should stay in suspension** |
| **Depth** | **2-4 m, sloping toward the flushing outlet** |
| **Length** | **From the settling time of the design particle — typically 30-60 m** |
| **Inlet transition** | **GRADUAL, to spread the flow evenly across the full width without jets** ← critical |
| **Flushing arrangement** | **A flushing gate and channel at the deep end, returning sediment to the river** |
| **Number of chambers** | **TWO or more, so one can be flushed while the other operates** ← |

> **The INLET TRANSITION is the detail that most often ruins a settling basin in practice.**

> **If the flow enters as a jet rather than spread evenly, most of the basin's cross-section is dead water while the flow shoots through a narrow core at high velocity — and the effective settling length is a fraction of the basin's actual length.**

> **So a basin of correct volume can perform very badly because of a few metres of poorly shaped approach**, and remedying it after construction means rebuilding the inlet.

> **The TWO-CHAMBER requirement is the operational equivalent: a single-chamber basin must be taken out of service to be flushed, which means shutting the plant — so in practice it is flushed rarely and fills up.**

> **Both details illustrate the same lesson as elsewhere in this subject: the structure provides the capability, and the benefit depends on the arrangement being operable in practice.**

**The consequence of sediment reaching the turbine, since that is what all this prevents:**

| Damage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Erosion of PELTON bucket splitters and cutwaters** | **Rounds the splitter, which then breaks the jet badly and loses efficiency** ← |
| **Erosion of Francis runner blades and labyrinth seals** | Efficiency loss and increased leakage |
| **Guide vane and needle-valve wear** | Loss of regulating precision, and leakage when closed |
| **Combined with CAVITATION, which erosion accelerates** | The two damage mechanisms compound each other |
| **Efficiency loss of several per cent per season** | The commercial cost |

> **The Pelton SPLITTER — the sharp ridge dividing the bucket — is the most sediment-sensitive part of any turbine: it must stay sharp to divide the jet cleanly, and a rounded splitter both loses efficiency and throws the flow unevenly.**

> **A Nepali high-head plant may lose 2 to 5 per cent efficiency in a single monsoon and require runner repair or replacement every few years — a cost that must appear in the operating budget from the outset.**

> **Which is why the sediment study is one of the most important parts of a Himalayan hydropower feasibility, and why a scheme's economics can turn on the sediment concentration of its river as much as on its flow.**

examTip.trick: **About 0.2 mm for a high-head Pelton; 0.2-0.3 mm for Francis; 0.3-0.5 mm for Kaplan.** The higher the head, the finer the particle that must go.
examTip.trap: **Erosion rate goes roughly as the CUBE of impact velocity, and v = √(2gH)** — so the same sediment is about NINETY times more erosive at 400 m than at 20 m. That is why high head demands fine removal.
examTip.mnemonic: **Settling velocity goes as d², so removing 0.05 mm instead of 0.2 mm needs a basin TEN TIMES longer** — 400 m instead of 40 m, unbuildable on a hillside. Himalayan sediment erosion is MANAGED, not eliminated.

questions.stem: In a run-of-river scheme, the structure placed immediately after the intake to remove coarse material before the water reaches the settling basin is the:
questions.solution:
**The GRAVEL TRAP.**

**What a gravel trap is and does:**

> **A GRAVEL TRAP is a short widened and deepened section of channel placed IMMEDIATELY after the intake.**

> **The widening and deepening slow the flow abruptly, so the GRAVEL and COARSE SAND that got past the intake rack settle at once.**

> **A flushing gate at its downstream end returns the collected material to the river.**

| Feature | Typical value |
|---|---|
| **Position** | **Immediately after the intake, before the headrace and the settling basin** ← |
| **Removes** | **Particles above about 2 mm — gravel and very coarse sand** |
| **Flow velocity through it** | **Reduced to about 0.6-1.0 m/s** |
| **Flushing** | **A gate and a steep flushing channel back to the river; flushed frequently, often daily in the monsoon** |
| **Length** | Short — a few times the channel width |

**Why it must come BEFORE the settling basin — the reason it exists as a separate structure:**

> **The SETTLING BASIN is designed to remove SAND down to about 0.2 mm, and its volume and length are computed for that purpose.**

> **If GRAVEL is allowed to enter it, the gravel deposits immediately at the basin's head — occupying the volume intended for sand and reducing the basin's effective length.**

> **And gravel is far harder to flush than sand: it does not move readily in the flushing flow, so it accumulates and must be dug out by hand.**

> **So a scheme without a gravel trap finds its expensive settling basin progressively filled with material a cheap short structure would have caught** — which is why omitting the gravel trap is a false economy that recurs in small schemes.

> **The general principle is the graded sequence: each structure catches what the previous one passed and what the next cannot handle.**

**Why the other options are wrong — each is a real structure elsewhere in the scheme:**

| Option | What it actually is and where |
|---|---|
| **(a) FOREBAY** | **A small basin at the END of the headrace, at the head of the PENSTOCK — provides a stilling area, a final settling opportunity and a small pondage** |
| **(b) SPILLWAY** | **Discharges surplus water — at the headworks, or as a side spillway along the headrace to protect it from overflow** |
| **(d) SURGE TANK** | **At the junction of a pressurised TUNNEL and the penstock — relieves water hammer** |

> **Option (a) is the most plausible distractor, because a forebay DOES settle sediment.**

> **The distinction is one of POSITION and PURPOSE: the forebay is at the DOWNSTREAM end of the conveyance, catching what has escaped everything upstream, while the gravel trap is at the UPSTREAM end catching the coarsest material first.**

> **And the sizes differ by an order of magnitude: the gravel trap catches material above 2 mm; the forebay catches the fine residue.**

**The complete layout of a run-of-river scheme, in order, since this question is about sequence:**

| Order | Structure | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Diversion WEIR / trench weir** | **Raise the level and admit water; reject boulders** |
| **2** | **INTAKE with rack** | Admit the design flow |
| **3** | **GRAVEL TRAP** | **Remove material above ~2 mm** ← |
| **4** | **SETTLING (desilting) BASIN** | **Remove sand down to ~0.2 mm** |
| **5** | **HEADRACE — canal, pipe or tunnel** | **Convey the water along the hillside at a gentle gradient** |
| **6** | **Side SPILLWAY along the headrace** | Discharge surplus and protect the channel |
| **7** | **FOREBAY** | **Final stilling and settling; a small pondage; the transition to pressurised flow** |
| **8** | **Trash rack and penstock inlet** | — |
| **9** | **SURGE TANK (if the conveyance is a pressurised tunnel)** | **Relieve water hammer** |
| **10** | **PENSTOCK** | **Carry the water down the steep drop under pressure** |
| **11** | **ANCHOR BLOCKS and saddle supports** | Restrain the penstock against thrust and movement |
| **12** | **POWERHOUSE — turbine, generator, controls** | Convert the energy |
| **13** | **TAILRACE** | Return the water to the river |

> **The FOREBAY deserves further note because it performs the most functions of any single structure in the list:**

| Function of the forebay | Note |
|---|---|
| **Transition from FREE SURFACE to PRESSURISED flow** | **The penstock starts here** ← |
| **A small POND to absorb short-term load changes** | Minutes of storage, not hours |
| **Final sediment settling** | The last chance before the machine |
| **Removal of floating trash at the rack** | — |
| **An overflow to spill surplus when the plant shuts down** | **Essential: when the turbine gates close, the headrace flow must go somewhere** ← |
| **A place for the intake gate and the air vent** | — |
| **Prevents AIR being drawn into the penstock** | **Requires adequate submergence over the penstock mouth** |

> **The OVERFLOW function is the safety-critical one: when the powerhouse trips, the turbine gates shut in seconds while the headrace is still delivering its full flow.**

> **Without an adequate forebay overflow, the water would back up and overtop the headrace channel along its length — washing out the hillside beneath it.**

> **So the forebay spillway must be able to pass the FULL design flow, and it is not a minor appurtenance.**

> **The AIR ENTRAINMENT requirement is the other detail worth knowing: if the water level over the penstock mouth is too shallow, a vortex forms and draws air into the penstock.**

> **Air in a penstock is seriously bad — it causes surging, noise, loss of output, and on collapse of the air pocket, pressure transients like water hammer.**

> **Hence a minimum submergence is specified over the intake mouth, and anti-vortex arrangements are provided where the depth is marginal.**

examTip.trick: **GRAVEL TRAP — immediately after the intake, removing material above about 2 mm before the settling basin.** The graded sequence: weir, intake, gravel trap, settling basin, headrace, forebay, penstock.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) forebay also settles sediment, but it sits at the DOWNSTREAM end** of the conveyance, catching the fine residue. The gravel trap is upstream, catching material an order of magnitude coarser.
examTip.mnemonic: **Gravel entering a settling basin deposits at its head, steals the volume meant for sand, and cannot be flushed out** — so omitting the gravel trap is a false economy. And the forebay OVERFLOW must pass the FULL flow, because when the turbine trips the headrace is still delivering.

questions.stem: An ANCHOR BLOCK on an exposed penstock is provided principally to:
options: Support the weight of the penstock at intervals along its length
Resist the unbalanced forces at bends and restrain the pipe against longitudinal movement
Prevent the penstock from being damaged by falling rock
Relieve the water hammer pressure in the penstock
questions.solution:
**To resist the unbalanced forces at bends and restrain the pipe against longitudinal movement.**

**The two kinds of support on an exposed penstock, which must be kept distinct:**

| Support | Function | Restrains |
|---|---|---|
| **SADDLE (or ring girder) SUPPORTS** | **Carry the WEIGHT of the pipe and its water between anchors** | **VERTICAL load only — the pipe is free to slide longitudinally** |
| **ANCHOR BLOCKS** | **Resist the unbalanced FORCES and fix the pipe's position** | **ALL directions — the pipe is rigidly held** ← |

> **Option (a) describes the SADDLE support, which is what makes it the designed distractor: both are supports, and they do different jobs.**

> **Saddles are spaced at intervals of typically 6 to 12 m and simply hold the pipe up.**

> **Anchor blocks are placed at every BEND — horizontal or vertical — and at intervals of perhaps 100 to 150 m on straight lengths.**

**The forces an anchor block must resist — and the largest is not the weight:**

| Force | Origin |
|---|---|
| **The BEND force (hydrodynamic thrust)** | **The change of momentum of the water as it turns, plus the pressure acting on the projected area of the bend — the DOMINANT force** ← |
| **Longitudinal component of the pipe and water weight** | On a slope, gravity pulls the pipe downhill |
| **FRICTION on the saddles as the pipe expands and contracts** | Thermal movement dragging on the supports |
| **Friction of the EXPANSION JOINT** | Sliding resistance |
| **Unbalanced pressure at an expansion joint or a reducer** | Pressure acting on the annular area |
| **Water hammer surge pressure** | Adds to the bend force during a transient |
| **Seismic force** | Where applicable |

> **The BEND FORCE is what makes anchor blocks necessary and it is worth seeing its magnitude:**

> **For a bend through an angle θ, the resultant thrust is:**

> **F = 2 (p A + ρ Q V) sin(θ/2)**

> **Take a 1.0 m diameter penstock (A = 0.785 m²) under 300 m of head (p = 2943 kPa), carrying 5 m³/s at 6.4 m/s, through a 45° bend:**

| Term | Value |
|---|---|
| **Pressure term p A** | **2943 × 0.785 = 2310 kN** |
| **Momentum term ρQV** | **1000 × 5 × 6.4 = 32 kN** |
| **Sum** | **2342 kN** |
| **F = 2 × 2342 × sin 22.5°** | **2 × 2342 × 0.383 = 1794 kN ≈ 183 tonnes** ← |

> **Nearly two hundred tonnes of thrust at a single 45° bend — which is why anchor blocks are massive concrete structures rather than brackets.**

> **And note which term dominates: the PRESSURE term is 2310 kN against the momentum term's 32 kN — a ratio of over seventy to one.**

> **So in a high-head penstock the bend thrust is essentially a PRESSURE effect, and the water's momentum is almost irrelevant.**

> **That is the opposite of the situation in a low-head, high-velocity conduit, and it is worth knowing which term to expect to dominate before computing either.**

**How the anchor block resists it:**

> **Almost entirely by its OWN WEIGHT and the friction and bearing it develops on the foundation.**

| Stability check | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Against SLIDING** | **Weight × friction coefficient ≥ the horizontal thrust, with a factor of safety of about 1.5** |
| **Against OVERTURNING** | **The resultant must pass within the base; factor of safety about 1.5** |
| **Foundation BEARING pressure** | Within the allowable value, with no tension at the heel |
| **The pipe's own stresses at the block** | The pipe is embedded and locally restrained |

> **Because the resistance comes from weight, anchor blocks are LARGE — commonly tens to hundreds of cubic metres of concrete for a substantial penstock, and they are among the more expensive items in a penstock's cost.**

> **Which produces a design conclusion worth stating: MINIMISE THE NUMBER OF BENDS.**

> **Every bend requires an anchor block, so a penstock alignment that follows the ground closely with many small bends may cost far more than a straighter one requiring more excavation.**

> **That is a genuine optimisation, and it usually favours a straighter line than the topography suggests.**

**EXPANSION JOINTS, which are the necessary companion to anchor blocks:**

> **A steel penstock changes length with temperature: the coefficient is about 12 × 10⁻⁶ per °C.**

> **For a 200 m length between anchors and a 30 °C temperature range:**

> **ΔL = 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 200,000 mm × 30 = 72 mm**

> **Over 70 mm of movement — which must be accommodated, or enormous thermal stresses develop.**

> **If the pipe were rigidly restrained at both ends, the thermal stress would be:**

> **σ = E α ΔT = 200,000 × 12×10⁻⁶ × 30 = 72 N/mm²**

> **That is a substantial fraction of the steel's capacity, added to the hoop and longitudinal stresses from pressure — and it exists whether or not the pipe is carrying water.**

> **So an EXPANSION JOINT is placed in each span between anchor blocks, allowing the pipe to slide on its saddles as it expands.**

| Element | Role in the system |
|---|---|
| **ANCHOR BLOCK** | **Fixes the pipe absolutely; takes all the unbalanced force** |
| **SADDLE supports between** | **Carry the weight and PERMIT sliding** |
| **EXPANSION JOINT in the span** | **Absorbs the length change** ← |

> **The three work as a system, and each requires the others: anchors without expansion joints overstress the pipe, and expansion joints without anchors leave the thrust unresisted.**

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Option | Comment |
|---|---|
| **(a) Support the weight at intervals** | **That is the SADDLE support's job** |
| **(c) Protect against falling rock** | **A real hazard on a Himalayan hillside, addressed by rock netting, protection sheds or burying the pipe — not by anchor blocks** |
| **(d) Relieve water hammer** | **A SURGE TANK or a pressure relief valve does that. An anchor block RESISTS the forces water hammer produces; it does not relieve the pressure** ← |

> **Option (d) contains a distinction worth being precise about: an anchor block is a STRUCTURAL response to the surge force, and a surge tank is a HYDRAULIC response that prevents the surge arising.**

> **Both appear in the same scheme, and they are not alternatives: the anchor blocks are designed for the surge pressure that the surge tank limits.**

examTip.trick: **Anchor blocks fix the pipe and take the unbalanced BEND thrust; SADDLES carry the weight and let it slide.** Anchors go at every bend; saddles every 6-12 m.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) describes the SADDLE support** — both are supports doing different jobs. And option (d) confuses a STRUCTURAL response (the block resists the surge force) with a HYDRAULIC one (a surge tank prevents the surge).
examTip.mnemonic: **F = 2(pA + ρQV) sin(θ/2) — and in a high-head penstock the PRESSURE term dominates by 70 to 1.** A 45° bend on a 1 m pipe under 300 m head gives about 180 tonnes, which is why anchor blocks are massive and why you MINIMISE BENDS.

questions.stem: The principal function of the DRAFT TUBE in a reaction turbine installation is:
options: To convey water from the penstock to the turbine runner
To regulate the discharge entering the runner
To dissipate the surplus energy of the water leaving the runner
To recover the kinetic energy at the runner exit and permit the machine to be set above the tailwater level
questions.solution:
**To RECOVER the kinetic energy at the runner exit and to permit the machine to be set ABOVE tailwater level.**

**What a draft tube is:**

> **A DRAFT TUBE is a gradually EXPANDING conduit connecting the runner exit of a REACTION turbine to the tailrace.**

> **It is always full of water and its outlet is always SUBMERGED below the tailwater level.**

**The two functions, both of which the answer must state:**

> **FIRST — RECOVERING THE KINETIC ENERGY AT THE RUNNER EXIT.**

> **Water leaves a reaction runner with appreciable velocity, and that velocity head would simply be lost if the water were discharged freely.**

> **The draft tube's gradual EXPANSION decelerates the flow, converting velocity head into PRESSURE head by Bernoulli's relation — creating a pressure BELOW ATMOSPHERIC at the runner exit and so increasing the effective head across the runner.**

> **The recovery is significant:**

| Turbine | Exit velocity head as a fraction of net head | Recovered by the draft tube |
|---|---|---|
| **Francis, medium head** | **2-5 %** | Most of it |
| **KAPLAN, low head** | **8-25 %** | **Most of it — and at low head this is a large fraction of the plant's output** ← |

> **For a Kaplan turbine the exit kinetic energy can be a QUARTER of the net head, so the draft tube is not a refinement but essential to the machine's viability.**

> **A low-head Kaplan without a draft tube would throw away a substantial part of its available energy.**

> **SECOND — PERMITTING THE MACHINE TO BE SET ABOVE TAILWATER.**

> **Because the draft tube is full and submerged, it forms a continuous water column from the runner down to the tailwater.**

> **That column acts as a SIPHON: the runner can sit ABOVE the tailwater level and still have the full head from headwater to TAILWATER acting across it.**

> **Without a draft tube, the turbine would have to be placed AT or BELOW tailwater level, and the head between the runner and the tailwater would be lost.**

> **The practical consequence is large: a powerhouse can be built at a convenient, dry, accessible level rather than excavated below the river.**

> **Which saves excavation, avoids dewatering during construction, and keeps the machinery above flood level.**

**Why option (c) is wrong — and it inverts the purpose:**

> **A draft tube RECOVERS energy; it does not DISSIPATE it.**

> **Dissipating energy is exactly what it must NOT do — every joule lost in the draft tube is a joule of output foregone.**

> **So the draft tube's expansion must be GRADUAL, precisely to avoid the turbulent losses that a sudden enlargement would cause.**

> **Energy DISSIPATION is the business of a stilling basin below a spillway — a different structure with the opposite intent.**

> **That inversion is what makes option (c) a well-made distractor: it names the right physical quantity and the wrong direction.**

**Option (a), for completeness:**

> **Conveying water TO the runner is the job of the SPIRAL (scroll) CASING and the GUIDE VANES.**

> **And option (b) — regulating the discharge — is the job of the GUIDE VANES (wicket gates) in a reaction turbine, or the SPEAR/NEEDLE VALVE in a Pelton.**

> **So the option set walks through the turbine's components in order and asks which one is at the exit.**

**The types of draft tube, since the choice matters:**

| Type | Description | Efficiency | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Straight conical (divergent)** | **A simple cone; the most efficient** | **~85-90 %** | **Vertical shaft, where depth permits** |
| **ELBOW (bend) type** | **Turns the flow to horizontal** | **~60-70 %** | **The standard for KAPLAN and large Francis — reduces excavation depth** ← |
| **Moody spreading (hydracone)** | A bell mouth with a central core | ~85 % | Where a wide outlet is wanted |
| **Elbow with a rectangular outlet** | Elbow flaring to a rectangle | ~60-70 % | Very large low-head machines |
| **Simple elbow** | Constant area | Low | Small machines |

> **The ELBOW type is much less efficient than a straight cone and is nevertheless the commonest choice — which is worth explaining, because it looks like a poor decision.**

> **A straight conical draft tube on a large low-head Kaplan would need to extend vertically for many metres below the runner, requiring very deep and expensive excavation in the river bed.**

> **An elbow turns the flow to horizontal within a much shallower depth, at the cost of some efficiency.**

> **So the choice trades EXCAVATION COST against EFFICIENCY, and for a large machine the excavation usually wins.**

> **That is a good example of a component chosen for constructability rather than performance, and of why the theoretically best option is not always the right one.**

**Why the draft tube is where CAVITATION appears — the critical design constraint:**

> **The draft tube creates a pressure BELOW atmospheric at the runner exit. That is its purpose.**

> **But if the pressure falls to the water's VAPOUR PRESSURE, the water BOILS at ambient temperature — CAVITATION — and the collapsing vapour bubbles pit and erode the runner blades and the draft tube liner.**

> **So the runner's SETTING LEVEL above the tailwater is limited, and the limit is expressed through the CAVITATION COEFFICIENT:**

> **σ = (H_a − H_v − H_s) / H**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **H_a** | **Atmospheric pressure head — LOWER AT ALTITUDE** ← |
| **H_v** | Vapour pressure head |
| **H_s** | **The SETTING — height of the runner above tailwater** |
| **H** | Net head |

> **The design requires σ to exceed a critical value σ_c that depends on the turbine's specific speed — and higher specific speed machines (Kaplans) are MORE cavitation-prone, so they need smaller settings or must be set BELOW tailwater.**

> **The ALTITUDE term deserves emphasis for Nepal, and it is a genuinely important practical point:**

| Altitude | Atmospheric head |
|---|---|
| **Sea level** | **10.3 m of water** |
| **1000 m** | **9.2 m** |
| **2000 m** | **8.1 m** |
| **3000 m** | **7.2 m** ← |

> **A powerhouse at 2000 m has about 2.2 m less atmospheric head available than one at sea level.**

> **That 2.2 m comes directly off the permissible setting, so a high-altitude machine must be set LOWER relative to its tailwater than an identical machine at sea level — meaning deeper excavation.**

> **A turbine selected from a manufacturer's sea-level data and installed in the Nepali hills without correcting for altitude will cavitate**, and that is a real and documented error rather than a textbook caution.

> **So the altitude correction is a required step in setting the powerhouse floor level, and it is one of the few places where Nepal's topography changes a machine's installation rather than merely its civil works.**

examTip.trick: **The draft tube does TWO things: RECOVERS the exit kinetic energy by gradual expansion, and lets the runner sit ABOVE tailwater by acting as a siphon.** Only option (d) states both.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) inverts the purpose** — a draft tube RECOVERS energy and must not dissipate it; every joule lost there is output foregone. Dissipation is a stilling basin's job.
examTip.mnemonic: **Kaplan exit velocity head can be 25 % of the net head**, so the draft tube is essential, not a refinement. And correct the cavitation setting for ALTITUDE: atmospheric head is 10.3 m at sea level but only 8.1 m at 2000 m — a machine set from sea-level data will cavitate in the hills.

questions.stem: In Nepal's road classification, the roads that connect district headquarters and important economic centres to the national highway network are classified as:
questions.solution:
**FEEDER ROADS.**

**Nepal's road classification, in order of hierarchy:**

| Class | Designation | Function | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| **NATIONAL HIGHWAY (NH)** | **H01, H02 …** | **The main arterial network — connects the country east to west and to the border crossings; the Mahendra (East-West) Highway is H01** | **Department of Roads** |
| **FEEDER ROAD (F)** | **F001, F002 …** | **Connect DISTRICT HEADQUARTERS and important economic centres to the national highways** ← | **Department of Roads** |
| **DISTRICT ROAD (D)** | **D…** | **Roads within a district, serving its internal traffic and connecting to the feeder network** | **Local level (district / municipality)** |
| **URBAN (municipal) ROAD** | — | Roads within a municipality | Municipality |
| **VILLAGE ROAD** | — | **Roads serving villages and rural settlements — the lowest tier** | Local level |

> **The essential distinction the question tests is between the FEEDER road and the DISTRICT road:**

> **A FEEDER road connects a district headquarters OUTWARD to the national network — it is the district's link to the country.**

> **A DISTRICT road serves traffic WITHIN the district and is a local-level responsibility.**

> **So the two differ in both function and authority, and option (c) is the designed distractor because both names contain "district".**

**Why the classification matters practically — it is not merely nomenclature:**

| Consequence of classification | Note |
|---|---|
| **WHO builds and maintains it** | **Department of Roads for highways and feeders; local government for district, urban and village roads** ← |
| **The FUNDING source** | Central budget against local budget and grants |
| **The DESIGN STANDARD applied** | **Design speed, carriageway width, geometric standards and pavement type all follow from the class** |
| **Right of way reserved** | Wider for higher classes |
| **Priority in maintenance and in emergency reopening** | Highways first |

> **The DESIGN STANDARD link is the one that matters most to an engineer: the Nepal Road Standard prescribes different geometric and structural standards for each class, so classifying a road determines its width, its curvature, its gradients and its pavement.**

> **A road built to village-road standards cannot later be promoted to a feeder road without substantial reconstruction — so the classification decision is made before design and constrains everything afterward.**

**The FUNCTIONAL classification, which is the other way of describing roads:**

> **Roads are also classified by the balance they strike between MOBILITY and ACCESS — and the two objectives conflict:**

| Functional class | Mobility | Access | Character |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ARTERIAL (expressway, highway)** | **HIGH — long distance, high speed** | **LOW — few access points, controlled** | **Movement through an area** ← |
| **COLLECTOR (sub-arterial)** | **Moderate** | **Moderate** | **Gathers traffic from local roads and delivers it to arterials** |
| **LOCAL (access) road** | **LOW** | **HIGH — access to every property** | **Movement within an area** |

> **The conflict is fundamental and worth stating: every access point — a driveway, a junction, a shop frontage — is a place where vehicles slow, turn and conflict, and therefore reduces the road's capacity and safety.**

> **So a road cannot serve both functions well, and the classification exists to decide which function each road will serve.**

> **RIBBON DEVELOPMENT along a highway is exactly the failure of that discipline: shops and houses build up along an arterial road, each with its own access, and the road progressively loses the mobility function it was built and paid for.**

> **The remedy is ACCESS CONTROL — service roads, limited junctions, and building setback lines enforced from the outset — and it is far easier to preserve than to recover.**

> **That is a genuinely important planning point in Nepal, where the East-West Highway has been substantially compromised by exactly this process, with market towns growing along it and reducing long-distance traffic to a crawl through each.**

**The IRC classification, since Nepali practice draws on it:**

| Class | Note |
|---|---|
| **EXPRESSWAY** | Fully access-controlled |
| **National Highway (NH)** | Arterial, connecting states/capitals |
| **State Highway (SH)** | Within a state |
| **Major District Road (MDR)** | Within a district |
| **Other District Road (ODR)** | Lower-order district roads |
| **Village Road (VR)** | Serving villages |

> **Nepal's system is a simplified version of that hierarchy, adapted to a smaller country and a unitary road authority — which is why the Nepali classes are fewer and the naming differs.**

**And the planning frameworks in which the classification sits:**

| Concept | Note |
|---|---|
| **NELSON'S / the SATURATION SYSTEM of road planning** | **Roads are prioritised by the utility they would provide — population served and agricultural produce carried — scored and ranked** |
| **Lucknow / Nagpur road plans (India)** | Historical target road-length formulae by area and population |
| **Road DENSITY (km per 100 km² or per 1000 population)** | **A common measure of a country's road provision; Nepal's is low, and very unevenly distributed between the Terai and the mountains** ← |
| **STAR and GRID patterns** | Network geometries |

> **The SATURATION SYSTEM deserves a note because it is the approach best suited to Nepal's circumstances: rather than pursuing an arbitrary target road length, it ranks candidate roads by the utility each would deliver — the population it would serve and the produce it would move — and builds in that order.**

> **In a country where the terrain makes every kilometre expensive and the resources are limited, ranking by utility rather than by target length is the defensible approach.**

examTip.trick: **FEEDER roads connect district headquarters OUTWARD to the national highways (Department of Roads). DISTRICT roads serve traffic WITHIN a district (local level).**
examTip.trap: **Option (c) is the designed distractor because both names contain "district"** — but they differ in function AND in which authority builds and maintains them.
examTip.mnemonic: **MOBILITY and ACCESS conflict: every access point reduces capacity and safety.** RIBBON DEVELOPMENT along a highway is that discipline failing — which is why access control is far easier to preserve than to recover, as the East-West Highway shows.

questions.stem: The stage of a highway alignment survey in which a rough ground inspection is made of the alternative routes identified from the map study is called the:
questions.solution:
**RECONNAISSANCE.**

**The four stages of a highway alignment survey, in order:**

| Stage | What is done | Output |
|---|---|---|
| **1. MAP STUDY** | **Study topographic maps, satellite imagery and existing records IN THE OFFICE; identify possible corridors** | **Alternative broad corridors, on paper** |
| **2. RECONNAISSANCE** | **A rough GROUND INSPECTION of those alternatives — walked or flown over, with hand instruments only** ← | **A short list of feasible alternatives, with obvious impossibilities eliminated** |
| **3. PRELIMINARY SURVEY** | **Instrumental survey of the short-listed routes — a traverse, levels, cross-sections; soil and material investigation; drainage and traffic studies** | **Comparison of alternatives; ONE route selected** |
| **4. FINAL LOCATION AND DETAILED SURVEY** | **Set out the chosen centre line on the ground; detailed levels, cross-sections, structure sites, land acquisition plans** | **Working drawings and quantities for construction** |

> **Note the progression: each stage covers FEWER alternatives in MORE detail.**

> **That is the essential logic of the sequence, and it is an economical one — the cheapest methods are used to eliminate the most options, and the expensive detailed work is done once, on the chosen line.**

> **A survey that began with detailed instrumental work on every corridor would waste most of its effort.**

**What the RECONNAISSANCE stage specifically looks for:**

> **The purpose is to detect, on the ground, the things a map does not show or shows badly:**

| Feature sought | Why a map may miss it |
|---|---|
| **Soft ground, marsh, poor soil, high water table** | **Not shown on topographic maps** ← |
| **LANDSLIDES, unstable slopes, evidence of past movement** | **Critical in Nepal, and readily visible on the ground while invisible on a map** ← |
| **Rock outcrops and the depth to rock** | Affects excavation cost enormously |
| **Sources of construction MATERIAL — quarries, sand, water** | Determines haulage cost |
| **Existing drainage patterns and flood marks** | Local knowledge and physical evidence |
| **Obligatory points — a bridge site, a pass, a settlement to serve** | Confirmed on the ground |
| **Land use, settlements, cultural and religious sites** | **Often the binding constraint, and rarely mapped** |

> **The LANDSLIDE point is the one that makes reconnaissance indispensable in Nepal: an alignment can look excellent on a contour map and cross an active slide that a walk over the ground reveals in minutes.**

> **Old slide scars, tension cracks, disturbed drainage, tilted trees and hummocky ground are all visible to an experienced eye and none of them appears on a map.**

> **An alignment taken across such ground will fail repeatedly for the life of the road, at a maintenance cost that dwarfs the saving the shorter route offered.**

> **So the reconnaissance is not a formality between the map study and the real survey — in mountainous terrain it is where the most consequential decisions are effectively made.**

**The instruments used at reconnaissance, which define the stage's character:**

| Instrument | Use |
|---|---|
| **Abney level or clinometer** | **Rough gradients** |
| **Hand-held GPS** | Position |
| **Barometer or altimeter** | Rough elevations |
| **Prismatic compass** | Rough bearings |
| **Pacing, tape, or a measuring wheel** | Rough distances |
| **Camera and notebook** | The most valuable of all |

> **All hand instruments, all rough — which is the point: reconnaissance is deliberately QUICK and APPROXIMATE, because its job is to eliminate rather than to measure.**

> **Precision at this stage would be wasted on alternatives that are about to be discarded.**

**The requirements of a GOOD alignment, since that is what the survey seeks:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **SHORT** | **The shortest route is the cheapest to build and to use — but rarely achievable** |
| **EASY** | **Easy to construct and to maintain; gentle gradients and curves; easy for traffic** |
| **SAFE** | **Adequate sight distance, stable slopes, safe geometry** |
| **ECONOMICAL** | **Least total cost — construction PLUS maintenance PLUS vehicle operating cost over the life** ← |

> **The fourth requirement subsumes the others and is the one that decides: the correct criterion is the TOTAL cost over the road's life, not the construction cost alone.**

> **A shorter alignment with steeper gradients costs less to build and more to use — every vehicle burns more fuel on every trip for decades.**

> **A longer, gentler alignment costs more to build and less to operate.**

> **Balancing them properly requires the vehicle operating costs and the traffic forecast, and in hill roads the answer often favours the longer, gentler line more strongly than intuition suggests.**

**The special controls in HILL ROAD alignment, since Nepal's roads are mostly hill roads:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **STABILITY of slopes** | **The dominant control — an unstable alignment cannot be maintained at any cost** ← |
| **DRAINAGE** | **The second control — most hill road failures are drainage failures** |
| **Ruling and limiting GRADIENT** | **5 % ruling and 6-7 % limiting in mountainous terrain, with an exceptional gradient beyond** |
| **Resisting length and grade compensation on curves** | Limits the sustained climb |
| **HAIRPIN BENDS** | **Located on a hillside as flat and stable as possible, never on a spur or a slide** |
| **Geological features — dip of strata, faults, springs** | **Cutting into a dip slope invites failure; springs mark groundwater** |

> **The DIP OF STRATA point is worth knowing because it distinguishes two apparently similar cuttings:**

> **A cutting into a slope where the rock strata dip INTO the hill is comparatively stable — the layers buttress one another.**

> **A cutting into a slope where the strata dip OUT of the hill, toward the road, is a prepared failure surface: removing the toe lets a slab of rock slide out along the bedding.**

> **The two cuttings look identical on a plan and behave entirely differently, and only a geological inspection on the ground distinguishes them.**

> **Which is a further argument for the reconnaissance stage, and for including a geologist in it — a point Nepal's road history illustrates repeatedly.**

examTip.trick: **Map study → RECONNAISSANCE → preliminary survey → final location survey.** Each stage covers FEWER alternatives in MORE detail.
examTip.trap: **Reconnaissance is deliberately rough — hand instruments only** — because its job is to ELIMINATE alternatives, not to measure them. Precision would be wasted on routes about to be discarded.
examTip.mnemonic: **Reconnaissance finds what a map cannot show: soft ground, springs, and above all LANDSLIDES.** An alignment can look excellent on a contour map and cross an active slide a walk reveals in minutes. And note the DIP of strata: dipping into the hill is stable, dipping out is a prepared failure surface.

questions.stem: As per IRC, the maximum superelevation permitted on a highway in plain and rolling terrain is:
questions.solution:
**7 per cent.**

**The IRC superelevation limits:**

| Situation | Maximum superelevation |
|---|---|
| **PLAIN and ROLLING terrain** | **7 % (1 in 15)** ← |
| **Hilly terrain NOT bound by snow** | **10 %** |
| **Snow-bound hilly terrain** | **7 %** |
| **URBAN roads with frequent intersections** | **4 %** |

> **All four values appear as options, so the situation stated in the stem must be matched.**

> **Option (a) 4 % is the URBAN limit and option (c) 10 % is the HILLY (non-snow) limit — both real values in the wrong context.**

**Why the maximum is limited at all — and the reason is SLOW vehicles:**

> **Superelevation is provided to help vehicles negotiate a curve: the banked surface directs part of the vehicle's weight toward the centre of the curve, supplying centripetal force.**

> **The design equation:  e + f = V² / (127 R)**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **e** | **Superelevation, as a ratio** |
| **f** | **Lateral friction coefficient — IRC takes 0.15 for design** |
| **V** | Speed in km/h |
| **R** | Radius in m |

> **A steeper bank helps a FAST vehicle. But it HARMS a SLOW one:**

> **A vehicle moving slowly, or stopped, on a steeply banked curve has its weight component acting DOWN the slope with insufficient centrifugal force to balance it.**

> **The consequences:**

| Effect on a slow or stopped vehicle | Note |
|---|---|
| **It tends to SLIDE DOWN the slope toward the inner edge** | **Especially on a wet or icy surface** ← |
| **A high-sided or top-heavy vehicle may OVERTURN inward** | A loaded truck or bus is vulnerable |
| **Load may shift** | Particularly loose or livestock loads |
| **Drivers steer away from the inner edge, using the road unevenly** | An operational nuisance |

> **So the maximum superelevation is set by the SLOW VEHICLE, not by the fast one.**

> **That is the key insight and it explains the whole table: the limit is lower where slow and stopped vehicles are more likely (urban roads with intersections, 4 per cent) and where the surface may be slippery (snow-bound, 7 per cent), and higher where traffic is fast and continuous and the terrain forces sharp curves (hilly, 10 per cent).**

> **The SNOW-BOUND case is the clearest demonstration: hilly terrain would justify 10 per cent, but where snow and ice reduce the available friction the limit is pulled back to 7 — because a vehicle sliding sideways on ice down a 10 per cent cross-slope has nothing to stop it.**

**The MINIMUM superelevation, which is the other end of the range:**

> **Superelevation is not provided below a certain value, because the CAMBER already supplies a cross-slope.**

> **The rule: if the calculated superelevation is less than the camber, the camber is simply retained on the outer half of the road and no separate superelevation is provided.**

> **And the practical minimum cross-slope for DRAINAGE is about 2 to 2.5 per cent, matching the camber.**

> **So the working range of superelevation is roughly 2.5 to 7 per cent on a plain-terrain highway** — a narrower band than the formula alone suggests.

**The IRC design procedure for superelevation, since it has a specific sequence:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Calculate e for 75 % of the design speed, IGNORING friction:  e = (0.75V)²/(127R) = V²/(225R)** ← |
| **2** | **If e ≤ 7 %, adopt it** |
| **3** | **If e > 7 %, limit e to 7 % and CHECK the safe speed by  V_safe = √(127R(0.07 + 0.15))** |
| **4** | **If the safe speed is less than the design speed, either increase the radius or restrict the speed with a warning sign** |

> **Step 1 is the distinctive feature and it is worth understanding: the design superelevation is computed for only THREE QUARTERS of the design speed, and with NO reliance on friction.**

> **The reason is exactly the slow-vehicle problem: designing the bank for the full design speed would produce a cross-slope too steep for the slower traffic that shares the road.**

> **So the bank is designed for a moderate speed, and FRICTION is left to supply the balance for vehicles travelling faster.**

> **That is a deliberate and sensible division of labour: the geometry serves the average, and friction covers the fast.**

**How superelevation is ATTAINED — the transition, which is where practice matters:**

| Stage | Action |
|---|---|
| **1. ELIMINATION of the crown** | **The outer half of the camber is rotated up to a level surface** |
| **2. ROTATION** | **The whole surface is rotated to the full superelevation** |
| **3. Fully attained at the start of the CIRCULAR curve** | ← |

> **The attainment takes place over the TRANSITION CURVE, the same length over which the curvature is introduced and the extra widening developed.**

> **The axis of rotation may be the centre line (keeping the centre level unchanged, preferred where drainage permits) or the inner edge (raising the whole surface, used where drainage requires it).**

> **The RATE of attainment is limited: not steeper than 1 in 150 for plain terrain, so that the surface does not appear or feel warped.**

> **And that rate requirement is one of the criteria fixing the TRANSITION LENGTH — the others being the rate of change of centrifugal acceleration and an empirical minimum.**

> **The longest of the three governs, which is a common pattern in geometric design: several independent criteria are computed and the most demanding is adopted.**

examTip.trick: **Maximum superelevation: 7 % plain and rolling, 10 % hilly (not snow-bound), 7 % snow-bound, 4 % urban.** All four appear as options, so match the terrain.
examTip.trap: **The maximum is set by the SLOW vehicle, not the fast one** — a stopped or slow vehicle on a steep bank slides or overturns inward. Which is why the snow-bound limit drops back to 7 % from hilly terrain's 10 %.
examTip.mnemonic: **IRC designs e for only 75 % of the design speed and IGNORES friction: e = V²/(225R).** Friction is left to cover the faster vehicles — the geometry serves the average. If e exceeds 7 %, cap it and check the safe speed.

questions.stem: The stopping sight distance for a design speed of 60 km/h, taking a reaction time of 2.5 s and a longitudinal friction coefficient of 0.36, is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 81 m.**

**The stopping sight distance formula:**

> **SSD = LAG distance + BRAKING distance**

> **SSD = 0.278 V t + V² / (254 f)**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **0.278 V t** | **LAG distance — travelled during the driver's perception-reaction time, at unchanged speed** |
| **V²/(254 f)** | **BRAKING distance — travelled while decelerating to rest** |
| **0.278** | Converts km/h to m/s (1/3.6) |
| **254** | **2 × 9.81 × 3.6² / 2 — the constant that lets V be entered in km/h** |

**The computation:**

> **Lag distance = 0.278 × 60 × 2.5 = 41.7 m**

> **Braking distance = 60²/(254 × 0.36) = 3600/91.44 = 39.4 m**

> **SSD = 41.7 + 39.4 = 81.1 m ≈ 81 m** ✓

> **IRC's tabulated value for 60 km/h is 80 m, which confirms the calculation.**

**The striking feature of the result — the two parts are nearly EQUAL:**

> **41.7 m of lag and 39.4 m of braking.**

> **So at 60 km/h, HALF the stopping distance is covered before the brakes are even applied.**

> **That is worth stating plainly because it is not widely appreciated: a driver's reaction time of two and a half seconds carries the vehicle over forty metres — the length of ten cars — before any deceleration begins.**

> **And the two components scale differently, which changes their balance with speed:**

| Component | Scales as |
|---|---|
| **LAG distance** | **V — LINEARLY** |
| **BRAKING distance** | **V² — as the SQUARE** ← |

| Speed | Lag (m) | Braking (m) | SSD (m) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **30 km/h** | **20.9** | **9.8** | **31** |
| **60 km/h** | **41.7** | **39.4** | **81** ← |
| **100 km/h** | **69.5** | **109.4** | **179** |

> **At 30 km/h the lag dominates; at 60 they are equal; at 100 the braking distance dominates and is nearly twice the lag.**

> **And note the total: DOUBLING the speed from 30 to 60 more than DOUBLES the SSD (31 to 81 m), and from 60 to 100 it more than doubles again.**

> **That non-linear growth is the fundamental reason speed matters so much for safety, and it is a stronger argument than any exhortation: the distance in which a driver can stop grows faster than the speed.**

**The REACTION TIME of 2.5 seconds — why so long:**

> **A laboratory reaction time is a few tenths of a second, so 2.5 s looks generous.**

> **It covers the whole PIEV process:**

| Stage | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **P — PERCEPTION** | **The driver sees the object** |
| **I — INTELLECTION** | **Recognises and understands what it is** |
| **E — EMOTION** | **Decides what to do — brake, swerve, or accept** ← the variable stage |
| **V — VOLITION** | **Acts — moves the foot to the brake** |

> **The INTELLECTION and EMOTION stages are what make the time so long and so variable: recognising a dark object as a stopped vehicle, and deciding to brake rather than steer, takes far longer than a simple reflex.**

> **IRC's 2.5 s is a design value covering most drivers in most conditions, including those who are inattentive, elderly, or unfamiliar with the road.**

> **Designing for a shorter reaction time would produce a road safe only for alert, expert drivers — which is not who uses roads.**

**The FRICTION coefficient, and why the longitudinal and lateral values differ:**

| Coefficient | IRC design value | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| **LONGITUDINAL friction f** | **0.35-0.40 (0.36 typical)** | **BRAKING — stopping sight distance** ← |
| **LATERAL friction f** | **0.15** | **CORNERING — superelevation and curve radius** |

> **The lateral value is much lower, and the reason is COMFORT rather than physics:**

> **The available friction is similar in both directions — a tyre can develop about 0.4 either way.**

> **But a lateral acceleration of 0.4g would throw passengers sideways and feel alarming, and it would overturn a high-sided vehicle.**

> **So the lateral value is limited to 0.15 for COMFORT and STABILITY, while the longitudinal value can use nearly the full available friction because hard braking is an emergency action that need only be tolerable, not comfortable.**

> **That distinction is worth holding, because using 0.36 in a curve calculation or 0.15 in a braking calculation is a large error in each case.**

**The other sight distances, since SSD is the minimum of a family:**

| Sight distance | Definition | Value at 60 km/h |
|---|---|---|
| **STOPPING (SSD)** | **Stop before an obstruction** | **80 m — the ABSOLUTE MINIMUM anywhere on a road** ← |
| **INTERMEDIATE (ISD)** | **Twice the SSD — allows limited overtaking** | **160 m** |
| **OVERTAKING (OSD)** | **Complete an overtaking manoeuvre safely** | **300 m** |
| **Safe sight distance at an uncontrolled intersection** | Enter or cross safely | By geometry |

> **The SSD must be available at EVERY point on a road, without exception — it is the distance in which a driver must be able to stop, and a road that does not provide it is unsafe by definition.**

> **On a TWO-WAY single-carriageway road with an obstruction on the road itself, the requirement doubles to twice the SSD, because two vehicles may be approaching one another.**

> **OVERTAKING sight distance is much longer — nearly four times the SSD — because the manoeuvre takes many seconds and involves an oncoming vehicle also closing the gap.**

> **Where OSD cannot be provided, the length is marked as a no-overtaking zone with a continuous centre line** — which is an operational remedy for a geometric deficiency, and the honest response when the terrain forbids the geometry.

**And the sight distance on a VERTICAL CURVE, since that is where SSD usually governs:**

> **The length of a SUMMIT curve is determined by the requirement to see over the crest:**

> **L = N S² / (4.4)  for  L > S**, with N the deviation angle and S the sight distance (SSD in metres), taking driver eye height 1.2 m and object height 0.15 m.

> **Note the S² term: the required curve length grows as the SQUARE of the sight distance, and the sight distance itself grows faster than the speed.**

> **So the length of a summit curve grows very rapidly with design speed — which is why high-speed roads need such long, flat vertical curves, and why raising a road's design speed can require extensive earthwork at every crest.**

examTip.trick: **SSD = 0.278Vt + V²/(254f) = 41.7 + 39.4 = 81 m.** IRC's tabulated value for 60 km/h is 80 m.
examTip.trap: **LONGITUDINAL friction is 0.36 (braking) but LATERAL friction only 0.15 (cornering)** — the lateral value is limited for COMFORT and overturning, not by available grip. Using one for the other is a large error.
examTip.mnemonic: **At 60 km/h the lag and braking distances are nearly EQUAL — half the stopping distance passes before the brakes are touched.** Lag scales as V, braking as V², so doubling the speed MORE than doubles the SSD. That is why speed matters so much.

questions.stem: In the California Bearing Ratio test, the standard load corresponding to 2.5 mm penetration is taken as:
questions.solution:
**1370 kg.**

**The CBR standard loads:**

| Penetration | Standard load | Standard unit pressure |
|---|---|---|
| **2.5 mm** | **1370 kg** ← | **70 kg/cm²** |
| **5.0 mm** | **2055 kg** | **105 kg/cm²** |
| **7.5 mm** | 2630 kg | 134 kg/cm² |
| **10.0 mm** | 3180 kg | 162 kg/cm² |
| **12.5 mm** | 3600 kg | 183 kg/cm² |

> **Only the first two are used in practice, and option (c) 2055 kg is the 5.0 mm value — the designed distractor, since both belong to the same short table.**

**How the CBR is computed:**

> **CBR (%) = (load carried by the specimen at the given penetration / standard load at that penetration) × 100**

> **The test is performed at BOTH 2.5 and 5.0 mm, giving two values.**

| Result | Action |
|---|---|
| **The 2.5 mm value is GREATER (the usual case)** | **Adopt the 2.5 mm value** |
| **The 5.0 mm value is greater** | **REPEAT the test. If it is confirmed, adopt the 5.0 mm value** ← |

> **The repeat requirement is worth knowing and is often omitted from summaries: normally the 2.5 mm ratio is the higher one, and a higher 5.0 mm ratio suggests something irregular about the specimen — a stone under the plunger, poor compaction, or a surface effect.**

> **So the procedure asks for confirmation before accepting the unusual result rather than simply taking the larger value.**

**What the test actually is, and why the values look arbitrary:**

> **A cylindrical PLUNGER of 50 mm diameter (area 19.35 cm², or 1935 mm²) is pushed into the specimen at a rate of 1.25 mm per minute, and the load is recorded against penetration.**

> **The STANDARD LOADS are the loads that a specimen of well-graded CRUSHED STONE from California carried in the original tests — hence the name.**

> **So the CBR is a RELATIVE measure: it expresses a soil's resistance as a percentage of that of a standard crushed rock.**

> **A CBR of 100 per cent means the material is as good as that crushed stone; 5 per cent means it is very much worse.**

> **The 70 and 105 kg/cm² pressures are simply 1370/19.35 and 2055/19.35 — so the loads and the pressures are the same information stated two ways.**

**Typical CBR values, which is what the number is used against:**

| Material | CBR (%) |
|---|---|
| **Highly plastic clay, poor subgrade** | **2-5** |
| **Silty clay, fair subgrade** | **5-10** |
| **Sandy clay, good subgrade** | **10-20** |
| **Well-graded gravel-sand subbase** | **20-50** |
| **Crushed stone base (WBM, WMM)** | **60-100** |
| **The California standard crushed stone** | **100 by definition** |

> **The pavement design is governed by the SUBGRADE CBR, and the relation is strongly non-linear: the total pavement thickness required falls rapidly as the subgrade CBR rises through the low values and much more slowly thereafter.**

> **So improving a subgrade from CBR 2 to CBR 5 saves a great deal of pavement thickness, while improving it from 15 to 20 saves very little.**

> **That is why subgrade improvement — replacing the top 300-500 mm with better material, or stabilising it with lime or cement — is so often economic on poor ground and rarely worth doing on good ground.**

**The test conditions, since the CBR is very sensitive to them:**

| Condition | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **SOAKING** | **The specimen is normally SOAKED FOR 96 HOURS (4 days) before testing** ← |
| **SURCHARGE weights** | **Annular weights of 2.5 to 5 kg placed on the specimen, representing the pavement above** |
| **Compaction** | **At the field density and moisture content to be achieved, or at OMC and maximum dry density** |
| **Swell measurement** | Recorded during soaking |
| **Penetration rate** | **1.25 mm/min** |

> **The SOAKING is the condition that matters most, and its purpose is genuinely important: the pavement must be designed for the WORST condition the subgrade will experience, which is when it is saturated after a monsoon.**

> **An unsoaked CBR can be several times the soaked value for a clayey soil — so designing on an unsoaked result would produce a pavement adequate in the dry season and failing in the wet.**

> **In Nepal, with its intense monsoon, the soaked CBR is unambiguously the value to design on, and using an unsoaked figure is a serious error rather than a conservative simplification.**

> **The SURCHARGE weights matter for the same reason: the subgrade in the field is confined by the pavement above it, and testing without that confinement understates its strength.**

**The CBR method's place in pavement design, stated honestly:**

| | **CBR method** | **Mechanistic-empirical methods** |
|---|---|---|
| **Basis** | **EMPIRICAL — thickness read from a chart against CBR and traffic** | **Layered elastic analysis; stresses and strains computed** |
| **Inputs** | **Subgrade CBR and the traffic in standard axles** | **Layer moduli, Poisson's ratios, axle loads and spectra** |
| **Output** | **Total and layer thicknesses** | **Predicted fatigue and rutting life** |
| **Used in** | **IRC 37 (older versions), and still widely in practice** | **IRC 37 (current), AASHTO, and most modern codes** |

> **The CBR method survives because it is simple, because the test is cheap and can be done with basic equipment, and because decades of pavement performance have been correlated with it.**

> **Its weakness is that the CBR is a PENETRATION resistance and not an elastic modulus, so it does not describe how a pavement layer distributes load — which is precisely what a pavement analysis needs.**

> **Modern practice therefore uses the RESILIENT MODULUS, with the CBR retained as a cheap correlate: M_R ≈ 10 × CBR (in MPa) is the commonest of several such relations.**

> **Which is a familiar pattern: a crude test with a large body of experience behind it persists alongside a better test with less, and the correlation between them is what carries the accumulated knowledge forward.**

examTip.trick: **1370 kg at 2.5 mm; 2055 kg at 5.0 mm** — equivalently 70 and 105 kg/cm² on the 19.35 cm² plunger.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) 2055 kg is the 5.0 mm value.** Normally the 2.5 mm ratio is the higher and is adopted; a higher 5.0 mm ratio requires the test to be REPEATED before it is accepted.
examTip.mnemonic: **Design on the SOAKED CBR (96 hours) with surcharge weights** — an unsoaked clay can test several times higher, giving a pavement that works in the dry season and fails in the monsoon. And thickness falls steeply as CBR rises from 2 to 5, barely at all from 15 to 20.

questions.stem: The softening point of bitumen is determined using the:
questions.solution:
**The RING AND BALL apparatus.**

**The test, and what it measures:**

> **A sample of bitumen is cast in a brass RING. A steel BALL of 3.5 g and 9.5 mm diameter is placed on it.**

> **The assembly is suspended in a water (or glycerine) bath, which is heated at a controlled rate of 5 °C per minute.**

> **The SOFTENING POINT is the temperature at which the bitumen softens enough for the ball to sink through it and fall a distance of 25 mm.**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Ball** | **Steel, 9.5 mm diameter, 3.5 g** |
| **Rate of heating** | **5 °C per minute** |
| **Fall distance** | **25 mm** |
| **Bath liquid** | **Water up to 80 °C; glycerine above** |
| **Typical softening point, paving bitumen** | **35-70 °C, depending on grade** |

> **The test is also called the RING AND BALL test, and the softening point is sometimes written R&B.**

**Why the other apparatus names are wrong — each belongs to a different material:**

| Apparatus | Material | Property measured |
|---|---|---|
| **VICAT** | **CEMENT** | **Setting time (initial and final), and consistency** |
| **LE CHATELIER** | **CEMENT** | **SOUNDNESS — unsoundness by expansion** |
| **CASAGRANDE** | **SOIL** | **LIQUID LIMIT (the percussion cup device)** |
| **RING AND BALL** | **BITUMEN** | **SOFTENING POINT** ← |

> **So the option set is drawn from three different materials, and knowing which apparatus belongs to which is the whole task.**

> **That is worth organising deliberately, because these apparatus names recur across the whole materials syllabus and are easily muddled.**

**Why bitumen has a SOFTENING POINT rather than a melting point:**

> **Bitumen is not a crystalline substance and has no sharp melting point.**

> **It is a VISCO-ELASTIC material whose stiffness changes CONTINUOUSLY with temperature — hard and brittle when cold, soft and fluid when hot, with no discontinuity between.**

> **So "softening point" is defined by an ARBITRARY BUT REPRODUCIBLE test condition — the temperature at which it becomes soft enough for a specified ball to sink a specified distance.**

> **It is an EMPIRICAL definition, and its value lies entirely in being reproducible: two laboratories following the procedure get the same answer, so grades can be compared and specified.**

> **That is worth understanding because it applies to most bitumen tests: penetration, ductility, viscosity and softening point are all defined by their procedures rather than by fundamental physics.**

**What the softening point is USED for:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Indicating the bitumen's HIGH-TEMPERATURE behaviour** | **A low softening point means the binder will soften and the pavement will RUT and BLEED in hot weather** ← |
| **Selecting a grade for the climate** | **A hot climate needs a HIGHER softening point (a harder binder)** |
| **Quality control on receipt** | Confirms the grade supplied |
| **Detecting whether bitumen has been overheated in the mixing plant** | **Overheating volatilises the lighter fractions and RAISES the softening point** |
| **With the penetration, indicating TEMPERATURE SUSCEPTIBILITY** | The penetration index |

> **The last row deserves explanation because it is the most useful derived quantity:**

> **The PENETRATION INDEX combines the penetration (a low-temperature/ambient measure) and the softening point (a high-temperature measure) to describe how STRONGLY the bitumen's consistency changes with temperature.**

> **A binder with LOW temperature susceptibility keeps a workable consistency over a wide range — which is what a pavement needs, since the same material must resist rutting at 60 °C in the sun and cracking at 0 °C on a winter night.**

> **A binder with HIGH susceptibility is soft in summer and brittle in winter — failing at both ends.**

> **That is why MODIFIED BITUMENS exist: adding polymers or crumb rubber flattens the temperature-consistency curve, raising the softening point without making the binder brittle when cold.**

> **They cost considerably more and are justified where the temperature range is extreme or the traffic is heavy.**

**The family of bitumen tests, since one question can ask for any:**

| Test | Measures | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| **PENETRATION** | **CONSISTENCY at ambient temperature** | **100 g needle, 5 seconds, 25 °C; result in 0.1 mm units** ← |
| **SOFTENING POINT (ring and ball)** | **High-temperature behaviour** | **Ball 3.5 g, heating 5 °C/min, 25 mm fall** |
| **DUCTILITY** | **Ability to stretch without breaking — an indicator of adhesion and elasticity** | **Briquette pulled at 50 mm/min at 27 °C; result in cm** |
| **VISCOSITY** | Flow resistance | Various — kinematic, absolute, or by orifice viscometer |
| **FLASH and FIRE POINT** | **SAFETY — the temperature at which vapours ignite** | **Pensky-Martens closed cup; flash point typically above 175 °C** |
| **SPECIFIC GRAVITY** | For volume-mass conversion | Pycnometer; about 0.97-1.02 |
| **LOSS ON HEATING** | Volatile content | — |
| **SOLUBILITY in trichloroethylene** | **PURITY — pure bitumen is almost entirely soluble; the residue is mineral matter** | Minimum 99 % |

> **The FLASH POINT is the one with immediate practical consequence: bitumen in a mixing plant or a boiler is heated to 150-170 °C, uncomfortably close to its flash point.**

> **Overheating a bitumen boiler has caused fires and serious injuries, and the flash point is why heating temperatures are specified as maxima and why direct flame contact with the tank wall is avoided.**

> **And note the DUCTILITY test's significance: a bitumen with low ductility is brittle and will not stretch with the pavement's thermal and traffic movements, so it cracks — which is why a minimum ductility is specified even though the test has no direct structural meaning.**

> **The grades themselves are named by their test values, which makes the nomenclature transparent:**

| Grade designation | Basis |
|---|---|
| **80/100, 60/70, 30/40** | **PENETRATION grades — the penetration in 0.1 mm units** |
| **VG10, VG20, VG30, VG40** | **VISCOSITY grades — the current IS 73 system, by viscosity at 60 °C** ← |
| **S65, A90 (older)** | Historical Indian designations |

> **Note that PENETRATION and VISCOSITY grading are different systems, and a penetration grade is not a viscosity grade** — a confusion that appears in examination questions and is worth guarding against.

examTip.trick: **RING AND BALL for bitumen's softening point.** The other three belong to other materials: VICAT and LE CHATELIER to CEMENT (setting time and soundness), CASAGRANDE to SOIL (liquid limit).
examTip.trap: **Bitumen has no melting point — it is visco-elastic with no discontinuity.** So the softening point is defined by an arbitrary but REPRODUCIBLE procedure, as are penetration, ductility and viscosity.
examTip.mnemonic: **Penetration (100 g, 5 s, 25 °C) plus softening point gives the PENETRATION INDEX — the temperature susceptibility.** A pavement must resist rutting at 60 °C and cracking at 0 °C, which is what modified bitumens are for. And 80/100 is a PENETRATION grade, not a viscosity grade.

questions.stem: As per IRC, the passenger car unit (PCU) value of a truck or bus in a mixed traffic stream is taken as:
questions.solution:
**3.0.**

**The IRC passenger car unit values:**

| Vehicle | PCU |
|---|---|
| **PASSENGER CAR, tempo, auto-rickshaw, agricultural tractor** | **1.0** |
| **Cycle** | **0.5** |
| **Motor cycle or scooter** | **0.5** |
| **Cycle rickshaw** | **1.5** |
| **Horse-drawn vehicle** | **4.0** |
| **Small light commercial vehicle** | **1.5** |
| **TRUCK or BUS** | **3.0** ← |
| **Truck-trailer, agricultural tractor-trailer** | **4.5** |
| **Hand cart** | **2.0** |
| **Bullock cart (large)** | **8.0** |
