> **Note that every option offered is a real PCU value from that table: 1.5 for a light commercial vehicle or cycle rickshaw, 0.5 for a two-wheeler, and 4.5 for a truck-trailer.**

> **So the option set requires the specific vehicle in the stem to be matched, and a candidate who recalls the table imperfectly will land on a neighbouring entry.**

**What a PCU IS and why the concept is needed:**

> **A traffic stream in South Asia contains vehicles of wildly different size, speed and manoeuvrability — bicycles, motorcycles, cars, trucks, tractor-trailers, bullock carts and pedestrians, often sharing an undivided carriageway.**

> **Counting them all as "vehicles" is meaningless for capacity purposes, because a truck consumes far more road space and imposes far more delay than a motorcycle.**

> **The PASSENGER CAR UNIT expresses each vehicle type's demand on the road AS A MULTIPLE OF A CAR'S.**

> **A traffic volume expressed in PCU per hour is then a meaningful measure of the load on the road, comparable between locations with different traffic composition.**

**What determines a vehicle's PCU — the factors:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Physical DIMENSIONS — length and width** | **A longer vehicle occupies more road length, including its headway** ← |
| **SPEED and acceleration** | **A slow vehicle causes queuing and overtaking demand behind it** ← |
| **The DIFFERENCE between its speed and the stream's** | The critical factor, more than the absolute speed |
| **Manoeuvrability and lateral placement** | A wobbling cycle needs more clearance than its width |
| **Gradient and geometry of the road** | **A truck's PCU RISES sharply on an upgrade, where it slows most** |
| **Traffic composition and volume** | PCU values are not truly constant |

> **The SPEED DIFFERENTIAL is the deeper reason a truck's PCU is 3 rather than something proportional to its length.**

> **A truck is perhaps two and a half times a car's length, which alone would give a PCU near 2.5.**

> **The remainder comes from its slower speed and poorer acceleration: it holds up the vehicles behind it, and each overtaking manoeuvre it provokes consumes road capacity in the opposing lane too.**

> **Which explains the gradient effect: on a steep upgrade a loaded truck may slow to 15 km/h while cars pass at 60, and its effective PCU can rise to 5 or more.**

> **That is why CLIMBING LANES are provided on long steep grades — a third lane letting the traffic stream pass the slow vehicles removes the capacity loss entirely, for the cost of one lane over the critical length.**

> **In Nepal's hill roads, where sustained gradients are the norm and loaded trucks are slow, the argument for climbing lanes at critical grades is unusually strong.**

**Why BULLOCK CARTS have such a high PCU — worth noting, since 8.0 looks extreme:**

> **A large bullock cart is slow (perhaps 5 km/h), wide, unable to be steered precisely, and cannot be expected to move over.**

> **On a two-lane road it effectively blocks its lane and forces every following vehicle into an overtaking manoeuvre using the opposing lane.**

> **So its consumption of road capacity is far out of proportion to its size, and 8.0 is a fair reflection of the delay it causes.**

> **The same reasoning gives a HAND CART 2.0 and a HORSE-DRAWN VEHICLE 4.0.**

> **Which illustrates the general point: PCU measures INTERFERENCE, not size — and the slowest vehicles interfere most.**

**Where PCU values are used:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **CAPACITY analysis** | **Comparing the traffic volume against the road's capacity in PCU/hour** ← |
| **Level of service determination** | The volume-to-capacity ratio |
| **Design of intersections, roundabouts and signals** | Approach volumes in PCU |
| **Deciding the number of lanes required** | — |
| **Warrants for traffic control devices** | Volume thresholds are stated in PCU |
| **Economic appraisal** | Delay and operating cost by vehicle type |

> **The IRC design capacities, for context:**

| Road | Capacity |
|---|---|
| **Single lane (3.75 m) two-way** | **About 2000 PCU/day** |
| **Two-lane (7.0 m) two-way** | **About 15,000 PCU/day** |
| **Four-lane divided** | **About 35,000 PCU/day** |
| **Two-lane, per hour** | **About 2000 PCU/hour, both directions** |

> **Note the striking non-linearity between the first two rows: widening from a single lane to two lanes multiplies the capacity by more than SEVEN, not by two.**

> **The reason is that on a single-lane road every meeting of opposing vehicles requires one to pull off onto the shoulder — so the road's capacity is limited by the frequency of those encounters rather than by the lane's throughput.**

> **Providing a second lane removes that interaction entirely, which is why the improvement is so disproportionate.**

> **That is an important practical conclusion for Nepal, where many roads are single-lane with passing places: widening to a true two-lane section is one of the highest-return road investments available, far more so than the length-based cost would suggest.**

examTip.trick: **Truck or bus = 3.0 PCU.** Car 1.0, two-wheeler and cycle 0.5, light commercial vehicle and cycle rickshaw 1.5, truck-trailer 4.5, bullock cart 8.0.
examTip.trap: **Every option offered is a real PCU from the same table** — 1.5, 0.5 and 4.5 all belong to other vehicles. Match the specific vehicle in the stem.
examTip.mnemonic: **PCU measures INTERFERENCE, not size** — which is why a bullock cart gets 8.0 and why a truck's PCU rises above 5 on a steep upgrade. Hence CLIMBING LANES. And note that widening a single lane to two lanes multiplies capacity by SEVEN, not two.

questions.stem: For the geometric design of a highway, the hourly traffic volume conventionally adopted as the design hourly volume is:
options: The average hourly volume for the year
The peak hourly volume of the year
The 10th highest hourly volume of the year
The 30th highest hourly volume of the year
questions.solution:
**The 30th HIGHEST HOURLY VOLUME of the year.**

**What that means:**

> **Rank all 8760 hourly volumes of the year from highest to lowest.**

> **The 30th value in that list is the DESIGN HOURLY VOLUME (DHV), also called the 30th highest hourly volume or the 30 HV.**

> **So the road is designed to operate satisfactorily for all but the 29 busiest hours of the year — during which it will be congested.**

**Why not the PEAK hour — the economic argument:**

> **Designing for the single busiest hour of the year would require a road substantially larger than the one that serves almost every other hour.**

> **The shape of the ranked hourly volume curve is what settles the matter:**

| Rank of the hour | Volume as a fraction of the peak hour |
|---|---|
| **1st (the peak)** | **100 %** |
| **10th** | **About 85-90 %** |
| **30th** | **About 75-80 %** ← |
| **100th** | **About 65-70 %** |
| **200th** | **About 60 %** |

> **The curve falls STEEPLY at first and then FLATTENS.**

> **So moving from the 1st to the 30th highest hour reduces the design volume by 20 to 25 per cent — a large saving — while moving from the 30th to the 100th saves only a further 10 per cent.**

> **The 30th hour sits at the KNEE of that curve, which is precisely why it was chosen: beyond it, further relaxation buys little, and before it, the cost of the extra capacity is disproportionate.**

> **That is a genuinely elegant piece of engineering economics: the design standard is placed where the marginal cost of capacity begins to exceed the marginal benefit of relieving congestion.**

**Why not the AVERAGE hourly volume — option (a):**

> **The average hourly volume is simply the AADT divided by 24, and it is far too low.**

> **A road designed for its average hour would be congested for a large part of every day, since traffic is concentrated into morning and evening peaks.**

> **The average conceals exactly the peaking the design must accommodate — which is the same objection as using the mean annual flow for a hydropower design.**

**How the DHV relates to the AADT — the K factor:**

> **DHV = K × AADT**, where K is typically 0.08 to 0.15 for rural highways — that is, the design hour carries 8 to 15 per cent of the day's traffic.

| Road type | K factor |
|---|---|
| **Rural highway with strong seasonal and weekend peaking** | **0.12-0.18 — a peaky pattern** |
| **Typical rural highway** | **0.10-0.15** |
| **URBAN road with regular commuting peaks** | **0.08-0.12 — flatter, because the peak repeats daily** ← |

> **The urban K is LOWER, and the reason is worth understanding: an urban road's peak hour occurs twice every working day, so the 30th highest hour of the year is very nearly as busy as the peak hour.**

> **A rural recreational route, by contrast, may have a few enormous holiday peaks and be quiet otherwise — so its 30th highest hour is far below its peak, and its K factor relative to the peak is higher.**

> **Which means the 30th-hour convention is more generous to a rural road than to an urban one, and urban design often uses a peak-hour analysis directly rather than the 30 HV.**

**The DIRECTIONAL DISTRIBUTION, which must be applied next:**

> **The DHV is a two-way volume. But a road's lanes must serve each direction, and traffic in the peak hour is usually UNBALANCED:**

> **Directional design hourly volume = DHV × D**, where D is the proportion in the heavier direction — typically 0.55 to 0.70.

> **A commuter route can be strongly directional — 70 or even 80 per cent inbound in the morning peak and outbound in the evening.**

> **That has a real design consequence: a four-lane divided road with two lanes each way may be congested inbound and half empty outbound during the same hour.**

> **Which is why REVERSIBLE or TIDAL FLOW lanes exist on some urban corridors — reallocating a lane to the heavy direction by time of day, which is an operational answer to a geometric constraint.**

**The other traffic volume measures, for context:**

| Measure | Definition | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **AADT (annual average daily traffic)** | **Total annual traffic ÷ 365** | **The basic measure; pavement design, economic appraisal** |
| **ADT** | Average over a shorter period | Where a full year's count is unavailable |
| **DHV (30th highest hour)** | **As above** | **GEOMETRIC design — number of lanes, capacity** ← |
| **PEAK HOUR VOLUME** | The busiest hour observed | Intersection and signal design |
| **PEAK HOUR FACTOR (PHF)** | **Peak hour volume ÷ (4 × the peak 15-minute volume)** | **Describes peaking WITHIN the hour** |
| **Standard axles (MSA)** | Cumulative equivalent axle loads | **PAVEMENT thickness design** |

> **Note the important division of labour in the last rows: GEOMETRIC design uses the DHV (a capacity question — how many vehicles at once), while PAVEMENT design uses cumulative STANDARD AXLES (a damage question — how much load over the life).**

> **The two are almost independent: a road carrying many cars needs lanes but little pavement thickness, while a road carrying few but very heavy trucks needs thickness but not lanes.**

> **So a quarry access road and a suburban commuter road can require completely different designs while carrying similar vehicle counts** — and confusing the two design inputs is a fundamental error rather than a detail.

> **The PEAK HOUR FACTOR deserves its place because it captures a further level of peaking: traffic within the peak hour is itself uneven, and a signalised intersection must handle the busiest 15 minutes rather than the hourly average.**

> **A PHF of 1.0 means perfectly uniform flow within the hour; 0.85 is typical; below 0.80 indicates sharp peaking that will produce queues even when the hourly volume is within capacity.**

examTip.trick: **The 30th HIGHEST hourly volume of the year** — so the road is congested for only the 29 busiest hours.
examTip.trap: **The 30th hour sits at the KNEE of the ranked-volume curve** — moving from the 1st to the 30th saves 20-25 % of capacity, but from the 30th to the 100th saves only 10 % more. That is why 30 was chosen, not 10 or 100.
examTip.mnemonic: **GEOMETRIC design uses the DHV (a capacity question); PAVEMENT design uses cumulative STANDARD AXLES (a damage question).** The two are nearly independent — many cars need lanes, few heavy trucks need thickness. Confusing them is a fundamental error.

questions.stem: In a RIGID pavement, the wheel load is transferred to the subgrade principally:
options: By grain-to-grain transfer through successive granular layers
By flexural action of the slab, which distributes the load over a wide area
By the subgrade alone, the slab contributing nothing
By the wearing course, which carries the load in shear
questions.solution:
**By FLEXURAL action of the slab, which distributes the load over a wide area.**

**The fundamental distinction between the two pavement types:**

| | **FLEXIBLE pavement** | **RIGID pavement** |
|---|---|---|
| **Load transfer** | **GRAIN TO GRAIN through successive layers, the load spreading in a cone** | **FLEXURAL (beam/plate) action of the slab, spreading the load over a wide area** ← |
| **Material** | **Bituminous surfacing on granular base and subbase** | **Cement concrete slab** |
| **Design based on** | **Total THICKNESS for the subgrade CBR and traffic** | **FLEXURAL STRENGTH of the concrete and the modulus of subgrade reaction** |
| **Stress on the subgrade** | **Higher — the spread is limited** | **LOW — distributed over a large area** |
| **Deflection under load** | **Larger, and recovered elastically** | Small |
| **Design life** | **10-15 years** | **30-40 years** |
| **Initial cost** | **LOWER** | **Higher (20-40 % more)** |
| **Maintenance** | **Frequent — periodic renewal of the surfacing** | **Very low — but repairs are difficult and disruptive** |
| **Requires good subgrade?** | **YES — the subgrade carries a large share** | **LESS critical — the slab bridges local weakness** ← |

> **Option (a) describes the FLEXIBLE pavement's mechanism, which is what makes it the designed distractor: it is the correct answer to the same question about the other pavement type.**

**Why the mechanisms differ so fundamentally:**

> **A FLEXIBLE pavement has NO significant flexural strength. Each granular layer transmits the load to the one below by grain-to-grain contact, and the stress spreads out at roughly 45 degrees as it descends.**

> **So the pressure on the subgrade depends entirely on the THICKNESS of material above it — which is why flexible pavement design is a thickness calculation.**

> **A RIGID pavement is a concrete SLAB with substantial flexural rigidity. It acts as a plate on an elastic foundation: a wheel load at one point is carried by BENDING over a radius of several metres.**

> **The pressure delivered to the subgrade is therefore low and spread over a wide area, and it depends on the SLAB'S STIFFNESS rather than on the thickness of material beneath.**

> **The practical consequence is the one in the last row of the table: a rigid pavement can BRIDGE a local soft spot in the subgrade, while a flexible pavement will simply deflect and fail over it.**

> **Which is why a concrete pavement is attractive over variable or poor subgrades, and over made ground or utility trenches.**

**The design theory for rigid pavements, since it follows from the flexural mechanism:**

> **WESTERGAARD'S analysis treats the slab as an elastic plate on a WINKLER foundation — a bed of independent springs characterised by the MODULUS OF SUBGRADE REACTION k.**

> **Three critical load positions are analysed:**

| Load position | Stress character | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **INTERIOR of the slab** | Bending, supported all round | Least critical |
| **EDGE of the slab** | **Higher stress — support on one side only** | |
| **CORNER of the slab** | **HIGHEST stress and greatest deflection — support on two sides only** ← |

> **The CORNER is the critical location, and that is why corner cracking is the characteristic distress of a concrete pavement and why corners receive special attention — dowel bars, thickened edges, or a stabilised subbase.**

> **The RADIUS OF RELATIVE STIFFNESS  l = [E h³ / (12 k (1 − μ²))]^{1/4}  measures how far the slab distributes a load, and it typically comes out at 0.6 to 1.0 m for a highway slab — so a wheel load is carried by a region a metre or so across, rather than by the small contact patch.**

**The other stress in a rigid pavement — and it is often the larger one:**

> **TEMPERATURE stresses in a concrete slab can EXCEED the traffic load stresses, which is a fact that surprises people.**

| Temperature effect | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **WARPING (curling) stress** | **A temperature DIFFERENCE between the top and bottom of the slab makes it try to curl; restrained by its own weight and by the subgrade, it develops bending stress** ← |
| **FRICTIONAL stress** | **Uniform temperature change makes the slab try to expand or contract; friction against the subbase restrains it, developing direct tension or compression** |

> **A slab whose surface is 15 °C hotter than its base — an ordinary afternoon condition — tries to curl upward at its edges, and the restraint generates tensile stress at the top of the slab.**

> **Combined with a wheel load at an edge or corner, that is the critical design case.**

> **And the frictional stress is what makes JOINTS necessary:**

| Joint | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **CONTRACTION (transverse) joints** | **Allow the slab to shrink and contract without cracking randomly — spaced 4.5 m or so** ← |
| **EXPANSION joints** | **Allow expansion; wider, with a filler, at longer intervals** |
| **LONGITUDINAL joints** | Between lanes; control warping cracks |
| **CONSTRUCTION joints** | At the end of a day's work |
| **TIE BARS across longitudinal joints** | Hold the lanes together |
| **DOWEL BARS across transverse joints** | **Transfer load across the joint while permitting movement** |

> **The DOWEL BAR is worth understanding: without it, a wheel crossing a joint is momentarily supported by one slab edge alone, and the edge stress is high.**

> **A dowel transfers part of the load to the adjacent slab, halving the effective edge loading — while remaining unbonded on one side so the slabs can still move relative to one another.**

> **So a dowel must transfer LOAD while permitting MOVEMENT, which is why it is a smooth round bar greased over half its length rather than a deformed bar.**

> **Getting that detail wrong — using a deformed bar, or bonding both ends — locks the joint, and the slab cracks somewhere else instead.**

**And a note on where each type is chosen:**

| Situation | Preferred pavement |
|---|---|
| **Heavy, channelised traffic; toll plazas; bus bays; ports** | **RIGID — resists rutting and standing loads** ← |
| **Poor or variable subgrade** | **RIGID — bridges weakness** |
| **Where maintenance access is difficult or costly** | **RIGID — long life, low maintenance** |
| **Staged construction, or where the alignment may change** | **FLEXIBLE — can be strengthened by overlay** |
| **Where good aggregate and bitumen are available cheaply** | Flexible |
| **Where cement is available but bitumen must be imported** | **Rigid — a real consideration in Nepal** |

> **The last row is a genuine factor in Nepal: cement is manufactured domestically while bitumen is imported, so the relative cost of the two pavement types there differs from the international norm — and concrete pavement is more competitive than a textbook comparison would suggest.**

> **And the RUTTING point deserves emphasis: a bituminous surface under a standing or slow-moving heavy load in hot weather deforms permanently, which is why bus stops, toll plazas and steep climbing lanes are so often concreted even on an otherwise flexible road.**

examTip.trick: **RIGID: flexural action of the slab spreads the load widely. FLEXIBLE: grain-to-grain transfer, the load spreading in a cone.** Option (a) is the correct answer for the other type.
examTip.trap: **A rigid pavement can BRIDGE a soft spot in the subgrade; a flexible one deflects and fails over it** — which is why concrete suits variable subgrades, made ground and utility trenches.
examTip.mnemonic: **TEMPERATURE (warping) stresses in a concrete slab can EXCEED the traffic stresses** — a 15 °C top-to-bottom difference is an ordinary afternoon. The CORNER is the critical load position, which is why dowel bars and corner details matter.

questions.stem: The pavement distress consisting of the progressive dislodging of aggregate particles from the surface, leaving it rough and pitted, is called:
questions.solution:
**RAVELLING.**

**The principal bituminous pavement distresses, defined and distinguished:**

| Distress | Appearance | Principal cause |
|---|---|---|
| **RAVELLING** | **Aggregate progressively dislodged; the surface becomes rough and pitted** ← | **INSUFFICIENT BINDER, or loss of adhesion between binder and aggregate (usually from water)** |
| **RUTTING** | **Longitudinal depressions in the wheel paths** | **Permanent deformation — of the bituminous layer (too soft a binder, too much binder) or of the layers beneath (inadequate thickness)** |
| **CORRUGATION (rippling)** | **Regular transverse ripples, like a washboard** | **Unstable mix — excess binder or rounded aggregate — plus traffic braking and accelerating** |
| **BLEEDING (flushing)** | **A film of binder on the surface; shiny, sticky, slippery when wet** | **EXCESS binder, or a binder too soft for the temperature** |
| **POTHOLES** | Bowl-shaped holes | Progression of ravelling or cracking, accelerated by water |
| **ALLIGATOR (fatigue) cracking** | **Interconnected cracks in a pattern like alligator hide, in the wheel paths** | **FATIGUE under repeated loading — the classic structural failure** |
| **Shoving** | Localised bulging and displacement | Unstable mix under braking or turning forces |
| **Stripping** | Binder separated from aggregate | **Water — the same mechanism as ravelling, seen from the material side** |
| **Edge breaking** | Loss of the carriageway edge | Inadequate shoulder support, water |

> **Note that RAVELLING and BLEEDING are OPPOSITE faults from the same variable:**

> **TOO LITTLE binder → the aggregate is not held → RAVELLING.**

> **TOO MUCH binder → it flushes to the surface → BLEEDING.**

> **So the binder content has an optimum, and erring in either direction produces a distinct and recognisable defect.**

> **That is precisely what the MARSHALL MIX DESIGN determines: the OPTIMUM BINDER CONTENT, at which stability, density, air voids and voids filled with bitumen are all satisfactory together.**

**Why WATER is the underlying agent in so many of these:**

> **Ravelling, stripping, potholes and edge breaking all have water as their principal accelerator, and the mechanism is worth understanding:**

> **Bitumen adheres to aggregate by physical and chemical bonding at the interface. WATER competes for that surface.**

> **In the presence of water — particularly under the pumping action of traffic on a wet pavement — the water displaces the binder from the aggregate surface, and the bond fails.**

> **The aggregate is then held only mechanically, and traffic plucks it out.**

| Factor | Effect on stripping and ravelling |
|---|---|
| **ACIDIC (siliceous) aggregate — quartzite, granite** | **MORE prone to stripping — water wets them preferentially** ← |
| **BASIC aggregate — limestone, basalt** | **Less prone — better affinity for bitumen** |
| **DUSTY or damp aggregate at mixing** | **The binder never bonds to the stone in the first place** ← |
| **ANTI-STRIPPING agents (amines, hydrated lime)** | Improve the bond chemically |
| **Poor drainage; water standing on or in the pavement** | The precondition for all of it |

> **The DUSTY OR DAMP AGGREGATE point is the practically important one: a coating of dust on the aggregate means the bitumen bonds to the dust rather than to the stone, and the mix is compromised from the moment it is made.**

> **Which is why aggregate must be washed if dusty and DRIED before mixing — and why a hot-mix plant's drier is not an optional refinement.**

> **And it explains a common site failure: a premix carpet laid on a damp or dusty existing surface ravels within a season, however good the mix, because the bond to the surface below never formed.**

**The MAINTENANCE responses, since identifying a distress is only useful if it leads to a treatment:**

| Distress | Treatment |
|---|---|
| **RAVELLING, early** | **A FOG SEAL or a slurry seal — restores binder at the surface** ← |
| **Ravelling, advanced** | **Surface dressing, or a thin overlay** |
| **BLEEDING** | **Blot with sand or coarse aggregate; in bad cases, remove and replace** |
| **RUTTING in the bituminous layer** | Mill off and replace with a stiffer mix |
| **RUTTING from the subgrade** | **STRUCTURAL failure — needs reconstruction or a substantial overlay, not a surface treatment** ← |
| **POTHOLES** | Cut to a regular shape, clean, tack coat, fill and compact — never merely thrown full of mix |
| **ALLIGATOR cracking** | **A structural deficiency — overlay designed for the remaining traffic, or reconstruction** |

> **The distinction between SURFACE and STRUCTURAL distress is the most important judgement in pavement maintenance:**

> **A SURFACE distress (ravelling, bleeding, minor cracking) is a defect of the wearing course and is cured by a surface treatment costing very little.**

> **A STRUCTURAL distress (alligator cracking, subgrade rutting, general deformation) means the pavement is inadequate for its traffic, and a surface treatment merely conceals it for a season.**

> **Applying a surface treatment to a structural failure is the commonest waste of a maintenance budget: the money is spent, the road looks better for a few months, and the underlying failure continues.**

> **Distinguishing the two requires looking at WHERE the distress is and WHAT PATTERN it follows — surface distresses are general or random, while structural ones follow the WHEEL PATHS.**

> **That single observation — is it in the wheel paths? — separates most cases correctly.**

**And the strongest general point about pavement maintenance:**

> **A pavement's condition deteriorates SLOWLY at first and then RAPIDLY: the curve is flat for most of the life and then falls away steeply.**

> **Maintenance applied EARLY, on the flat part, is cheap and restores the pavement to nearly new condition.**

> **The same defect left until the curve has fallen requires reconstruction at many times the cost.**

> **The figure commonly quoted is that a rupee spent on timely preventive maintenance saves four to five spent on later rehabilitation — and while the exact ratio varies, the shape of the argument is well established.**

> **Which makes PREVENTIVE maintenance the highest-return activity in road management, and its chronic underfunding the commonest failure of road administration** — because the benefit is invisible, consisting entirely of a deterioration that did not happen.

examTip.trick: **RAVELLING — aggregate progressively dislodged, from TOO LITTLE binder or loss of adhesion.** BLEEDING is its opposite: TOO MUCH binder flushing to the surface.
examTip.trap: **Ravelling and bleeding are opposite faults from the same variable**, which is why Marshall mix design exists — to find the OPTIMUM binder content where neither occurs.
examTip.mnemonic: **Ask: is the distress in the WHEEL PATHS?** If yes, suspect STRUCTURAL failure needing an overlay; if general or random, it is a SURFACE defect a cheap seal will cure. Treating a structural failure with a surface seal is the commonest waste of a maintenance budget.

questions.stem: In FIRST-ANGLE projection, the top view (plan) of an object is placed:
options: To the left of the front view
To the right of the front view
questions.solution:
**BELOW the front view.**

**The two projection systems, and the rule that distinguishes them:**

| | **FIRST-angle projection** | **THIRD-angle projection** |
|---|---|---|
| **Object sits** | **BETWEEN the observer and the plane of projection** | **The PLANE sits between the observer and the object** |
| **TOP view (plan)** | **BELOW the front view** ← | **ABOVE the front view** |
| **Left-side view** | **Placed on the RIGHT** | **Placed on the LEFT** |
| **Right-side view** | **Placed on the LEFT** | **Placed on the RIGHT** |
| **Used in** | **India, Nepal, Europe — the ISO convention** | **USA, Canada, Japan** |

> **The single rule that generates the whole table:**

> **In FIRST angle, the view is projected THROUGH the object onto a plane BEHIND it — so each view appears on the side OPPOSITE to the direction from which it was taken.**

> **In THIRD angle, the object is projected FORWARD onto a plane in FRONT of it — so each view appears on the SAME side as the direction from which it was taken.**

> **Hence: looking DOWN at the object in first angle puts the plan BELOW; in third angle it puts the plan ABOVE.**

> **Reasoning it out that way is far more reliable than memorising four rows, and it settles the side views at the same time.**

**The physical picture, which makes it stick:**

> **FIRST ANGLE: imagine the object resting on the paper and being SQUASHED FLAT — the top folds down below, the left side folds over to the right.**

> **THIRD ANGLE: imagine the object inside a GLASS BOX and the box being UNFOLDED — the top opens upward, the left side opens to the left.**

> **The "glass box unfolding" image for third angle and the "squash flat" image for first angle recover both conventions in a few seconds.**

**Why the distinction matters — and it matters a great deal:**

> **A drawing read in the wrong convention gives a MIRRORED object.**

> **A component with a feature on its left will be manufactured with the feature on its right — and the error is not always obvious, because both readings produce a plausible-looking object.**

> **Which is why every drawing must carry a PROJECTION SYMBOL in or near the title block:**

| Symbol | Convention |
|---|---|
| **A truncated cone with the SMALL circle toward the LEFT view position** | **FIRST angle** |
| **The same cone with the SMALL circle toward the RIGHT** | **THIRD angle** |

> **The symbol is itself a frustum of a cone drawn in the convention it denotes — so it demonstrates the convention rather than merely naming it, which is an elegant piece of standardisation.**

> **A drawing without the symbol is incomplete, and on an international project it is a genuine hazard: a Nepali consultant's first-angle drawings sent to an American fabricator, or the reverse, will be misread unless the symbol is there and is noticed.**

**The SIX principal views, and how many are actually needed:**

| View | Direction |
|---|---|
| **FRONT elevation** | From the front |
| **TOP view / PLAN** | From above |
| **BOTTOM view** | From below |
| **LEFT side elevation** | From the left |
| **RIGHT side elevation** | From the right |
| **REAR elevation** | From behind |

> **Six are possible; THREE are usually sufficient — front, top and one side — and the guiding principle is to use the MINIMUM NUMBER OF VIEWS THAT DESCRIBES THE OBJECT COMPLETELY.**

> **Additional views are not thoroughness but clutter: each one must be drawn, checked and revised, and every extra view is another place for an inconsistency to hide.**

> **Which view to choose as the FRONT is the draughtsman's first decision, and the conventions are:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **Choose the view showing the most CHARACTERISTIC shape** | The one by which the object is recognised |
| **Choose the view with the FEWEST HIDDEN LINES** | **Hidden detail is harder to read than visible detail** ← |
| **Show the object in its NATURAL or FUNCTIONAL position** | A beam horizontal, a column vertical |
| **Choose the LONGEST dimension horizontally** | Fits the sheet better |

**The other projection types, for context, since "projection" covers more than these two:**

| Projection | Character |
|---|---|
| **ORTHOGRAPHIC (first and third angle)** | **Multiple 2-D views, all true to scale — the basis of all working drawings** ← |
| **ISOMETRIC** | **A single pictorial view; all three axes at 120°, all equally foreshortened to 0.816 (usually drawn full size on an isometric scale)** |
| **Oblique (cavalier, cabinet)** | One face true, the depth axis at an angle |
| **PERSPECTIVE** | **Converging lines to vanishing points — realistic, but NOT to scale, so it cannot be measured from** |
| **Auxiliary view** | A view on a plane inclined to the principal planes, to show an inclined face truly |
| **Section** | A cut through the object, revealing internal detail |

> **The critical practical distinction is between ORTHOGRAPHIC and PERSPECTIVE:**

> **An orthographic view is TO SCALE and can be measured — which is why every working drawing is orthographic.**

> **A perspective view LOOKS right and cannot be measured, because objects diminish with distance.**

> **So perspective belongs in a presentation drawing for a client and never in a construction drawing** — and issuing a perspective as a working drawing, or scaling a dimension off one, is a real and occasionally consequential mistake.

> **The same caution applies in a milder form to any drawing: a dimension should be READ from the figures written on it, never SCALED off the paper — because prints stretch, photocopies rescale, and a revised drawing may have had a figure changed without the geometry being redrawn.**

> **Hence the note "DO NOT SCALE" that appears on properly prepared drawings, and hence the rule that a missing dimension must be queried rather than measured.**

examTip.trick: **FIRST angle: the plan goes BELOW the front view, and the LEFT view goes on the RIGHT.** Third angle is the reverse of both. India and Nepal use first angle.
examTip.trap: **Reason it out rather than memorising: FIRST angle projects THROUGH the object onto a plane behind, so each view lands on the OPPOSITE side.** Third angle projects forward, so views land on the SAME side. Picture "squash flat" against "unfold a glass box".
examTip.mnemonic: **A drawing read in the wrong convention gives a MIRRORED object** — which is why the truncated-cone projection symbol is mandatory. And a PERSPECTIVE view is not to scale, so it can never be a working drawing; even on orthographic drawings, READ the figures, never scale the paper.

questions.stem: On a drawing prepared to a scale of 1:100, a wall 4.5 m long is drawn as a line of length:
questions.solution:
**45 mm.**

**The computation:**

> **A scale of 1:100 means one unit on the drawing represents 100 of the same units on the object.**

> **Drawn length = actual length / 100 = 4500 mm / 100 = 45 mm** ✓

> **Working in MILLIMETRES throughout is what makes this trivial: 4.5 m = 4500 mm, divided by 100 gives 45 mm directly.**

> **The commonest error is a factor of ten in the metre-to-millimetre conversion, and options (a) 4.5 mm and (b) 450 mm are exactly that error made in each direction.**

> **So the safeguard is a single written step: convert to millimetres FIRST, then divide.**

**A useful shortcut for the scales actually used:**

> **At 1:100, ONE METRE becomes TEN MILLIMETRES — a clean 1 cm per metre.**

> **So 4.5 m is 4.5 centimetres, that is 45 mm.**

> **The equivalent shortcuts for the common scales are worth having, because they let a drawing be read or checked at a glance:**

| Scale | One metre becomes | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **1:1** | **1000 mm (full size)** | Details, templates |
| **1:5** | 200 mm | Large-scale details |
| **1:10** | **100 mm** | **Reinforcement and joint details** |
| **1:20** | 50 mm | Details, staircases |
| **1:50** | **20 mm** | **Building plans, sections, bar bending** |
| **1:100** | **10 mm** ← | **General building plans and elevations** |
| **1:200** | 5 mm | Large building plans, layouts |
| **1:500** | **2 mm** | **Site plans** |
| **1:1000** | **1 mm** | **Site and location plans** |
| **1:2500 to 1:50,000** | Less than 1 mm | **Topographic and location maps** |

> **Note the preferred series: 1, 2, 5 and their decimal multiples.**

> **Scales such as 1:30 or 1:75 are avoided because they cannot be read with a standard scale rule — which is a practical constraint that has shaped the convention.**

**REPRESENTATIVE FRACTION, since the term is used interchangeably:**

> **RF = drawing length / actual length**, both in the same units.

> **So a scale of 1:100 has RF = 1/100, and a map at 1:50,000 has RF = 1/50,000.**

| Scale type | RF | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **FULL size** | **1/1** | RF = 1 |
| **REDUCING scale** | **Less than 1** | **All architectural and engineering drawings** ← |
| **ENLARGING scale** | **Greater than 1** | Small components, machine details |

> **And note which is the LARGER scale, since the terminology inverts:**

> **1:50 is a LARGER scale than 1:100, because its RF (1/50) is the larger fraction — and the object is drawn BIGGER.**

> **So a "large-scale drawing" shows a SMALL area in GREAT detail, and a "small-scale drawing" shows a LARGE area with little detail.**

> **That inversion catches people constantly, and the reliable check is to ask which drawing shows the object BIGGER — that is the larger scale.**

**The three kinds of scale, since drawings and maps use different ones:**

| Kind | Form | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **ENGINEER'S / numerical scale** | **"1:100" or "1 cm = 1 m"** | Stated as a ratio or an equivalence |
| **REPRESENTATIVE FRACTION** | **1/100** | The same thing as a fraction |
| **GRAPHICAL (bar) scale** | **A divided line drawn on the sheet** | **Survives PHOTOCOPYING and rescaling — the numerical scale does not** ← |

> **The GRAPHICAL scale's advantage is genuinely important and often overlooked: if a drawing is photocopied at a reduced size, or printed to a different paper size, the printed numerical scale becomes a LIE while the bar scale rescales with the drawing and stays true.**

> **Which is why every map and every drawing likely to be reproduced should carry a bar scale as well as a stated ratio** — and it is another reason for the "do not scale" rule on working drawings, where dimensions are read from figures instead.

**The scales specific to surveying, for completeness:**

| Scale | Construction | Reads |
|---|---|---|
| **PLAIN scale** | Divided into main and sub-divisions | **TWO dimensions — units and tenths** |
| **DIAGONAL scale** | **Sub-divided by a diagonal construction** | **THREE dimensions — units, tenths and hundredths** ← |
| **VERNIER scale** | A sliding auxiliary scale | Three dimensions, more precisely |
| **Comparative scale** | Two scales of different units to the same RF | Converts between unit systems |
| **Scale of chords** | For setting out and measuring angles | Angles without a protractor |

> **The DIAGONAL SCALE's principle is worth a sentence because it is ingenious: dividing a short length into ten parts directly would give divisions too small to read, so the length is drawn as the base of a triangle and subdivided along the DIAGONAL, where the same ten divisions are spread over a much greater length.**

> **Similar triangles then give the required hundredths at a readable spacing — obtaining precision from geometry rather than from finer draughtsmanship.**

> **It is a device from the age of hand drawing, and it survives on the syllabus because the geometrical reasoning is instructive even where the instrument is obsolete.**

examTip.trick: **Convert to MILLIMETRES first: 4.5 m = 4500 mm, ÷ 100 = 45 mm.** At 1:100, one metre becomes 10 mm — so 4.5 m is 4.5 cm.
examTip.trap: **Options (a) and (b) are the metre-to-millimetre conversion wrong by a factor of ten in each direction.** One written conversion step prevents both.
examTip.mnemonic: **1:50 is a LARGER scale than 1:100** — the object is drawn bigger, so the fraction is larger. And a GRAPHICAL bar scale survives photocopying while the printed ratio becomes a lie, which is why maps carry both.

questions.stem: A sum of Rs 1,00,000 is invested at 10 % per annum compounded annually. Its value at the end of 3 years is:
questions.solution:
**Rs 1,33,100.**

**The compound interest relation:**

> **F = P (1 + i)ⁿ**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **P** | **Present sum (principal)** | **1,00,000** |
| **i** | **Interest rate per period** | **0.10** |
| **n** | **Number of periods** | **3** |

**The computation:**

> **F = 1,00,000 × (1.10)³**

> **(1.10)³ = 1.331**

> **F = Rs 1,33,100** ✓

> **The cube of 1.1 is worth knowing outright: 1.1² = 1.21, and 1.21 × 1.1 = 1.331.**

> **And the pattern continues neatly — 1.1⁴ = 1.4641, which is option (d), the value after FOUR years.**

**Why each distractor is placed as it is — every one is a specific error:**

| Option | Origin |
|---|---|
| **(a) Rs 1,33,100** | ✓ |
| **(b) Rs 1,30,000** | **SIMPLE interest: 1,00,000 + 3 × 10,000 = 1,30,000** ← the designed trap |
| **(c) Rs 1,21,000** | **The value after TWO years, (1.1)² = 1.21** |
| **(d) Rs 1,46,410** | **The value after FOUR years, (1.1)⁴ = 1.4641** |

> **Option (b) is the important one, because it tests whether SIMPLE and COMPOUND interest are held apart:**

| | **SIMPLE interest** | **COMPOUND interest** |
|---|---|---|
| **Formula** | **F = P(1 + in)** | **F = P(1 + i)ⁿ** |
| **Interest earned on** | **The PRINCIPAL only** | **Principal AND accumulated interest** ← |
| **After 3 years here** | **Rs 1,30,000** | **Rs 1,33,100** |
| **Growth** | **LINEAR** | **EXPONENTIAL** |

> **The difference over three years is only Rs 3,100 — about 3 per cent — which is why the two are easily confused at short durations.**

> **But the gap widens dramatically:**

| Years | Simple interest | Compound interest | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| **3** | **1,30,000** | **1,33,100** | **3,100** |
| **10** | **2,00,000** | **2,59,374** | **59,374** |
| **20** | **3,00,000** | **6,72,750** | **3,72,750** |
| **30** | **4,00,000** | **17,44,940** | **13,44,940** |

> **Over thirty years the compound value is more than FOUR TIMES the simple value.**

> **That divergence is the whole reason engineering economics uses compound interest exclusively: infrastructure projects have lives of twenty to fifty years, and over those spans the distinction is not a refinement but the dominant term.**

> **A thirty-year appraisal done on simple interest would be wrong by a factor of four.**

**The DOUBLING TIME, which is the most useful mental tool here:**

> **The RULE OF 72: money roughly DOUBLES in (72 / interest rate in per cent) years.**

> **At 10 per cent: 72/10 = 7.2 years.**

> **Check: 1.1^7.2 = 1.99** ✓ — accurate to one per cent.

| Rate | Doubling time by the rule | Actual |
|---|---|---|
| **6 %** | **12.0 years** | **11.9** |
| **8 %** | **9.0 years** | **9.0** |
| **10 %** | **7.2 years** | **7.3** |
| **12 %** | **6.0 years** | **6.1** |

> **The rule is remarkably accurate over the range of rates that actually occur, and it lets any compound growth question be sanity-checked instantly.**

> **Here: three years is less than half a doubling period, so the answer must be well below 2,00,000 and somewhat above 1,30,000 — which selects option (a) without computing anything.**

**The interest factors used in engineering economics, since this is the first of a family:**

| Factor | Symbol | Expression | Converts |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Single payment COMPOUND AMOUNT** | **(F/P, i, n)** | **(1+i)ⁿ** | **P → F** ← |
| **Single payment PRESENT WORTH** | **(P/F, i, n)** | **1/(1+i)ⁿ** | **F → P (DISCOUNTING)** |
| **Uniform series COMPOUND AMOUNT** | **(F/A, i, n)** | **[(1+i)ⁿ − 1]/i** | **A → F** |
| **SINKING FUND** | **(A/F, i, n)** | **i/[(1+i)ⁿ − 1]** | **F → A** |
| **Uniform series PRESENT WORTH** | **(P/A, i, n)** | **[(1+i)ⁿ − 1]/[i(1+i)ⁿ]** | **A → P** |
| **CAPITAL RECOVERY** | **(A/P, i, n)** | **i(1+i)ⁿ/[(1+i)ⁿ − 1]** | **P → A** ← |

> **Note that the factors come in RECIPROCAL PAIRS: (F/P) and (P/F), (F/A) and (A/F), (P/A) and (A/P).**

> **So only three need to be remembered and the others are their reciprocals — which halves the memory load and provides a check on any recalled expression.**

> **The CAPITAL RECOVERY factor is the one most used in practice: it converts a capital cost into an equivalent ANNUAL cost, which is how a project's capital and running costs are brought to a common basis for comparison.**

> **For a Rs 1,00,000 investment at 10 per cent over 3 years, the capital recovery factor is 0.4021 — so the equivalent annual cost is Rs 40,210.**

> **That is the figure a project appraisal actually uses, because it can be added directly to the annual operating cost to give a total annual cost comparable between alternatives with different lives and different capital-to-running-cost balances.**

**And a word on the DISCOUNT RATE, since it is the parameter that matters most:**

> **The whole apparatus above is driven by the interest or discount rate, and small changes in it change conclusions:**

> **At a HIGH discount rate, future benefits are heavily discounted, so projects with early returns are favoured and long-lived infrastructure looks poor.**

> **At a LOW rate, distant benefits retain their weight, and capital-intensive long-life projects — dams, railways, water supply — become attractive.**

> **So the choice of discount rate is not a technical detail but a policy decision about how much weight the future is to be given** — and it is the single most contested number in any large project's appraisal.

examTip.trick: **F = P(1+i)ⁿ = 1,00,000 × 1.1³ = 1,00,000 × 1.331 = Rs 1,33,100.** Worth knowing: 1.1² = 1.21, 1.1³ = 1.331, 1.1⁴ = 1.4641 — and options (c) and (d) are the 2-year and 4-year values.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) Rs 1,30,000 is SIMPLE interest.** The gap is only 3 % over three years but over thirty years compound gives more than FOUR times as much — which is why engineering economics uses compound interest exclusively.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rule of 72: money doubles in 72/i years — 7.2 years at 10 %.** Three years is under half a doubling, so the answer must sit between 1,30,000 and 2,00,000. And the interest factors come in RECIPROCAL PAIRS, so only three need remembering.

questions.stem: The discount rate at which the net present value of a project becomes exactly zero is called the:
questions.solution:
**The INTERNAL RATE OF RETURN (IRR).**

**The definition:**

> **The IRR is the discount rate i* at which:**

> **NPV = Σ [Cash flow in year t / (1 + i*)ᵗ] = 0**

> **Equivalently, it is the rate at which the present worth of the BENEFITS exactly equals the present worth of the COSTS.**

> **So the IRR is the project's own rate of return — the effective interest rate the invested money earns.**

**How the decision is made — the IRR must be compared with something:**

> **The IRR alone says nothing. It is compared with the MINIMUM ATTRACTIVE RATE OF RETURN (MARR), also called the hurdle rate or the cost of capital:**

| Comparison | Decision |
|---|---|
| **IRR > MARR** | **ACCEPT — the project earns more than the money's alternative use** ← |
| **IRR = MARR** | Indifferent |
| **IRR < MARR** | **REJECT — the money would do better elsewhere** |

> **Which is why option (c) is such a well-made distractor: the MARR is the value the IRR is JUDGED AGAINST, and the two are used in the same sentence constantly.**

> **But the MARR is an EXTERNAL parameter — set by the organisation from its cost of capital and its risk appetite — while the IRR is INTERNAL to the project, computed from its own cash flows.**

> **That is exactly what the word "internal" in the name denotes: it depends on nothing but the project's own numbers.**

**The four principal appraisal criteria, compared:**

| Criterion | Measures | Decision rule | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| **NET PRESENT VALUE (NPV)** | **The project's net worth today, in money** | **Accept if NPV > 0 at the MARR** | **Requires the discount rate to be chosen first; gives an absolute figure, so it favours large projects** |
| **INTERNAL RATE OF RETURN (IRR)** | **The project's own return, as a percentage** | **Accept if IRR > MARR** ← | **Multiple or no solutions with irregular cash flows; can mis-rank alternatives** |
| **BENEFIT-COST RATIO (BCR)** | **PW of benefits ÷ PW of costs** | **Accept if BCR > 1** | Sensitive to what is classified as a cost against a disbenefit |
| **PAYBACK PERIOD** | **Time to recover the initial investment** | **Accept if shorter than a threshold** | **IGNORES everything after the payback, and (in its simple form) ignores the time value of money entirely** ← |

> **The PAYBACK PERIOD's weakness deserves emphasis because the method remains popular despite it:**

> **A project that recovers its cost in three years and then produces nothing scores better on payback than one that recovers in five years and then produces handsomely for thirty.**

> **So payback measures LIQUIDITY and RISK EXPOSURE rather than profitability — it answers "how soon is my money back?" and not "is this worth doing?".**

> **It is a useful supplementary check, particularly where capital is scarce or the political horizon is short, and it is not a substitute for NPV or IRR.**

**Why NPV is theoretically the soundest criterion — and where IRR misleads:**

> **NPV measures the actual increase in wealth, in money, at the organisation's own cost of capital. It is additive across projects and it always ranks alternatives correctly.**

> **The IRR has two genuine defects worth knowing:**

| Defect | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **MULTIPLE IRRs** | **If the cash flow changes sign more than once — a major mid-life replacement, or decommissioning costs at the end — the polynomial has several roots, and there is no single IRR** ← |
| **Mis-ranking of alternatives of different SIZE** | **A small project can have a high IRR and a tiny NPV. Choosing by IRR would prefer earning 40 % on Rs 1 lakh to earning 15 % on Rs 10 crore** ← |
| **Implicit reinvestment assumption** | The IRR assumes interim cash flows are reinvested at the IRR itself, which may be unrealistic |

> **The SIZE problem is the practically important one, and the remedy is the INCREMENTAL analysis: compare alternatives two at a time by computing the IRR on the DIFFERENCE in their cash flows, and accept the extra investment if that incremental IRR exceeds the MARR.**

> **Done properly, incremental IRR analysis gives the same ranking as NPV — which is reassuring, and it means the IRR can be used correctly, just not naively.**

> **So why is the IRR so widely preferred in practice despite its defects? Because a PERCENTAGE is intuitive and comparable across projects of any size, and because it does NOT require a discount rate to be agreed before the calculation.**

> **In a setting where the appropriate discount rate is genuinely contested — which describes most public infrastructure appraisal — being able to report "this project returns 14 per cent" and let the reader apply their own hurdle is a real advantage.**

**Where these criteria are applied in civil engineering:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Choosing between design alternatives** | **A thicker pavement now against more maintenance later; a larger pipe against higher pumping costs** ← |
| **Deciding whether to build at all** | Project justification |
| **Timing an investment** | Build now or build later |
| **Choosing an ECONOMIC diameter, thickness or capacity** | The same trade-off in a continuous variable |
| **Replacement analysis** | When to replace ageing plant |
| **Public project appraisal, including non-monetary benefits** | Economic rather than financial analysis |

> **The last row raises the distinction that matters most in public works:**

| | **FINANCIAL analysis** | **ECONOMIC analysis** |
|---|---|---|
| **Viewpoint** | **The project owner's — actual money in and out** | **SOCIETY'S — all costs and benefits, whoever bears them** |
| **Prices used** | **Market prices, including taxes and subsidies** | **SHADOW (economic) prices, with transfers removed** |
| **Includes** | Revenues and expenditures | **Time savings, accident reduction, health benefits, environmental costs** ← |
| **Discount rate** | The cost of capital | The social discount rate |

> **A rural road frequently fails a FINANCIAL test — it collects no tolls and generates no revenue — while passing an ECONOMIC test comfortably, because the value of the travel time saved, the produce brought to market and the access to health care and schooling far exceeds its cost.**

> **So a public infrastructure project must be appraised economically, and applying a financial test to it would reject almost every road, water supply and school in the country.**

> **That distinction is the single most important thing a civil engineer should understand about project appraisal, because it determines whether the analysis measures the right thing at all.**

examTip.trick: **IRR — the discount rate making NPV zero**, that is, where the present worth of benefits equals that of costs. "Internal" because it depends on nothing but the project's own cash flows.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) MARR is what the IRR is JUDGED AGAINST** — accept if IRR > MARR. The MARR is external (the cost of capital); the IRR is internal to the project.
examTip.mnemonic: **IRR's real defect is SIZE: 40 % on Rs 1 lakh beats 15 % on Rs 10 crore by IRR and loses badly by NPV.** Use INCREMENTAL IRR to fix it. And for public works, ECONOMIC analysis (time saved, accidents avoided) not FINANCIAL — a rural road fails the second and passes the first.

questions.stem: In PERT, an activity has an optimistic time of 4 days, a most likely time of 6 days and a pessimistic time of 14 days. Its expected time is:
questions.solution:
**7.0 days.**

**The PERT expected time (a weighted mean of the three estimates):**

> **t_E = (t_o + 4 t_m + t_p) / 6**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **t_o** | **OPTIMISTIC time — everything goes right** | **4** |
| **t_m** | **MOST LIKELY time — the modal estimate** | **6** |
| **t_p** | **PESSIMISTIC time — everything goes wrong** | **14** |

**The computation:**

> **t_E = (4 + 4×6 + 14)/6 = (4 + 24 + 14)/6 = 42/6 = 7.0 days** ✓

**The important feature of the result — the expected time EXCEEDS the most likely time:**

> **t_m = 6 days, but t_E = 7 days.**

> **The reason is the ASYMMETRY of the estimates: the pessimistic time is 8 days ABOVE the mode while the optimistic time is only 2 days BELOW it.**

> **The distribution is therefore SKEWED to the right, and its mean lies to the right of its mode.**

> **That skew is not an artefact — it reflects reality. An activity can be delayed almost without limit (weather, a late delivery, a labour dispute, a design change) but it can only be accelerated so far.**

> **So the downside is fatter than the upside, and PERT's weighted formula captures it.**

> **Option (a) 6.0 days is the MOST LIKELY time offered as the expected time — the designed trap, and it understates the duration by exactly the amount the skew contributes.**

> **And that understatement is systematic: a project planned on most-likely durations throughout will run late, because every activity's true mean exceeds its mode.**

> **Which is one of the more useful things PERT teaches, and it explains a phenomenon everyone has observed without being able to name.**

**The VARIANCE and the standard deviation, since PERT's purpose is probabilistic:**

> **σ = (t_p − t_o) / 6   and   σ² = [(t_p − t_o)/6]²**

> **Here: σ = (14 − 4)/6 = 10/6 = 1.667 days, so σ² = 2.78 days².**

> **The RANGE divided by six comes from the assumption that the optimistic and pessimistic estimates span about six standard deviations of a beta distribution — that is, that they are near-extreme values rather than confidence limits.**

> **So an activity with widely separated estimates has a large variance and is UNCERTAIN, and one with close estimates is well understood.**

> **This activity's σ of 1.67 days against a mean of 7 is substantial uncertainty — about 24 per cent — which flags it as one worth investigating further.**

**How the variances are used — probability of completion:**

> **The variances of the activities ON THE CRITICAL PATH are ADDED (variances add; standard deviations do not):**

> **σ_project = √(Σ σ²_critical activities)**

> **Then, treating the project duration as normally distributed by the central limit theorem:**

> **Z = (Target date − Expected duration) / σ_project**

> **And the probability of meeting the target is read from the standard normal table.**

| Z | Probability of completion |
|---|---|
| **−1.0** | **16 %** |
| **0** | **50 %** ← at the expected duration |
| **+1.0** | **84 %** |
| **+1.64** | **95 %** |
| **+2.33** | **99 %** |

> **The Z = 0 row carries a genuinely important lesson: at the EXPECTED duration, the probability of completion is only 50 PER CENT.**

> **A project promised on its PERT expected date is a coin toss.**

> **To offer a date with 90 or 95 per cent confidence, a CONTINGENCY of 1.28 to 1.64 standard deviations must be added.**

> **That is the single most practically valuable output of a PERT analysis, and it converts a scheduling exercise into a statement about risk — which is what a client actually needs.**

**PERT against CPM — the comparison that always follows:**

| | **PERT** | **CPM** |
|---|---|---|
| **Time estimates** | **THREE — probabilistic** | **ONE — deterministic** |
| **Orientation** | **EVENT-oriented** | **ACTIVITY-oriented** |
| **Suits** | **RESEARCH and DEVELOPMENT; novel work where durations are uncertain** ← | **CONSTRUCTION and repetitive work where durations are known from experience** ← |
| **Cost** | **Not originally treated** | **COST-TIME trade-off is central — crashing** |
| **Origin** | **US Navy, Polaris missile programme, 1958** | **DuPont, plant maintenance, 1957** |
| **Dummy activities** | Used | Used |

> **In modern practice the two have largely MERGED — commercial software offers three-point estimates and cost-loading together — so the distinction is now more historical than operational.**

> **But the underlying question it poses remains live and is worth asking of any programme: ARE THESE DURATIONS KNOWN OR GUESSED?**

> **A construction programme for a familiar building type on a known site has durations known from experience, and a single estimate is honest.**

> **A programme for a novel structure, an unfamiliar site or unproven methods has durations that are guesses, and presenting them as single figures conceals the uncertainty rather than removing it.**

> **CRASHING, from the CPM side, deserves a note since it is the other half of the subject: shortening a project by adding resources to CRITICAL activities, at the least cost per day saved.**

> **The essential points are that only CRITICAL activities are worth crashing (shortening a non-critical activity changes nothing), that the cheapest critical activity is crashed first, and that as the critical path shortens NEW critical paths appear — so the analysis must be redone after each step.**

> **And crashing is pursued only until the cost of a further day saved exceeds the benefit of saving it, which is where the optimum project duration lies: not the shortest achievable, but the least costly.**

examTip.trap: **Option (a) 6.0 is the MOST LIKELY time.** The expected time EXCEEDS it because the estimates are skewed right — delay is nearly unbounded while acceleration is limited. A project planned on most-likely durations runs late systematically.
examTip.mnemonic: **At the PERT expected duration the probability of completion is only 50 %** — a promised date needs 1.28σ for 90 % or 1.64σ for 95 %. Variances ADD along the critical path; standard deviations do not.

questions.stem: The principal limitation of a bar (Gantt) chart as a project planning tool is that:
options: It cannot show the duration of activities
It cannot show the progress achieved against the plan
It does not show the interdependence of activities or which of them are critical
It cannot be prepared for a large project
questions.solution:
**It does not show the INTERDEPENDENCE of activities or which of them are CRITICAL.**

**What a bar chart does and does not show:**

| Shows | Does NOT show |
|---|---|
| **The activities, listed** | **WHICH activity depends on which** ← |
| **The DURATION of each, as a bar length** | **Which activities are CRITICAL** ← |
| **The START and FINISH dates** | **The FLOAT available on non-critical activities** |
| **Progress, if the bars are shaded** | **The EFFECT of a delay on the rest of the project** |
| **Overlap and concurrency, visually** | **Why an activity is scheduled when it is** |

> **Options (a) and (b) are simply false — a bar chart shows durations by definition, and progress is routinely shown by shading or by a second bar.**

> **Option (d) is false as well: bar charts are prepared for very large projects, usually summarised at a high level.**

> **The real limitation is the one in option (c), and it is a limitation of the FORM rather than of the practitioner.**

**Why the missing dependencies matter so much:**

> **Consider a bar chart showing an activity due to start on 1 May.**

> **The chart does not tell you WHY 1 May: is it because the preceding excavation finishes then, because the reinforcement is delivered then, or merely because someone drew it there?**

> **So when the excavation runs two weeks late, the chart cannot tell you what else moves.**

> **The planner must rework the whole chart by judgement, and the judgement is not recorded — which means:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **No systematic way to update the plan** | **Every revision is a fresh act of judgement** ← |
| **No way to know which delays matter** | **A three-week delay to a non-critical activity may cost nothing; a one-day delay to a critical one costs a day** |
| **No basis for evaluating a claim for extension of time** | **The contractual consequence — a delay's effect cannot be demonstrated** ← |
| **No basis for crashing or resource decisions** | Which activity to accelerate is unknown |
| **Cannot compute float** | So resources cannot be levelled intelligently |

> **The CONTRACTUAL consequence is the one that has driven the adoption of network methods more than any technical argument:**

> **When a contractor claims an extension of time, the question is whether the event complained of actually DELAYED THE COMPLETION — and that can only be demonstrated on a network showing the critical path.**

> **A bar chart cannot support or refute such a claim, so disputes on bar-chart projects are settled by argument rather than by analysis.**

> **Which is why modern contracts routinely REQUIRE a network programme, and why delay analysis has become a specialist field built entirely on the critical path concept.**

**The comparison with network methods:**

| | **BAR (Gantt) chart** | **NETWORK (CPM/PERT)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Dependencies** | **NOT shown** | **Shown explicitly, as the logic** ← |
| **Critical path** | **Not identified** | **Identified** |
| **Float** | **Not computable** | **Computed for every activity** |
| **Updating** | **By judgement** | **By recomputation** |
| **Ease of reading** | **EXCELLENT — anyone can read it** ← | **Requires training** |
| **Suits** | **COMMUNICATION and reporting** | **ANALYSIS and control** |

> **Note the fifth row, because it explains why the bar chart has not been displaced despite its limitation:**

> **A bar chart is IMMEDIATELY LEGIBLE to anyone — a client, a foreman, a minister, a shopkeeper affected by the works.**

> **A network diagram is not, and a network presented to a lay audience conveys almost nothing.**

> **So modern practice uses BOTH, and uses each for what it does well:**

> **The NETWORK is the analytical model — it holds the logic, computes the critical path and the floats, and is what gets updated.**

> **The BAR CHART is the OUTPUT — generated from the network, showing the same schedule in a form people can read.**

> **Every scheduling package works this way: the user enters activities, durations and DEPENDENCIES, the software computes the network, and the display is a bar chart with the dependency arrows drawn on it — a LINKED bar chart, which is the best of both.**

> **So the honest answer to "bar chart or network?" is that the question is obsolete: the bar chart is the view and the network is the model.**

**The other planning techniques, for completeness:**

| Technique | Character |
|---|---|
| **BAR / GANTT chart** | **Time against activity; the standard reporting form** ← |
| **LINKED bar chart** | **A bar chart with dependency arrows — the modern default** |
| **NETWORK: activity-on-arrow (AOA)** | **Arrows are activities, nodes are events; needs DUMMY activities** |
| **NETWORK: activity-on-node (AON, precedence)** | **Nodes are activities, arrows are dependencies; no dummies needed — the form software uses** ← |
| **LINE OF BALANCE (LOB)** | **For REPETITIVE work — housing units, pipeline lengths, floors of a tower; plots progress against location** |
| **Time-chainage (time-location) diagram** | **For LINEAR projects — roads, railways, tunnels; distance against time on one chart** |
| **S-curve** | **Cumulative progress, cost or man-hours against time; the standard monitoring tool** |
| **Milestone chart** | Key dates only, for high-level reporting |

> **The TIME-CHAINAGE diagram deserves particular mention for Nepal's road and canal projects: it plots distance ALONG the alignment against time, so each activity appears as a sloping band whose gradient is its rate of progress.**

> **Its great advantage is that CLASHES become visible immediately — two activities occupying the same chainage at the same time show as crossing bands, which no bar chart would reveal.**

> **For a linear project it conveys in one diagram what a bar chart cannot express at all**, and it is under-used relative to its value.

> **And the LINE OF BALANCE serves the same purpose for repetitive work, its object being to keep the crews moving at a BALANCED rate so that no trade catches up with the one in front — which is the central scheduling problem of repetitive construction and is invisible on a conventional bar chart.**

examTip.trick: **A bar chart shows WHEN activities happen but not WHY** — no dependencies, no critical path, no float. Options (a) and (b) are simply false: durations and progress are both shown.
examTip.trap: **The consequence that drove adoption of networks is CONTRACTUAL** — an extension-of-time claim can only be demonstrated on a network showing the critical path. A bar chart can neither support nor refute one.
examTip.mnemonic: **Modern practice uses both: the NETWORK is the model, the BAR CHART is the view** — which is exactly how scheduling software works. And for LINEAR projects use a TIME-CHAINAGE diagram, where clashes appear as crossing bands.

questions.stem: A contract in which the contractor is paid a fixed rate for each unit of work actually executed, measured on completion, is called a:
questions.solution:
**An ITEM-RATE or UNIT-PRICE contract.**

**The principal contract types compared:**

| Type | Basis of payment | Who carries the QUANTITY risk | Suits |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ITEM-RATE (unit price, schedule of rates)** | **A fixed rate per unit, times the quantity ACTUALLY executed and measured** | **The EMPLOYER** ← | **Most civil works, where quantities cannot be known exactly in advance** |
| **LUMP-SUM** | **One fixed total price for the whole defined work** | **The CONTRACTOR** | **Work fully defined before tender — buildings with complete drawings** |
| **COST-PLUS-PERCENTAGE** | **Actual cost plus an agreed percentage as profit** | **The EMPLOYER entirely** | **Emergency work; work of unknown extent** |
| **COST-PLUS-FIXED-FEE** | **Actual cost plus a fixed sum** | Employer, but the fee is capped | As above, with better incentive |
| **PERCENTAGE-RATE** | **Contractor bids a percentage above or below a departmental schedule of rates** | Employer | Small departmental works |
| **LABOUR (piece-work) contract** | **Labour only; the employer supplies materials** | Employer supplies materials | Small works; where the employer can procure better |
| **TARGET COST** | Cost against a target, with the saving or overrun shared | Shared | Collaborative projects |
| **BOT / BOOT / concession** | **The concessionaire finances, builds and operates, recovering from tolls or tariffs** | **The concessionaire** | Large infrastructure with a revenue stream |

> **The QUANTITY RISK column is the most useful way to organise these, because it identifies what each type is really for.**

**Why the item-rate contract dominates civil engineering — the reason is the nature of the work:**

> **Civil works quantities cannot be known exactly before construction:**

| Uncertainty | Example |
|---|---|
| **The depth of excavation to sound foundation** | **Not known until the excavation is made** ← |
| **The quantity of rock against soft material** | Boreholes sample a tiny fraction of the volume |
| **The extent of dewatering required** | Depends on the season and the ground |
| **The volume of unsuitable material to be removed** | Discovered as work proceeds |
| **Grouting quantities, pile lengths** | Determined by the ground |

> **A LUMP-SUM contract for such work would force the contractor to price an unknown quantity — and a rational contractor would price the WORST CASE, or would price optimistically and then litigate.**

> **Neither serves the employer: the first is expensive, and the second is expensive and acrimonious.**

> **The ITEM-RATE contract resolves it by separating the two things properly:**

> **The CONTRACTOR prices the RATE — which is within their expertise and control, being a matter of their productivity, plant and organisation.**

> **The EMPLOYER carries the QUANTITY — which is a matter of the ground and the design, being within the employer's knowledge and responsibility.**

> **That allocation of risk to the party best able to assess and manage it is the fundamental principle of sound contracting, and the item-rate contract is its clearest application.**

**The consequences of item-rate contracting, which must be managed:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **All work must be MEASURED** | **Requires a measurement standard, a measurement book, and staff to measure — an administrative burden** ← |
| **The final cost is NOT known at award** | **Only the rates are fixed; the total depends on the quantities executed** |
| **UNBALANCED bidding is possible** | **See below — the principal abuse** ← |
| **Variations are priced from the schedule** | An advantage: changes have pre-agreed rates |
| **Disputes shift from price to measurement and classification** | Is this rock or hard soil? |

> **UNBALANCED (or front-loaded) BIDDING is the abuse worth understanding, because it is common and it is detectable:**

> **A contractor who believes the bill of quantities UNDERSTATES an item quotes a very high rate for it, and compensates with a low rate on an item they believe is overstated.**

> **The tender total looks competitive, and the contractor profits when the quantities turn out as expected.**

> **Front-loading is a related version: high rates on early items (excavation, site clearance) and low rates on later ones, improving the contractor's cash flow at the employer's expense.**

> **The defences are to examine the RATE ANALYSIS behind unusual rates, to compare item rates against the engineer's own estimate item by item rather than only comparing totals, and to specify that grossly unbalanced rates may be a ground for rejection.**

> **Comparing only the bottom line — which is the natural thing to do — is precisely what makes the tactic work.**

**Why COST-PLUS-PERCENTAGE is the weakest form, since it is worth being clear:**

> **The contractor is reimbursed their actual cost plus a percentage of it.**

> **So the contractor's PROFIT RISES WITH THE COST — there is a positive incentive to spend more.**

> **That is a perverse incentive of the plainest kind, and it is why cost-plus-percentage is confined to genuine emergencies where speed overrides everything and no time exists to define the work.**

> **COST-PLUS-FIXED-FEE removes the perversity — the fee does not grow with the cost — and is preferred wherever a cost-reimbursable form is genuinely necessary.**

> **And a TARGET COST arrangement goes further, sharing savings and overruns so that the contractor gains from economy.**

> **The general lesson is one worth carrying beyond contracts: examine what a payment mechanism REWARDS, because that is what it will produce.**

**The tendering procedures, briefly, since they accompany the contract types:**

| Procedure | Note |
|---|---|
| **OPEN competitive tender** | **Advertised publicly; the default for public works, and the most transparent** ← |
| **LIMITED / selective tender** | From a pre-qualified or approved list |
| **PRE-QUALIFICATION then tender** | **For large or technically demanding works — capability assessed before price** |
| **NEGOTIATED contract** | Directly with one contractor; exceptional, and requires justification |
| **Two-envelope (technical and financial)** | **Technical proposals evaluated before financial ones are opened** |
| **Quality and cost based selection (QCBS)** | **For CONSULTANCY, where the cheapest is rarely the best** ← |

> **The QCBS point is worth stating because it corrects a common misconception: for CONSTRUCTION, the lowest evaluated responsive bid is generally the right award, since the specification defines the product.**

> **For DESIGN and CONSULTANCY it is not, because the product IS the consultant's judgement, and buying judgement at the lowest price is a poor bargain.**

> **Hence quality-and-cost-based selection, typically weighting technical quality at 70 to 80 per cent and price at 20 to 30 — an arrangement that recognises what is actually being purchased.**

examTip.trick: **ITEM-RATE (unit price): a fixed rate per unit times the quantity ACTUALLY measured.** The contractor prices the RATE; the EMPLOYER carries the QUANTITY.
examTip.trap: **Organise the types by WHO CARRIES THE QUANTITY RISK** — employer in item-rate, contractor in lump-sum, employer entirely in cost-plus. That single column tells you what each form is for.
examTip.mnemonic: **Watch for UNBALANCED bidding: high rates on items believed understated, low on those overstated.** Comparing only the bottom line is what makes it work — compare item by item. And note that cost-plus-PERCENTAGE rewards spending more, which is why it is confined to emergencies.

questions.stem: The sum deducted from each running bill and held by the employer until the defect liability period expires is called:
questions.solution:
**RETENTION MONEY.**

**The securities and deposits in a construction contract, in the order they arise:**

| Item | When | Purpose | Typical amount |
|---|---|---|---|
| **EARNEST MONEY / BID SECURITY** | **Submitted WITH the tender** | **Ensures the bidder does not withdraw the bid or refuse to sign the contract if awarded** | **1-3 % of the estimated cost** |
| **PERFORMANCE SECURITY / security deposit** | **On award, before signing** | **Ensures the contract is performed; forfeited on default** | **5-10 % of the contract price** |
| **MOBILISATION ADVANCE** | **Early, on request, against a bank guarantee** | **Helps the contractor establish the site and procure plant — recovered from later bills** | **10-20 %, recovered progressively** |
| **RETENTION MONEY** | **Deducted from EACH running bill** | **Held against defects; ensures the contractor returns to rectify them** ← | **5-10 % of each bill, capped at 5 % of the contract price** |
| **Release of retention** | **Half on completion, half at the END of the DEFECT LIABILITY PERIOD** | — | — |

> **The distinctive feature of RETENTION MONEY, which the stem points to, is its TIMING: it is deducted PROGRESSIVELY from each payment and released AFTER the defect liability period.**

> **Earnest money and bid security come BEFORE the contract exists; performance security comes AT its formation; retention accumulates DURING the work and is released AFTER it.**

> **So the four secure four different risks at four different stages, and option (a) and (b) — which are in fact the same thing under two names — belong to the tendering stage.**

**Why retention money exists — the specific risk it addresses:**

> **Defects in construction frequently do not appear until the work has been in use for a season or two:**

| Defect | When it appears |
|---|---|
| **Leaking roof or waterproofing** | **The first monsoon** ← |
| **Settlement cracks** | Months after loading |
| **Failure of a plaster or paint finish** | Weeks to months |
| **Blocked or mis-graded drainage** | The first heavy rain |
| **Pavement defects from poor compaction** | The first wet season under traffic |
| **Faulty joinery, ironmongery, fittings** | Through use |

> **A contractor paid in full on completion has no financial reason to return and rectify — and pursuing them through the courts costs more than the repair.**

> **Retention money reverses that: the contractor is holding an unpaid balance that is released only after the defect liability period, so returning to fix a defect is cheaper for them than forfeiting the retention.**

> **So the mechanism works by ALIGNING THE CONTRACTOR'S INTEREST with the employer's rather than by relying on obligation or enforcement — which is why it is effective where a mere contractual duty would not be.**

**The DEFECT LIABILITY PERIOD, since the retention's release depends on it:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Typical duration** | **12 months from completion; sometimes 24 for major works** |
| **What it covers** | **Defects arising from the CONTRACTOR'S materials or workmanship** ← |
| **What it does NOT cover** | **Fair wear and tear, misuse by the employer, or defects in the EMPLOYER'S design** |
| **Also called** | Maintenance period, defects notification period |
| **At its end** | **A final inspection, the defect liability certificate, and release of the remaining retention** |

> **The exclusion of DESIGN defects is the important distinction, and it is where disputes concentrate:**

> **A crack caused by BAD CONCRETE is a workmanship defect and the contractor's liability.**

> **A crack caused by an INADEQUATE SECTION in the design is the designer's responsibility, not the contractor's, and the contractor is entitled to be paid for rectifying it.**

> **Establishing which it is requires investigation, and it is one of the commonest and most contested questions on a defects claim.**

> **Note that the defect liability period is NOT a warranty period in the sense of extinguishing all liability at its end: a LATENT defect — one concealed and not reasonably discoverable — may remain actionable for far longer under the general law.**

> **So a contractor is not free of a structural defect after twelve months merely because the certificate was issued.**

**The MOBILISATION ADVANCE, since option (c) names it and it is the odd one out:**

> **It is the only item in the list that moves money TOWARD the contractor rather than securing money for the employer.**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Purpose** | **Enable the contractor to establish the site, bring plant and buy initial materials** |
| **Justification** | **A contractor's largest cash need is at the START, before any bill can be raised** ← |
| **Security required** | **An unconditional BANK GUARANTEE for the full amount** |
