| **Recovery** | **Deducted proportionally from running bills, fully recovered before the work is complete** |
| **Interest** | Interest-free in some conditions of contract, interest-bearing in others |

> **The economic case for a mobilisation advance is real and worth understanding: without it, only well-capitalised contractors can tender, and competition narrows to the largest firms.**

> **A capable but small contractor may be unable to fund three months of work before the first payment, and would either not bid or would bid at a rate loaded with the cost of borrowing.**

> **So the advance broadens competition and lowers prices — provided it is properly secured by a bank guarantee and properly recovered.**

> **Where it is NOT properly secured, it is simply a gift at the public's risk, and the abuse of unsecured advances is a recurring problem in public procurement.**

**The payment cycle in full, since these items sit within it:**

| Stage | Document |
|---|---|
| **Work executed and measured** | **MEASUREMENT BOOK entries, jointly signed** |
| **Contractor submits a claim** | **RUNNING (interim) BILL** |
| **Engineer certifies** | **INTERIM PAYMENT CERTIFICATE, less retention, less advance recovery, less any deductions** |
| **Employer pays within the stipulated period** | — |
| **Work completed** | **COMPLETION CERTIFICATE; half the retention released** |
| **Final measurement and account** | **FINAL BILL** |
| **Defect liability period expires** | **DEFECT LIABILITY CERTIFICATE; the remaining retention released; performance security returned** |

> **The MEASUREMENT BOOK deserves a closing note because it is the document on which everything else rests: it is a legal record, written in ink, jointly signed by the contractor's and the employer's representatives at the time of measurement, and not alterable afterward.**

> **Payment follows measurement, and measurement follows the book — so a poorly kept measurement book undermines the whole payment chain and is the most common source of audit objection on public works.**

> **Which is why its rules are strict to the point of seeming pedantic: no erasures, no pencil, no blank spaces, corrections initialled, and every page accounted for.**

examTip.trick: **RETENTION MONEY — deducted from EACH running bill, released half on completion and half at the end of the defect liability period.** Its distinguishing feature is the TIMING.
examTip.trap: **The four securities cover four stages: earnest money/bid security BEFORE the contract, performance security AT its formation, retention DURING the work, released AFTER.** Options (a) and (b) are the same thing under two names.
examTip.mnemonic: **Retention works by ALIGNING the contractor's interest, not by imposing a duty** — returning to fix a defect is cheaper than forfeiting the money. And the defect liability period excludes DESIGN defects, which is where the disputes concentrate.

questions.stem: A registered engineer discovers, during construction, a design error that could endanger the occupants of a building. The client instructs the engineer to say nothing. The engineer's professional obligation is to:
options: Keep the matter confidential, since the duty of confidentiality to the client is paramount
Inform the client and, if the client will not act, notify the appropriate authority
Take no action until the client gives instructions in writing
Resign from the commission quietly, without making any report
questions.solution:
**Inform the client and, if the client will not act, notify the appropriate authority.**

**The governing principle:**

> **The FIRST and PARAMOUNT duty of an engineer is to the SAFETY, HEALTH AND WELFARE OF THE PUBLIC.**

> **That duty OVERRIDES the duty of confidentiality to a client and the duty of loyalty to an employer.**

> **Every recognised engineering code of ethics states it in substantially the same words, and it is the first canon in almost all of them.**

> **So the hierarchy is settled, and it is not a matter of judgement between competing duties of equal weight:**

| Rank | Duty |
|---|---|
| **1** | **PUBLIC safety, health and welfare** ← |
| **2** | **The client's or employer's legitimate interests** |
| **3** | **The profession's standing** |
| **4** | Self-interest |

**Why confidentiality does NOT prevail — and it is worth being precise:**

> **The duty of confidentiality is real and important: an engineer must not disclose a client's commercial information, designs or affairs.**

> **But confidentiality protects a client's LEGITIMATE interests. It does not extend to CONCEALING A DANGER TO THIRD PARTIES.**

> **A client has no legitimate interest in the concealment of a hazard to the people who will occupy the building, and so there is no confidentiality to breach.**

> **Which means option (a) mistakes the nature of the duty rather than misranking two genuine ones.**

**Why option (d) — quiet resignation — is inadequate, and this is the subtler point:**

> **Resigning removes the ENGINEER from the situation. It does nothing about the DANGER.**

> **The building will still be built with the defect, and the occupants will still be at risk — and now nobody who knows about it is involved.**

> **So a quiet resignation protects the engineer's own position while abandoning the people the duty exists to protect.**

> **It is the option that FEELS most professional and is in fact the least so.**

> **Resignation may well be a proper step ALONGSIDE reporting — an engineer cannot continue to lend their name to work they know to be unsafe — but resignation INSTEAD of reporting is a failure of the primary duty.**

> **Option (c) fails for a related reason: awaiting instructions defers action indefinitely while the risk continues, and a client who has already instructed silence is unlikely to instruct otherwise in writing.**

**The proper SEQUENCE of steps, since "report it" is not the whole answer:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **VERIFY the finding — be sure the error is real, and quantify the risk. A false alarm damages everyone and the engineer's credibility with it** ← |
| **2** | **Document it: the calculation, the drawing, the observation, dated** |
| **3** | **Raise it FIRST with the client, in writing, setting out the risk and the remedy** |
| **4** | **Give the client a reasonable opportunity to act — most clients will** |
| **5** | **If the client will not act, notify the AUTHORITY — the building permit authority, the local body, or the Nepal Engineering Council** |
| **6** | **Consider whether to continue on the commission at all** |
| **7** | **Keep a complete record throughout** |

> **Step 1 is not a delaying tactic but a professional requirement: an engineer must be RIGHT before making an allegation that will stop a project and impugn a colleague.**

> **And step 3 matters because it is both fair and effective: most clients, told plainly and in writing that a defect endangers occupants, will act — because their own liability is at stake once they have been informed.**

> **So going to the client first is not weakness; it is the step most likely to fix the problem quickly.**

> **The escalation to the authority is the recourse when that fails, and it is a recourse the engineer is obliged to use rather than merely permitted to.**

**Why the profession is regulated at all — the underlying logic, which this question illustrates:**

> **Engineering is licensed because the public CANNOT ASSESS the competence or the safety of engineering work for themselves.**

> **A building's occupants cannot inspect its structural calculations. They rely entirely on the engineer's competence and honesty.**

> **That INFORMATION ASYMMETRY is what justifies a licensing regime: the public is asked to trust a professional they cannot check, and in exchange the profession accepts regulation, a code of conduct, and liability.**

> **So the privileges of registration — the exclusive right to practise, to sign drawings, to certify work — are granted in return for accepting duties that sometimes conflict with the engineer's own interest.**

> **An engineer who conceals a danger for a client's convenience has taken the privileges and declined the duty, and that is precisely the conduct the disciplinary provisions exist to address.**

**The NEC's disciplinary powers, since they give the code force:**

| Power | Note |
|---|---|
| **Investigate a complaint of professional misconduct** | On complaint or on its own motion |
| **Warn or reprimand** | For lesser matters |
| **SUSPEND registration for a period** | **The engineer cannot legally practise during it** |
| **REMOVE the name from the register** | **The most severe sanction — a permanent bar** ← |
| **Refer matters involving criminal conduct to the authorities** | Where a law has been broken |

> **The sanction that matters is REMOVAL FROM THE REGISTER, because in a licensed profession it ends the career rather than merely penalising an act.**

> **That is what gives a code of ethics practical force: without a registration that can be withdrawn, a code is only an exhortation.**

**The other principal canons of engineering ethics, for completeness:**

| Canon | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Hold PARAMOUNT the safety, health and welfare of the public** | ← the first and governing canon |
| **Perform services only in areas of one's COMPETENCE** | **Do not accept work you are not qualified to do** |
| **Issue public statements only in an OBJECTIVE and truthful manner** | No misleading claims |
| **Act for each client or employer as a FAITHFUL AGENT** | Loyalty, subject to canon 1 |
| **Avoid DECEPTIVE acts** | Including in seeking work |
| **Conduct oneself HONOURABLY and lawfully, so as to enhance the profession's standing** | — |
| **Continue PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT** | **And provide opportunities for the development of engineers under one's supervision** |
| **Avoid CONFLICTS OF INTEREST, and disclose them where they arise** | Full disclosure to all affected parties |

> **The COMPETENCE canon is worth noting alongside the safety canon, because the two together cover most real ethical failures in engineering practice: work concealed when it should have been reported, and work accepted when it should have been declined.**

> **Neither failure usually arises from bad intent. Both arise from commercial pressure — the wish to keep a client, or to win a commission — which is why the canons are written as absolutes rather than as considerations to be balanced.**

examTip.trick: **PUBLIC safety, health and welfare is the PARAMOUNT duty** — it overrides confidentiality to a client and loyalty to an employer. That hierarchy is settled, not a balance to be struck.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) quiet resignation FEELS most professional and is the least so** — it removes the engineer from the situation and does nothing about the danger. Resignation may accompany reporting; it cannot replace it.
examTip.mnemonic: **VERIFY first, then tell the CLIENT in writing, then escalate to the AUTHORITY if they will not act.** Being right before making the allegation is a professional requirement, and most clients act once informed — because their own liability then attaches.

questions.stem: The tenure of the members elected to the Nepal Engineering Council from the Nepal Engineers' Association is:
questions.solution:
**Four years.**

**The provision:**

> **Under the Nepal Engineering Council Act, FIVE members are ELECTED to the Council from among the members of the NEPAL ENGINEERS' ASSOCIATION, and their tenure is FOUR YEARS.**

> **They are the only DIRECTLY ELECTED members of the Council — every other member is nominated, appointed or ex officio.**

**The Council's full composition, since this fact belongs to a set:**

| Position | Number | Appointed by | Qualification |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CHAIRMAN (President)** | **1** | **Nominated by GoN** | **Bachelor's + 15 years** |
| **VICE CHAIRMAN** | **1** | **Nominated by GoN** | **Bachelor's + 10 years** |
| **Members, one from each province** | **7** | **Nominated by GoN** | **Bachelor's + 7 years; at least THREE women** |
| **President of the NEA** | **1** | **Ex officio** | — |
| **Members ELECTED from the NEA** | **5** | **Directly ELECTED** | **Tenure FOUR YEARS** ← |
| **Campus chief of an engineering campus** | **1** | Nominated by GoN | — |
| **Representative, Institute of Engineering, TU** | **1** | Nominated by GoN | — |
| **Representative of universities teaching engineering** | **1** | Nominated by GoN | — |
| **Members nominated BY THE COUNCIL itself** | **2** | **By the Council** | **Bachelor's + 7 years; at least ONE woman** |
| **MEMBER SECRETARY (Registrar)** | **1** | — | **Bachelor's + 10 years** |

> **So the Council has about twenty-one members drawn through four distinct routes — government nomination, direct election, ex officio membership and the Council's own nomination.**

**Why the elected members matter to the Council's character:**

> **A regulator composed entirely of government appointees would lack LEGITIMACY with the profession it regulates, and would be suspected of serving the government rather than the public.**

> **A regulator composed entirely of elected practitioners would risk becoming a GUILD — protecting its members rather than the public, and reluctant to discipline its own.**

> **The five elected members give the profession a genuine voice and a stake in the Council's decisions, while remaining a minority within a body whose majority comes through other routes.**

> **That balance is deliberate, and it is the standard design of professional regulators worldwide.**

> **The FOUR-YEAR tenure serves the same purpose: long enough for an elected member to learn the work and contribute to continuity, short enough that the electorate can change the representation.**

**The NEC facts most often examined, gathered as a set:**

| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| **NEC Act** | **2055 BS (1998 AD)** |
| **NEC Regulation** | **2057 BS** |
| **First amendment to the Act** | **2079/05/05** |
| **Bachelor's programme recognition** | **2066/06/23** |
| **Master's programme recognition** | **2076/09/06** |
| **Nature of the Council** | **An AUTONOMOUS body** |
| **Who approves its rules** | **Government of Nepal** |
| **Chairman's qualification** | **Bachelor's + 15 years** |
| **Vice chairman's qualification** | **Bachelor's + 10 years** |
| **Registrar / Member Secretary** | **Bachelor's + 10 years** |
| **Provincial members** | **7 (at least 3 women)** |
| **NEA-ELECTED members** | **5, tenure FOUR years** ← |
| **Members nominated by the Council** | **2 (at least 1 woman)** |
| **Minimum qualification to register** | **A Bachelor's degree in engineering** |
| **The NEA's own legal basis** | **The Social Service Act** |

> **This is a small, closed body of facts and it appears in almost every sitting, sometimes more than once in the same paper.**

> **So it is among the cheapest marks in the examination, and the practical advice is to learn the set AS A SET rather than meeting each fact separately.**

> **The internal logic helps a great deal: the SENIORITY requirement rises with the office — 7 years for a member, 10 for the vice chairman and the registrar, 15 for the chairman — and every constituency (government, profession, universities, the Council itself) is represented.**

> **Reasoning from that structure recovers most of the table even if the individual numbers are not separately remembered.**

**What the NEC actually does, since the composition exists to serve its functions:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **REGISTER engineers, and maintain the register** | **The core function — a bachelor's degree is the minimum qualification** ← |
| **RECOGNISE engineering qualifications and institutions** | Which degrees qualify for registration |
| **Prescribe the professional CODE OF CONDUCT** | And enforce it |
| **Take DISCIPLINARY action for professional misconduct** | **Warning, suspension, or removal from the register** |
| **Conduct the REGISTRATION (license) EXAMINATION** | **The examination this portal prepares candidates for** ← |
| **Classify engineers by category and discipline** | Graduate, professional, and by field |
| **Advise the Government on engineering matters** | An advisory role |

> **The REGISTRATION EXAMINATION is the function most directly relevant here, and its purpose is worth stating plainly: a degree certifies that a candidate completed a course of study, while the license examination certifies a MINIMUM COMPETENCE TO PRACTISE.**

> **The two are different claims, and only the second protects the public.**

> **A degree is awarded by a university on its own standards, which vary; a license is granted by the regulator on a single national standard, which is what makes it a meaningful assurance.**

> **Which is why the examination is broad rather than deep — covering the whole of civil engineering practice rather than testing any part of it to research level — because it asks whether a candidate is safe to practise, not whether they are expert.**

> **That understanding is genuinely useful for a candidate: the examination rewards BREADTH and sound fundamentals across every subject, and it does not reward mastery of a favourite topic at the expense of the rest.**

> **A candidate strong in structures and weak in irrigation will do worse than one who is competent everywhere — because the paper takes ten questions from each of ten chapters and cares equally about all of them.**
